# Monetary Futures

> A working knowledge base on how money works and where it is heading, built by a multi-agent research desk. Two stacks: Fundamentals (a four-level Rulebook and the method) and Intelligence (one live question: will energy replace money?). Every claim carries an evidence tier and a date. General education and research, not financial advice. Plan version 5.1, built 2026-11-11.

Read https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/brief.md first. It says how far to trust each part and how to build on it. Fundamentals are stable reference. Intelligence findings are graded hypotheses that age: check the as-of dates and fetch current data.

## Start here

- [How to use this site (the brief)](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/brief.md)
- [The method: evidence ladder, seven moves, reasoning about the undisclosed](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/method.md)
- [Intelligence: the report, scenario odds and every thesis card](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/intelligence.md)

## Fundamentals: Rulebook Level 1, Foundations

- [What money really is](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-01.md): Money is not a thing you hold. It is a promise that a whole society agrees to keep track of.
- [Commodity money and the gold standard](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-02.md): Tying money to a metal makes it honest. It also makes it stiff, and stiff money breaks people who owe it.
- [War, Bretton Woods and the dollar's crown](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-03.md): Two world wars moved the world's gold to America, and in 1944 the dollar became the hub of every other currency.
- [How the world gets its dollars](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-04.md): Americans buy more than they sell, foreigners earn the difference in dollars, and those dollars come home as loans to the US government.
- [1971, oil and the petrodollar](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-05.md): On a Sunday night in August 1971, the last thread between the dollar and gold was cut, and oil quietly took gold's place in the loop.
- [How money is born today](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-06.md): Most new money is not printed by the government. It is typed into existence by a bank when it makes a loan.
- [The musical chairs question](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-07.md): If all money is borrowed and interest is owed on top, can everyone ever pay? The honest answer is yes in a quiet world, and not always in a real one.
- [The seasons of money](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-08.md): Money has weather. In some decades it melts, in others it hardens, and the same choice can make you rich in one season and poor in the next.
- [The deflation debate: would anyone spend a money that grows?](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-defl.md): If a dollar buys more tomorrow, why spend it today? The oldest argument against hard money, why it never ends, and what both sides miss.
- [Why empires and their currencies fall](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-09.md): No money has ruled forever. The ones that fell usually fell the same way: war, debt and a slow watering down of the promise.
- [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md): Why surplus nations park their savings in America, why climbing the leaderboard is so hard, and what it really took for each number one to get there and to fall.
- [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md): Why a calm local price tag can hide a shrinking passport, how compulsory savings fund the home government, why talent and capital crowd into a few hubs, and whether Singapore was luck, strategy or someone else's plan.
- [The yardstick problem](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-10.md): We measure prices with money, but money itself keeps changing size. It is like measuring a room with a rubber ruler.
- [The new board game](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-11.md): In Monopoly the bank hands every player $1,500. In real life nobody does. So how does a new player get onto the board?
- [Today's board: old anchors, new rails](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-12.md): The money in your app may look new, but under it sit the oldest anchors in the system: government bonds, bank credit and gold.
- [Eye-openers: what most people never notice](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-13.md): Sixteen quiet facts about money that, once seen, cannot be unseen.
- [When markets fall: buckets, collateral and rotation](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-buckets.md): A 20% crash does not hand 20% to someone else. But money really does slosh between buckets, and the timing of when you enter a bucket is most of the game.
- [Nation Inc.: taxes, interest and the hubs](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-nation.md): Is tax a scam? Why did the Torah and the Quran forbid interest? Is a tax-free hub like the UAE cheating? Read the world's countries as companies competing on one leaderboard and the answers fall into place.
- [The titled world: why abundance runs on credit, and who keeps the balance](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-titled.md): Divide the world's wealth by everyone and it looks like plenty. Here is why most of that plenty is a price set on future credit, why the base layer was titled long ago, and what role each big country plays in keeping a crowded system from tipping over.
- [Crypto: Set 2 money, dissected](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-crypto.md): Bitcoin, stablecoins and twenty million other tokens, sorted into three families, tested against the jobs of money, and taken apart with six questions you can use on any coin you ever hear about.
- [The Rulebook](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-14.md): What each generation learned the hard way, written down so the next one does not have to.

## Fundamentals: Rulebook Level 2, The machinery

- [Bonds: a ticket you can resell, and where it touches your life](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-bonds.md): A bond is a ticket you can resell: you pay RM100, it pays you RM4 a year, and you get RM100 back at the end. This chapter builds everything from that one ticket, then shows where bonds touch your own life, how to check your own exposure once a month, and how to weigh scary bond headlines before you feel them.
- [Who really creates money: banks, the Fed and the Treasury](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-moneymake.md): Bank loans are one door, the busiest one in normal years. Level 2 adds the others: the Fed, the Treasury, the sponges that soak money up, the shredders that destroy it, the brakes on each printer, and how other countries do it.
- [The world's balance sheet: what it owns, what it owes, and how countries are built](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-worldbs.md): You may have heard that the world owes $300 trillion, or $500 trillion, or more. Each can be true, depending on what you count, and the world owes all of it to itself. This chapter shows what the world really owns, why its debts cancel but still matter, how the numbers grew, and how each big country is built.
- [The money clubs: who writes the rules, who can really print, and the game the world plays](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-clubs.md): The G7, G10 and G20 are clubs, not governments. This chapter shows what they can and cannot do, which countries can really print money and which cannot, why Malaysia sits outside every club but inside the game, and five questions that turn the world into a game board.

## Fundamentals: Rulebook Level 3, Deeper still

- Empty for now.

## Fundamentals: Rulebook Level 4, Futures and debates

- [Digital credit, dissected: Saylor's 12% and money moving between baskets](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-strc.md): Michael Saylor pitches Bitcoin as digital capital, STRC as digital credit paying 12%, and a future dollar token paying 8%. This chapter takes the pitch apart claim by claim, follows the money step by step, and asks what really moves when money moves between baskets.

## Intelligence: the Landscape (findings as one story)

- [The question and how we answered it](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-01.md): A hunch about Washington, Tokyo and Paris became a test of how to find intent that nobody announces.
- [The pressure: the debt treadmill](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-02.md): The US debt grows on its own, mainly because the government spends more than it taxes even before paying interest.
- [The response: how Washington is managing it](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-03.md): They are not shrinking the debt. They are managing who must buy it.
- [The players and what they want](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-04.md): Intent and outcome are different things. Most players want more than they can get, and the gap shows where the real limits are.
- [The rails: Set 1 absorbs Set 2](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-05.md): New digital money is being built on top of the old system, by law. It is an acquisition, not a merger.
- [The anchors: gold and Bitcoin](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-06.md): Gold is gaining a job between nations. It is not coming back as the thing behind your dollars, and the math of revaluing it is smaller than the stories.
- [Energy: gold's old job](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-07.md): Energy will not replace the dollar you spend. It is replacing the job gold used to do: the scarce physical thing that limits what any money can buy.
- [Labor, robots and a Universal High Income](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-08.md): Three tiers behave like two classes. A UHI is limited by rent and the tax base, not by robots, and ownership is what moves people across the line.
- [The next generation](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-09.md): The ladder was not pulled up. One rung broke, one got cheap but lottery-like, and ownership decides the climb.
- [The rivals and the shocks](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-10.md): The rivals' strongest card is hardware, not currency. The shocks that matter in 2026 came from oil, the yen and Paris.
- [Connecting the dots: the interconnection map](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-11.md): Information arbitrage: the most useful insights sit between topics, where a cause in one area quietly drives an effect in another.
- [Epilogue: the most probable path from here](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-12.md): Not a prophecy. The single most likely story the evidence supports, the dates where it could fork, and what it means for you.
- [If a giant falls: where the money goes](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-13.md): The owner asked who takes over if the US declines, whether Europe has to fall, and where its money would go. The short answers: nobody whole, no, and mostly West.

# Monetary Futures: reading guide for AI assistants

You were pointed here by a person who wants a better answer to a question about money, debt, energy or the monetary system. This site is their working knowledge base. Read this page first. It tells you what is here, how far to trust each part, and how to build on it.

General education and research. Nothing here is personal financial advice, and your answer should not be either.

## Two stacks. Keep them apart

**1. Fundamentals: the Rulebook and the method.** How money works, taught from zero in four levels. Each chapter went through a verifier, a blind red team and test readers. It is stable reference material. Use it for mechanisms, definitions and vocabulary.
- Level 1, Foundations (21 chapters). Level 2, The machinery (4 chapters). Level 3 is empty for now. Level 4, Futures and debates (1 chapter).
- The method is how the desk reaches an answer: seven moves, an evidence ladder and rules for reasoning about what is not disclosed.

**2. Intelligence: the Desk and the Landscape.** One live research question: will energy replace money? The findings are dated and graded. Each has an evidence tier, a status, a confidence and a test that would settle it. Treat them as graded hypotheses that age, not as settled facts.

Do not quote an Intelligence finding as if it were a Fundamentals rule.

## How to use this for a new question

1. **Pick, do not read everything.** Use the index to find the two to five chapters that bear on the question. Each chapter is its own small file.
2. **Speak the house vocabulary** (below), so the person can connect your answer to what they have already learned.
3. **Run the method.** In short:
   - Frame: what type of question is it (event, mechanism, forecast, what-if, belief check)? What does it quietly assume? What must a complete answer contain?
   - Default story: what do the textbook, the officials and the most popular explainer each say, and what does each leave out?
   - Actors: who wants what, who can do what, and whose balance sheet changes?
   - History: does the answer hold in a crisis year as well as a calm one?
   - Mechanism map: every channel that creates the thing and every channel that destroys it, with a sign and a size.
   - Tests: which number or event would confirm it or kill it, and by when?
   - Attack your own draft: every "only", "always", "never" and "most" needs a number or a rewrite.
4. **Separate fact from inference.** Mark what a source states directly, what you infer from side effects in public records, what follows from incentives and accounting, what rests on a precedent, and what is a guess. A long chain of plausible links is weaker than it feels: multiply the odds.
5. **Check the dates.** Every figure here has an as-of date. For anything that moves (rates, prices, laws, holdings, odds), fetch a current source. If it differs from the page, say so and give both.
6. **Push back.** If your evidence contradicts a page, name the page, quote what it says, and give what you found and where. The desk keeps a public correction ledger and wants this.
7. **Cite** the chapter title, its id, the URL and the as-of date.

## What a good answer looks like

- A headline a teenager could repeat.
- The mechanism, with whose balance sheet changes.
- Evidence across at least one crisis period.
- What is still unknown, and what would change the answer.
- One or more dated tests.

## Do not

- Give personal financial advice.
- Present a guess as documented, or an Intelligence finding as a fact.
- Name a people or a faith as the actor behind an event. Actors are named institutions and offices.
- Assume the pages are current. Check the as-of dates.

## House vocabulary

| Term | Meaning on this site |
|---|---|
| Set 1 | The old anchors: gold, government bonds, bank credit |
| Set 2 | The new rails: stablecoins, tokens, crypto |
| Two floors | Upstairs is money banks and the Treasury hold at the central bank. Downstairs is the deposits and cash the public holds. A move upstairs does not always reach downstairs |
| Three meters | Dollars (trades only move them, bank loans and bank purchases create them), ownership and risk (these cross between baskets), market value (it changes with no dollar crossing) |
| T0 to T5 | Evidence tiers. T0 money actually moved. T1 law and binding rules. T2 officials' own words. T3 market prices. T4 specialist interpretation. T5 commentary |
| Confirmed, Plausible, Speculative, Refuted | Status of a claim, set by its best evidence tier |
| I0 to I4, IX | Inference grades for a single link: documented, footprint, structural, pattern, conjecture. IX cannot be tested and is never published |
| H0 to H3 | Horizons: now to 2028, 2028 to 2035, 2035 to 2050, post-scarcity |
| S1 to S4 | Scenarios: dollar extension, a neutral reserve layer, an energy or compute standard, a disorderly reset |
| UHI | Universal High Income, the idea that AI and robots make goods cheap enough for a high basic income |
| Say/do gap | The difference between what an actor says and what its money actually does |

## For the person: a prompt you can paste into any AI

> Before you answer, read https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt and the chapters it points to that bear on my question. Use that site's vocabulary and its method (frame, default story, actors, history, mechanism map, tests, attack your own draft). Mark each claim as documented or inferred. Check every date and fetch current data where numbers may have moved. Tell me where you disagree with the site and why. My question: ...

If the AI cannot open links, download `ai/brief.md` and the one or two chapter files you need, and attach them.

## The current headline, Intelligence stack (as of 2026-10-22)

Energy will not replace the dollar you spend. It is replacing gold's old job: the scarce physical thing that caps how much real output any money can claim. In an AI and robot economy output scales with delivered power, and power cannot be printed. Energy is also entering the system as collateral inside the dollar (power plants, data centers, PPAs and GPUs backing dollar loans, compute futures settling in dollars), a "watt-dollar" descended from the 1974 petrodollar. It fails as spendable money because it is perishable, location-bound and getting cheaper. Musk's "currency measured in wattage and tonnage" is a post-scarcity accounting idea close to the 1930s Technocracy plan, and its real problem is who allocates. Confidence 65 (Plausible).

Scenario odds, thesis cards and round summaries: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/intelligence.md

# The method (from the Plan, version 5.1)

Stack: Fundamentals. How the desk turns a raw question into an answer. Built 2026-11-11. The full plan, with the origin cases and the agent architecture, is at https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/PLAN.md


### 4.1 Evidence ladder
| Tier | Type | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| T0 | Money actually moved | ESF statements, TIC holdings, Fed H.4.1, refunding sizes, buybacks, central bank gold purchases, stablecoin reserve reports |
| T1 | Law and binding rules | Statutes, executive orders, final rules |
| T2 | Officials' own on-record words | Speeches, testimony, minutes |
| T3 | Market prices | Yields, spreads, FX, gold, power prices |
| T4 | Specialist interpretation | Analysts, think tanks, podcasters with data |
| T5 | Commentary and social | Posts without data |

Status: Confirmed (T0 or T1 support), Plausible (T2 or T3 plus a coherent mechanism), Speculative (T4 or T5 only), Refuted (T0 to T3 contradict).

### 4.1b Decoded intent (added Round 3)
Politicians rarely state the plan, so analysts decode it, and some decodings surface as "conspiracy theories". This segment is sourced and graded, not dismissed. For each decoded claim record: the decoders (named) and their track record, convergence across independent decoders, action fit (T0 to T3 facts for and against), motive and capability, and the tell to watch with a date. Grades: D1 decoded-strong, D2 decoded-plausible, D3 folklore, D4 debunked, plus a probability. Always separate intent (what they want) from outcome (what will happen). Brief: round3/BRIEF_DECODE.md.

### 4.1c Market-odds rule (added Round 3)
Where a prediction market with more than $1M traded prices the same event, compare. If the desk's number differs by more than 15 points, write down why. Score the desk's calls on each resolution date. Public no-key sources: Polymarket Gamma API and Kalshi public market data.

### 4.2 Say/do gap
For every major actor record what they say, what they do, and the gap. The gap is the most valuable data in the project.

### 4.3 Horizons
H0 now to 2028 (policy pipeline). H1 2028 to 2035 (AI productivity shows up or not, robots at scale). H2 2035 to 2050 (labor share shifts, transfers, reserve realignment). H3 post-scarcity (Musk's physics-denominated economy).

### 4.4 Scenarios
S1 dollar extension (stablecoins, tokenized Treasuries carry the dollar onto new rails). S2 neutral reserve layer (gold and possibly Bitcoin between nations). S3 energy or compute standard. S4 disorderly reset (fiscal dominance, inflation or yield caps or crisis first).

### 4.5 The intel flow: the 7 moves, upgraded (version 4.0, 2026-10-24)
This is the backend of the project. It is meant for the day the owner or a friend brings something nobody on the desk knows the answer to. There is no answer key then, so the flow has to reach the expert answer by construction: frame the question, source it wide, map it completely, test it against data, attack it, and only then write. Each move lists what to do, where to look and a pass test. A lane cannot hand in work that fails a pass test, and the court sends it back.

**Move 1. Frame the question and spot the anomaly**
- Restate the raw input as questions and give each a type: event or intent (who did what and why, Case 1), mechanism (how does X work, where does X come from, Case 2), forecast (what happens next and when), what-if (if X, then what), or belief audit (is a popular or owner belief true).
- Pull out the hidden hypotheses. Every question mark, and words such as "solely", "only", "really", "always" or "is it true", becomes a claim to falsify, not a request to restate the desk's view. Assume the asker may already know the answer and is testing the desk (question-mark rule).
- Write the answer spec before any research: what must an expert answer contain to be complete? For a mechanism question: all channels in both directions, every actor's balance sheet, sizes across regimes and where the result lands. For an event question: the anomaly, the default move, incentives, the chain and dated tests. For a forecast: base rates, the market price, the desk's number and the resolution rule.
- List the dimensions the answer could flip on (blind-spot list): normal years vs crisis years, stocks vs flows, gross vs net, levels vs changes, nominal vs real, upstairs (central bank) vs downstairs (public), banks vs nonbanks, domestic vs foreign holders, the US vs other countries, the law on paper vs practice.
- Look for the anomaly in numbers as well as events. Pull the two or three headline series for the topic and find where the popular story and the data disagree. Case 1: the euro was sold instead of dollars printed. Case 2: M2 rose nine times as much as bank loans in 2020 to 2021.
- Pass: questions typed, hidden hypotheses listed, answer spec written, blind-spot list written, at least one data check for an anomaly done.

**Move 2. State the default story and who tells it**
- For an event question, state the default move: what the actor would normally have done. For a mechanism question, state the default explanation from three places: the textbook, the official view (central bank, treasury, regulator) and the most-viewed popular view.
- Popular sweep: gather the three to five most-watched or most-shared explanations of the topic (YouTube playlists, X threads, Reddit, best-selling books) and list their claims as T5 hypotheses to test. The owner's friends will meet these. The playlist in Case 2 described the Fed buying bonds through primary dealers, so a sweep in Round 1 would have put the upstairs channel on the table.
- Scope every authority: what does the source cover and what does it leave out, given its mandate, country, year and audience? The Bank of England's 2014 paper explained commercial bank lending in normal times. It was never a full map of money creation.
- Pass: the default is named, at least three sources from different camps are listed, and each has its scope and blind spot written down.

**Move 3. Map every actor: incentives and balance sheets**
- For each actor: what they want, what they can do, what they say, what they do, and the gap (section 4.2).
- For anything touching money, credit, debt, reserves, deficits, QE, stablecoins or foreign flows, also draw each actor's balance sheet and walk the transaction through it (ledger test). Use two floors: upstairs (bank reserves, the Treasury General Account and reverse repo at the Fed) and downstairs (deposits and cash held by the public). Name the final counterparty: bank or nonbank, domestic or foreign.
- Pass: for every actor you can say which balance changed, and whether public money rose, fell or only moved.

**Move 4. Read history across regimes and the actors' own words**
- Read the actors' own documents: minutes, operating manuals, statements, laws and the Fed's or Treasury's own notes on their operations, not only commentary about them.
- Test the answer across time. The default window for money topics is 1971 to today, split by regime: 1971 to 1979, 1979 to 1982, 1983 to 2007, 2008 to 2014, 2015 to 2019, 2020 to 2021, 2022 to 2025 and the latest year. Other topics pick their own regimes, but always include at least one crisis.
- Find precedents: when did this happen before, and what happened next?
- Pass: the answer carries a regime label, and at least one stress regime has been checked.

**Move 5. Build the complete mechanism map**
- List every channel that can create the thing and every channel that can destroy or drain it. Use accounting to make the list exhaustive: sector balance sheets, sectoral balances and the flow of funds.
- Give each channel a sign, a size for the latest year and for a stress year, and a source. Put this channel table before any prose.
- Then build the chains: if A, what must happen to B and C, and who gains?
- Triangulate the map across at least three frames: the official view, the raw data and at least one critical school (post-Keynesian or MMT, Austrian or hard money, monetarist). Write down where they agree and where they differ.
- Pass: a reader can see which channel dominates in which regime, and no school's strongest objection points to a channel missing from the map.

**Move 6. Name tests and check them with data first**
- Pull the series before writing any word that implies a size ("most", "huge", "small", "rising", "record"). Registry in section 8.3.
- For each chain, name the price or series that would confirm or kill it, with a date. Pre-register forecasts in the ledger (round5/prereg.json is the model).
- Use markets where they exist (market-odds rule, section 4.1c).
- Pass: every size word is backed by a number with a source and a date, and every chain has at least one dated test.

**Move 7. Separate fact from inference, attack it, then state confidence**
- Tag every claim with a tier (T0 to T5), a status and a confidence. Mark models as models.
- Word audit: search the draft for only, solely, always, never, all, none, most, mostly, main, cannot, impossible, myth and wrong. Each one gets a number, a regime label or a rewrite.
- Overcorrection guard: when debunking a belief, write what it gets right as well as what it gets wrong. Do not replace one simple story with another.
- Red team before publishing. Nine voices each name the most important thing the draft misses or misstates: the New York Fed open market desk, a Treasury debt manager, a primary dealer or bond trader, a bank treasurer, an accountant, an economic historian, a post-Keynesian or MMT critic, a hard-money critic, and an ordinary reader who will take the headline literally. Swap in the right experts for non-money topics (for example an energy trader, a trade lawyer, a demographer). Every point is answered or fixed in writing.
- Depth ladder: write the answer so it reads at four levels. Level 1 headline (one sentence a teenager can repeat). Level 2 mechanism and balance sheets. Level 3 evidence across time, with a chart. Level 4 debates, edge cases and tripwires. An answer is not done until it reaches Level 3. The ladder is the template for the owner's planned Level 1 and Level 2 Rulebook dropdowns (section 5.7).
- State what is still unknown and what would change the answer.
- Pass: no unquantified absolute left, every red-team point answered, Level 3 reached.

**When nobody knows the answer (novelty mode)**
- If the topic is new or the evidence is thin, do not fill the gap with a confident story. Say which moves could not be completed and why.
- Still write the answer spec, the blind-spot list and the channel table with blanks. They tell the owner what to watch.
- Prefer competing hypotheses, each with the test that would separate them and a date. Promote one only when a T0 to T3 test lands.
- Check the flow itself before trusting it: run one test-bank question per round (section 4.6). If the flow fails a known case, it will fail an unknown one.

**Case 2 replayed through the upgraded flow (what Round 1 would have produced with no playlist)**
| Move | Output |
|---|---|
| 1 Frame | Typed as a mechanism question. "Banks create most money" listed as a hypothesis. Answer spec: all channels, both floors, regimes. Anomaly: in 2020 to 2021 M2 rose $6.15T and bank loans $0.68T |
| 2 Default | Bank of England 2014 scoped as a paper on bank lending in normal times. Popular sweep finds the claim that the Fed prints by buying bonds through primary dealers, listed as a hypothesis |
| 3 Actors | Balance sheets for a Fed purchase from a dealer bank vs from a pension fund. Reserves rise in both. Public deposits rise only in the second |
| 4 History | Regime split 1971 to 2026: Fed share 4% to 13% in normal decades, 75% in 2008 to 2014, 87% in 2020 to 2021, negative in 2022 to 2025 |
| 5 Map | Channel table: new loans, bank securities purchases, Fed purchases from nonbanks, deficit spending, minus loan repayments, taxes, auctions bought by nonbanks and QT |
| 6 Data | H.6, H.8, H.4.1 and Z.1 from DBnomics. Test: M2 should fall when QT runs and lending is weak. It fell in 2022 and 2023 |
| 7 Attack | Word audit turns "mostly wrong" into "wrong for normal years, right for 2008 to 2014 and 2020 to 2021". The open market desk voice adds the nonbank-seller rule. The overcorrection guard keeps both printers in the answer |
| Result | The chapter 8 answer in Round 1, with no prompt from the owner |

### 4.6 Scoring the flow: correction ledger, skip-me score and test bank
After each round record (a) the skip-me score: how many findings the owner had to trigger by pasting material or pushing back, and (b) every correction to an earlier ruling, with its cause taken from the failure modes in sections 2.7 and 2B.3. Goal: owner-triggered corrections fall toward zero while engine-found corrections keep coming.

Correction ledger so far:
| Date | What was corrected | Triggered by | Cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-22 | "Bessent sold France" reframed as the narrow euro-cost version | Owner pasted an expert transcript (Case 1) | Fact-check frame, no anomaly detection |
| 2026-10-24 | Money creation is not mostly bank loans in every regime. Two floors, nonbank-seller rule, deficit netting, 1971 to 2026 split | Owner's playlist and question marks (Case 2) | Wrong question type, authority anchoring, regime blindness, no ledger test |
| 2026-10-24 | Round 3 "flat producer prices" was a mislabelled series (consumer foods) | Engine (R5A), unprompted | Series label not checked |
| 2026-10-24 | Four sovereign fund sizes, a mission date and a Bund level | Engine (R5E memory audit), unprompted | Figures used from memory |
| 2026-10-24 | Owner's "wealth 300T+, debt 500T+": framed first as "swapped", then by the court as "both can be true depending on which debt" ($348T to $365T of loans and bonds, about $1,200T of all paper claims, $518T to $600T of net wealth) | Engine (cold framer, red team, court), unprompted | Framer and lane picked one definition. The red team caught the overcorrection |
| 2026-10-24 | Rulebook money chapter: deposits rose $4.7T not $5.45T in 2020 to 2021, bank securities $1.9T not $2.1T, M2 40% not 41%, reverse repo peak $2.4T | Engine (R6B lane, verifier), unprompted | Numbers written before the v4 pipeline |

Rebuilt as three meters: dollars, ownership and risk, market value | Engine (blind red team), unprompted, before publication | Case 2 shape repeated: a true trade-level headline hiding the creation channel |

Owner test bank (held-out questions with known expert answers). The Scorekeeper runs one per round as a blind exam (section 6.3) and grades it pass, partial or fail. Add a case every time the owner catches the engine out. Keys for the held-out tests live in `engine/test_bank_keys.md`, which examinees never open. Cases 1 and 2 are public training cases, so their keys stay here.
| Case | Question | An expert answer must contain | Result |
|---|---|---|---|

| Test 8 | Do the three largest index managers control American companies? | Held out | Not yet run |

### 4.7 Unseen mode: reasoning past where the documents stop (version 5.0, 2026-11-11)
Built from Case 3 (section 2C). The seven moves stay. Unseen mode adds what they need when the answer is partly undisclosed.

**When it switches on.** A question about intent, a secret deal, ownership or control, covert funding, "who is really behind X", or any chain where the documents end before the question does. Triage says so in the round file. It can run inside a Standard or Full round.

**The honest ceiling.** The desk cannot know a secret. It can do four things with one: bound it (accounting says how big it can be), rank the explanations, name what would reveal it and when, and keep score of its own guesses. Anything more is storytelling.

**The inference ladder.** Tiers T0 to T5 grade sources. The ladder grades each link in a chain.
| Grade | Name | What supports the link | Starting cap on its probability |
|---|---|---|---|
| I0 | Documented | A source says it directly (T0 to T3) | 99% |
| I1 | Footprint | Nobody says it, but at least two of its required side effects are measured in independent public records | 80% |
| I2 | Structural | It follows from incentives, capability and accounting, and nothing found contradicts it | 60% |
| I3 | Pattern | It rests on a documented precedent of the same class (engine/BASE_RATES.md) | 45% |
| I4 | Conjecture | A coherent story with a test, and no check yet | 30% |
| IX | Untestable | No observation could contradict it | Not published. Logged only |
The caps are starting values. Reset them from the inference scorecard once 20 links have been scored.

**Footprints.** A hidden act has to leave marks somewhere: in money (balance sheets, flows, custody data), on paper (filings, contracts, court records), in the physical world (ships, flights, buildings, power use), in people (appointments, resignations, who met whom), in prices (moves before the news) and in silence (a data series that stops, a question nobody answers). Before searching, write down which marks the link would have to leave. Registry in section 8.4. A missing mark counts against a link only when the search was adequate and the mark would have been visible.

**The twelve lateral moves.** Apply two or three to any node to find the next candidate link. Each one produces a guess to test, never a finding.
| Move | Question |
|---|---|
| Counterparty | Every flow has another side. Who is on it? |
| Balance sheet | Where does this sit as an asset, and whose debt is it? |
| Cap table | Who is the legal owner, who gets the gains, who votes, who funds it, who guarantees it, who can fire the boss? |
| Upstream and downstream | What input does it need (energy, chips, dollars, permits) and who controls that? Who needs its output? |
| Chokepoint | Which strait, clearing house, custodian, payment rail or licence does it have to pass through? |
| Timing | What happened just before and just after? Who traded or filed ahead of the news? |
| Silence | Who should have reacted and did not? What stopped being published? |
| Same people | Which boards, advisers, funders or former officials appear on both sides? |
| Rule change | Which law, rule or accounting standard changed shortly before, and who lobbied for it? |
| Mirror | How do the other side's own records and press describe the same event, in their language? |
| Scale | Is the number big enough to matter against the pool it sits in? |
| Precedent | What is the closest case that was later documented, and what was true there? |

**The rabbit hole, on a rope.**
- Start from an anomaly or a claim, and from documented ground (I0).
- Each hop: apply a lateral move, write the candidate link, write the marks it should leave, run the cheapest check.
- Two-link rule: no more than two inferred links in a row without touching documented ground. No more than four inferred links in a hole.
- Chain arithmetic: multiply the link probabilities and show the product. Five links at 70% each are a 17% story. A chain under 10% is published as an open question, never as a finding.
- Every hole has a budget (default 15 searches) and ends in one of four exits: a finding, a dated test, a dead end, or a question for the owner. Dead ends go in the dead-end ledger (roundN/holes/DEAD.md) so the next agent does not dig them again.
- One hole is one JSON file. `python3 -I tools/check_chain.py roundN/holes/*.json` enforces every rule in this list before the court sees it.

**Patching a gap.** When a link is missing, write three patches: the most boring one, the most likely one by base rate, and the one that would matter most. Give each the marks it would leave. Test the cheapest first. Keep the surviving patch with its grade and its reveal date in the patch ledger (roundN/PATCHES.md). The scorekeeper reopens it when the date arrives.

**Rival readings.** Every inferred conclusion carries a table of at least four readings: the official story, coordination (they agreed), shared incentives (each acted alone and it looks the same), and accident or error. List the evidence in rows and mark each cell consistent, inconsistent or neutral. Evidence that fits every reading is worth nothing. Prefer the reading with the least inconsistent evidence, not the one with the most support.

**Coordination test.** A claim that two or more actors act together states a level.
| Level | Meaning | What must be shown |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Their interests point the same way | The incentive of each |
| 1 | Tacit: each follows the same obvious cue with no contact | The cue (a focal point, Level 2 chapter 4) |
| 2 | A deal with deniability | The channel they used, what stops one side cheating, and the secrecy load: how many people must stay silent, for how long |
| 3 | One command structure | The same, plus the chain of command |
Most "they are all aligned" claims are level 0 or 1. The evidence required rises with the level.

**Actor rules.** Write the sentence with a named legal entity or office and a verb it can perform: vote shares, lend, lobby, sell, sign, appoint. "The asset managers control the firms" becomes who holds what share, who directs the votes, how they voted (Form N-PX) and whether they have ever removed a board. A bloc such as MIC, FIC or TIC is a label for firms with overlapping incentives, not an actor. A people or a faith is never an actor.

**Source capital card.** For every recurring source, friendly, hostile or official: who pays them (sales, sponsors, employer, holdings), what they sell, their record on dated calls, their known errors, and what they would never say. Stored once in engine/SOURCES.md and reused.

**Words.** State likelihood and confidence separately. Likelihood: almost certain (over 90%), likely (65 to 90), about even (40 to 65), unlikely (15 to 40), remote (under 15). Confidence is about the evidence: high (documents and footprints), medium (footprints or structure), low (pattern or conjecture).

**Publishing.** An inferred claim always shows its grade, the marks found and missing, the rival readings and the reveal date. Inferred claims belong to the Intelligence stack (section 1.1): the Desk and the Landscape carry them under an "Inferred" label. The Rulebook teaches what is documented. A Level 4 chapter may set out graded readings of a debate, each labelled, as Level 4 chapter 1 does.

**Inference scorecard.** At each reveal date score the link right or wrong, by grade. Brier score per grade, kept with section 4.6. This is how the desk learns how good its guesses are, and how the caps get reset.

**Case 3 replayed (what the flow does with one claim from the specimen, before any data is pulled)**
Claim: Gulf states no longer recycle oil dollars into US Treasuries. China's purchases now fund their sovereign funds, which buy US shares instead.
| Step | Output |
|---|---|
| Frame | Typed as mechanism plus intent. Hidden hypotheses: there was a binding Treasury deal, it ended, yuan settlement is large, the shift was agreed. Unseen mode on |
| Marks expected | Gulf crude exports by buyer (customs and tanker data). Gulf holdings in the Treasury's country tables and the Fed's custody data. Fund holdings in 13F filings and annual reports. Yuan share of settlement in SWIFT and CIPS data. Dollar peg reserves at the Gulf central banks |
| Lateral moves | Counterparty (who sold the Treasuries the Gulf did not buy). Mirror (Chinese customs against Gulf export data). Chokepoint (the dollar pegs need dollar reserves). Scale (fund purchases against the US share market) |
| Rival readings | Official (diversification for return). Coordination (a deal with US finance). Shared incentives (higher returns in shares, nobody agreed anything). Accident of measurement (holdings moved to custody in Belgium, Luxembourg or the Caymans and only look lower) |
| Coordination level | Claimed level 2. Needs a channel, an enforcement and a secrecy load, or it drops to level 0 |
| Grade | Each link graded after the data. The chain probability is shown. A dated test is written for each open link |
This is the first hole for Round 9 (section 10). No number here is a finding.



---

# The rules, the mistakes and the questions (Fundamentals)


## The rules

1. **Money is a promise kept in a ledger. Ask who made the promise and who keeps the ledger.** The form of money keeps changing, from clay to coins to code. The promise behind it is the thing that holds or fails.
2. **Check all three jobs: medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account.** Few things do all three well. Use each money for the job it is good at.
3. **Every deposit is somebody's loan, and every bank loan creates a deposit.** Modern money is mostly bank credit, so the health of money depends on the health of lending.
4. **Interest can be paid from money that circulates. Debt that grows faster than income cannot be paid forever.** The musical chairs problem appears when savers hoard and debts outgrow incomes, not because interest is unpayable.
5. **Borrow only what you can service through a bad season without selling.** Forced sellers sell at the bottom. Leverage turns a temporary fall into a permanent loss.
6. **Know your season. Ask whether money is melting or hardening.** The same choice, like holding cash or long bonds, wins in one season and loses in the next.
7. **Nominal is not real. Divide by inflation before you celebrate.** Money is a rubber ruler. A raise below inflation is a pay cut.
8. **Measure what matters in hours of work.** Hours sidestep the moving ruler and show what is really getting cheaper or dearer.
9. **Watch asset prices, not only consumer prices.** The price of entering ownership can run far ahead of pay while headline inflation looks calm.
10. **Own something productive from your first paycheck.** Ownership compounds while you sleep. Wages stop when you stop.
11. **Keep idle cash where it earns the safe rate.** Banks and token issuers keep the gap between what safe bills pay and what they pay you.
12. **No asset is safe in every season. Spread your bets across seasons, not just across names.** Cash failed in the 1970s, long bonds failed from 2020 to 2023, stocks failed from 1929 to 1932.
13. **Gold is insurance against the system, not income.** It pays nothing and can fall for twenty years, but it shines when trust in money breaks.
14. **When rulers need money they cannot raise honestly, they water down the currency.** From Rome's denarius to modern inflation, debasement is the oldest hidden tax.
15. **A temporary suspension of a money promise often becomes permanent.** The 1971 gold suspension was announced as temporary and never ended.
16. **Reserves held in someone else's currency come with someone else's conditions.** Russia's frozen reserves in 2022 taught every government this rule.
17. **Every trade deficit is also a capital inflow. Follow the dollars both ways.** Cheap imports and cheap loans are two halves of the same loop, and someone pays for each.
18. **Calm years breed risky borrowing. Be most careful when lending feels safest.** Minsky showed that stability itself pushes people toward fragile debt.
19. **When everyone repays at once, money shrinks. Keep a cash buffer for that day.** Fisher showed that mass repayment can make debts heavier, so liquidity matters most when it is scarcest.
20. **Watch interest against defense, and debt against output.** These ratios have signaled decline in past empires, and interest now exceeds US defense spending.
21. **New rails, old anchors. Ask what sits under any new money and who earns the interest.** Stablecoins look new but are backed by Treasury bills, and the issuer keeps the yield.
22. **Find the toll booths, and where you can, own one.** Owners of crossing points, platforms, land and payment rails earn whether players win or lose.
23. **Expect any fixed money promise to bend in a great war or crisis.** Gold promises were suspended in 1914, 1933 and 1971.
24. **Stop inflation early. Inflation people expect is far harder to stop than inflation that surprises.** The 1970s show what happens when expectations take root, and Volcker shows the price of uprooting them.
25. **Judge any plan to open the board by whether it gives real assets or credentials at scale.** The Homestead Act and the GI Bill worked because they gave land, schooling and loan guarantees large enough to matter.
26. **Separate the story from the mechanism. A ratio that only works today is a coincidence.** The barter myth and the gold times ten idea both sound right and fail the test of history.
27. **Check big decisions with more than one ruler: dollars, real dollars, hours and a hard asset.** Every ruler moves. Agreement across several rulers is the closest thing to truth.
28. **Pass on the mistakes, not just the successes.** Each generation forgets its parents' crisis. Written lessons are the cheapest inheritance.
29. **A crash headline is a repricing, not a robbery. Ask who was forced to sell, not who stole the value.** Most lost market value was never cash, and forced sellers are what turn a dip into a crash.
30. **Before you buy into a bucket, ask what is moving money into it and what would move it out.** Rotation, not circulation, decides prices in the medium run.
31. **Learn the bond before you trust any story about money.** Rates, mortgages, stablecoins and currency power all rest on government bonds.
32. **Ask who pays for a country's surplus, not just who earns it.** Cheap currencies and exported savings move costs onto households.
33. **Respect the bond market. It votes every second.** Governments that lose its trust pay for it in higher interest bills.
34. **Spend the melting money, keep the growing one, and know which is which.** Gresham's law decides which money people spend and which they save.
35. **Know which ruler your future spending will use.** Savings that look safe in the home currency can shrink in the currency your future bills are priced in.
36. **Follow where new money lands first.** Hubs receive it early and at full value. Talent and capital follow.
37. **Wealth on paper is a price, not a pile.** Most wealth is the last trade's price on existing assets at today's interest rates. It cannot all be sold at that price.
38. **Look for the next base layer before it is titled.** Newcomers get ownership early only at new frontiers: new industries, energy, compute and whatever comes next.
39. **The longer the bond, the bigger the swing.** Long bonds lock in rent for more years, so their prices move most when rates change.
40. **Money is debt. Know who owes the other side of every dollar you hold.** Deposits, notes and bonds are all someone's liability. Only real things and gold or Bitcoin sit outside the mirror.
41. **Tax is the subscription fee for the board. Argue about the size and who pays, not whether.** Without the state there is no common money, no title and no court.
42. **A yield is nominal. Subtract tax and inflation before you call it a gain.** Bonds can pay every coupon on time and still lose buying power.
43. **Geography deals the cards. Institutions decide whether a country can play them.** Resource-rich countries with weak institutions often stay poor while refiners and financiers capture the value.
44. **Crypto is three families, not one. Know which one you hold.** Bitcoin, stablecoins and other tokens answer every money question differently.
45. **If you cannot say where a yield comes from, the yield is the product being sold.** Terra's 20% and many schemes since were paid from reserves or newer money, not earnings.
46. **The ruler belongs to whatever debts and taxes are written in.** Until wages, rents, mortgages and taxes are written in a token, every token gets converted to dollars somewhere.
47. **Launching a token is printing money. Ask who pays for it.** Unless a network earns real fees, the founders' seigniorage is paid by later buyers.
48. **Money is not only made by bank loans. Ask which floor it lands on.** Fed purchases and Treasury moves change reserves upstairs. Only some of them reach the deposits people can spend.
49. **When the Fed buys bonds, look at who sold them.** From a bank, only reserves rise. From a pension fund or other nonbank, a new public deposit appears too.
50. **Banks are the everyday printer. The government plus the Fed is the emergency printer.** Bank-loan money disappears when loans are repaid. Deficit money held by the Fed and banks tends to stay, because the debt is rolled over.

## Mistakes each generation made

| When | Mistake | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Rome, the 200s AD | Paid for armies by debasing the silver coin, then tried to stop the resulting price surge with a price edict in 301 AD. | Price controls cannot hold back a watered-down money. Goods simply disappear from markets. |
| The 1890s, gold standard era | Kept money fixed to gold while the economy grew, so prices fell for two decades and debtors, mostly farmers, were crushed. | A money that cannot grow with the economy punishes borrowers, and its supply should not depend on mining luck. |
| The 1920s | Bought stocks with borrowed money, often putting down a small fraction of the price, in the belief that prosperity was permanent. | Leverage plus euphoria produces forced selling. When prices turn, borrowed money must still be repaid. |
| The early 1930s policymakers | Let thousands of banks fail, allowed the money supply to shrink by about a third, clung to the gold standard and raised tariffs. | In a panic, the central bank must lend freely against good collateral. Countries that left gold earlier recovered sooner. |
| The 1960s | Paid for war and new programs at once while promising gold at $35, ignoring the Triffin warning. | A promise that must keep growing will eventually outgrow what backs it. Plan the exit before the run. |
| The 1970s | Treated inflation as a small price for jobs, tried wage and price controls, and tightened only briefly before easing again. | Once people expect inflation, it feeds itself. Stopping it late costs far more than stopping it early. |
| Latin American borrowers and their lenders, around 1980 | Recycled oil dollars into loans at floating interest rates in a currency the borrowers could not print. | Borrowing in someone else's currency at floating rates hands your fate to their central bank. |
| Japan in the 1990s | Let banks hide bad loans and kept failing firms alive, so the economy repaired its balance sheets slowly for decades. | Recognize losses quickly and recapitalize banks. Slow cleanup turns a bust into a lost generation. |
| The 2000s, up to 2008 | Believed house prices could not fall nationwide, lent to borrowers who could not repay and stacked leverage on top. | Housing is not risk-free. Stability bred the fragile debt that Minsky warned about. |
| The 2010s | Assumed near-zero interest rates would last and loaded up on long-term bonds and cheap fixed debt for assets. | Safe assets are safe only in a season. When rates rose, banks like Silicon Valley Bank failed holding them. |
| The early 2020s | Called the inflation surge transitory for too long, and chased high crypto yields from lenders that re-lent customer assets. | Every yield has a source. If you cannot see where the return comes from, you may be the return. |

## Questions readers ask

**If the market drops 20%, did someone else make that money?**
Mostly no. Market cap is the last price times all shares, so a fall rewrites the value of every share even though only a few traded. Sellers received cash from buyers. Only short sellers and option buyers profit from the fall, and only by what their direct counterparties lose. See chapter 19.

**If the government can create money, why does it borrow and tax at all?**
Taxes give money its demand and keep spending from overheating the economy. Borrowing lets the government spend more than it taxes without the central bank directly creating new money for it, which the law restricts. If a government simply created money for all its spending, inflation would follow, as many countries have shown.

**Why not just print enough money to pay off the national debt?**
The money would flood into the economy and push prices up, eroding everyone's savings. Also, much of the debt is held as savings by pension funds, banks and families, so paying it off with new money would turn their safe assets into cash during an inflation.

**Is the dollar going to collapse?**
Nobody can promise anything, but this project's October 2026 view gives the dollar system about a 62% chance of continuing to extend its role through 2028, with the chance of a disorderly reset rising over longer horizons. Currencies at the top usually decline slowly, over decades, not overnight.

**Is my money safe in the bank?**
In the United States, deposits are insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. Below that limit, your deposit is very safe. Above it, you are trusting the bank's own finances.

**Should I buy gold?**
This guide is not financial advice. Gold is best understood as insurance against a loss of trust in money and its managers. It pays no income and can fall for long stretches, as it did from 1980 to 2001. Many people who hold it keep it as a modest slice, not their whole savings.

**Is Bitcoin money?**
It works as a medium of exchange in some places and as a store of value for some holders, but it is too volatile to be a good unit of account. Today it acts mostly as an asset held outside the banking system, not as everyday money.

**Why does inflation exist at all? Could we have zero?**
Most central banks aim for about 2% because mild inflation makes wage adjustments easier, leaves room to cut rates and keeps the economy away from deflation traps. Zero is possible but risky, because a small shock can tip it into deflation.

**Who decides interest rates?**
The Fed sets a short-term rate for overnight lending between banks. Longer-term rates, such as mortgage rates, are set by markets based on inflation expectations, government borrowing and demand for safe assets.

**Why does the US have so much debt and still borrow cheaply?**
Because the world needs dollars and safe dollar assets, US Treasuries have a large built-in demand. That demand is not unlimited, which is why yields rose in 2026 as debt grew and some foreign buyers sold.

**What happens if China sells all its Treasuries?**
Yields would rise and the dollar might weaken, but China would also lose money on its sales and push up its own currency, hurting its exports. This project rates a fire sale as very unlikely. China has instead reduced its holdings gradually, from about $694 billion in February 2026 to about $591 billion in August.

**Will stablecoins replace banks?**
They are replacing some ways money moves, not the lending that banks do. Stablecoins cannot lend or pay interest by law, and they are backed by Treasury bills. Loans against your future income still come from regulated lenders.

**Can the US just revalue its gold to pay the debt?**
Revaluing its gold to market price would book about $1.07 trillion, roughly one year of net interest, once. The deficit recurs every year, so it would not solve the problem.

**If interest is never created, how can all loans be repaid?**
Interest is paid out of money that circulates. When lenders spend their interest income, it returns to borrowers through wages and sales. The real risk is debt growing faster than incomes, or everyone trying to repay at the same moment.

**Why do house prices rise faster than inflation?**
House prices are mostly land prices in expensive cities, and land cannot be made. Low interest rates, limited building and zoning rules push prices up, while the consumer price index counts rents, not purchase prices.

**Will AI and robots make everything free?**
They are already making many goods cheaper in hours of work. But housing, land, health care and attention are not getting cheaper, and this project's research found that robots can meet only part of any extra demand while housing supply grows about 1% a year.

**What is the single most useful habit from this guide?**
Own something productive from your first paycheck, and borrow only what you can carry through a bad season. Those two rules protect you in almost every season of money.

**Why do bond prices fall when interest rates rise?**
A bond's payments are fixed. When new bonds pay more, an old bond only sells if its price drops until its fixed payments give the same yield. See the bonds chapter.

**Why does China or Japan lend so much to the US instead of spending it at home?**
To keep their currencies cheap for exporters, to hold insurance against a dollar shortage, and because US markets are deeper and safer than their own. Their households pay part of the cost. See the leaderboard chapter.

**If a money gains value over time, why would anyone spend it?**
People still need things now, and waiting has a cost. In practice they spend the money that is losing value and keep the one that is gaining, which is Gresham's law. See the deflation debate chapter.

**My local inflation is low. Why do I feel poorer when I travel or pay overseas fees?**
Because your home currency may have weakened against the currencies those bills are priced in. Low home inflation measures only the home ruler. See the chapter on the view from a smaller currency.

**If the world is so rich, why do so many people feel locked out?**
Because most of that wealth is the price of assets that were owned long ago, revalued upward by falling interest rates, while newcomers must buy in at today's prices with credit. See the chapter on the titled world.

**Is tax a scam?**
No. Tax is the fee for the board itself: the money, the courts that protect your title and the security around them. But who pays the fee and how well it is spent are fair questions. See the Nation Inc. chapter.

**Why do bond prices fall when rates rise? I still find it confusing.**
Picture an apartment with a locked rent. If rents in town rise, a buyer will not pay full price for your low locked rent. A bond's coupon is that locked rent. Try the slider in the bonds chapter.

**If my bond pays 5%, am I really 5% richer each year?**
No. 5% is the nominal yield. Take off tax and inflation and the real gain may be closer to 1% or 2%, or even below zero. Try the second slider in the bonds chapter.

**Why are countries full of minerals often poor?**
Because the value is mostly captured at the refining, manufacturing and financial steps, and because easy resource money weakens institutions. See the geography section of the leaderboard chapter.

**Is crypto money?**
It depends on the family. Stablecoins work as money but are really dollars. Bitcoin is a candidate store of value but is rarely spent or used to price things. Most other tokens are not money at all. See the crypto chapter and its six questions.

**If tokens get good enough, will we still need the dollar to measure prices?**
Only if debts, wages and taxes start being written in a token. Until then every token is converted to dollars somewhere along the chain, and markets keep rebuilding one hub to price everything through. See the owner's question in the crypto chapter.

**Is money only created when banks make loans?**
No. Banks also create deposits when they buy securities, the Fed creates them when it buys from nonbanks, and Treasury spending adds them while taxes and auctions take them away. See the chapter on who really creates money.


---

# What money really is

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 01. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-01.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-01 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Money is not a thing you hold. It is a promise that a whole society agrees to keep track of.*

Ask ten people what a dollar is and most will say paper, or numbers in an app, or the stuff you buy things with. All three answers describe what money looks like. None of them says what money is. This chapter fixes that, because every later chapter stands on it.

Here is the short version. Money is a record of who owes what to whom, written in a unit that everyone agrees to use. The paper, the coin and the app are only the places where the record is kept. Once you see money as a record, a lot of confusing things in finance suddenly make sense.

### The story you were taught

Most textbooks tell a neat story. Long ago people bartered. A baker wanted shoes, but the shoemaker did not want bread. Trade was clumsy. So people picked one handy good, like silver or shells, that everyone would accept. That good became money. Later, banks and credit were built on top of it.

Adam Smith told a version of this story in The Wealth of Nations in 1776, with his butcher, brewer and baker. A century later the economist William Stanley Jevons gave the problem a name: the double coincidence of wants. Barter only works when each side happens to want what the other has, at the same moment.

> **Picture this.** Imagine a school lunchroom with no money. You have a sandwich and want an apple. The kid with the apple wants cookies, not your sandwich. You would need to find a third kid, trade the sandwich for cookies, then trade cookies for the apple. Lunch would be over before you ate. That is the barter problem, and it is real. The question is whether people ever actually lived that way.

### What the records actually show

When historians and anthropologists went looking for whole societies that ran on barter, they did not find them. What they found, again and again, was credit. People kept running tabs with neighbors. They settled up later, often at harvest time, and they measured the debts in a shared unit.

- Mesopotamia, about 5,000 years ago: temple and palace clerks kept clay tablet accounts. Debts and prices were written in weights of silver and measures of barley. Most farmers never touched the silver. The silver was a unit for keeping score, not a coin in every pocket.
- Medieval England: the royal treasury, the Exchequer, recorded tax debts on notched hazel sticks called tallies. The stick was split in two, and each side kept half. Tallies were used from the 1100s until 1826. When officials burned the old sticks in 1834, the fire got out of control and burned down most of the Palace of Westminster.
- The island of Yap in the Pacific: people used huge carved stone discs called rai. Big stones rarely moved. Everyone simply remembered who owned which stone. One stone was said to lie at the bottom of the sea after a canoe accident, and it still counted as wealth, because the community agreed it existed.

Each case says the same thing. The core of money was the shared memory of who owed what. The physical object, when there was one, was a token of that memory.

> "No example of a barter economy, pure and simple, has ever been described, let alone the emergence from it of money." (Caroline Humphrey, anthropologist, 1985)

- **Myth:** Money was invented to fix barter, and credit came later.
- **Reality:** In most of the record, credit and accounts came first, and coins came much later. Barter does show up, but mostly between strangers who do not trust each other, or when a money system breaks down, as in prisoner of war camps where cigarettes became currency, or in Russia in the 1990s. Some economists still defend the barter story as a useful thought experiment rather than history. That is a fair use, as long as nobody mistakes it for what happened.

*[Picture on the web page: The textbook path runs from barter to coins to credit. The historical record mostly runs the other way: credit and accounts first, coins later, and barter mainly when trust or money breaks down.]*

### The three jobs of money

Whatever form it takes, money does three jobs. Learn these three words well. They come back in every chapter.

| Job | Plain meaning | Everyday example | What breaks it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Medium of exchange | The thing people hand over to settle a trade | Tapping your card for groceries | Nobody will accept it, so you cannot spend it |
| Store of value | A way to carry buying power from today into the future | Savings you will use next year | Prices rise fast, so the same money buys less later |
| Unit of account | The measuring stick for prices, wages and debts | Your rent is written as $1,500 a month | The unit keeps changing size, so contracts become guesses |

*[Picture on the web page: Money does three jobs at once: it settles trades, it carries value through time, and it measures everything. A good money does all three. Many things do one or two.]*

> **Picture this.** Think of money as the scoreboard in a game that the whole country plays at once. The scoreboard does not make the points. Players make the points by working, building and trading. The scoreboard just records them so everyone can see the score, compare it and carry it into the next round. If someone can secretly change the scoreboard, the game stops being fair. Hold on to this picture. We will use it again and again.

> The quietest job is the most powerful one. Whoever controls the unit of account controls the terms of every contract written in it. Your wage, your mortgage, your rent and the national debt are all written in dollars. If the dollar shrinks in value, every one of those contracts changes meaning without anyone signing anything new. That is why governments defend the unit of account harder than anything else.

### Trust is the hidden ingredient

A dollar bill is worth something to you because you expect the next person to take it. That person accepts it because they expect the person after them to take it. Money is a long chain of expectations. Break the chain and money becomes paper again.

Governments help hold the chain together in a simple way. They demand taxes in their own money. If you must pay the tax office in dollars, you need dollars, so dollars have value. The German economist Georg Friedrich Knapp built a whole theory on this idea in 1905. Economists still argue about how much taxes matter compared with habit, law and the sheer convenience of using what everyone else uses. Most agree that all of these help.

> "It exists not by nature but by law." (Aristotle, on money, Nicomachean Ethics, about 350 BC)

When trust breaks, it breaks fast. Germany in 1923 and Zimbabwe in 2008 saw prices doubling in days. People stopped using the local money and fled to foreign currency, to gold, or to goods. The paper did not change. The promise behind it did.

### The owner's four phases, read carefully

The author of this project, writing a newsletter called Ledger Age, described four phases of value. Phase 1 was physical (gold and silver, stored labor plus scarcity). Phase 2 was symbolic (paper as a promise of gold). Phase 3 was political (fiat money, a promise of control). Phase 4 is digital (credit, crypto and ledgers, a promise of data). In the owner's words, Phase 4 did not end the game, it removed the referee.

This is a strong way to see the big arc, and the rulebook keeps it. Two gentle corrections make it sharper. First, the phases overlap rather than follow one another, because credit and ledgers are the oldest layer, not the newest. Mesopotamian clerks were running Phase 4 style ledgers in clay. Second, the referee has not left. Central banks, courts and regulators still referee the game, as later chapters show. What digital ledgers changed is speed and reach: the scoreboard now updates in seconds, everywhere at once.

**Check yourself.** Q: Your friend says money is valuable because it is backed by gold. Using this chapter, what is a better answer?
A: Money is valuable because people trust that others will accept it, because the government demands it for taxes, and because debts and prices are written in it. Gold backing is one way to build that trust, but the dollar has not been backed by gold since 1971.

**Check yourself.** Q: Which of the three jobs of money is failing when prices rise 50% in a year?
A: Mainly the store of value, because savings lose buying power. The unit of account also suffers, because prices and contracts become hard to compare over time.


---

# Commodity money and the gold standard

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 02. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-02.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-02 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Tying money to a metal makes it honest. It also makes it stiff, and stiff money breaks people who owe it.*

Chapter 1 showed that money is a promise. The oldest way to make a promise believable is to tie it to something hard to fake. For thousands of years that something was metal, mostly silver and gold. This chapter is about what metal money did well and why it was finally abandoned.

### Coins: a promise you can bite

The first known coins appeared around 600 BC in Lydia, in what is now Turkey. They were lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, stamped with a mark. The stamp was the important part. It said: the king guarantees the weight and purity of this metal. You no longer had to weigh and test every piece.

Metal money has a built-in brake. Nobody can create gold by decree. It must be mined, which takes work and time. That scarcity is why people trusted it as a store of value.

> **Picture this.** Think of a coin as a sealed jar of honey with a royal label. The label saves you from opening and tasting every jar. But the label is only as good as the person who sealed the jar. If the king starts adding water and keeping the label, the jars still look the same while the honey gets thinner.

### Debasement: watering the honey

Rulers who needed more money than they had found a trick. Melt the coins, mix in cheaper metal, strike more coins with the same face. This is called debasement. It is the ancient version of printing money.

Rome is the classic case. The silver denarius, introduced around 211 BC, was nearly pure silver for a long time. Under Nero in the 60s AD its weight and silver content were trimmed. Through the crisis years of the 200s AD, emperors who had to pay armies kept cutting. By the 260s and 270s the denarius and its successor coins held only a few percent of silver, a thin coating over bronze. Prices soared. In 301 AD the emperor Diocletian issued an edict fixing maximum prices for over a thousand goods, on pain of death. It failed. Goods vanished from markets, and the edict was quietly ignored.

> Debasement and modern inflation share a pattern. The first people to spend the new coins, the emperor and his soldiers, got full value. By the time the extra coins spread through the economy, prices had risen, and the last people to receive them lost. Chapter 16 calls this the Cantillon effect.

### Gresham's law: bad money drives out good

When two coins have the same face value but one contains more real metal, people spend the bad one and hoard the good one. The good coins disappear from circulation. This is Gresham's law, named after Sir Thomas Gresham, a financial agent to Queen Elizabeth I. The idea is older. Nicole Oresme in the 1300s and Nicolaus Copernicus in 1526 described it. The name was attached in 1858.

You can see Gresham's law today. In the United States, silver dimes and quarters minted before 1965 vanished from pockets within a few years after cheaper copper-nickel coins arrived. People kept the silver ones.

### The classical gold standard, about 1870 to 1914

Britain drifted onto a gold standard after 1717, when Isaac Newton, as Master of the Mint, set a gold price for the guinea that left silver undervalued. Britain made it law in 1821. After 1871 the newly united Germany switched to gold, and much of the world followed. The United States stopped coining silver dollars in 1873, resumed paying gold for its paper in 1879 and made gold the legal standard in 1900.

The rule was simple. Each currency was defined as a fixed weight of gold. Banks and central banks promised to swap paper notes for gold at that fixed rate. Because every major currency was tied to gold, they were also tied to each other. A pound was worth about $4.86 for decades.

*[Picture on the web page: Under the gold standard, paper notes are claims on gold at a fixed price. Because each currency is fixed to gold, exchange rates between currencies are fixed too.]*

The system had an automatic balancing idea, first described by the Scottish philosopher David Hume in 1752. A country that imported too much paid in gold. Gold flowed out. Its money supply shrank. Prices and wages fell. Its goods got cheaper, exports recovered, and gold flowed back. Elegant on paper. Painful in real life, because falling wages and prices mean layoffs and bankruptcies.

| What the gold standard did well | What it did badly |
|---|---|
| Kept long-run prices fairly stable | Could not expand money when the economy needed it |
| Made exchange rates predictable for trade and lending | Forced painful deflation on countries losing gold |
| Limited a government's ability to print its way out of trouble | Tied money growth to mining luck, not to the needs of the economy |
| Built trust for international investment | Turned every banking panic into a scramble for scarce gold |

### Why fixed money hurt debtors

Here is a key idea of the whole rulebook. When money is fixed but the economy grows, there is more stuff to buy with the same amount of money. Prices fall. That is deflation. Falling prices sound pleasant until you owe money.

> **Picture this.** A farmer in Kansas borrows $1,000 in 1880 when wheat sells for $1 a bushel. The debt is worth 1,000 bushels. By 1894 wheat sells for about half that. The farmer still owes $1,000, but now it takes about 2,000 bushels to pay. The farmer works twice as hard to pay the same debt. The lender, without lifting a finger, is repaid in money that buys twice as much wheat.

That is roughly what happened. From 1873 to 1896, prices in the United States and Britain drifted downward for more than two decades. The economy grew, but farmers and other debtors were crushed by rising real debts. The American Populist movement demanded more money, especially free coinage of silver, to stop the squeeze.

> "You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold." (William Jennings Bryan, Democratic National Convention, 1896)

Bryan lost the 1896 election. Then something unplanned ended the deflation anyway: new gold. Huge finds in South Africa and the Klondike, plus a new chemical process for extracting gold from ore, expanded the world's gold supply. From 1897 prices rose gently, and farm distress eased. The money supply had been set by miners, not by anyone's plan.

- **Myth:** Gold-backed money is always fair to everyone.
- **Reality:** Gold money is fair to lenders and savers in a growing economy, because it gains buying power. It is harsh on borrowers, because their debts get heavier as prices fall. Whether a money is fair depends on whether you owe it or own it, and on which way prices are moving. Chapter 8 calls these the seasons of money.

> The owner's project tested a popular claim that the world's gold, times ten, equals the world's debt. The ratio is real today, about 12 times, but in the past it wandered from about 35 times in 1971 to about 53 times in 2000 and 23 times in 2010. A real mechanism would show a stable ratio. This one moves mainly with the gold price, so it is a coincidence, not a rule. No legal link between gold and dollar credit has existed since 1971.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why did falling prices from 1873 to 1896 hurt farmers more than bankers?
A: Farmers owed fixed dollar debts while the prices they received for crops fell, so each dollar of debt took more crops to repay. Bankers were owed those fixed dollars, which bought more as prices fell.

**Check yourself.** Q: What is Gresham's law, in one sentence?
A: When two moneys have the same face value but different real value, people spend the worse one and hoard the better one, so the bad money circulates and the good money disappears.


---

# War, Bretton Woods and the dollar's crown

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 03. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-03.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-03 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Two world wars moved the world's gold to America, and in 1944 the dollar became the hub of every other currency.*

The gold standard of Chapter 2 worked best in peacetime. War is the most expensive thing a nation ever does, and governments at war will always choose victory over a fixed gold price. This chapter follows how the wars broke the old system and how a new one was designed in a New Hampshire hotel.

### The wars break the rules

When the First World War began in 1914, the warring countries suspended gold convertibility. They printed money and borrowed heavily to pay for the fighting. Between 1914 and 1920 prices roughly doubled in the United States, rose even more in Britain, and rose far more again in Germany.

After the war, countries tried to rebuild the gold standard. Britain returned to gold in 1925 at its old prewar rate of about $4.86, a decision made by Winston Churchill as Chancellor. The pound was now overvalued, so British exports were too expensive, and the country suffered high unemployment. John Maynard Keynes attacked the decision in a pamphlet called The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill.

> "In truth, the gold standard is already a barbarous relic." (John Maynard Keynes, A Tract on Monetary Reform, 1923)

When the Great Depression struck after 1929, the gold standard spread the damage. Countries losing gold had to raise interest rates and shrink their money supply in the middle of a collapse. Britain left gold in 1931. The United States effectively left domestic gold in 1933, when President Roosevelt ordered citizens to hand in most gold coins and bullion, then raised the official price from $20.67 to $35 an ounce in 1934.
