Research by economists Barry Eichengreen and Jeffrey Sachs found that countries that left gold earlier generally recovered sooner.

### Why America ended up with the gold

Through the 1930s and the Second World War, gold poured into the United States. Europeans sent gold to safety. Allied countries paid for American weapons, food and fuel. By the late 1940s the US government held roughly two thirds of all the gold owned by the world's governments. America also had the only large industrial economy that had not been bombed.

> **Picture this.** Imagine a long poker night where every player keeps losing chips to one player who also owns the casino's only working kitchen. By dawn that player holds most of the chips. When the others want to start a new game, they have little choice but to use that player's chips as the house standard. That is roughly the position of the United States in 1944.

### Bretton Woods, July 1944

In July 1944, delegates from 44 Allied nations met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. Two men shaped the talks. Keynes, for Britain, proposed a new international clearing unit called bancor, which would push both deficit and surplus countries to adjust. Harry Dexter White, for the US Treasury, proposed a system built around the dollar. The country with the gold won the argument.

- The US dollar was fixed to gold at $35 an ounce. Foreign central banks, not private citizens, could swap dollars for gold at that price.
- Other currencies were pegged to the dollar at fixed rates, allowed to move only about 1% either way. Pegs could be changed only for a serious imbalance.
- The International Monetary Fund (IMF) was created to lend to countries with short-term payment problems, so they would not need to devalue or crash their economies.
- The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, now part of the World Bank, was created to finance rebuilding and development.

*[Picture on the web page: Bretton Woods, 1944: other currencies pegged to the dollar, and the dollar pegged to gold at $35 an ounce. The dollar became the hub, gold the anchor.]*

> This made the dollar the hub of a wheel. To defend its peg, a country needed a stock of dollars to buy its own currency when it fell. So central banks around the world began to hold dollars, and soon US Treasury bills, as their main reserves. The reserve role of the dollar, which still shapes your mortgage rate today, was born in this design.

### A system that worked, then strained

For about two decades the system delivered. Europe and Japan rebuilt quickly. The United States gave about $13 billion in Marshall Plan aid from 1948 to 1952, which put dollars into European hands. Trade grew fast, and inflation was mostly moderate. Many economists call the 1950s and 1960s a golden age of growth.

But the system had a crack in its foundation, spotted early by the Belgian economist Robert Triffin. He laid it out in testimony to Congress in 1959 and in a book in 1960.

### The Triffin dilemma

The world needed more and more dollars as trade grew. The only way foreigners could get more dollars was for the United States to send more dollars abroad than it took back, by buying imports, investing overseas, or spending on military bases and aid. Year after year, that piled up dollars in foreign hands.

But each of those dollars was a claim on American gold at $35. As foreign dollar holdings grew, they eventually exceeded the gold the US held. By the early 1960s that line had been crossed. If everyone asked for gold at once, the US could not pay.

> **Picture this.** A popular bakery issues tickets, each good for one loaf. Tickets are so trusted that the whole town uses them as money. The town grows and wants more tickets. The bakery keeps printing them, but it cannot bake much more bread. Every new ticket makes the town happier today and the bakery's promise weaker tomorrow. If the bakery stops printing, the town's trade seizes up. If it keeps printing, one day a crowd shows up wanting bread for every ticket. That is the Triffin dilemma.

The dilemma is this. If the US stops supplying dollars, the world economy runs short of money. If it keeps supplying them, confidence in the gold link erodes. Either way, the system is on a timer.

Governments tried patches. In 1961 the US and European central banks formed the London Gold Pool to hold the market price of gold at $35. France, under President Charles de Gaulle, began swapping its dollars for gold and publicly called for a return to a pure gold standard in 1965. The French finance minister Valery Giscard d'Estaing complained of America's exorbitant privilege: the ability to pay for things with its own currency that others must earn. The Gold Pool collapsed in 1968. The countdown to 1971, the subject of Chapter 5, had begun.

- **Myth:** The US took the world's gold by force or trickery.
- **Reality:** Most of it arrived through ordinary channels: European capital fleeing war and instability in the 1930s, and Allied payments for American goods during the war. The result gave the US enormous leverage at Bretton Woods, but it was mostly the product of the US being the safe, unbombed workshop of the world, not a heist.

> The United States still holds about 261.5 million ounces of gold, about 8,134 tonnes, according to the Treasury's own records for September 2026. It books that gold at $42.22 an ounce, a price set by law in 1973, so the official value is about $11 billion. At market prices it is worth about $1.08 trillion. The gap is a fossil of the Bretton Woods era still sitting in today's government accounts.

**Check yourself.** Q: Under Bretton Woods, could an American citizen walk into a bank and swap dollars for gold?
A: No. Only foreign central banks and governments could convert dollars to gold at $35. American citizens were not even allowed to own most gold bullion from 1933 until 1975.

**Check yourself.** Q: State the Triffin dilemma in two sentences.
A: The world needed a growing supply of dollars, which the US could only provide by running deficits with the rest of the world. But the more dollars piled up abroad, the less believable the promise to convert them into gold became.


---

# How the world gets its dollars

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 04. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-04.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-04 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Americans buy more than they sell, foreigners earn the difference in dollars, and those dollars come home as loans to the US government.*

Chapter 3 ended with a puzzle. The world wants dollars. How does it get them? The answer is the most important circuit in modern finance. Once you see it, you will notice it in the price of your phone, your mortgage rate and the news about sanctions.

### The loop in one breath

1. Americans, as a group, buy more goods and services from the world than they sell to it. This is the trade or current account deficit.
2. Paying for those imports sends dollars abroad. Foreign exporters now hold dollars.
3. The exporters, or their central banks, need somewhere safe to keep those dollars that also pays interest.
4. The deepest, safest place is US government debt: Treasury bills, notes and bonds. So they buy Treasuries, or other US assets such as stocks, companies and property.
5. The dollars flow back into the US financial system, help fund the US government's deficit and keep US interest rates lower than they would otherwise be.
6. With rates lower and goods cheap, Americans keep buying, and the loop turns again.

*[Picture on the web page: The recycling loop: the US deficit sends dollars abroad, foreigners earn them by exporting, and they send them back by buying US Treasuries and other US assets.]*

> **Picture this.** Imagine a family that shops every day at a neighbor's store and pays with IOUs. The neighbor does not cash the IOUs. Instead, the neighbor deposits them right back with the family, which pays a little interest. The family keeps shopping, the neighbor keeps selling, and the neighbor's pile of IOUs keeps growing. Both are happy as long as the neighbor trusts the family's IOUs. That is the dollar loop, in kitchen terms.

### Level one: you, the individual

The loop touches your life in at least two ways, even if you never think about foreign exchange.

- Cheap imports. Because foreign makers are happy to be paid in dollars and to hold them, Americans can buy goods from all over the world at low prices. The project's time price data show a television costs roughly 99.5% fewer hours of work than in 1993. Clothing, electronics and toys are cheap partly because of this loop.
- Lower borrowing costs. When foreigners buy Treasuries, they push up their prices and push down their yields. Since mortgage rates and car loan rates follow Treasury yields, American borrowers benefit. One well known study by Francis and Veronica Warnock estimated that foreign buying lowered the 10-year Treasury yield by close to a percentage point in the mid-2000s.

The flip side for individuals is quieter. If your job was in a factory that competed with imports, the same loop may have cost you that job. More on that below.

### Level two: businesses

Picture a Japanese carmaker selling cars in Ohio. It is paid in dollars. It needs yen to pay its workers at home, so it can sell the dollars. But if every exporter sold dollars at once, the yen would soar and Japanese goods would become expensive. So a lot of those dollars stay as dollars. Some are invested by the company in US factories and assets. Some are swapped with Japanese banks and pension funds, who buy Treasuries. Some are absorbed by Japan's central bank and Ministry of Finance as reserves.

The same pattern holds for a Chinese electronics maker, a German machine builder or a Gulf oil company. The project's files show a modern version: Gulf sovereign funds now recycle their dollars into US artificial intelligence infrastructure as owners, for example a roughly $40 billion deal by MGX and BlackRock for a large data center company.

> When a foreign company sells you a product, it often ends up lending you, the US taxpayer, the money you paid it. Your dollars leave as payment and come back as a loan to the US government. The trade deficit and the foreign holding of US debt are two sides of the same coin.

### Level three: governments

At the top level, foreign governments hold dollars as reserves: a rainy day fund to defend their currency, pay for imports in a crisis and reassure investors. As of August 2026, Japan held about $1,068 billion of US Treasuries, the United Kingdom about $1,010 billion and China about $591 billion, according to US Treasury data gathered by this project. Foreign official accounts held about $2.55 trillion in custody at the New York Fed in mid-October 2026.

For the US government the loop brings two powers. First, it can borrow cheaply and at enormous scale, because the world needs its debt as a safe asset. Second, because most international payments pass through dollar accounts at US banks, the US can cut a country or a company out of the system. In 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine, Western governments froze roughly $300 billion of Russia's central bank reserves. That showed every government on earth that dollar reserves come with a political condition.

*[Picture on the web page: The same dollar loop seen at three levels: individuals get cheap imports and lower loan rates, businesses earn dollars and invest them in US assets, governments hold Treasuries as reserves while the US gains borrowing and sanctions power.]*

### Why the model works

| Pillar | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Deep markets | The US has about $31.8 trillion of marketable Treasury debt. You can buy or sell billions in minutes without moving the price much. No other safe asset is that large or liquid. |
| Rule of law | Courts enforce contracts and property rights fairly reliably, even for foreigners. Investors fear arbitrary seizure less in the US than in most alternatives. |
| Network effects | Oil, commodities, loans and trade are already priced in dollars, so everyone needs dollars, so more things get priced in dollars. Like a language, the more people use it, the harder it is to switch. |
| Open capital account | Money can enter and leave the US freely. China, the largest rival economy, still restricts this, which limits the yuan as a reserve. |
| Military and alliances | The US security umbrella over allies such as Japan, South Korea, Germany and the Gulf states gives them extra reasons to hold dollars. |

### What the model costs

- Hollowed industry. A strong dollar makes US exports expensive and imports cheap. Economists David Autor, David Dorn, Gordon Hanson and coauthors estimated that the surge of Chinese imports in the 2000s cost around a million US manufacturing jobs, and perhaps two million jobs in all. Whole towns felt it.
- Persistent deficits. The US has run trade deficits almost every year since the mid-1970s. Foreign claims on the US keep growing.
- Borrowing becomes easy, maybe too easy. With the world eager to buy its debt, Washington faces little market pressure to balance its budget, until the price of borrowing finally rises, as Chapter 16 shows it now has.
- Dependence on foreign buyers. If foreign governments slow their buying or sell, US rates rise. In 2026 Japan's Treasury holdings fell about $171 billion from February to August as it defended the yen, and long-term US yields rose.

- **Myth:** The trade deficit shows the US is losing.
- **Reality:** Economists disagree about what drives the deficit. One view, associated with Ben Bernanke's 2005 'global saving glut' speech, says foreigners save too much and push their savings into the US, so the deficit is partly caused abroad. Another view, argued by Michael Pettis and others, says surplus countries hold down their own consumption, which forces deficits onto the US. A third view blames low US saving. All three agree the deficit is the mirror image of foreign capital flowing into the US, and that this brings benefits and real costs to different groups of Americans.

> "The dollar is our currency, but your problem." (John Connally, US Treasury Secretary, to European finance ministers, 1971)

Connally said this as the Bretton Woods system cracked. It captures the deal in one line. Because the world holds dollars, American decisions about the dollar land on everyone else. The next chapter shows the moment that line was spoken in earnest.

**Check yourself.** Q: If foreign central banks stopped buying US Treasuries, what would likely happen to US mortgage rates, and why?
A: They would likely rise. Fewer buyers for Treasuries means lower prices and higher yields, and mortgage rates follow Treasury yields.

**Check yourself.** Q: Name one benefit and one cost of the dollar loop for an ordinary American.
A: Benefit: cheaper imported goods and lower loan rates. Cost: jobs lost in industries that compete with imports, and a government that can borrow without much discipline.


---

# 1971, oil and the petrodollar

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 05. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-05.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-05 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*On a Sunday night in August 1971, the last thread between the dollar and gold was cut, and oil quietly took gold's place in the loop.*

Chapter 3 ended with a timer. Foreign governments held more dollars than the US held gold. Chapter 4 showed why the world kept piling up dollars anyway. This chapter is the moment the timer ran out, and the surprising thing that happened next.

### The run on the bakery

Through the late 1960s, US spending rose on two fronts at once: the Vietnam War abroad and the Great Society programs at home. Inflation crept up. Foreign central banks looked at their growing piles of dollars and at America's shrinking pile of gold, and started asking for gold. In the summer of 1971 Britain reportedly asked to protect a large part of its dollar holdings. The bakery in our Chapter 3 picture had a crowd at the door.

### August 15, 1971

President Richard Nixon gathered his advisers at Camp David and then went on national television on a Sunday evening. He announced a package: a 90-day freeze on wages and prices, a 10% surcharge on imports, and the step that changed the world's money.

> "I have directed Secretary Connally to suspend temporarily the convertibility of the dollar into gold or other reserve assets." (Richard Nixon, televised address, August 15, 1971)

Temporarily turned out to mean permanently. Foreign central banks could no longer swap dollars for gold. The dollar was now backed by nothing physical at all. It was backed by the US government's promise, the US economy, and the fact that the whole world already used it.

*[Picture on the web page: Before August 1971: dollar convertible to gold at $35 for foreign central banks. After: the gold window closed, and by 1973 the major currencies floated against each other.]*

### From fixed to floating

Governments tried to patch the system. In December 1971 the Smithsonian Agreement devalued the dollar to $38 an ounce of gold and reset other pegs. In February 1973 the official price was raised again to $42.22. By March 1973 the major currencies gave up pegs and began to float, meaning their prices against each other were set every day by markets.

> That $42.22 is still in the US government's books today. The Treasury values its 261.5 million ounces of gold at exactly $42.2222 an ounce, as of September 2026, while the market price is around $4,100. A number set in a 1973 emergency is still sitting in the national accounts.

- **Myth:** Gold still backs the dollar.
- **Reality:** It does not. No one can swap dollars for gold at a fixed price, and no law ties the amount of dollars to the amount of gold. The US government still owns a lot of gold, but it is an asset on the shelf, not a backing for the currency. What anchors the dollar today is the taxing power of the US government, the size of the US economy, and the Federal Reserve's management of interest rates.

### Oil enters the loop

Two years after Nixon's announcement, in October 1973, Arab members of OPEC (the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) imposed an oil embargo on the United States and other countries over the Arab Israeli war. Oil prices roughly quadrupled within months, from about $3 a barrel to about $12. Suddenly, oil exporters were collecting a flood of dollars.

Where would that flood go? In 1974, US Treasury Secretary William Simon traveled to Saudi Arabia. The two governments reached an understanding. Saudi Arabia would invest a large share of its oil earnings in US Treasury securities, through special arrangements that kept its purchases out of the normal auctions and kept its holdings secret. In return the US offered military cooperation and security. Oil continued to be priced in dollars, which was already the norm.

The details stayed hidden for decades. In 2016 a Freedom of Information Act request by Bloomberg News uncovered the arrangement, and the US Treasury published Saudi Arabia's Treasury holdings for the first time.

> **Picture this.** Recall the neighbor who deposits the family's IOUs right back with the family. Now give that neighbor a gas station that every driver in the world must use, with prices quoted in the family's IOUs. The neighbor's pile of IOUs grows enormously, and the neighbor parks it with the family. That is the petrodollar: oil priced in dollars, and the oil money recycled into US government debt.

### What the petrodollar was, and what it was not

- It was three things: oil invoiced in dollars, Gulf oil surpluses recycled into Treasuries and US banks, and a security relationship between Washington and Riyadh.
- It was not the dollar's backing. The dollar would remain the world's main currency without it, because of the pillars in Chapter 4.
- It is not suddenly over. A viral story claimed a 50-year petrodollar pact expired in June 2024. This project's research found that claim false. There was no such dated pact to expire.
- It is fading slowly. Saudi Arabia now holds about $141 billion of Treasuries, about 1.5% of foreign holdings, and in 2026 Gulf states borrowed in markets more than they recycled. Electric vehicles are slowly eating into oil demand.

> In the 1970s, banks also recycled petrodollars by lending them to developing countries in Latin America. When US interest rates jumped in the early 1980s, those borrowers could not pay. Mexico defaulted in 1982 and much of Latin America lost a decade. Recycled money always lands somewhere, and the landing is not always soft.

### The Great Inflation

With no gold anchor and two oil shocks (1973 and again after the Iranian revolution in 1979), US inflation climbed through the decade. Consumer price inflation peaked near 14.8% in early 1980. Savers who held cash or long-term bonds watched their wealth melt. Workers saw wages chase prices in a race they kept losing. Borrowers with fixed-rate loans, by contrast, quietly gained, because they repaid in cheaper dollars.

Policymakers tried wage and price controls, which caused shortages, and stop and go policy, which tightened just long enough to cause pain and then loosened again before inflation was beaten. People came to expect inflation, and expectations started to drive it.

### Volcker breaks the fever

In August 1979 President Jimmy Carter appointed Paul Volcker to chair the Federal Reserve. On October 6, 1979, Volcker announced a new approach that let interest rates rise as high as needed to slow money growth. The federal funds rate, the Fed's key rate, reached close to 20% in 1980 and 1981. Mortgage rates went above 18%.

The cure was brutal. The US went through two recessions in quick succession. Unemployment reached 10.8% at the end of 1982. Farmers drove tractors to Washington to protest. But inflation fell to around 3% by 1983, and the Fed earned back its credibility. A 40-year era of falling interest rates began, which Chapter 8 calls the long bond summer.

| Year | Event | What it meant for money |
|---|---|---|
| 1971 | Gold window closed | The dollar became a pure promise |
| 1973 | Floating rates, oil embargo | Currencies traded freely, oil prices quadrupled |
| 1974 | US and Saudi arrangement | Oil dollars recycled into Treasuries |
| 1979 | Second oil shock, Volcker appointed | Inflation peaked, then rates soared |
| 1982 | Deep recession, Mexico default | Inflation broken, debt crisis abroad |

The owner's Ledger Age series listed five effects of 1971: the dollar became a pure promise, unlimited printing became possible, inflation became the default, the petrodollar arrived, and cheap credit flowed to those who could borrow and buy assets. All five are well supported, with one sharpening. Printing became possible without a gold limit, but it is not unlimited in practice. The limits moved from metal to politics and markets: how much inflation voters will tolerate, and how much debt the bond market will absorb at what price. Volcker proved the limit is real when it is enforced.

**Check yourself.** Q: After 1971, what does the dollar's value rest on, if not gold?
A: On trust in the US government and its taxing power, the size and openness of the US economy, the Fed's management of interest rates and inflation, and the network effect of the whole world already using dollars.

**Check yourself.** Q: Who gained and who lost in the 1970s inflation?
A: Borrowers with fixed-rate loans and owners of real assets like gold, land and oil gained. Savers in cash and bonds, people on fixed incomes and workers whose wages lagged prices lost.


---

# How money is born today

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 06. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-06.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-06 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Most new money is not printed by the government. It is typed into existence by a bank when it makes a loan.*

With gold gone, where does new money come from? Most people imagine a government printing press. That picture is mostly wrong. This chapter shows the actual machinery, step by step, with a simple set of books. It is the chapter to reread if any later one feels confusing.

### Three kinds of dollars

Not all dollars are the same kind of thing. There are layers, each a promise from a different promiser.

| Layer | Who promises | Who can hold it | Rough size, US, 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base money: paper cash and bank reserves | The Federal Reserve | Cash: anyone. Reserves: only banks and a few institutions with Fed accounts | Bank reserves about $2.96 trillion (week to 21 October 2026) |
| Bank deposits | Your commercial bank | Anyone with a bank account | About $19.6 trillion (September 2026) |
| Treasury securities | The US government | Anyone, through a broker or bank | About $31.8 trillion of marketable debt held by the public |

The money you use day to day is almost all the second layer: bank deposits. When you pay with a card or an app, you are moving bank deposits. Paper cash is a small share.

### Loans create deposits

In 2014 the Bank of England, the central bank of the United Kingdom, published a short paper that surprised many readers. It described what bankers already knew.

> "Whenever a bank makes a loan, it simultaneously creates a matching deposit in the borrower's bank account, thereby creating new money." (Bank of England, Money creation in the modern economy, 2014)

A bank does not lend out a pile of savings it was holding. It writes two new entries in its books at the same moment. Let us watch it happen.

> **Worked example.** Maria borrows $20,000 from her bank to buy a car. Before the loan, the bank's books show nothing about Maria. The moment the loan is approved, the bank adds an asset: a $20,000 loan that Maria owes the bank. It also adds a liability: a $20,000 deposit in Maria's account that the bank owes Maria. Both sides grow by $20,000. Maria's own books mirror this: she now has a $20,000 deposit (an asset) and a $20,000 debt (a liability). No one else's deposit went down. The economy has $20,000 more money than it had a minute ago.

*[Picture on the web page: Double-entry: the bank records a new loan as an asset and a new deposit as a liability at the same instant. The deposit is new money.]*

1. Maria pays the car dealer. Her deposit moves to the dealer's account, maybe at another bank.
2. Between the two banks, the payment settles in reserves at the Federal Reserve. Banks keep reserve accounts at the Fed for exactly this.
3. The dealer now has $20,000 in deposits. The money keeps circulating, paying wages, suppliers and taxes.
4. As Maria repays the loan, her payments cancel both her debt and an equal amount of deposits. Repaying a bank loan destroys money, just as making one created it.

> When you deposit your paycheck, you are lending money to your bank. Your deposit is the bank's debt to you. You are an unsecured lender, protected by government deposit insurance up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. This is why bank runs happen: depositors are creditors who can all ask for their money back at once.

### What limits banks, then?

If banks can create money by lending, why not lend infinitely? Because lending has real limits, just not the ones in the old textbook.

- Capital rules: regulators require banks to fund a share of their loans with their owners' money, so losses hit shareholders first.
- Borrower demand: someone has to want the loan and be judged able to repay it.
- Profit: the loan must earn more than it costs the bank to fund and manage.
- Interest rates: the Fed sets the price of reserves, which ripples out to the price of every loan. Higher rates mean fewer borrowers.

- **Myth:** Banks can lend about ten times their reserves, so every dollar of base money becomes ten dollars of loans.
- **Reality:** This is the old money multiplier from textbooks, and the owner's notes used it, for example multiplying gold or Bitcoin by ten. The Bank of England's 2014 paper, which the owner also cites, says the reverse: banks lend first, and the central bank supplies reserves as needed at its chosen interest rate. In the United States, reserve requirements have been zero since March 2020. There is no fixed multiplier. The binding limits are capital, demand, profit and the interest rate. The owner's instinct that money is debt is correct. The fixed ten times rule is not. And when the Fed buys bonds, new public deposits appear only if the seller is a nonbank, such as a pension fund. Level 2 chapter 2 shows the two floors.

### The government's part: the Treasury

The US Treasury is the government's money manager. It keeps its main checking account, the Treasury General Account, at the Federal Reserve. In the week to 21 October 2026 it held about $952 billion. When the government spends, say on a Social Security payment, money moves from that account to the recipient's bank. The recipient's deposit rises and the bank's reserves at the Fed rise. Government spending adds money to the private economy.

When you pay taxes, the reverse happens. Your deposit falls, your bank's reserves fall, and the Treasury's account at the Fed rises. Taxes drain money out of the private economy.

Because the government spends more than it taxes, it borrows the difference. It does this through primary auctions. Treasury announces how many bills, notes and bonds it will sell. A group of 25 large banks and dealers, called primary dealers, must bid. Pension funds, money market funds, foreign central banks and individuals bid too, directly or through the dealers. Buyers pay with deposits and reserves, which move into the Treasury's account.

> The Fed is not allowed to buy new Treasuries straight from the government at auction, apart from rolling over bonds it already owns. When the Fed does buy Treasuries, it buys them from banks and investors in the open market. That is what quantitative easing was: the Fed creating reserves to buy bonds that were already out there.

### The owner's loop, corrected and kept

The owner sketched the money circuit as Treasury to Fed to banks to public to IRS (the tax office) to Treasury. That is a real loop, and the core insight, that modern money is a circuit of debts, is right. Here it is with the parts in their correct places.

1. Congress decides spending and taxes. Treasury spends from its account at the Fed, which adds deposits for the public and reserves for their banks.
2. Treasury covers the gap between spending and taxes by auctioning Treasury securities to dealers, banks, funds, foreigners and individuals, not to the Fed directly.
3. Banks create most new money by making loans to households and businesses. The Fed does not hand banks money to lend. It sets the interest rate on reserves and lends to banks against good collateral when needed.
4. The public spends, saves and repays loans. Repaying bank loans destroys deposits.
5. The public pays taxes to the IRS, which moves deposits and reserves back into Treasury's account at the Fed.
6. The Fed sometimes buys or lets run off Treasury securities in the open market, and when it makes a profit it sends it to the Treasury.

The owner also wrote that the Fed controls the speed of credit expansion, not the amount. That is close to right. The Fed sets the price of money, the interest rate, and banks and borrowers decide the quantity at that price. In September 2026 the Fed, now chaired by Kevin Warsh, raised its target rate to 3.75 to 4.00%, a sign that it is trying to slow the speed.

**Check yourself.** Q: Maria repays her entire $20,000 car loan. What happens to the money supply?
A: It shrinks by $20,000. Her repayment cancels both her loan, an asset of the bank, and an equal amount of deposits, a liability of the bank. Money created by a loan is destroyed when the loan is repaid.

**Check yourself.** Q: Does the Federal Reserve lend money to the Treasury when the government runs a deficit?
A: Not directly. The Treasury borrows by selling securities at auction to dealers and investors. The Fed may later buy some of those securities in the open market, which is one reason people say the Fed finances deficits indirectly.


---

# The musical chairs question

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 07. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-07.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-07 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*If all money is borrowed and interest is owed on top, can everyone ever pay? The honest answer is yes in a quiet world, and not always in a real one.*

Chapter 6 showed that money is born as debt. That raises a question almost everyone hits sooner or later, and the owner of this project put it in a sharp form.

> "Imagine I give a person my own currency YYY$10, but I tell them they must pay me back 5% interest, but no matter how much they work they can't repay if there is only YYY$10 in circulation." (The owner of this project, in their own words)

It feels like musical chairs. Ten chairs, ten and a half people. Someone must always be left standing, or someone must always borrow more to keep the music playing. Let us test the intuition carefully, because it is half right, and the half that is right matters a great deal.

*[Picture on the web page: The worry: YYY$10 in circulation, YYY$10.50 owed. If the stock of money is all there is, someone must default or borrow more.]*

### Why it feels impossible

The worry treats money as a fixed pile, a stock. You hand out 10. You ask for 10.50 back. There are only 10 in existence. Arithmetic seems to say no.

The missing piece is time. Money is not used once. It moves. The same coin can pay many debts in a year, because each person who receives it spends it again. Economists call how often money changes hands its velocity. Debts are paid from flows over time, not from the stock all at once.

### The real mechanism: the lender spends

> **Picture this.** You are the lender on a small island. You lend YYY$10 to Bea, a fisher, at 5% a year. Each year Bea owes you YYY$0.50 of interest. Where does she get it? From you. You need to eat, so you buy YYY$0.50 of fish from Bea each year. She takes that YYY$0.50 and pays you the interest. Next year, the same thing. The money supply never changes. It stays at YYY$10. Bea pays her interest forever. Nobody is left standing.

| Year | Money in circulation | Bea's loan | Interest Bea pays you | You spend back on fish | Anyone short? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | YYY$10 | YYY$10 | YYY$0.50 | YYY$0.50 | No |
| 2 | YYY$10 | YYY$10 | YYY$0.50 | YYY$0.50 | No |
| 10 | YYY$10 | YYY$10 | YYY$0.50 | YYY$0.50 | No |
| Total over 10 years | Still YYY$10 | Still YYY$10 | YYY$5.00 paid | YYY$5.00 spent | No |

Interest is a payment for a service, the use of money over time. As long as the person who receives interest spends it back into the economy, on goods, wages, rent or taxes, the money circulates and can be earned again. Even repaying the principal is possible. Bea can sell you more fish over time and pay down the YYY$10. When she finishes, the money she borrowed is gone, because the loan that created it is gone. That is not a failure. It is the loop from Chapter 6 running in reverse.

Economists who modeled this carefully, including critics of mainstream economics such as Steve Keen, have shown that a pure credit economy can pay interest in a steady state without needing endless new loans. So the strict version of the musical chairs claim, that interest can never be paid without more debt, is not correct.

- **Myth:** Because banks only create the principal and never the interest, the system needs ever more debt just to pay interest, or it collapses.
- **Reality:** Interest is paid out of the circulating flow of money, and banks spend their interest income on salaries, rent, dividends and taxes, which puts it back into circulation. In a steady state, interest can be paid indefinitely. The real dangers come from somewhere else, and they are listed below.

### Where the intuition is right

Now the important part. The owner's instinct points at real weaknesses. They are just different from the arithmetic one.

- Savers who do not spend. If the people receiving interest save it instead of spending it, money piles up with them and drains from everyone else. If savers as a group want their savings to keep growing, someone else must keep going deeper into debt. This is an accounting fact, made famous by the economist Wynne Godley: for every saver accumulating financial assets, some sector, households, businesses, government or foreigners, must be adding debt.
- Debt can outgrow income. Paying interest is possible. Paying more and more interest on debts that grow faster than incomes is not sustainable. Global debt is about $365 trillion, roughly 310% of world output, according to the Institute of International Finance in 2026.
- Repayment destroys money. If many borrowers try to pay down debt at once, deposits vanish, spending falls, prices and incomes drop, and the remaining debts get harder to pay.
- Panics need cash now, not over time. In a crisis everyone wants to settle at once. Then the stock of money really is too small for the pile of claims, unless a central bank steps in.

> "The more the debtors pay, the more they owe." (Irving Fisher, The Debt-Deflation Theory of Great Depressions, 1933)

Fisher saw this in the Great Depression. When everyone sells assets and cuts spending to repay debt, prices fall. Falling prices make each remaining dollar of debt heavier. Paying down debt can make debt burdens worse.

### Minsky: stability breeds instability

The economist Hyman Minsky described three kinds of borrowers. Hedge borrowers can pay both interest and principal from income. Speculative borrowers can pay interest from income but must keep rolling over the principal. Ponzi borrowers cannot even pay the interest from income, and must borrow more or sell assets that they hope keep rising.

Minsky's key idea is that long calm periods push people from the first kind toward the third. Good times make lenders and borrowers confident, so they take on more debt against rising asset prices. Then a small shock, like a dip in house prices, reveals that many borrowers were Ponzi borrowers all along. The 2008 crisis is often called a Minsky moment, a phrase coined by economist Paul McCulley.

*[Picture on the web page: The debt treadmill: when debt grows faster than income, the interest bill rises, so more borrowing is needed just to keep pace. Calm years tempt more people onto the faster belt.]*

### Why credit growth became structural after 1971

Under gold, a bank boom eventually ran into a gold shortage and stopped. After 1971 that brake was gone. Each time a slump threatened, central banks could cut rates and governments could borrow, so recessions were shorter but debt rarely got cleared out. Over decades, debt grew faster than incomes. The system became like a bicycle that is stable only while it keeps moving forward.

The US government is the clearest current case. According to Treasury data gathered by this project, the government spent about $7.40 trillion in fiscal year 2026 and collected about $5.40 trillion, a deficit of about $1.99 trillion. Even before interest, it ran a primary deficit of about $941 billion, close to 2.9% of the economy. Interest itself cost about $1.05 trillion. The average rate on its marketable debt is about 3.5%, but new borrowing costs closer to 4.9%, and about 36% of the debt reprices within a year. Unless deficits shrink or rates fall, the interest bill climbs on its own.

> The owner's notes say there is only about $15,000 of liquid money per person on earth against about $346 trillion of global debt, and conclude that we live in a world of scarce settlement capacity, not scarce money. The figures need updating: world broad money is now about $19,500 per person, and global debt is about $365 trillion. But the insight is sharp. Normally debts are paid slowly from flows, so a small stock of money services a huge stock of debt. In a panic, everyone wants settlement at once, and the stock is far too small. That is exactly why central banks act as lenders of last resort in a crisis.

**Check yourself.** Q: In the island story, what single behavior would turn the YYY$10 economy into a real musical chairs game?
A: If you, the lender, stopped spending your interest and hoarded it. Then money would drain out of circulation into your savings, and Bea would eventually be unable to pay without borrowing more or defaulting.

**Check yourself.** Q: Is it true that interest can never be paid without new loans?
A: No. In a steady state, interest can be paid indefinitely as long as interest income is spent back into circulation. The real risks are debt growing faster than income, savers hoarding, mass repayment shrinking the money supply, and panics.


---

# The seasons of money

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 08. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-08.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-08 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Money has weather. In some decades it melts, in others it hardens, and the same choice can make you rich in one season and poor in the next.*

So far we have looked at how money is made. Now we look at how it behaves over time. Prices do not move in a straight line. They move in long seasons, some inflationary, some deflationary. Most people live through only two or three seasons, so they assume the one they grew up in is normal. The rulebook exists so you do not make that mistake.

### Two kinds of weather

- Inflation: prices in general rise, so each unit of money buys less. Debts get lighter in real terms. Savings in cash shrink in real terms.
- Deflation: prices in general fall, so each unit of money buys more. Debts get heavier in real terms. Cash gains real value, but jobs and incomes usually suffer.

> **Picture this.** Think of money as ice. In a warm season, inflation, ice held in your hand melts, so you want to turn it into something that does not melt, like a house or a tool, and owing ice to someone is cheap because it shrinks while you owe it. In a cold season, deflation, ice keeps its shape and even grows, so holding ice is smart and owing ice is dangerous because your debt grows heavier.

### A timeline of seasons, 1870 to 2026

*[Picture on the web page: Seasons of money from 1870 to 2026: inflationary eras (wars, the 1970s, 2021 onward) and deflationary or disinflationary eras (1873 to 1896, 1929 to 1933, 1982 to 2020).]*

| Years | Season | Main cause | Who tended to win | Who tended to lose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1873 to 1896 | Long deflation | Gold standard, money growth slower than output | Lenders, savers | Farmers and other debtors |
| 1897 to 1914 | Mild inflation | New gold discoveries | Debtors, farmers | Fixed-income holders, slightly |
| 1914 to 1920 | War inflation | War spending, gold suspended | Debtors, governments | Savers, bondholders |
| 1929 to 1933 | Deflationary collapse | Bank failures, money supply fell about a third | Holders of safe cash | Debtors, workers, banks |
| 1941 to 1951 | War and postwar inflation with capped rates | War debt, Fed held rates down | The government as debtor | Savers in bonds and deposits |
| 1966 to 1981 | The Great Inflation | Deficits, oil shocks, loose policy, no gold anchor | Fixed-rate borrowers, owners of gold and real assets | Savers, bondholders, fixed incomes |
| 1982 to 2007 | Disinflation, long bond summer | Volcker's credibility, globalization | Bondholders, stock owners | Late borrowers at high fixed rates |
| 2008 to 2020 | Low inflation, zero rates | Debt overhang after 2008, cautious banks | Asset owners | Savers earning nearly nothing |
| 2021 to 2023 | Inflation surge | Pandemic spending, supply shocks, energy | Borrowers with low fixed mortgages | Renters, savers, long bond holders |
| 2024 to 2026 | Sticky, energy-led inflation | Oil shock, deficits, AI investment boom | Owners of energy and real assets | Wage earners whose pay lags prices |

The last row comes from this project's 2026 data. US consumer energy prices rose about 20.4% over a year, oil traded near $98 a barrel in October, and a key inflation measure ran at 5.0% annualized in the second quarter. Real hourly pay fell about 0.7% in the year to September 2026. The Fed under Kevin Warsh raised rates in September 2026, against the President's wishes.

> Financial repression is the polite name for a quiet trick governments use to shrink debt. They keep interest rates below inflation, so lenders to the government lose real value every year. Economists Carmen Reinhart and Belen Sbrancia showed in 2011 that the US and UK used this after the Second World War to cut their debt burdens substantially. A mild version is happening now: the average interest rate on US government debt is about 3.2 to 3.5%, while nominal income has grown about 5.7% a year over the past decade, so inflation is quietly shrinking the debt relative to the economy.

### Why governments prefer mild inflation

- It shrinks debt. A government that owes trillions benefits when each future dollar is worth a little less.
- Wages are sticky downward. People resist pay cuts. With mild inflation, a business can let real wages adjust by giving smaller raises instead of cutting pay, which keeps more people employed.
- It leaves room to cut rates. If inflation is 2% and rates are 4%, a central bank can cut rates enough to make borrowing cheap in real terms during a slump. With zero inflation, there is less room.
- Deflation is scarier. Once people expect falling prices, they delay buying, firms delay hiring, and debts grow heavier. That spiral is hard to stop.

New Zealand adopted the first formal inflation target in 1990. The Federal Reserve formally adopted a 2% target in 2012. The owner calls inflation a circulation incentive, a leaking bucket that pushes people to spend or invest rather than hoard cash. That is a fair description of how a mild target works, and it is also why holding idle cash is a slow loss in most modern seasons.

> "Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon." (Milton Friedman, 1963)

Friedman's line is famous and partly true. Over long periods, sustained high inflation does come with fast money growth. But most economists today add that supply shocks, like the oil embargoes of the 1970s or the 2026 energy shock, can drive prices up for a while even without fast money growth, and that expectations matter a great deal. Where scholars disagree is how much weight to give each.

### Deflation traps

The United States from 1929 to 1933 is the classic trap. About 9,000 banks failed. The money supply fell by about a third, as Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz documented. Prices fell by about a quarter. Unemployment reached about 25%. Fisher's debt deflation, from Chapter 7, ran at full speed.

Japan is the modern case. After its stock and property bubble burst around 1990, banks were slow to admit losses, households and firms paid down debt for years, and prices drifted slightly downward for much of the period from the late 1990s to the early 2010s. The Nikkei stock index did not regain its 1989 peak until 2024. The economist Richard Koo called this a balance sheet recession: everyone repaying debt at once, so nobody borrows to spend.

### A store of value changes jobs with the season

Here is a subtle point that most people never notice. An asset is not simply safe or risky. It is a tool that works in some seasons and fails in others.

| Asset | Works as a store of value in | Fails in | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cash and savings accounts | Deflation | Inflation | Cash gained real value in 1930 to 1933, lost it in the 1970s |
| Long-term government bonds | Disinflation and deflation | Inflation and rising rates | Great from 1982 to 2020, lost close to half their market value from 2020 to 2023 |
| Gold | Inflation, crisis and loss of trust | Disinflation with high real rates | Rose from $35 to $850 by January 1980, then fell to around $255 by 1999 to 2001 |
| Fixed-rate debt (as a borrower) | Inflation | Deflation | A 3% mortgage from 2021 became a gift as prices rose |
| Stocks of strong companies | Moderate inflation and growth | Deep deflation and very high real rates | Fell sharply in 1929 to 1932 and in 1973 to 1974 |

> Gold is usually called an inflation hedge, but from 1980 to 2001, a period that still had inflation, gold lost most of its value in real terms. What gold really hedges is a loss of trust in the money or the people managing it. When trust is high and real interest rates are high, gold tends to struggle. When trust falls, gold shines. In 2025 central banks bought about 863 tonnes of gold, a sign that some governments trust the system less.

- **Myth:** There is one safe asset you can buy and forget.
- **Reality:** Safety depends on the season. Long-term US government bonds are free of default risk, but holders lost close to half their market value from 2020 to 2023 as rates rose. Cash is safe from crashes but loses value to inflation. The most reliable protection is to understand which season you are in and to avoid betting everything on one season continuing.

**Check yourself.** Q: You have a fixed-rate mortgage and inflation jumps to 8%. Are you better or worse off in real terms?
A: Better off as a borrower, as long as your income keeps up. Your fixed payments and remaining debt shrink in real terms because each dollar you repay buys less.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why did Japan's long stagnation happen even though interest rates were near zero?
A: Households, firms and banks were focused on repairing their balance sheets after the 1990 bust, so they paid down debt instead of borrowing to spend. Cheap money did not help when nobody wanted to borrow.


---

# The deflation debate: would anyone spend a money that grows?

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 09. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-defl.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-defl . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*If a dollar buys more tomorrow, why spend it today? The oldest argument against hard money, why it never ends, and what both sides miss.*

Chapter 8 showed that money has seasons. This chapter takes one question from the cold season and follows it all the way down, because it sits under almost every fight about gold, Bitcoin and central banks. The question is simple: if I know my $1 will buy more tomorrow, why would I spend it today?

### The case against a growing money

1. Prices are expected to fall, so people wait to buy cars, homes and machines.
2. Shops and factories sell less, so they cut prices further and cut jobs.
3. Workers who lose income spend even less. Borrowers find their debts heavier, because the money they owe is worth more while their income shrinks.
4. Defaults rise, banks pull back, and the loop feeds itself. Economists call this a deflationary spiral. Irving Fisher described its debt side in 1933 and called it debt deflation.

This is why almost every major central bank aims for a little inflation, usually 2%, rather than zero or falling prices. The cases they point to are the Great Depression and Japan's lost decades, both in chapter 8.

### The case for a growing money

- You still need things today. Food, rent, medicine and school fees do not wait. People keep buying phones and televisions even though they know next year's model will be cheaper and better.
- Waiting has a cost. A sofa you buy next year is a year without a sofa. Economists call this time preference: people value having things sooner.
- History has good deflations. From the 1870s to the 1890s US prices fell for years while output, railways and industry grew fast, because new technology made things cheaper to produce.
- The data are weaker than the fear. A 2015 Bank for International Settlements study covering about 140 years and up to 38 economies found only a weak link between falling consumer prices and slower growth, mostly driven by the Great Depression. The damage came mainly from falling property prices combined with private debt.
- Discipline. When money cannot be printed, governments and companies must fund projects from real savings, so fewer bad projects get started.

### Why the fight never ends: two sides, two different deflations

*[Picture on the web page: The same falling prices with opposite causes. Good deflation starts with cheaper production. Bad deflation starts with collapsing demand and heavy debt.]*

The argument goes in circles because each side pictures a different deflation. The hard-money side pictures good deflation: things get cheaper because we got better at making them, incomes hold steady, and every paycheck buys more. The central-bank side pictures bad deflation: prices fall because nobody is buying, while debts stay fixed. Both have happened. Which one you get depends mostly on one thing: how much debt is in the system when prices start to fall.

> Today's world carries record debt. The US government alone owes $40.44T. In a deflation every one of those dollars gets heavier to repay. That is the real reason no heavily indebted government will choose a deflationary money. The debate sounds like it is about shoppers delaying purchases. Underneath, it is about who carries the debt.

### Spend the worse money, keep the better one

An older rule explains what people actually do when they can choose between two monies. It is Gresham's law: bad money drives out good. People spend the money that is losing value and hoard the one that is gaining. In Tudor England people spent the clipped and debased coins and kept the full-weight ones at home.

> **Picture this.** On 22 May 2010 a programmer named Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas, the first well-known purchase of real goods with Bitcoin. At about $86,000 a coin in early October 2026, those coins would be worth roughly $860 million. After stories like that, almost nobody spends Bitcoin on pizza. They spend dollars and keep the Bitcoin. That is Gresham's law in a single slice.

So a money expected to grow tends to become a store of value, while a money that slowly melts becomes the one people spend. That is why the medium of exchange argument against deflationary money is partly right and partly beside the point. People do not stop spending. They spend the other money. Today that other money is the dollar, or a dollar stablecoin, sitting next to gold or Bitcoin in the same wallet.

| Question | Mild-inflation camp | Hard-money camp |
|---|---|---|
| Will people stop spending? | Enough of them to start a spiral | No, needs and time preference keep them buying |
| What about debt? | Inflation shrinks debts in real terms | Debt should be smaller to begin with |
| Who gains? | Borrowers, including governments | Savers and lenders |
| Who loses? | Savers and people on fixed incomes | Borrowers and the heavily leveraged |
| Wages | Mild inflation lets real wages adjust without cutting paychecks | Falling prices raise real wages without raises |
| Best evidence | 1929 to 1933, Japan after 1990 | 1870s to 1890s, technology prices today |

- **Myth:** Falling prices always mean a weak economy.
- **Reality:** Prices of televisions, computers and phones have fallen for decades while the industries making them boomed. What hurts is falling prices plus heavy debt plus collapsing demand, not falling prices alone.

> This matters for the future this desk studies. Robots, AI and cheap solar push the cost of making things down, a good-deflation force. A debt-heavy system cannot let that show up as falling prices, so it creates enough new money to keep prices rising gently. The productivity gain does not vanish. It flows to whoever receives the new money first and to owners of scarce things such as land, energy and platforms. That is the link to the Cantillon effect and the platform toll booths in chapter 16.

**Check yourself.** Q: If prices are expected to fall 2% a year, why might a family still buy a fridge today?
A: Because it needs a fridge now. Waiting a year to save 2% means a year without a fridge. Real needs and time preference keep spending going. A spiral starts when incomes fall and debts bite, not from cheaper prices alone.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why do most people spend dollars and keep gold or Bitcoin?
A: Gresham's law. When two monies circulate side by side, people spend the one expected to lose value and hoard the one expected to gain.


---

# Why empires and their currencies fall

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 10. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-09.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-09 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*No money has ruled forever. The ones that fell usually fell the same way: war, debt and a slow watering down of the promise.*

The dollar has been the world's main money for about a century. Before it, other currencies held that role and lost it. This chapter walks through the most famous cases, looks for the common pattern, and then asks honestly what is different today. It is the chapter where humility matters most, because history rhymes but never repeats exactly.

### Rome: the long watering down

Chapter 2 told the story of the denarius. Rome's army and borders were enormously expensive. As conquest slowed, new silver stopped arriving, but the bills kept coming. Emperors filled the gap by debasing the coin. By the late 200s AD the coinage had collapsed, prices had soared and the state increasingly collected taxes in goods rather than in its own worthless coins.

> The story has a twist that few people know. The emperor Constantine introduced a gold coin, the solidus, in the early 300s. In the eastern half of the empire, which became Byzantium, the solidus kept its gold content for roughly 700 years, until it was debased in the 1000s. It was the dollar of the medieval Mediterranean. A money can stay honest for centuries when the state that issues it chooses to keep it so.

### Spain: rich in silver, poor in the end

In 1545 Spanish colonizers found a mountain of silver at Potosi, in today's Bolivia. Silver from Potosi and Mexico flooded into Spain for over a century, and the Spanish silver coin, the piece of eight, became a world money used from China to the American colonies.

Yet the Spanish crown went bankrupt again and again. Philip II stopped payments to his bankers in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596. The silver was spent on wars across Europe and on imports, and it flowed out as fast as it came in. Prices across Europe rose several-fold over the 1500s, an episode called the price revolution. Historians still debate how much of that inflation came from American silver and how much from population growth. What is clear is that easy money without a productive base did not make Spain lastingly strong.

### The Dutch: the first modern financial center

In the 1600s the small Dutch Republic became the trading and financial center of Europe. Amsterdam created the Dutch East India Company in 1602, one of the first companies with tradable shares, and the Bank of Amsterdam in 1609, whose bank money was trusted across Europe. Dutch guilders and bills of exchange financed world trade.

Decline came through a mix of costly wars with England and France, rising debt, and loss of trading edge as Britain grew. A disastrous war with Britain from 1780 to 1784 hit hard. It later emerged that the Bank of Amsterdam had secretly lent heavily to the struggling East India Company and the city, which undermined trust in its money. The company was dissolved in 1799 and the bank was wound down in 1819.

### Britain: the pound sterling

Britain built the most successful money of the 1800s. The Bank of England, founded in 1694, and the gold standard of Chapter 2 made sterling the currency of world trade and London the world's banker. Britain carried enormous debt after the Napoleonic Wars, more than twice its economy, but the Industrial Revolution grew the economy fast enough to carry it. High debt alone did not sink Britain.

Two world wars did. Britain sold overseas investments and borrowed heavily from the United States to fight. After 1945 it was a large debtor with a weakened industry. The decline of sterling then took decades: a convertibility crisis in 1947, American financial pressure during the Suez crisis of 1956, a devaluation in 1967, and a loan from the IMF in 1976. The economist Barry Eichengreen showed that the dollar actually overtook sterling as a reserve currency as early as the mid-1920s, fell back in the 1930s, and only pulled clearly ahead after the Second World War. Changes at the top are slow and messy, not sudden.

### The common pattern

*[Picture on the web page: A common pattern in past declines: rising power and trust, a peak with a trusted currency and financial center, then war costs, rising debt, debasement or inflation, and a rival taking the lead. A framework, not a law.]*

1. A rising power wins trust through productive strength, trade and sound money.
2. Its currency becomes the world's preferred money, and its capital becomes the financial center. Borrowing becomes cheap.
3. Cheap borrowing funds wars, overseas commitments and consumption. Debt rises faster than the productive base.
4. To pay the bills, the state debases its coin or inflates its paper, and trust starts to fade.
5. A rival with stronger production offers an alternative. The center of money moves, usually after a great war.

A popular chart, often shown by investment firms, lists the leading currencies of the last 600 years with lifespans of roughly 80 to 110 years each: Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands, France, Britain and the United States. Treat it with care. Historians argue about whether reserve currency even means much before the 1800s, the dates are rough, and as the sterling story shows, top currencies often share the stage for decades. The chart is a conversation starter, not a countdown clock.

### Dalio's big cycle: one framework

The investor Ray Dalio, in his 2021 book Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order, describes a big cycle of empires. He tracks measures such as education, innovation, competitiveness, economic output, share of world trade, military strength, financial center strength and reserve currency status. In his account, empires rise as education and innovation improve, peak when their currency and financial center dominate, and decline as debts mount, money is printed, wealth gaps widen, internal conflict grows and a rival rises.

The framework is useful because it makes you look at many measures at once. It is not a law of nature. Critics point out that the sample of empires is small, that the stages are easier to see in hindsight than in real time, and that very different histories get squeezed into one shape. Use it as a checklist for questions, not a calendar for predictions.

> "If something cannot go on forever, it will stop." (Herbert Stein, economist and adviser to Presidents Nixon and Ford, 1980s)

### What looks familiar now

- Interest now costs more than defense. In fiscal year 2026 the US paid about $1,052 billion in net interest against about $965 billion for national defense, the third year in a row. The historian Niall Ferguson has argued that a great power spending more on debt service than on defense is a warning sign.
- Debt rising faster than the economy. US debt held by the public is about 100% of GDP, and the deficit was about $1.99 trillion in 2026.
- Allies hedging. Foreign official holdings of Treasuries at the New York Fed fell about $254 billion from February to October 2026, and central banks bought about 863 tonnes of gold in 2025.
- A tax base leaning on wages. About 86% of federal receipts in 2026 came from individual income and payroll taxes, while machines and capital are taking a larger share of income.

### What is genuinely different

- No ready successor. The euro has no single government bond market and no single treasury behind it. China keeps controls on money leaving the country, which limits the yuan as a reserve. This project's research found that rivals' strongest cards today are in hardware, like rare earth magnets, batteries and solar technology, not in currency.
- US debt is in its own currency. Spain owed its bankers in silver it could not create. The US owes dollars it can create. It is unlikely to default outright. The risk is inflation and higher interest rates, which is a slower, quieter kind of decline.
- Digital rails may extend the dollar's reach. Most of the growth in dollar stablecoins went to holders outside the US, spreading dollar use rather than shrinking it.
- Network effects are global and instant. Payments, oil, loans and contracts all run on dollar plumbing, and switching costs are enormous.

| Scenario (this project's desk view) | Now to 2028 | 2028 to 2035 | 2035 to 2050 |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1: the dollar system extends, absorbing new rails | 62% | 45% | 32% |
| S2: a neutral layer (for example gold or a neutral token) gains a real role | 15% | 22% | 28% |
| S3: energy or compute becomes a monetary anchor | 1% | 3% | 10% |
| S4: a disorderly reset | 22% | 30% | 30% |

These are this project's own judgment, made in October 2026, not facts. Notice two things. The dollar stays the most likely single outcome for years. But the chance of something messier grows the further out you look. Both of those can be true at once.

**Check yourself.** Q: What do Rome, Spain and Britain have in common in the decline of their money?
A: Each faced war costs and debts larger than their productive base could carry, leaned on debasement, borrowing or inflation to pay, and saw trust and leadership shift to a stronger rival.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why is Dalio's big cycle a framework rather than a law?
A: It is based on a small number of historical cases, its stages are clearer in hindsight than in real time, and very different histories are fitted to one shape. It is useful for asking questions, not for predicting dates.


---

# The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 11. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-leader.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-leader . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Why surplus nations park their savings in America, why climbing the leaderboard is so hard, and what it really took for each number one to get there and to fall.*

Imagine every country on a leaderboard ranked by how much the world trusts its money. Near the top is a strange fact: some of the hardest working, highest saving nations on earth send a large share of their savings to the United States, a country that saves little and borrows a lot. To understand why, you need three ideas: deep markets, governance incentives and game theory.

### What makes a market deep

A deep market is one where you can put in or take out enormous sums, quickly, at a fair price, and trust that the rules will not change on you. Few markets qualify. The US Treasury market is the deepest. Its qualities read like a checklist.

*[Picture on the web page: The qualities that make savers worldwide choose one market over their own.]*

- Size: tens of trillions of dollars of bonds, so even a central bank can buy or sell billions without moving the price much.
- Liquidity: buyers and sellers are always there, every hour, through dealers, futures and repo.
- Rule of law: independent courts, contracts that hold, and property that is not taken on a whim.
- Open doors: money can leave whenever the owner wants. No exit queue, no permission slip.
- A trusted central bank and a currency others already use for trade, debt and oil.
- Hedging tools: futures, swaps and options let holders protect themselves.
- Security: the military and alliances that protect trade routes and the system itself.

> Notice the trade-off hidden in that list. The US gives up some control (it lets money in and out freely and lets courts bind the government) and in return earns the world's trust. Countries that want to keep tight control of their money cannot offer the same deal. That single trade-off explains much of the leaderboard.

### Why surplus countries send their savings to America

When an exporter in Japan, China, Korea, Taiwan or the Gulf sells to the world, it earns dollars. If all those dollars were converted into local currency, the local currency would rise, exports would get dearer and factories would lose orders. So, often through the central bank, the dollars are kept as dollars and parked in the safest dollar asset available: Treasuries.

1. Stay competitive: holding the dollars instead of selling them keeps the home currency cheap and exports flowing.
2. Buy insurance: after the 1997 Asian crisis, countries that ran short of dollars were forced into painful IMF programs. Many vowed never again and built large dollar reserves.
3. No deep home alternative: many local bond markets are too small, too controlled or too easy to freeze to hold trillions.
4. Protect the wealthy: elites in less secure systems prefer assets where courts protect property, so private money follows the official money abroad.
5. Oil and commodities: these are priced in dollars, so exporters earn dollars and often recycle them through sovereign wealth funds.

### How that trickles down into the home economy

Parking savings abroad is a governance choice, and ordinary citizens pay part of the bill. A deliberately cheap currency makes imports, fuel and foreign goods dearer for households. Savings that could have financed homes, wages or local businesses instead finance American borrowing. Exporters and the state gain, households consume less than they produce. On the other side, Americans enjoy cheap imports and cheap credit while factory towns hollow out, as chapter 4 showed. Each side's elite chose the arrangement, and each side's workers live with its costs.

> **Picture this.** Two neighbors. One works long hours, sells most of what it makes to the other, and lends the payment back so the other can keep buying. The lender's family lives modestly. The borrower's family lives well but its workshop goes quiet. Neither can easily stop: if the lender stops lending, its buyer disappears. If the borrower stops buying, the lender's factory stalls. That is the quiet bargain behind the dollar.

Economist Larry Summers called this mutual dependence a 'balance of financial terror' in 2004. Each side holds the other hostage, which is why sudden moves are rare and why the game is played with signals, slow shifts and patience.

### The game theory of the leaderboard

*[Picture on the web page: A currency war as a prisoner's dilemma. Each country is tempted to cheat, and if both do, both lose.]*

- A coordination game: everyone uses the dollar because everyone else does. Switching only pays if many switch together, and the first to switch pays the most. That is why the leader keeps its place long after its advantages fade.
- A prisoner's dilemma: each country gains by weakening its currency or adding tariffs, but if all do it, trade shrinks and all lose. The 1930s round of competitive devaluations and tariffs is the classic case.
- A repeated game: nations meet again and again, so reputation matters. A country that keeps its promises can borrow cheaply for centuries. One that breaks them pays for decades.
- A war of exhaustion: rivals drain each other through arms races, sanctions and tariff wars. History suggests leaders more often fall from overstretch and debt than from being overtaken in a single contest. Historian Paul Kennedy called this imperial overstretch.
- The elite trap: a country rises on cheap labor and heavy investment, but climbing higher requires giving up control: floating the currency, opening the capital account, independent courts. The elites who profit from control often block those steps. Economists Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson describe this as extractive institutions resisting inclusive ones. It is one reason so many countries stall in the middle of the leaderboard.

- **Myth:** The country with the biggest economy automatically gets the top currency.
- **Reality:** Currency leadership lags economic leadership by decades. The US economy passed Britain's in the 1870s, yet sterling remained a leading reserve currency into the 1940s and beyond. Trust, habit and deep markets take generations to move.

### How the number ones rose, and how they fell

| Leader | Its edge | How it slipped | Debt record |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rome | Roads, legions, control of the Mediterranean trade lake | Endless wars, coin debasement, inflation, splits | Silver content of the denarius collapsed over the third century |
| Portugal | Atlantic coast, navigation skill, the sea route to Asian spices | Small population stretched across oceans | Absorbed into the Spanish crown in 1580 |
| Spain | American silver and a vast Habsburg empire | Wars on many fronts, silver-fuelled inflation | Philip II defaulted on royal debts in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596 |
| Netherlands | Trade hub, merchant culture, the Bank of Amsterdam (1609), the first great joint-stock company (VOC, 1602) | Wars with England and France, rising rivals | Defeat in the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War (1780 to 1784), French conquest in 1795 |
| Britain | Island safety, coal and industry, the Royal Navy, credible public debt after 1688 and the Bank of England (1694) | Two world wars, empire costs, rising America | Stopped paying its WWI debts to the US after 1934, devalued sterling in 1949 and 1967, IMF loan in 1976 |
| United States | Two oceans, a resource-rich continent, immigration, rule of law, deep capital markets, inventive culture | Today's test: debt, polarization, rivals in hardware | Changed gold clauses in 1933 and ended gold convertibility in 1971, but has always paid its bonds in dollars |

Notice the pattern. Defaults and devaluations rarely end an empire in one blow. They are symptoms of a deeper strain: spending on war and status that the productive economy can no longer carry. France shows how fast it can turn political: a partial default in 1770 and a debt crisis in the 1780s led to the calling of the Estates General in 1789 and the Revolution.

### What it really takes to be number one

- Produce: a real economy that makes things the world wants.
- Protect: security for trade routes and allies.
- Promise: institutions that make debt credible, so the state can borrow cheaply in a crisis. Britain after 1688 and Hamilton's America after 1790 both won wars partly because lenders trusted them.
- Plumbing: deep, open financial markets that others can use.
- People: a culture of work, saving, invention and trust in contracts.
- Place: geography that protects and connects, from Britain's channel to America's two oceans.

No single leader had all six forever. Each rose when its mix fit the technology and trade of its age, and each faded when debt, war and complacency ate the mix away. The open question for this century is whether the United States can keep its plumbing and promise strong enough to outlast the strain on the other pillars, and whether any rival is willing to give up enough control to offer a deeper market.

### Geography deals the cards, and the deck keeps changing

Place is one of the six pillars, but what makes a place valuable changes with technology. Every era has its own rare and needed thing, and the countries sitting on it get a turn near the top. Then the technology moves, and yesterday's treasure can lose its value almost overnight.

*[Picture on the web page: What the world found rare and needed, era by era. The places that held it rose. Some lost it when technology changed.]*

Chile's nitrate mines made it rich in the late 1800s, because nitrate was needed for fertilizer and explosives. In 1913 German chemists began making nitrogen in factories, and the boom ended. Botswana grew faster than almost any country from 1965 to 1995 on diamonds, and is now strained because laboratory-grown stones have pushed natural diamond prices down. Today the rare and needed things are battery metals, rare earths, chips, cheap power and compute.

### Rich ground, poor people: the resource curse

Having the cards is not the same as winning the hand. South Africa mines about 70% of the world's platinum, 46% of its chromium and 40% of its manganese, according to the US Geological Survey, and holds most of the world's platinum-group reserves. Yet its official unemployment rate was 33.6% in the second quarter of 2026, and 47.4% for people aged 15 to 34. The Democratic Republic of the Congo mines about 72% of the world's cobalt, the metal in most rechargeable batteries, yet remains one of the poorest countries on earth and has suffered decades of war.

*[Picture on the web page: Who captures the value of a mineral. The miner keeps the smallest share. China refines about 79% of the world's cobalt.]*

Economists call this the resource curse. Its parts fit together. Easy money from the ground lets rulers govern without taxing or serving citizens. Armed groups fight to control the mines. A flood of export dollars lifts the currency and makes every other industry uncompetitive, which is called Dutch disease after the Netherlands' gas boom of the 1960s. And the money is made at the next steps, refining, manufacturing and finance, which happen elsewhere.

- **Myth:** Resource-rich countries stay poor because of their culture or because people are out of touch with modern money habits.
- **Reality:** Habits such as saving in banks, paying tax and trusting contracts do matter, but research points mainly to institutions, and habits follow institutions. People save and invest where titles are safe and money holds its value. Colonial economies were built to dig and ship raw materials out. In South Africa, apartheid barred most people from owning land, skilled jobs and good schools until 1994, and since then power cuts, failing rail and ports, and corruption exposed by the state capture inquiry have held growth back. Change the institutions and the habits change with them.

The exceptions prove the rule. Norway built strong institutions before it found oil, then saved the oil money abroad in a fund that now owns about 1.5% of every listed company in the world. Botswana negotiated a partnership with the diamond company De Beers and spent the money on schools, health and roads. Geography deals the cards. Institutions decide whether a country can play them.

> Watch who refines, not just who digs. Indonesia banned exports of raw nickel ore in 2020 to force refining at home, and China's grip on refining battery metals and rare earths gives it more leverage than any mine does. On the country leaderboard, the processing step and the financial step are where rare things turn into power.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why might a country with huge savings choose to lend them to the US instead of spending them at home?
A: To keep its own currency cheap for exporters, to hold insurance against a dollar shortage, because its home markets are too small or controlled to hold the savings, and because its elites trust US courts with their wealth.
