Its households pay part of the cost through dearer imports and lower consumption.

**Check yourself.** Q: South Africa mines about 70% of the world's platinum. Why has that not made most South Africans rich?
A: Because the value is captured mostly at later steps and by owners, while the institutions that turn resource money into broad jobs, skills and ownership were weakened by history and poor governance. Rare ground pays only when institutions let it.


---

# The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 12. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-em.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-em . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Why a calm local price tag can hide a shrinking passport, how compulsory savings fund the home government, why talent and capital crowd into a few hubs, and whether Singapore was luck, strategy or someone else's plan.*

Most of this Rulebook looks at money from the top, from Washington and the dollar. This chapter looks at it from the ground in a smaller economy. Malaysia is the worked example because its story touches every idea in this book, but the same logic applies to Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines, Turkey, South Africa and most of the roughly 180 currencies on earth.

### The comfortable picture

A Malaysian worker sees a reassuring picture. Consumer inflation was 1.8% in September 2026 by the statistics department's count. The Employees Provident Fund (EPF), where most private-sector workers' retirement money must go by law, paid a 6.15% dividend for 2025 on investment assets of about RM1.41 trillion. Savings grow faster than prices. Why worry?

The picture is true, but it is measured with only one ruler: the ringgit, inside Malaysia. There is a second ruler most people never check.

### Two rulers: the home price tag and the passport price tag

*[Picture on the web page: What one ringgit buys abroad, then and now. Rates are approximate. The 1997 figures are before the Asian crisis.]*

Before the 1997 Asian crisis a US dollar cost about 2.50 ringgit. In October 2026 it costs about 4.08. So a ringgit buys roughly 39% fewer dollars than it did 29 years ago. Against the Singapore dollar the slide is steeper, from about 1.75 ringgit per Singapore dollar in early 1997 to about 3.2 in 2026. Inside Malaysia the loss is hidden, because local prices move gently. Outside, it shows up the moment you pay an overseas tuition bill, a foreign hospital, a holiday, an imported phone or anything priced in dollars.

- Imported goods: fuel, food ingredients, machines, medicines and electronics are often priced in dollars. A weaker ringgit raises their cost in ringgit.
- Education and health abroad: a family saving for a child's degree in the US or Britain is really saving in dollars or pounds, whatever its account says.
- Travel and work options: the same salary buys fewer days abroad, and moving to a richer country costs more.
- Assets priced globally: shares of global companies, gold and Bitcoin all cost more ringgit when the ringgit falls.

> **Be fair to both sides.** Currencies swing both ways. The ringgit weakened to about 4.80 per dollar in early 2024, its weakest since the 1998 crisis, then strengthened to about 4.08 by October 2026. Short moves reverse. For a lifetime of savings the long trend is what counts, and since 1997 the passport ruler has shrunk.

### Why the home price tag looks so calm

- Subsidies and price controls. The government absorbs part of the cost of fuel, electricity and some foods. In September 2026, for example, protection on household electricity bills was widened from 600 to 800 kWh a month, which helped pull the utilities index down. The cost does not disappear. It moves onto the government's budget, and later onto taxes, debt or a subsidy cut.
- The basket. Official inflation tracks an average household's local shopping. It does not include overseas school fees or the cost of moving abroad.
- Local wages and rents set many prices, and they move slowly.

### How Washington reaches a Malaysian wallet

1. The Fed raises rates or the Treasury sells more bonds, so dollar yields rise.
2. Global money leaves smaller markets to earn more in dollars, more safely. Foreign holders sell local bonds and shares.
3. The local currency falls. Imports get dearer, so inflation is imported even though nothing changed at home.
4. The local central bank must choose: raise its own rates to defend the currency, which hurts local borrowers and businesses, or let the currency fall and accept dearer imports.
5. Either way, households pay for a decision made in Washington. When the Fed eases or the dollar weakens, the flow reverses, which is part of why the ringgit strengthened in 2025 and 2026.

### The rule no small economy can escape

*[Picture on the web page: The impossible trinity. A country can hold only two corners at once. Each side of the triangle is a choice with a cost.]*

Economists call it the impossible trinity. A country cannot at the same time fix its exchange rate, let money flow freely in and out, and set its own interest rates. It must give one up. The US keeps free flows and its own rates, and lets the dollar float. Malaysia in September 1998 chose differently: it imposed capital controls and pegged the ringgit at 3.80 to the dollar, keeping control of its rates. The peg lasted until July 2005. Singapore chose a third path: it keeps money flowing freely and steers its exchange rate, and accepts that its interest rates largely follow world rates.

### Captive savings: the EPF and the home government

The EPF is one of the largest pension funds in Asia, and also the biggest single holder of Malaysian government bonds, with about 28% of them according to the fund's statement for December 2023. Its policy is to place about 70% to 80% of new money inside Malaysia. About 39% of its assets were overseas in late 2025, and in 2024 the overseas part, about 37% of assets, earned about half of all investment income.

> This is the same captive-demand playbook Level 2 chapter 1 showed in Washington, where stablecoins are required by law to hold Treasury bills. A government with a large pool of compulsory savings has a reliable buyer for its debt at home. That keeps its borrowing cheap and its markets steady. The cost is that workers' retirement money is concentrated in the same economy that pays their wages, in the same currency.

To be fair, the EPF has done well in ringgit, and the leak is slower than many fear. The ringgit's fall against the dollar since 1997 works out to roughly 1.7% a year, so a 6% ringgit dividend is still very roughly 4% a year in dollar terms. The leak is real but quiet. It matters most for people whose future spending will happen abroad.

### When the local economy hits bottom

The real test comes in a crisis. In 1997 and 1998 the ringgit fell from about 2.50 to about 4.88 per dollar at its worst in January 1998, roughly halving what Malaysian savings were worth in world terms within months. Stocks crashed, companies with dollar debts were crushed, and the government reached for capital controls. Malaysia recovered, but the lesson stayed: in a crisis, people with only local assets and a local passport have the fewest exits. People with income or savings in a strong currency, or skills that are paid in one, have options.

Malaysia remains deeply tied to the outside world. Its trade is larger than its whole economy, it is a key link in the world's chip supply chain, and its exporters earn dollars. That openness brought decades of growth. It also means a US recession, a tariff war or a Fed shock reaches Malaysian jobs within months. The same holds for most economies outside the few big hubs.

### Why money and talent crowd into a few places

*[Picture on the web page: New dollars ripple outward. The closer to the center, the earlier they arrive and the more they buy when they do.]*

Chapter 16 describes the Cantillon effect: whoever receives new money first spends it before prices rise. At world scale, new dollars are created in New York and Washington and land first in US banks, US markets and a handful of hubs such as London, Singapore, Hong Kong, Dubai and Zurich. Commodity exporters and factory economies receive them later, through trade. Households in smaller economies receive them last, often after their currency has already moved.

- Capital goes where returns, rule of law and exits are best.
- Talent follows capital, because that is where the jobs, the strong-currency salaries and the investors are.
- Capital follows talent, because investors want to be near founders, engineers and deal makers.
- The loop feeds itself. Each hub's lead makes the next arrival more likely. That is why successful businesses and entrepreneurs end up in the same few cities out of more than 190 countries.

Malaysia feels this loop directly. About 1.8 million Malaysians live abroad, and roughly 60% of them are in Singapore, according to a 2024 New Straits Times report citing World Bank work. The World Bank's chief economist Indermit Gill pointed to the currency gap as one reason educated Malaysians move there.

### Singapore: anomaly, strategy, or someone else's plan?

Singapore is an island with no farmland, little water and no natural resources, separated from Malaysia in August 1965. Within two generations it became one of the richest places on earth. Some people decode this as a plan by American money managers to plant a financial outpost in Asia. Here is the record, run through this project's decoding method.

| What happened | Who drove it | What it suggests |
|---|---|---|
| 1960 to 1961: Dutch economist Albert Winsemius leads a UN mission, reports in 1961 and becomes Singapore's long-time economic adviser | Singapore's government, with UN help | A home-grown plan with outside advice |
| 1968: Singapore abolishes the tax on interest paid to foreign depositors. Bank of America opens the first Asian Currency Unit, starting the Asian Dollar Market | Singapore's government and a US bank, together | Singapore made itself the dollar's hub in the Asian time zone, and US banks were glad to use it |
| 1971: the Monetary Authority of Singapore is set up. From 1981 monetary policy steers the exchange rate instead of interest rates | Singapore | A deliberate choice inside the impossible trinity |
| 1974 and 1981: Temasek and GIC are founded to invest national savings around the world | Singapore | National savings sent abroad by design, unlike most countries |
| 1990: an agreement gives US forces access to Singapore facilities. Changi Naval Base later hosts US aircraft carriers | Singapore and the US | A security umbrella traded for strategic usefulness |
| Location on the Strait of Malacca, one of the busiest sea lanes on earth | Geography | An advantage no plan could create |

> **The decode verdict.** Planted by American money managers: D3, folklore, about 10% likely as stated. No evidence shows Washington designed Singapore. Strategically welcomed by them: D1, decoded-strong, about 80% likely. Singapore's leaders deliberately made their island useful to the dollar system and to US security in Asia, and the US, its banks and its navy had every reason to support that. It was Singapore's plan, built to fit the American system. Small size let the plan be run tightly, and geography made it pay.

That is why Singapore is hard to copy. It needed a strategic location, leaders able to make long-term choices, rule of law trusted by foreign money, English as a working language, and the willingness to plug into the world's dominant system rather than fight it. Most countries have one or two of these. Very few have all of them at once.

### Tying it together

1. A decision in Washington moves dollar yields.
2. Global money flows toward or away from smaller markets, and their currencies move.
3. Home inflation stays calm, partly because subsidies absorb the shock, while the passport price tag changes.
4. Compulsory savings such as the EPF recycle most local money into the home government and home market, in the home currency.
5. Money reaches the hubs first. Talent follows money, and money follows talent.
6. In a crisis, people with only local assets and local options have the fewest exits.
7. A few places, like Singapore, escaped by choosing to become hubs themselves. That took geography, discipline and decades.

- **Myth:** My country's inflation is only 2%, so my savings are safe.
- **Reality:** Safe on the home ruler. Measure them also on the passport ruler: what they buy in dollars, in a foreign degree or in the cost of moving. Both rulers matter, and the second one moves with decisions made abroad.

> This is general education, not advice. The lesson people usually draw is to know which ruler their future spending will use. If your life will be lived at home, the home ruler matters most. If your children may study or work abroad, part of your savings is really owed in another currency. Skills that are paid in global terms are the most portable asset a person can own.

**Check yourself.** Q: The Fed raises rates and the ringgit falls 10% against the dollar. Malaysian inflation stays at 2%. Has anything changed for a family saving for a child's degree in the United States?
A: Yes. The degree is priced in dollars, so it now costs about 11% more ringgit. The home price tag stayed calm, but the passport price tag rose.


---

# The yardstick problem

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 13. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-10.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-10 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*We measure prices with money, but money itself keeps changing size. It is like measuring a room with a rubber ruler.*

Chapter 8 talked about prices rising and falling. But compared to what? Every price is measured in money, and money's value is itself moving. This chapter gives you the tools to see through the moving ruler: nominal versus real, time prices, and the difference between consumer prices and asset prices.

> **Picture this.** Imagine measuring your child's height every year with a tape measure made of rubber that stretches a little each year. The marks say your child grew 10 centimeters. But the tape stretched 4. Your child really grew about 6. Money is that rubber tape. Every price, wage and savings balance you see is read off a tape that keeps stretching.

*[Picture on the web page: A stretching yardstick: if the ruler (money) stretches, numbers rise even when the real thing has not grown. Real values strip out the stretch.]*

### Nominal and real

- Nominal means the number on the label, in today's money. Your salary is $50,000. A house costs $417,500.
- Real means the number adjusted for the change in money's buying power, so you can compare across time.
- The basic formula: real value equals nominal value divided by (1 plus inflation). The same idea works for growth rates: real growth is roughly nominal growth minus inflation.

> **Worked example.** You earn $50,000. You get a 3% raise, to $51,500. Prices rose 5% over the same year. In last year's dollars your new pay is $51,500 divided by 1.05, which is about $49,048. Your nominal pay went up $1,500. Your real pay went down about $950, or about 1.9%. You can buy less than last year, even though your paycheck says you got a raise.

The same logic applies to savings. This project found that the average US savings account paid about 0.38% in 2026. With inflation running around 3.5% that year, the real return on that savings account was roughly minus 3% a year. A Treasury bill paying about 4.25% at the same time had a real return of a little under plus 1%. Both are very safe. The real results are very different.

> When the news says the economy grew 5%, ask: nominal or real? In the second quarter of 2026 US nominal GDP grew at about an 8.5% annualized rate, but real GDP grew only about 2.2%. Most of the nominal growth was the ruler stretching.

### Time prices: measuring in hours of life

One way around the rubber ruler is to measure prices in hours of work. How many hours must an ordinary worker labor to buy something? This sidesteps the changing size of the dollar, because wages and prices are both in the same money. The owner wrote, time is the real currency for now. Time prices take that seriously.

| Item | Then | Now | Change in hours of work |
|---|---|---|---|
| All consumer prices (the CPI basket) | 1990 | 2026 | About 19% fewer hours |
| Food at home | 1990 | 2026 | About 24% fewer hours |
| New cars, adjusted for quality | 1990 | 2026 | About 54% fewer hours |
| Televisions | 1993 | 2026 | About 99.5% fewer hours |
| Median existing home, full price | 1990 | 2026 | About 42% more hours (about 9,000 to 12,800 hours) |
| Monthly payment on a median home | early 2020 | 2026 | About 40 to 68 hours a month |
| Family health insurance premium | 1999 | 2025 | About twice the hours (429 to 861) |
| Published public 4-year college tuition | 1995 to 1996 | 2025 to 2026 | About 58% more hours |

These figures come from this project's research, using the average hourly wage of production and nonsupervisory workers: about $10.20 in 1990 and $32.60 in September 2026. A few 1990 inputs are from memory sources and not perfectly verified, so read the house rows as approximate. The pattern, though, is strong and confirmed by independent studies.

> Goods that can be made in factories and traded across borders keep getting cheaper in hours of work. Things tied to land, local services and institutions, like housing, health care and college, keep getting more expensive. Your hour buys more food and electronics than in 1990, and less of a house than in 2020. Most arguments about whether life is getting better or worse are really people looking at different halves of this table.

### Asset inflation versus consumer inflation

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the prices of things people buy to use: food, rent, fuel, clothes, medical care. It does not include the prices of things people buy to own: stocks, bonds and houses as investments. For housing, CPI counts rent and an estimate of what owners would pay to rent their own homes, not the purchase price.

That gap matters. From February 2020 to 2026, average hourly pay rose about 32.5% and consumer prices about 30.3%, so real pay barely moved. Over a similar period, house prices rose about 59% and the S&P 500 stock index about 140%. If you only watch CPI, you miss that the price of entering ownership ran far ahead of pay.

| Measure, about 2020 to 2026 | Rise |
|---|---|
| Average hourly pay | About 32.5% |
| Consumer prices (CPI) | About 30.3% |
| House prices | About 59% |
| S&P 500 stock index | About 140% |

- **Myth:** If inflation is low, your money is holding its value.
- **Reality:** Low consumer inflation means your money holds its value for buying groceries and gadgets. It says nothing about whether your money can still buy a house, a business or a share of the stock market. When new money flows mainly into assets, consumer inflation can stay modest while ownership slips out of reach. This is asset inflation, and it is invisible in the headline number.

### Other rulers people propose

Some people say: measure everything in gold. Gold is not a stable ruler either. In the year to October 2026 gold went from a high of about $5,586 an ounce to about $4,131. Others say: measure everything in energy, such as kilowatt-hours. This project worked through the arithmetic. Because solar panels have become dramatically cheaper (module costs fell from about $132 per watt in 1975 to about $0.27 in 2024, in today's dollars), a fixed kilowatt-hour tends to buy less over time. Goods priced in kilowatt-hours would show inflation, not stability, while energy keeps getting cheaper.

There is no perfect ruler. The practical skill is to know which ruler you are using, and to check important decisions with more than one: dollars, real dollars, hours of work and perhaps a hard asset.

**Check yourself.** Q: Your rent rises from $1,500 to $1,575 and your pay rises from $4,000 to $4,100 a month. Did rent take a bigger or smaller share of your pay?
A: Bigger. Rent went from 37.5% of pay to about 38.4%, because rent rose 5% while pay rose only 2.5%.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why can house prices double while official inflation stays moderate?
A: Because the consumer price index counts rents and an estimate of owners' rental cost, not the purchase price of homes as assets. Asset prices can surge without showing up in the headline inflation number.

# The new board game

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 14. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-11.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-11 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*In Monopoly the bank hands every player $1,500. In real life nobody does. So how does a new player get onto the board?*

The owner asked a question that sits under every fear about the future of money.

> "If a new board game runs but no players have the starting money, how can a new player with no royal lineage and no inherited wealth start?" (The owner of this project, in their own words)

This chapter answers it in three parts: how money actually enters the board, the ladder of rungs a newcomer climbs, and what history says about times when the ladder was rebuilt. Then it looks at the routes open in 2026, using this project's own research.

### How money enters the board

In Monopoly, every player starts with $1,500 from the bank. In the real economy there is no starting allowance. Chapter 6 showed the real doors through which money arrives.

- Wages and sales: a business pays you for your work or buys what you make. This is the main door for most people.
- Bank loans: a bank creates a deposit when it lends to you. This door opens only if a lender believes you can repay, often because you already have income or something to pledge.
- Government spending and transfers: the government pays wages, contracts and benefits, which adds money to private hands. Programs like child tax credits, education grants and, in some proposals, universal income payments enter here.

> **Picture this.** The real board game has no starting cash pile. Instead there are three ways onto the board. You can work for a player already on it, who pays you. You can persuade the bank to lend you chips, which usually requires showing chips you already have or wages coming in. Or the game's organizer can hand out chips, which happens rarely and in small amounts. Most players start through the first door, then use the chips they earn to climb.

*[Picture on the web page: Entering the board: money arrives through wages and sales, bank loans, or government spending. Each door leads to the ladder: job, savings, credit, collateral, ownership.]*

### The ladder of rungs

1. Job: trade time and skill for income. This gives you a flow of money.
2. Savings: keep part of that flow. This gives you a stock of money and a buffer against shocks.
3. Credit: a record of reliably repaying small debts. This lets lenders trust you with larger ones.
4. Collateral: an asset you can pledge, like a house deposit, equipment or a business's sales history. This unlocks cheaper and larger loans.
5. Ownership: a share of something that earns without your time, like a home, a business or stocks. This is where wealth compounds.

Each rung converts what you have into what you need for the next one. Wages become savings. Savings plus a repayment record become credit. Credit plus savings buy collateral. Collateral and its income become ownership. The owner's Ledger Age series describes three mindsets: the Worker chases today's cash, the Investor studies the maze, and the Architect borrows tomorrow's cash today, puts it to work and owns the maze. The ladder is the path from Worker to Architect.

- **Myth:** The Architect's play is simple: borrow at about 6% and invest in stocks that return about 13.6% a year.
- **Reality:** Borrowing to own assets is how many fortunes were built, and the owner is right that ownership, not wages, decides who keeps up. But the 13.6% is a recent ten-year average, not a promise. From 2000 to 2009 the S&P 500 returned roughly nothing. Borrowed money must be repaid on schedule even when assets fall, which is how the 2008 crisis ruined many leveraged owners. The Architect's rule of survival is to borrow only what you can service through a bad season without selling.

### When the ladder was rebuilt before

| Program | What it gave non-owners | Scale | Who was left out |
|---|---|---|---|
| Homestead Act, 1862 | Free land, the main productive asset of the age, for living on and farming it | About 270 million acres, about 10% of US land. Nearly 4 million claims, about 1.6 million completed deeds | Native nations whose land it was, and many Black Americans in practice |
| Public high school movement, about 1910 to 1940 | A free credential that raised earning power | The share of young people with a high school diploma rose from about 9% to about half | Many Black students in segregated, underfunded schools |
| GI Bill, 1944 | Paid education and government-backed home loans for veterans | About 7.8 million of 16 million veterans trained. Nearly 2.4 million home loans from 1944 to 1952 | Many Black veterans, through local discrimination, and most women |

Each reopening gave non-owners a productive asset or a credential that was large relative to the economy, and paired it with credit. Each also had exclusions, and the people left out became the next generation shut outside the board. The research of Raj Chetty and colleagues found that 90% of Americans born in 1940 out-earned their parents, against only about 50% of those born in the 1980s.

### Today's routes, from this project's research

| Rung | What the 2026 data say |
|---|---|
| First job | Unemployment for ages 20 to 24 was 8.0% in September 2026, down from 9.2% a year earlier. Entry roles in fields exposed to AI are thinning, and recent graduates face 5.6% unemployment against 4.2% overall. |
| Credit file | Under age 21, a credit card needs independent income or a cosigner. Realistic paths: authorized user on a parent's card, a secured card, or a credit-builder loan. |
| Savings and housing | The broken rung. Median first-time home buyer age is a record 40. Saving a 10% down payment on a median home at 10% of young pay took about 6.2 years in 1990 and about 10 years now. About 49% of adults under 30 live with a parent. |
| Launching a business | The cheap but steep rung. A digital brand can launch for about $525 to $2,850, a small physical brand for about $1,900 to $7,400. But median solo founder revenue fell 23% in 2025 while the top tenth rose 19%, and platforms charge a growing toll for attention. |
| Ownership | The bottom half of US households hold about 0.58% of directly held stocks and funds. Since late 2019, the top 10% took about 67.5% of the $78 trillion rise in household wealth, and the bottom half about 3.1%. |
| Child accounts | Trump Accounts give a $1,000 seed to children born 2025 to 2028. The seed alone grows to about $2,400 in today's money by 18 at 5% real return. Adding $50 a month reaches about $19,500. Today's 18-year-olds get no seed. |

> The owner worried that people living on a universal income would lose access to credit and assets, locking out their children. Under current law, this project found that worry is not supported: a steady benefit can count as income for a loan, roughly $69,000 of mortgage capacity per $1,000 a month. The real dividing line is not income source but ownership. Wage earners and benefit receivers are squeezed in the same places, housing, health cover and energy. The three tiers behave like two classes: owners, and people who depend on an income stream.

### What actually moves a newcomer up

- Get an income door open early, ideally in work that AI complements or that needs physical trust and licensing.
- Build a thin credit file before you need it, and never miss a payment.
- Own something from your first paycheck, even a small, diversified slice of the stock market. Ownership compounds while you sleep.
- Treat a cheap business launch as a skills and equity lottery ticket, not a plan to quit everything.
- Watch housing supply politics in your city. Broad, by-right zoning, as in Auckland after 2016, lowered rents in a measurable way. Land, not the house, is most of the price in expensive cities.

**Check yourself.** Q: In the real economy, what are the three doors through which money reaches a new player?
A: Wages or sales from someone already on the board, loans from a bank that creates new deposits, and government spending or transfers.

**Check yourself.** Q: What did the Homestead Act, public high schools and the GI Bill have in common?
A: Each gave non-owners a productive asset or credential that was large relative to the economy, often paired with credit, and each excluded some groups, who were left behind.


---

# Today's board: old anchors, new rails

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 15. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-12.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-12 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*The money in your app may look new, but under it sit the oldest anchors in the system: government bonds, bank credit and gold.*

Every chapter so far has built toward this one. Here is the board as it stands in October 2026. The owner divided it into two sets. Set 1 is gold, Treasury bonds and bank credit. Set 2 is stablecoins, tokens and crypto rails. The big question is whether Set 2 replaces Set 1. This project's answer, after three rounds of research, is no. Set 1 is absorbing Set 2. In the project's phrase, it is an acquisition, not a merger.

### The layers of money today

*[Picture on the web page: The layers of money in 2026: gold at the base for nations, then central bank money, bank deposits and Treasuries, with tokens and stablecoins sitting on top and backed by Treasuries.]*

| Layer | What backs it | Size, from this project's data | Who uses it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gold | Nothing but itself. No issuer, no promise | About 222,600 tonnes above ground, worth about $29.6 trillion. Central banks hold about 39,000 tonnes | Central banks as a neutral reserve, savers as insurance |
| Central bank money | The Fed's balance sheet and its legal authority | Fed total assets about $6.76 trillion. Bank reserves about $3.0 trillion | Banks, the government, and you through paper cash |
| Treasuries | The taxing power of the US government | Gross federal debt about $40.4 trillion. Marketable debt about $31.8 trillion | Everyone: foreign governments, banks, funds, stablecoin issuers |
| Bank deposits | Bank loans, bank capital and deposit insurance up to $250,000 | About $19.6 trillion of US deposits | Households and businesses for daily money |
| Stablecoins | By law, cash, bank deposits and Treasury bills of 93 days or less | About $304 billion, flat for a year. Tether about $183 billion, USDC about $73 billion | Traders, cross-border users, people in weak-currency countries |
| Bitcoin and crypto | Scarcity by code and network belief, no issuer | About 20.1 million bitcoin at about $84,000, roughly $1.7 trillion | Holders seeking an asset outside the system |

### Set 1: three jobs, not one layer

- Gold is the neutral reserve. It has no issuer to default and cannot be frozen if you hold it at home. Central banks bought about 863 tonnes in 2025. That buying rose after Russia's reserves were frozen in 2022.
- Treasuries are the prime collateral. Stablecoins, banks, money funds and foreign governments all hold them. They are the asset that the rest of the system stands on.
- Bank credit decides who can borrow against future income. A mortgage, a car loan or a first business loan still needs someone who studies your income and absorbs the loss if you fail.

### Set 2: new rails on old anchors

Stablecoins are tokens on a blockchain that promise to be worth one dollar each. Under the US GENIUS Act, from January 18, 2027, every compliant stablecoin must be backed by cash, bank deposits or Treasury bills of 93 days or less. That means every new compliant stablecoin dollar is new demand for Set 1 assets. Offshore coins are not bound the same way: Tether's USDT also reported about $8.4 billion of Bitcoin and $19.1 billion of gold in its reserves on 30 September 2026. Stablecoins cannot pay holders interest by law. And they cannot lend. They move money, they do not create credit.

> Stablecoin issuers keep the interest. When you hold a dollar stablecoin, the issuer invests your dollar in Treasury bills and keeps the yield. Circle, the issuer of USDC, earned about $668 million of reserve income in one quarter of 2026 and paid about 61.5% of it to distribution partners such as Coinbase. Across the market, this float is worth roughly $11.7 billion a year at a 4.25% bill rate. Idle stablecoins cost you the interest you could have earned.

- **Myth:** Crypto will replace banks, so people with savings will stop borrowing from banks.
- **Reality:** Crypto is replacing some rails, how money moves and settles, not the balance sheet behind it. All crypto-backed lending was about $56 billion in mid-2026, roughly 0.4% of US bank loans, and it only lends against assets you already own. A loan against your future income still comes from a regulated lender. Banks are adapting too: JPMorgan launched a deposit token on a public blockchain in 2025.

- **Myth:** Bitcoin's 21 million coins, times ten, can support about $300 trillion of credit.
- **Reality:** That figure works out to bitcoin at the same total value as all gold, about $1.43 million per coin, then multiplied by ten. Real crypto lending runs the other way: borrowers pledge about $2 of crypto to borrow $1, and all crypto-backed lending is about 0.05 times bitcoin's value, not 10 times.

### Digital central bank money

- United States: a federal ban on a retail central bank digital currency is now law, carried in the same bill as a 2026 housing act. The Fed cannot issue a retail digital dollar. Digital dollars will come from private stablecoins and bank tokens.
- Europe: a digital euro is under negotiation, with a holding cap of around 3,000 euros discussed and issuance in 2029 at the earliest.
- China: the digital yuan, e-CNY, runs domestic pilots, including programmable payments that expire. The cross-border mBridge platform has settled about $55 billion in total. Saudi Arabia left it in May 2025.

### Energy as collateral and ceiling

This project's central research question was whether energy will become money. The answer: energy will not replace the dollar you spend. It is taking over gold's old job as the scarce physical thing that caps how much real output any money can claim. In an economy of AI and robots, output grows with delivered electric power, and power cannot be printed.

Energy is also entering the system as collateral inside the dollar. Power plants, data centers, long electricity contracts and computer chips back new dollar loans. The project calls this the watt-dollar, a descendant of the 1974 petrodollar. US data centers used about 176 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2023, about 4.4% of US power, and projections for 2028 range from 325 to 580. Consumer energy prices rose about 20.4% in the year to September 2026.

*[Picture on the web page: Energy as collateral and as ceiling: dollar loans are increasingly backed by power plants, data centers and chips, while delivered power caps how much real output money can buy.]*

Energy fails as everyday money because a kilowatt-hour is perishable, tied to a place, and keeps getting cheaper as solar spreads. Elon Musk's suggestion of a currency measured in watts and tonnage is closer to a post-scarcity accounting idea, similar to the 1930s Technocracy movement's energy certificates. Its real problem is the same as every planned money: who decides the allocations.

> The rivals' strongest card is hardware, not currency. China's money moves, like selling some Treasuries or building alternative payment rails, have little bite so far. Its export controls on rare earth magnets, battery materials and, since October 2026, solar manufacturing know-how go straight at the watt-dollar, because the US Treasury can issue bills but not magnets.

### The toll booths

On any board, some players earn by owning the squares others must cross. In 2026 the biggest toll booths are not always banks.

| Toll booth | What it charges | From this project's data |
|---|---|---|
| Banks on savings | The gap between what they pay you and what safe bills pay | Average savings 0.38% against bills about 4.25%. On $50,000 that is about $1,935 a year kept by the bank |
| Stablecoin issuers | The full interest on reserves | Holders get 0% by law. Float worth about $11.7 billion a year |
| Online marketplaces | Fees and ads on each sale | Advertising reached about 41.9% of Amazon's seller services revenue in early 2026, up from 23.5% in 2019. Etsy's take rate rose from 16.5% to 24.2% |
| Dollar plumbing | Access to the payment system itself | Sanctions can cut a country out. Hormuz shipping tolls in 2026 were partly demanded in yuan |
| Land | Rent and price of location | Land is about 68% of single-family home value in San Jose and Los Angeles, about 40% nationally |

**Check yourself.** Q: Under the GENIUS Act, what must back a compliant US stablecoin, and who earns the interest?
A: Cash, bank deposits and Treasury bills of 93 days or less. The issuer and its distribution partners earn the interest. Holders cannot be paid interest by the issuer.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why does this project say energy is replacing gold's old job rather than the dollar?
A: Because delivered energy is the scarce physical limit on how much real output money can buy, as gold once was, and energy assets increasingly back dollar loans. But a kilowatt-hour is perishable, local and getting cheaper, so it fails as spendable money.


---

# Eye-openers: what most people never notice

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 16. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-13.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-13 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Sixteen quiet facts about money that, once seen, cannot be unseen.*

Each chapter so far has hidden a few surprises. This chapter gathers them in one place, with a few new ones. Each is something that sits in plain sight in the official numbers, yet most people go their whole lives without noticing it. Read them slowly. For each one, ask yourself where it touches your own money.

### About your own money

> 1. Your bank deposit is a loan you made to the bank. The balance in your account is the bank's debt to you. You are an unsecured lender, protected by deposit insurance up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. Above that, you are trusting the bank's books. That is why depositors ran from Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023.

> 2. Banks create money when they lend. They do not lend out your savings. A new loan creates a new deposit at the same instant, as the Bank of England explained in 2014. In the United States, reserve requirements have been zero since March 2020. Bank lending is limited by capital, demand, profit and the interest rate, not by a fixed multiple of reserves.

> 3. Treasury bills are the cash of the rich. In 2026 the average US savings account paid about 0.38%, while a three-month Treasury bill paid about 4.25%. On $50,000 that is about $190 a year against about $2,125. Wealthier savers and companies keep their cash in bills and money market funds. Many ordinary savers leave it in accounts that pay almost nothing, and the bank keeps the difference.

> 4. Most money is not cash at all. Paper notes and coins are a small share of the money supply. Most money is bank deposits, which are entries in ledgers. When people say the government prints money, what usually grows is ledger entries at banks and at the Fed.

### About the government's money

> 5. Inflation is a silent tax. No law is passed and no vote is taken, yet inflation moves buying power from people holding money and fixed-rate claims to people who owe money, and the largest debtor is the government. In 2026 the average interest rate on US government debt was about 3.2 to 3.5%, while nominal income had grown about 5.7% a year over the decade. That gap quietly shrinks the debt relative to the economy, paid for by bondholders and savers.

> "There is no subtler, no surer means of overturning the existing basis of society than to debauch the currency." (John Maynard Keynes, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, 1919)

> 6. Seigniorage: issuing money is profitable. A $100 bill costs a few cents to print and buys $100 of goods. More importantly, the Fed buys interest-paying bonds with money it creates, earns the interest, and in normal years sends its profits to the Treasury. Stablecoin issuers have found a private version: they take your dollar, buy Treasury bills and keep the yield.

> 7. The Fed can lose money and keep running. From late 2022, the Fed paid more interest on bank reserves than it earned on its bonds. Instead of asking for a bailout, it recorded the losses as a deferred asset, an IOU to itself to be repaid from future profits before it resumes sending money to the Treasury. A central bank that creates its own currency cannot run out of it. It can only lose credibility.

> 8. Interest on the national debt now exceeds defense. In fiscal year 2026 the US spent about $1,052 billion on net interest and about $965 billion on national defense. Interest was higher in 2024, 2025 and 2026. Interest took about 19.5% of all federal revenue. About 36% of the government's marketable debt reprices within a year, so if rates stay high, the bill keeps climbing.

> 9. US gold is still booked at $42.22 an ounce. The Treasury owns about 261.5 million ounces of gold and records it at the 1973 legal price, about $11 billion in total. At market prices it is worth about $1.08 trillion. Revaluing it would raise about one year of interest payments, once. It is a one-time gain, not a fix for deficits that recur every year.

> 10. Workers carry most of the federal tax load. In 2026 about 86% of federal receipts came from individual income and payroll taxes, and only about 7% from corporate taxes, down from about 11% two years earlier as companies expensed huge investments in AI. As machines take a larger share of income, this tax base is under quiet pressure.

### About the world's money

> 11. Sanctions run through dollar plumbing. Most international payments pass through dollar accounts at US banks. That gives Washington the power to cut a country, bank or person out of the system. When Western governments froze about $300 billion of Russia's reserves in 2022, every central bank noticed. Central banks then bought gold at a record pace, about 863 tonnes in 2025, because gold held at home cannot be frozen by someone else.

> 12. The Cantillon effect. In the 1700s the banker and writer Richard Cantillon noticed that new money does not reach everyone at once. Those who receive it first spend it before prices rise. Those who receive it last face higher prices first. This project's data refine the idea: in 2020 and 2021, checks sent directly to households lifted the bottom half's share of wealth from 1.7% to 2.4%. But owners of assets captured most of the dollar gains. Since late 2019 the top 10% took about 67.5% of the $78 trillion rise in household wealth.

> 13. Stablecoin issuers keep the interest. Under the GENIUS Act, holders of compliant US stablecoins cannot be paid interest by the issuer. The issuer invests the reserves in Treasury bills and keeps the yield, often sharing it with distributors. At a 4.25% bill rate, the whole market's float is worth about $11.7 billion a year. Each $1,000 left idle in a stablecoin gives up about $42.50 a year.

> 14. Mortgage rates are set more by the bond market than by the Fed. The Fed sets a short-term rate. Mortgage rates follow long-term Treasury yields, which reflect inflation fears, debt supply and foreign demand. In October 2026 the Fed's rate was 3.75 to 4.00%, while the 10-year Treasury yield was about 5.13% and the 30-year about 5.42%. In late 2024 the Fed cut rates and long-term yields rose anyway.

> 15. Safe assets are only safe in a given season. Long-term US Treasury bonds have essentially no risk of default, yet they lost close to half their market value from 2020 to 2023 as rates rose. Silicon Valley Bank failed in 2023 largely because it held safe bonds bought in a different season. Safety is a property of an asset in a season, not of the asset alone.

> 16. Platforms are the new toll booths. Producing goods has not become cheaper in dollar terms since 2019, but the cut taken by platforms has grown. Advertising rose from about 23.5% to about 41.9% of Amazon's seller services revenue between 2019 and early 2026. Etsy's take rate rose from 16.5% to 24.2%. None of this shows up as a separate line in the consumer price index.

**Check yourself.** Q: Pick the eye-opener that most affects you this month, and say why.
A: Any is fine. For many readers it is number 3: moving idle savings from a near-zero account to a Treasury bill or government money market fund can earn many times more for the same safety. For others it is number 14, because mortgage rates do not simply follow the Fed.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why can the Fed lose money without failing?
A: Because it creates the currency its debts are paid in. It records losses as a deferred asset to be covered from future profits. Its real risk is a loss of credibility, not running out of money.


---

# When markets fall: buckets, collateral and rotation

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 17. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-buckets.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-buckets . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*A 20% crash does not hand 20% to someone else. But money really does slosh between buckets, and the timing of when you enter a bucket is most of the game.*

Every big market drop brings the same post: the market lost a trillion dollars today, so someone on the other side must have made a trillion. It feels like conservation of money. If value left one place, it must have arrived somewhere. That intuition is mostly wrong, and understanding why it is wrong is one of the most useful things in this whole rulebook.

### Market cap is a price tag, not a pile of cash

Market capitalization is a simple multiplication: the last price anyone traded at, times every share that exists. It is a valuation. It is not money sitting in a vault. When the price moves, the whole tag is rewritten, even though only a few shares actually changed hands.

*[Picture on the web page: A company with 1,000 shares. Ten shares trade at a lower price and the value of all 1,000 shares is rewritten.]*

1. A company has 1,000 shares. The last trade was at $100, so its market cap is $100,000.
2. Bad news arrives. A nervous seller offers 10 shares and the best bid is $80. They trade.
3. The last price is now $80, so the market cap is now $80,000. Twenty thousand dollars of value is gone.
4. How much cash changed hands? Ten shares at $80, which is $800. The seller got $800 in cash. The buyer paid $800 in cash and got shares.
5. Nobody received the missing $20,000. It was never cash. It was an estimate of what all the shares were worth, and the estimate went down.

- **Myth:** When the stock market drops 20%, someone on the other side profited by that same 20%.
- **Reality:** Most of the drop is a repricing of paper value that nobody collects. Every share sold had a buyer who paid cash for it, so cash only changes hands, it does not appear from the crash. The people who do profit from a fall (short sellers, buyers of put options) win only what the other side of those specific contracts loses, which is a small slice of the headline number.

> **Picture this.** Your street has 100 houses. One neighbor sells in a hurry for 20% below what similar houses fetched last month. An appraiser now marks every house on the street 20% lower. The street lost millions on paper in one afternoon, yet only one family actually sold, and one family actually bought. Nobody walked away with the millions. That is what a market crash headline is.

### So does money just circulate? Not quite. It moves between buckets

The owner of this project put the next idea well: money is not a fixed pie that only circulates. It moves through different buckets, at different times, and each bucket sits on top of other buckets as collateral. That is right, with two refinements. First, the pie is not fixed: banks create money when they lend and it disappears when loans are repaid (chapter 6), so the total in the buckets can grow or shrink. Second, valuations move far more than money does, because a small flow of cash into a bucket can reprice everything already in it.

*[Picture on the web page: Money rotates between buckets, and the buckets are stacked: one bucket's value is pledged to borrow money that fills the next.]*

- Cash and bills: the safe bucket. It fills up when people are scared.
- Bonds: fill up when people expect rates to fall or want steady income.
- Stocks: fill up when people expect profits to grow.
- Property: fills up when credit is cheap, because most of it is bought with loans.
- Gold: fills up when people distrust the system or the currency.
- Crypto and frontier assets: fill up last in a boom and empty first in a bust.

### Collateral on top of collateral

Here is where the owner's phrase is exactly right. A bucket's value is often pledged to borrow money that fills another bucket. Stocks are pledged for a margin loan. Bonds are pledged in repo (a short loan backed by bonds) to buy more bonds. A house is pledged for a mortgage, and the bank pledges the mortgage to borrow from someone else. When prices rise, the collateral is worth more, so you can borrow more, so prices rise further. When prices fall, the same chain runs backwards: the lender asks for more collateral (a margin call), you must sell, the selling pushes prices lower, and the next borrower gets a margin call. That is why falls are often faster than rises.

> The scary days in markets are rarely about people changing their minds. They are about collateral. In 2008 it was mortgage bonds pledged in repo. In 2022 British pension funds had to sell government bonds to meet margin calls on their hedges, which pushed bond prices down, which caused more margin calls, until the Bank of England stepped in. Watch who is forced to sell, not who wants to sell.

### Early, late, and the price of being first

Because money rotates, timing matters. The first money into a bucket buys before the crowd, when the story is uncertain and the bucket might stay empty. It takes the most risk and, when it is right, earns the largest return, sometimes an outlier return. The last money in buys after prices have risen, when the story is obvious and everybody agrees. It takes a different risk: that it is buying from the early money on its way out. Neither is free money. The early buyer is paid for carrying uncertainty and being wrong often. The late buyer pays for comfort.

| When you enter a bucket | What you are paid for | Main risk |
|---|---|---|
| Early (before the crowd) | Carrying uncertainty and illiquidity | Being wrong or too early, the bucket stays empty |
| Middle (as flows arrive) | Riding the repricing as others join | Mistaking a crowded trade for a safe one |
| Late (after the story is obvious) | Comfort and confirmation | Buying from early money that is leaving |

### What moves money between buckets

- Interest rates and liquidity: when central banks make money cheap, it flows outward toward riskier buckets. When money gets dear, it flows back toward cash and bills.
- Credit: lending creates new money that lands in some bucket first, usually property and financial assets (the Cantillon effect from chapter 16).
- Supply and demand: new shares, new bonds and new coins dilute a bucket. Buybacks and scarcity concentrate it.
- Fear and narrative: stories move flows faster than numbers do.
- Rules: laws that force holders into a bucket (like stablecoin reserves that must hold Treasury bills) fill that bucket by design.
- Rigging: it exists (insider trading, pump and dump schemes, spoofing) and is illegal in most markets, but most rotation is explained by the five forces above.

**Check yourself.** Q: The stock market falls 20% and headlines say $10 trillion was wiped out. Where did the $10 trillion go?
A: Mostly nowhere. It was the paper value of all shares at the last traded price. The cash that changed hands in the selling went from buyers to sellers. Short sellers and put buyers gained only what their direct counterparties lost, a small fraction of the headline.


---

# Nation Inc.: taxes, interest and the hubs

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 18. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-nation.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-nation . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Is tax a scam? Why did the Torah and the Quran forbid interest? Is a tax-free hub like the UAE cheating? Read the world's countries as companies competing on one leaderboard and the answers fall into place.*

**In short**
- Each country works like a company: a finance department, a currency desk, billing, legal, security, sales and HR.
- Tax is the subscription fee for the board itself: the money, the courts that protect your title and the security around them. It is not a scam, but who pays it and how well it is spent are fair fights.
- Old religious bans on interest were early tools to stop debt from turning into permanent ownership. Islamic finance today still runs inside a dollar system built on interest.
- Tax-free hubs like the UAE compete for people and capital that other countries paid to raise. It is legal and deliberate, and it is the leaderboard at work.

### Read every country as a company

The fastest way through the jargon is to stop picturing countries as flags and start picturing them as companies. There are about 195 of them. Each has departments, staff, customers, a balance sheet, a credit rating and rivals. The leaderboard from chapter 11 is the ranking of these companies.

*[Picture on the web page: A country drawn as a company. The names change from place to place. The jobs do not.]*

| A company is judged on | A country is judged on | Today's example |
|---|---|---|
| Credit rating | Its credit rating and bond yields | US 10-year yield 5.13% (October 2026) |
| Market share | Its currency's share of world reserves | US dollar 56.70%, Chinese yuan 2.11% (IMF data) |
| Revenue | Its tax base and output | Taxes on work carry about 86% of US federal receipts |
| Debt and cash | Public debt and reserves | US debt $40.44T, interest $1,051.8B a year |
| Brand and trust | Rule of law and kept promises | The pillars of a deep market in chapter 11 |
| Talent | Who moves in and who moves out | About 60% of the Malaysian diaspora lives in Singapore |

### Is tax a scam?

A popular argument says tax is theft, or a scam that takes from workers and hands to elites. Go back to the board game from chapter 14. The game has been running for thousands of years, and it only works because someone keeps the board, issues the money, records who owns which square and stops players from simply seizing each other's property. That someone is the state, and the subscription fee is tax. Without it there is no common money, no court to defend your title deed, no land registry, no police and no army. You would be left trading by barter, and anyone stronger could take your land.

Tax also gives the money its value. Adam Smith noticed in 1776 that a ruler who demands taxes in a certain paper money gives that paper value. The German economist Georg Friedrich Knapp built a whole theory on the idea in 1905. Every American must pay federal tax in dollars, so every American needs dollars. That steady demand is one reason the dollar is accepted everywhere, long before anyone thinks about gold or oil.

The critics are not wrong about everything. Who pays matters. In the US, taxes on income and payroll carry about 86% of federal receipts, while gains on assets are taxed only when sold and can escape tax when passed on at death. Inflation is a tax nobody votes on. Spending can be wasteful or captured by insiders. So the honest verdict is: tax is not a scam. It is a fee. The real fights are over how big the fee is, who pays it, and whether the company spends it well.

- **Myth:** Tax is a scam. Without the state I would keep everything I earn.
- **Reality:** Without the state there is no money to earn in, no court to enforce your pay and no title to your home. The fair question is not whether to pay the fee, but whether it is set and spent fairly.

### Why the holy books forbade interest

The Torah forbids lending at interest to a fellow member of the community (Exodus 22:25, Leviticus 25:36 to 37), while Deuteronomy 23:19 to 20 allows it with a foreigner. The Quran forbids riba and warns those who take it (Al-Baqarah 2:275 to 279). Medieval Christianity banned usury for centuries as well. Three traditions, far apart, reached the same rule. Why?

Because in an ancient farming world, interest on debt could grow faster than any harvest. A bad year forced a family to borrow, the interest compounded, and soon the family handed over its land, then its labor, sometimes its children. Debt turned into permanent ownership by the lender. The same book of Leviticus prescribed a Jubilee every fiftieth year, when land returned to its original families. Mesopotamian kings regularly declared clean slates that cancelled farmers' debts. These were resets built into the rules, so the board could never become permanently titled to a few. It is the same pressure chapter 19 describes today.

> **Picture this.** Imagine Monopoly with one extra rule: every fifty laps, every street returns to the family that first held it, and all loans are torn up. Nobody can win forever, and nobody is a tenant forever. That was the Jubilee.

Islamic finance today, estimated at about $5 trillion to $6.5 trillion of assets in 2025 depending on who counts, replaces interest with sharing and trading. Instead of lending at interest, a bank can share the profits and losses of a venture, buy a house and sell it to you at a fixed markup paid in installments, or lease it to you. Islamic bonds, called sukuk, pay returns tied to real assets.

> Two catches. First, many products end up paying something very close to interest in a different wrapper. In November 2007 the leading scholar Muhammad Taqi Usmani said that about 85% of sukuk did not comply with Islamic law because of buyback promises that guaranteed the money back, and the standards body AAOIFI tightened its rules in 2008. Second, the Gulf currencies are pegged to the dollar, so their interest rates follow the Federal Reserve. Interest-free finance still lives inside a dollar system that runs on interest.

### The UAE: no income tax. Cheat, or strategy?

The UAE charges no personal income tax. It added a 5% VAT in 2018, a 9% corporate tax from June 2023 on profits above AED 375,000, and a 15% minimum tax on large multinationals from 2025. Much of the state's income comes from oil and gas, state companies and fees, and its sovereign funds are among the largest in the world. Its dirham is pegged to the dollar.

The result is a magnet. Henley and Partners estimated that about 9,800 millionaires would move to the UAE in 2025, more than to any other country. In company terms, the UAE hires experienced staff whose schooling, health care and early careers were paid for by other countries' taxpayers, at the moment those people earn the most. The home country trained them. The hub collects their best years and their capital.

> **The decode verdict.** Cheating: no. It is legal and openly announced. A deliberate strategy to attract wealth built elsewhere: D1, decoded-strong, about 85%. Lucrative: yes, as long as oil income funds the state, the dollar peg holds and the region stays safe. Singapore, Switzerland, Monaco, Ireland for companies, and others play versions of the same game. The OECD's 15% global minimum tax, agreed by more than 130 countries in 2021, was the big countries' attempt to limit it.

> The leaderboard leader plays by different rules. The United States is the only major country that taxes its citizens' full income wherever they live. Eritrea, the other usual example, charges its citizens abroad a flat 2%. An American who moves to Dubai still files a US tax return, and leaving for good means giving up citizenship and possibly paying an exit tax. Since 2010 a law called FATCA has made banks around the world report Americans' accounts. Only the company that owns the world's main currency and its payment pipes can keep its staff on the payroll after they leave.

### Why this usually takes years to see

Taxes, interest, pegs, hubs, ratings and reserves are usually taught in different courses, each with its own jargon and messy charts, and rarely with the history and geopolitics that explain why they exist. That is why understanding money usually takes years of relooping. Read the countries as companies on one leaderboard, and the pieces snap into one picture: who issues the money, who pays the fee, who trains the talent, who collects it, and who sets the rules.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why does a country that charges no income tax still need a state, a currency and courts?
A: Because the board still needs a keeper. The UAE funds its state mainly from oil, state companies and fees instead of income tax, but it still issues the dirham, runs courts and registries and provides security. The fee is collected another way.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why did ancient rules ban interest or cancel debts?
A: Because compounding interest in a farming world turned bad harvests into lost land and lost freedom. Bans and jubilees stopped debt from turning into permanent ownership by lenders.


---

# The titled world: why abundance runs on credit, and who keeps the balance

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 19. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-titled.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-titled . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Divide the world's wealth by everyone and it looks like plenty. Here is why most of that plenty is a price set on future credit, why the base layer was titled long ago, and what role each big country plays in keeping a crowded system from tipping over.*

This is the last chapter before the Rulebook, and it pulls the whole book together around one thought experiment. Take everything the world owns, divide it by everyone alive, and ask: if there is so much, why do so many people feel they are locked out?

### The thought experiment: divide it all

UBS estimates the world's personal wealth at about $470 trillion at the end of 2024. Divided by about 8.2 billion people, that is roughly $57,000 for every man, woman and child, or about $230,000 for a family of four. On paper the world is rich. Yet the same report finds that about 42% of adults own less than $10,000, while about 1.5% own more than $1 million.

*[Picture on the web page: The equal share on paper against what adults actually hold. Brackets from the UBS Global Wealth Report 2025, end of 2024.]*

### Now divide the base layer instead

The $57,000 is a nominal number. It is a price, measured in dollars at today's interest rates, not a quantity of things. To see the real pie, divide the base layer instead.

*[Picture on the web page: Each person's equal share of the world, first in paper, then in real things. Cropland from FAO (2023), energy from the Energy Institute (2025).]*

Each person's share of the world's cropland is about 0.2 hectares, roughly a quarter of a football pitch, to grow all of their food. Their share of all the energy humanity used in 2025, about 600 exajoules, is about 20,000 kWh a year, the same as 23 old 100-watt bulbs burning day and night, to run every farm, factory, truck, home and data center on their behalf. Savills' value for all the world's farmland works out to about $5,800 a person. Measured in things, the world is far less abundant than $57,000 suggests. Measured in claims, it looks rich, because claims can multiply faster than farmland or power plants.

> This is why the price of the base layer tends to climb in a credit-driven world. Each new round of credit creates more claims chasing the same farmland, the same city plots and the same energy. The claims multiply and the base layer does not, so its price rises. Owners of the base layer get richer without making anything new.

### Why the pie is smaller than it looks

- Most wealth is a price, not a pile. About two thirds of the world's net worth is real estate, and Savills values all the world's property at about $393 trillion at the start of 2025. Those values come from the last sales, as chapter 17 showed with market caps. If everyone tried to sell at once to share out the money, the price would collapse.
- Prices are future income divided by the interest rate. When rates fell from the early 1980s to 2021, the same buildings and companies became worth far more without producing more. McKinsey found that global net worth rose from about $156 trillion in 2000 to about $514 trillion in 2020, while for every $1 of new investment, liabilities grew almost $4, about $2 of it debt. Most of the new wealth was revaluation, not new things.
- Every financial asset is someone else's debt or someone's future income. Global debt reached about $365 trillion in mid-2026, about 310% of world output, according to the Institute of International Finance. A bond, a deposit or a loan is a claim on a borrower's future earnings. Count the claim as wealth and you must also count the debt.
- What can really be shared each year is output, not prices. The world produces roughly $115 to $120 trillion of goods and services a year, about $14,000 per person, and most of that already pays for wages, rents, interest and taxes.

*[Picture on the web page: A wide stack of claims balanced on a narrow base of real things. The higher the layer, the more it depends on future credit.]*

So the abundance we see is partly real, in machines, knowledge, networks and food, and partly a bet on future production, financed by credit and priced at today's interest rates. That is the owner's insight in plain terms: much of the world's apparent abundance is priced on future credit. When rates rise, as they did in 2026, the bet is repriced and the paper abundance shrinks, even though not one building or factory disappears.

### Money is debt, and debt is money

There is a deeper reason the paper pie and the real pie differ. Almost all modern money is somebody's debt. Chapter 6 showed that a bank loan creates a deposit. Your bank balance is the bank's debt to you. A dollar bill is a liability of the Federal Reserve, which holds mostly government bonds against it, and those bonds are the government's debt, to be paid from future taxes. Money is debt, and debt is money. If every loan in the world were repaid tomorrow, most of the money would vanish with them.

*[Picture on the web page: Every dollar someone owns is matched by a debt someone else owes. Only real things, gold and Bitcoin sit outside the mirror.]*

- To grow the money supply, the system must grow debt. That is why total wealth and total debt keep rising together.
- Paying debt down shrinks money. When too many people do it at once, as in 1929 to 1933, money disappears and prices fall.
- Add up the whole world and every financial asset cancels out against someone's debt. What remains, the world's true net worth, is the value of its real things: land, buildings, machines and the rest of the base layer.
- The exceptions are things that are nobody's IOU: gold, Bitcoin, land and goods. That is exactly why people run to them when they start to doubt the debts.

> So the $57,000 is not $57,000 of stuff. Much of it is deposits, bonds and pension claims, each matched by a debt somewhere else, owed by a company, a bank or a government that must pay it from future income. Net out the IOUs and what is left is the base layer plus the machines and buildings on top, priced at whatever today's interest rates allow.

### A world already titled

Underneath the claims sits the base layer: land, water, minerals, energy, ports, sea lanes, the best city plots, radio spectrum. Almost all of it was claimed long ago, recorded in a title registry or held by a state. Chapter 14 asked how a new player gets onto a board where no one gives out starting money. The harder truth is that the squares are already owned. Newcomers do not arrive on an empty board. They arrive as tenants.

When the base layer was up for grabs, it was often fought over with armies. European powers divided Africa among themselves after the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885. Japan pushed into Southeast Asia in 1941 after the United States cut off its oil. Iraq invaded oil-rich Kuwait in 1990. Today the contest is mostly fought with money instead: tariffs, sanctions, export controls on chips and rare earths, and who gets to price oil, finance mines and hold the world's savings. The wars over title turned into wars over price and access, though the older kind has not disappeared.

### The generational seat at the table

Within countries, the same pattern runs between generations. In the United States, households headed by baby boomers, born from 1946 to 1964, hold about 52% of household net worth in mid-2026, while millennials and Gen Z together hold about 11%, according to analyses of the Federal Reserve's distributional accounts. Households headed by someone under 40 held about 6.6% in early 2026, down from about 12% in 1989. Older people always own more than younger ones, but the gap has widened, because the assets the older generation bought were revalued upward by falling rates, and the young must buy the same assets at the higher price, usually with credit.

> **Picture this.** A Monopoly game where the first players bought every street while it was cheap. Late players start with only cash and pay rent on every lap. The bank keeps lending the late players money so the game can go on, because a game in which nobody can pay rent ends for the owners too.

> That last line is the key to the whole system. Owners need newcomers. Rents, mortgages, share prices and pension promises only hold if new buyers and tenants keep paying. So the system cannot lock newcomers out completely. It lets them in through wages, credit and a little inflation, on terms that keep the owners' titles valuable. This is the quiet balance the money managers of the world are actually running.

### Four levers that keep the balance

1. Credit: lend newcomers the price of a seat. It keeps asset prices up and lets the young buy in, at the cost of decades of payments to lenders.
2. Inflation: quietly shifts value from savers and lenders to borrowers, who are often younger. It shrinks old debts and lifts wages in money terms. Chapter 9 showed why indebted systems choose it.
3. Taxes and transfers: pensions, health care, child accounts and income support move part of the owners' income to people without assets. Chapter 14 and the Desk looked at what a universal income can and cannot carry.
4. New frontiers: new industries create new things to own before they are titled. Railways, oil, the internet and now AI, compute, energy and space are where newcomers can get title early.

When all four levers fail at once, history offers darker resets. The historian Walter Scheidel argued in The Great Leveler (2017) that across recorded history only four forces have reliably shrunk inequality on a large scale: mass-mobilization war, transformative revolution, state collapse and deadly pandemics. The levers above exist, in large part, to keep those four away.

### Who plays which role

*[Picture on the web page: A simplified map of the roles. Real countries mix several roles, and roles change over time.]*

| Who | Role in the system | What it gets | What it risks |
|---|---|---|---|
| United States | Issues the reserve currency, borrows and buys from the world, guarantees security | Cheap borrowing, consumption, power | Debt, hollowed industry, division at home |
| China | The world's workshop and a giant saver, now the main rival in hardware | Jobs, technology, influence | Dependence on foreign buyers, low household spending |
| Japan, Germany, Korea, Taiwan | High-tech exporters that lend their surpluses back | Jobs and steady surpluses | Weak home demand, exposure to US policy |
| Gulf states and other energy exporters | Supply the base-layer fuel and recycle surpluses through state funds | Wealth and security ties | Oil price swings, dependence on protection |
| Resource exporters such as Australia, Brazil, Canada, Indonesia and Africa's miners | Supply minerals and food | Income in boom years | Price swings and fights over title |
| Hubs: UK, Switzerland, Singapore, Hong Kong, UAE | Custodians, bankers, courts and meeting places | Fees and talent | Dependence on trust and openness |
| India and other large, young economies | Labor and tomorrow's buyers | Growth | Entering on terms set by others |
| IMF, World Bank, BIS, WTO | Referees and lenders of last resort | Stability | Questions about whose rules they enforce |

Each role balances the others. Exporters need the US to keep buying. The US needs them to keep lending. Energy and resource exporters need both. Hubs need everyone to keep trusting the pipes. Countries also change roles: Britain went from workshop to banker, and China from workshop to rival. Every role change is a moment of stress for the whole system, which is why this desk watches the China truce, the Gulf and Japan so closely.

### Sovereign wealth funds: the countries' investment arms

Chapter 18 drew every country as a company with an investment arm. That arm is the sovereign wealth fund: a state-owned fund that turns a country's surplus, usually from oil, gas or trade, into ownership of assets around the world. Global SWF counted sovereign funds holding more than $15 trillion at the end of 2025. There are well over a hundred of them, but about a dozen giants hold most of the money, so twelve is a good number to remember.

*[Picture on the web page: The five jobs a sovereign fund can do. Most big funds do two or three at once.]*

| Fund | Country | Money from | Main job | Size |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Government Pension Fund Global | Norway | Oil and gas | Saver. Owns about 1.5% of all listed companies | $2.39T (June 2026, published) |
| China Investment Corporation | China | Foreign reserves | Reserve investor | $1.57T total assets (end 2024, published) |
| SAFE Investment Company | China | Foreign reserves | Reserve investor, publishes nothing | about $1T or more (estimate) |
| Abu Dhabi Investment Authority | UAE | Oil | Saver with a global portfolio | about $1.18T (estimate) |
| Kuwait Investment Authority | Kuwait | Oil | Saver. Roots in 1953, the oldest of its kind | about $1T (estimate) |
| Public Investment Fund | Saudi Arabia | Oil and state assets | Developer and strategic arm: new cities, sports, games | about $905B (2025, published) |
| GIC | Singapore | Government reserves | Reserve investor | hundreds of billions (estimate) |
| Qatar Investment Authority | Qatar | Gas | Saver and strategic arm, trophy assets abroad | hundreds of billions (estimate) |
| Exchange Fund | Hong Kong | Reserves | Stabilizer behind the Hong Kong dollar peg | about $530B (HK$4.15T, end 2025, published) |
| Investment Corporation of Dubai | UAE | State companies | Holding company for the airline, banks and property | about $429B |
| Mubadala | UAE | Oil and state assets | Developer: chips, energy, health | about $358B |
| Temasek | Singapore | State companies | Owner of national champions | S$518B, about $400B (March 2026, published) |

Sizes are approximate. Norway publishes its value every quarter, but several giants, including ADIA, GIC and China's SAFE, publish no official figure, so trackers estimate them and do not always agree. The UAE alone runs four funds above $250 billion: ADIA, Investment Corporation of Dubai, Mubadala and ADQ.

- Stabilizer: a shock absorber that saves in boom years and spends when oil or export prices crash.
- Saver: turns a resource that will run out into a permanent stake in the world's companies, for generations not yet born.
- Reserve investor: earns more on a country's surplus dollars than Treasury bills would.
- Developer: builds new industries at home so the country is not stuck selling one raw material. Malaysia's Khazanah Nasional plays this role.
- Strategic arm: buys stakes, ports, chip plants, football clubs and game studios abroad, which bring influence and access as well as returns.

> Read these funds through this chapter's lens. They convert a base layer that will run out, oil and gas, into titles on the rest of the world: shares, buildings, ports and companies. Norway turned its oil into about 1.5% of every listed company on earth. A small country cannot hold the deep-market crown, but it can buy a slice of the board itself. It is also how much of the petrodollar from chapter 5 comes back to the US and Europe, not only into Treasuries but into their companies.

The fund idea also touches the universal income debate. Alaska's Permanent Fund, built from oil revenue and worth about $89 billion, pays every eligible resident a yearly dividend: $1,200 in 2026, made up of $1,000 plus a $200 energy relief payment. It is the closest thing in the United States to a citizen's share of a titled base layer. The United States has historically had no national fund of this kind. A February 2025 executive order asked for a plan for one, and whether it becomes real is a tell worth watching.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why would an oil country rather own a slice of the world's companies than spend all its oil money at home?
A: Because oil runs out and its price swings. Spreading the money across the world's companies turns a temporary resource into permanent, diversified income, and avoids flooding the home economy with cash it cannot absorb, which would cause Dutch disease.

### Decoding the balance: a plan, or incentives?

> **The decode verdict.** A secret global plan by money managers to keep newcomers out forever: D3, folklore, about 10% as stated. Policy that consistently protects asset prices, because owners vote, lend, fund campaigns and hold the pension savings: D1, decoded-strong, about 80%. After 2008 and again in 2020 central banks moved quickly to support asset prices. Nobody needs to coordinate. Each actor's incentive points the same way: keep the titles valuable, keep the newcomers paying, and keep the four horsemen away.

> This is why the future this desk studies matters so much. Robots, AI and cheap energy could enlarge the base layer itself. If newcomers can own a share of that new capacity before it is titled, the gap can close. If the same owners title it first, the gap widens.
