Who gets title to the new base layer of energy, compute, data and orbit is the ownership question of this generation.

### The whole book in one chain

1. Money is a trusted promise (chapter 1). Its anchor moved from metal to the dollar to government bonds (chapters 2 to 6 and Level 2 chapter 1).
2. Banks create most money as loans, so the system needs ever more credit (chapter 6 and Level 2 chapter 2).
3. The seasons decide who wins, borrowers or savers, and debt decides which season governments choose (chapters 7 and 8).
4. Nations compete for the deep-market crown, and smaller currencies live by its rules (chapters 11 and 12).
5. The ruler we measure with keeps shrinking (chapter 13).
6. Newcomers start on a board with no free money, and new rails are laid on old anchors (chapters 14 and 15).
7. Paper values are claims on the future and can fall fast (chapters 16 and 17).
8. Every country runs like a company on that leaderboard, with taxes as its subscription fee and hubs competing for its talent (chapter 18).
9. Underneath it all, money is debt, the abundance on paper rests on credit, and the base layer was titled long ago. The system's real job is balancing owners and newcomers without calling the horsemen.

- **Myth:** If the world's wealth were shared out, everyone would be comfortable.
- **Reality:** Only on paper. Most of that wealth is the price of homes and companies at today's interest rates. Sell it all to divide it and the price collapses. What could really be shared is each year's output, about $14,000 per person, and most of it already pays for wages, rents, interest and taxes.

**Check yourself.** Q: Global personal wealth is about $470 trillion. Why can't it simply be handed out as $57,000 to each person?
A: Because most of it is the price of existing assets, valued at the last trade and at today's interest rates, and much of it is matched by debts. Selling it all to share it out would crash the price. What is really available each year is output, about $14,000 per person.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why does a system that favors owners still lend money to newcomers?
A: Because owners need newcomers to keep paying rent, interest and share prices. If newcomers could pay nothing, the owners' titles would lose their value. Credit keeps the game going.


---

# Crypto: Set 2 money, dissected

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 20. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-crypto.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-crypto . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Bitcoin, stablecoins and twenty million other tokens, sorted into three families, tested against the jobs of money, and taken apart with six questions you can use on any coin you ever hear about.*

**In short**
- Chapter 1 said money is a trusted record of who can claim what. Crypto is a new way to keep that record: a shared ledger that no single bank or government runs.
- There are three very different families. Bitcoin is a scarce asset that is nobody's debt. Stablecoins are digital dollars backed by Treasury bills. Everything else is closer to a share in a platform, a loyalty point or a lottery ticket.
- Lumping them together as 'crypto' is the most common mistake. Each family answers the money questions differently.
- So far Set 2 is not replacing Set 1. Stablecoins carry dollars onto new rails, and Bitcoin competes with gold as a neutral store. Set 1 is absorbing Set 2.
- To judge any token, ask six questions: who issues it, whose debt is it, what anchors it, which job of money does it do, who can freeze it, and where does its return come from.

**Five words for this chapter.** 
- **Ledger:** A record of who owns what. Every money in history has been one.
- **Blockchain:** A ledger copied across thousands of computers, updated in blocks and very hard to change afterward.
- **Token:** A unit recorded on a blockchain. It can stand for a coin, a dollar, a share or a vote.
- **Keys:** The secret password that moves your tokens. Lose it and nobody can restore it.
- **Stablecoin:** A token built to stay worth $1, usually backed by dollars and Treasury bills.

### Why crypto matters for what money is

Go back to chapter 1. Money is not the paper or the metal. It is a trusted record of who can claim what, and the fight has always been over who keeps the record: the temple, the king, the goldsmith, the central bank, the commercial bank. Crypto's real invention, published in 2008, is a record kept by a network instead of a keeper. The rules are written in code, anyone can check the ledger, and no single party can quietly edit it.

> **Picture this.** On 3 January 2009 the first Bitcoin block was created with a newspaper headline written into it: 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks', from The Times of London. Whoever built it was making a point in the middle of the financial crisis: here is a money whose ledger no bank can lose and no government can inflate. The creator, known only as Satoshi Nakamoto, has never been identified.

That is why crypto belongs in this book. It is the first serious attempt since gold to create money that is nobody's debt and nobody's ledger. Chapter 19 showed that almost all modern money is someone's IOU. Bitcoin is the deliberate exception. Whether or not it succeeds, it forces every government to answer an old question in a new form: who should keep the record?

### Set 1 and Set 2

This project splits the money world into two sets. Set 1 is the old anchors: gold, government bonds and bank credit. Set 2 is the new rails: blockchains, stablecoins and tokens. After three research rounds the desk's finding is that Set 1 is absorbing Set 2, an acquisition rather than a merger. Stablecoins must hold Treasury bills by law, Wall Street sells Bitcoin through exchange-traded funds approved in January 2024, and asset managers are moving Treasury funds onto blockchains.

*[Picture on the web page: Each new rail ends up tied back to an old anchor.]*

### The three families

*[Picture on the web page: Three families that share a technology and little else. Sizes from mid-October 2026.]*

### Family 1: Bitcoin, digital gold

- Fixed supply: the code caps it at 21 million coins. About 20.08 million had been mined by August 2026, and an estimated 10% to 20% of those are lost forever with forgotten keys.
- Slowing issuance: new coins are created as a reward for running the network, and the reward halves about every four years. The last halving, in April 2024, cut it to 3.125 coins per block.
- Nobody's debt: there is no issuer to redeem it and no one who owes you anything. On chapter 19's mirror it sits beside gold.
- Size: about $80,900 a coin and about $1.63 trillion in total on 15 October 2026, roughly 60% of all crypto by value.
- Wild swings: it fell about 77% from its November 2021 peak to November 2022, and has had several falls of that size.
- Governments are circling: a March 2025 executive order created a US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve from coins already seized in court cases. The Treasury Secretary said in August 2025 the US would not buy more.

Test it against the three jobs of money. As a store of value it is a real candidate, scarce and owed by no one, but its swings are far too large for most people's savings. As a medium of exchange it is rarely used, because, as chapter 9 showed with the 10,000-bitcoin pizza, people spend the money that melts and keep the one they expect to grow. As a unit of account it barely exists: almost nothing is priced in Bitcoin. Its realistic job is a neutral store of value next to gold.

### Family 2: Stablecoins, dollars on new rails

A stablecoin is a token that tries to stay worth exactly $1. A company holds dollars and short-term Treasury bills, issues a token for each dollar deposited and destroys it when the dollar is taken back out. In October 2026 stablecoins totaled about $303.8 billion, led by Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC. Under the GENIUS Act, signed in July 2025 and taking full effect on 18 January 2027, compliant issuers must hold reserves in cash and Treasury bills of 93 days or less, and may not pay holders interest. The issuer keeps the interest on the bills.

> Stablecoins are Set 1 wearing Set 2 clothes. They carry the dollar to anyone with a phone, including savers in weak-currency countries like those in chapter 12, and every new compliant stablecoin dollar is a new buyer of US Treasury bills. Offshore coins are not bound the same way: Tether's USDT also reported about $8.4 billion of Bitcoin and $19.1 billion of gold in its reserves on 30 September 2026. Stablecoins already hold about 4.27% of all T-bills. That is why Washington legalized private stablecoins while a January 2025 executive order blocked work on a Federal Reserve digital dollar for the public. A stablecoin is a dollar IOU, so on chapter 19's mirror it sits on the debt side.

Stable does not mean safe. In March 2023 USDC briefly fell to about 87 cents when $3.3 billion of its reserves were stuck at the failing Silicon Valley Bank. In May 2022 TerraUSD, a so-called algorithmic stablecoin backed mainly by its own sister token instead of dollars, collapsed from about $40 billion to almost nothing within days.

### Family 3: everything else

More than 20 million tokens had been created by 2025, most through do-it-yourself launch sites, and CoinGecko counts more than half of the ones it tracks as already dead. The survivors follow a handful of business models.

| Type | What it is | Business goal | Closest old cousin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Platform tokens | Fuel to run apps on a blockchain, such as Ether (about $288B in October 2026) | Collect fees from everyone who uses the network | A share in a toll road |
| Exchange and company tokens | Issued by a crypto business | Discounts, loyalty, raising money | Loyalty points, or shares without shareholder rights |
| Governance tokens | Votes over how a protocol is run | Steer and fund the project | Voting shares |
| Tokenized real assets | Bonds, funds or property recorded on a blockchain, such as BlackRock's BUIDL | Faster, cheaper settlement | The same asset with a new ledger |
| Meme coins | Jokes and online communities | Attention and speculation | A lottery ticket |

Tokenized US Treasury funds grew about fiftyfold from early 2024 to about $16 billion by August 2026, which is the clearest sign of Set 1 moving onto Set 2 rails. Most of the rest are not money at all in the sense of chapter 1. They are claims on a business, a network or a hope.

> **Not crypto, but a cousin.** A central bank digital currency uses some of the same technology for the opposite purpose: the state keeps the ledger and can see every payment. China's e-CNY is the largest. Since January 2026 its wallet balances count as deposits at commercial banks and can earn interest. Bitcoin was built to take the ledger away from the state. A central bank digital currency brings it closer.

### How to dissect any token: six questions

*[Picture on the web page: Six questions that work on any coin, old or new. The last one catches most scams.]*

1. Who issues it, and can they make more? Find the supply rule and who is able to change it.
2. Whose debt is it? If someone must redeem it, it is an IOU and you are trusting them. If no one owes it, its value rests only on demand.
3. What anchors its value? Reserves, scarcity, fees from a working network, or nothing but attention.
4. Which job of money does it do: spend, store or measure? Or is it really a share, a coupon or a lottery ticket?
5. Who runs the ledger, and who can freeze or change it? An issuer that can freeze your coins is a bank in all but name.
6. Where does the return come from? If it pays a yield, someone must be paying it. If you cannot name who, the yield may be paid with newer investors' money.

*[Interactive tool on the web page: Try it. Pick a token and read its dissection. Compare Bitcoin with a stablecoin, then with a meme coin.]*

> Question six would have saved a lot of people in 2022. Terra's Anchor platform paid about 20% a year on its stablecoin when most dollar savings paid under 2%, and at its peak held about $14 billion. The return was topped up from reserves rather than earned, so when the reserves ran low the whole structure collapsed. The same question applied to the FTX exchange, which collapsed in November 2022 after customer deposits were moved to its sister trading firm.

### Where crypto sits on the layers of money

*[Picture on the web page: Bitcoin sits beside gold at the narrow, solid bottom because it is nobody's debt. Stablecoins sit on top of Treasuries. Most other tokens belong with the riskiest claims near the top.]*

- **Myth:** Crypto is backed by nothing, so it is all worthless.
- **Reality:** Some tokens are backed by nothing and are worth nothing. Stablecoins are backed by dollars and bills. Bitcoin is backed by nothing in the way gold is backed by nothing: its value rests on scarcity and demand. Judge each one with the six questions, not by the label.

- **Myth:** Bitcoin will replace the dollar.
- **Reality:** Not as things stand. Almost nothing is priced in Bitcoin, few people spend it, and its swings are too large for wages and rent. Its realistic job is a neutral store of value next to gold. The challenger on the spending side is the stablecoin, and that is the dollar itself.

### Why it matters for the future this desk studies

- It tests who keeps the record. Every government now has to choose between private stablecoins, a state digital currency, or leaving the old bank ledger alone.
- It extends the dollar. Stablecoins are becoming one of the largest new sources of demand for US Treasury bills, the captive demand Level 2 chapter 1 described.
- It offers a neutral store. If trust in all government debts weakens, Bitcoin and gold are the two assets that are nobody's IOU. The desk's scenario of a neutral reserve layer stands at about 15% to 2028, 23% from 2028 to 2035 and 28% from 2035 to 2050.
- It moves the ledger itself. Tokenized Treasuries and funds could make settlement instant, which changes who earns the float, the fees and the data.

### The owner's question: what if the dollar ruler disappears?

> **The owner's question.** Today everything, a share, a company bond, a token, has an easy measuring stick, because the dollar is there. Remove that layer, and we would probably learn to price things in Bitcoin. But right now crypto keeps getting absorbed into Set 1, because most of the world still settles in currencies. If tokens get good enough that nobody needs to convert Solana into stablecoins to buy things, and so many tokens can exist, where does their value come from? It still seems to come from base-layer credit and bond money. And if anyone lucky enough, a lottery winner or someone with a big enough yield, can launch their own token, it looks like a utopia. The opportunity seems enormous, and this is where it stops making sense.

This is chapter 1's question in its newest form: what makes something money, and who decides how everything is measured? It untangles in five pieces, followed by the questions worth carrying with you.

### 1. The ruler is the hardest job of money

Money has three jobs: spend, store and measure. Crypto has made real progress on the first two. The third, being the ruler everything is priced in, is the hardest, and no token has won it. When you pay with a token through a crypto debit card, the shop's price was set in dollars and your token was sold for dollars at the till. The conversion is invisible, not absent. The European Central Bank finds crypto and stablecoins below 1% of in-store payments in the euro area, in both 2024 and 2026.

*[Picture on the web page: Why the dollar keeps the ruler: every link in an ordinary life is a dollar contract.]*

The ruler belongs to whatever debts and taxes are written in. Your salary, your rent, your landlord's mortgage, the bank's loans, the government's bonds and your taxes are all dollar contracts. A token can become the ruler only when those debts start being written in it. Chapter 18 showed that taxes give a money its value. El Salvador tested the opposite. It made Bitcoin legal tender in 2021, but its debts, wages and taxes stayed in dollars, use stayed low, and in January 2025, as part of a $1.4 billion IMF deal, it made accepting Bitcoin optional and dropped the state's promise to convert it to dollars.

### 2. Many monies, one ruler: why markets always rebuild a hub

*[Picture on the web page: Six monies with no common ruler need 15 exchange rates. With one ruler in the middle, each needs only one price.]*

If every token traded directly against every other, each pair would need its own price. With 10 monies that is 45 exchange rates. With 1,000 it is 499,500. With the more than 20 million tokens created by 2025 it would be about 200 trillion. Nobody can think in that many prices, so markets always choose one hub that everything else is priced through. That is how barter turned into money in chapter 1, and it is happening again inside crypto, where most trading runs through a dollar stablecoin, Ether or Bitcoin acting as the hub.

*[Interactive tool on the web page: Try it. Slide from 2 monies to 20 million and watch how many exchange rates you would need without a common ruler.]*

> **This happened before.** From 1837 to 1863 America had no national paper currency. Hundreds of banks printed their own notes, and each note traded at its own discount depending on the bank's reputation and how far away it was. Shopkeepers kept bank note reporters, booklets listing what each note was worth and which ones were forgeries. It was a world of many tokens. It ended when Congress taxed state bank notes at 10% in 1865, and their circulation fell from $143 million to $4 million within two years. The ruler went back to one national dollar.

The economist Friedrich Hayek argued in 1976, in The Denationalisation of Money, that private monies should compete and the public would choose the most stable one. Crypto is the first large-scale test of his idea. So far the public keeps choosing the most stable token on offer, and that token is a dollar.

### 3. Where a token's value really comes from

Your instinct is half right. Today almost every token's price is a dollar price, and most of the money that buys tokens was born as dollar credit, so crypto prices tend to rise when dollar credit is easy and fall when it tightens. But the deeper source of any money's value is the base layer from chapter 19: the real goods, work and assets people will hand over for it. A token is worth what someone will give up to hold it. If everyone held tokens and nobody produced anything, every token would buy nothing.

> Bitcoin is scarce, but crypto is not. One coin can be capped at 21 million while anyone can launch a new one in minutes, and more than 20 million have been launched. Each new token is a new claim competing for the same real goods, the same attention and the same buyers' dollars. That is chapter 19's picture again: the claims multiply, and the base layer does not.

### 4. The lottery winner who launches a token

*[Picture on the web page: The life of a typical launch. Bars show the price. The dashed arrow is where the dollars go.]*

Launching a token is printing money, and the profit has an old name: seigniorage, from chapter 16. A token costs almost nothing to create. When its founders sell part of it for dollars, they turn newly printed units into real buying power, exactly as a government does when it issues money. That buying power comes from the buyers. Unless the token's network produces something people pay for, the founders' gain is the later buyers' loss. That is why the utopia feels so big: the power to issue money has been opened to everyone, but the pool of real goods all those monies can buy has not grown with it.

| What a project does | Creates value or captures it? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Runs a network people pay to use | Creates | Users pay fees for a real service, such as settlement or storage |
| Moves a real asset onto a faster ledger | Creates | Cheaper, quicker settlement saves real costs |
| Launches a token and sells it to later buyers | Captures | Seigniorage moves dollars from late buyers to early ones |
| Pays a high yield from new deposits | Captures, then collapses | Returns come from newer money, as at Terra in 2022 |

### 5. So where is the real opportunity?

- New rails: cheaper, faster payments across borders, especially for people in weak-currency countries, mostly using dollar stablecoins.
- Settlement: tokenized Treasuries and funds that settle in seconds, cutting into the float and fees banks earn today.
- Money for machines: AI agents paying each other per request, which this project found already happens mostly in dollar tokens.
- Early title to new networks: owning part of a network people truly pay to use, before it is titled. Chapter 19's rule applies: look for the next base layer before it is titled.
- The ruler itself: if trust in all government debt ever broke, the next ruler would be whatever is hardest and most widely accepted. Gold did that job for thousands of years, Bitcoin is a candidate, and this project's founding question asks whether energy could be one. The desk puts an energy or compute standard at about 1% to 2028, 3% from 2028 to 2035 and 10% from 2035 to 2050.

The opportunity is real but narrower than it looks. Most of the lasting value is in building rails and owning networks that produce something. Much of the rest is seigniorage passing from late buyers to early ones.

### Questions worth carrying with you

**Check yourself.** Q: If your salary were paid in Solana, what would you pay your rent in, and what is your landlord's mortgage written in?
A: Dollars, and dollars. Every link in the chain is a dollar contract, so the token is converted somewhere even when you never see it. The ruler changes only when the debts change.

**Check yourself.** Q: If Bitcoin became the ruler, what would happen to everyone with a mortgage?
A: If Bitcoin kept rising against goods, prices in Bitcoin would fall and debts written in Bitcoin would get heavier every year. Chapter 9's deflation debate applies: borrowers lose, savers win, and with no central bank there is no lender of last resort in a crisis.

**Check yourself.** Q: Who would set interest rates in a world of a thousand tokens?
A: No one centrally. Each token's lenders and borrowers would set their own, and the most trusted token's rate would become the benchmark, the way the Treasury yield is today. The hub returns.

**Check yourself.** Q: When AI agents pay each other, which ruler will they use?
A: So far the dollar, through stablecoins. Machines need stable prices even more than people do, because they price millions of tiny transactions. A machine economy is more likely to strengthen the dollar ruler than replace it, unless energy or compute itself becomes the unit.

**Check yourself.** Q: If anyone can launch a token, what stops the world from drowning in money?
A: Nothing stops the launching. What stops the drowning is that buyers ignore most tokens, which is why more than half are already dead. Free issuance makes money cheap to create and trust expensive to earn.

> General education, not advice. Crypto adds risks that bank money does not have: lost keys with no reset button, hacks, scams that target newcomers, exchanges that fail with customers' money inside, and rules that can change by executive order. Anyone who holds it should know which of the three families they own, and the answer to all six questions.

**Check yourself.** Q: Is a dollar stablecoin closer to Bitcoin or to a bank deposit?
A: To a bank deposit. It is an IOU from an issuer, backed by dollars and Treasury bills, worth a dollar only as long as the issuer can redeem it. Bitcoin is nobody's IOU.

**Check yourself.** Q: A new token promises 30% a year, paid in the token itself. Which of the six questions matters most?
A: Question six: where does the return come from? If the yield is paid in newly created tokens or from newer investors' money, the high number is a warning, not a feature.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why do people spend dollars and stablecoins but hold Bitcoin?
A: Gresham's law from chapter 9: people spend the money they expect to lose value and keep the one they expect to gain.


---

# The Rulebook

Rulebook Level 1 (Foundations), chapter 21. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-14.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-14 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*What each generation learned the hard way, written down so the next one does not have to.*

Families pass down recipes, tools and stories. They rarely pass down money lessons, because money talk feels private or shameful, and because each generation's crisis feels unique while it is happening. So each generation relearns the same lessons at full price. This chapter is the remedy: a short rulebook, and a list of the mistakes behind it.

> "Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it." (George Santayana, The Life of Reason, 1905)

### How to use the rulebook

1. Read the rules once straight through. Most will now feel obvious, because the chapters built them.
2. Pick three rules that you are breaking today. Write them where you will see them.
3. Before any big money decision, such as a loan, a house, a business or an investment, scan the list and ask which rules apply.
4. Read the mistakes list with someone younger than you. Ask which mistake they think their own generation is making now.
5. Add your own rule when life teaches you one. A rulebook that stops growing stops being useful.

### The shape of the rules

| Group | What the rules protect | Chapters |
|---|---|---|
| What money is | Your understanding: see the promise behind the paper | 1, 2, 6, 20, L2.1, L2.2 |
| Seasons and rulers | Your savings: know what melts and what hardens | 8, 9, 12, 13 |
| Debt | Your freedom: never become a forced seller | 7, 17 |
| Power and plumbing | Your judgment: see who sets the rules and who earns the tolls | 3, 4, 5, 10, 11, 15, 16, 18 |
| Getting on the board | Your future: turn income into ownership | 14, 19 |

> **Picture this.** Think of the rulebook as a ship's logbook kept across generations. Each captain wrote down the storms they met, the rocks they hit and the stars that guided them home. The next captain cannot avoid every storm. But a captain who has read the log will recognize the sky before the storm arrives.

The full rulebook and the generational mistakes follow this chapter. They are written to be copied, shared and argued with. They are general education about how money works, not financial advice for any particular person. Where a rule touches your own situation, test it against your own numbers, and against a second opinion.

**Check yourself.** Q: Which rule from the whole guide would have saved the most people in 2008?
A: Several apply, but the strongest is: borrow only what you can service through a bad season without selling. Many households and banks were forced sellers when house prices fell.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why does each generation repeat money mistakes?
A: Because the last crisis fades from memory, calm years breed confidence, and each new boom tells a story about why this time is different. Writing lessons down and passing them on is the cheapest defense.


---

# Bonds: a ticket you can resell, and where it touches your life

Rulebook Level 2 (The machinery), chapter 01. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-bonds.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-bonds . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*A bond is a ticket you can resell: you pay RM100, it pays you RM4 a year, and you get RM100 back at the end. This chapter builds everything from that one ticket, then shows where bonds touch your own life, how to check your own exposure once a month, and how to weigh scary bond headlines before you feel them.*

**In short**
- A bond is a ticket: you pay RM100, get RM4 a year, and get your RM100 back at the end.
- You can keep it or resell it through a dealer. That resale market is the secondary market.
- Yields up, prices down. A single bond held to the end still pays back its RM100. A bond fund never ends, so its dips are real when you sell.
- Bonds touch you through EPF, loans, the ringgit, prices and taxes, even if you never buy one.
- Rising yields hurt people holding long bonds today and help people who will save for years, if yields stay above inflation.
- Once a month, check four dials and six questions, and weigh scary headlines on the SCALES.

**Built on Level 1: recall these before you start.** 
- [What money really is](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-01.md): Money is a promise that a whole society keeps track of. A bond is a promise with a date and a price.
- [How money is born today](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-06.md): Money comes in layers: cash and bank reserves, then bank deposits, then government bonds.
- [The yardstick problem](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-10.md): The ruler is rubber. Every yield you see is before inflation.
- [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md): A Malaysian saver measures with two rulers: what money buys at home and what it buys abroad.

**Map of this chapter: A bond is a ticket you can resell**
- The ticket: RM100 in, RM4 a year (see [What money really is](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-01.md))
- The seesaw: Yields up, prices down (see [The yardstick problem](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-10.md))
- The resale stall: The dealer's gap (see [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md))
- How you own bonds: EPF first (see [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md))
- Where bonds touch you: Loans, ringgit, taxes (see [Nation Inc.: taxes, interest and the hubs](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-nation.md))
- Risks and cushions: 2008 against 2022 (see [When markets fall: buckets, collateral and rotation](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-buckets.md))
- Your monthly gauge: Four dials, six questions (see [The seasons of money](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-08.md))
- The SCALES filter: Weigh a headline (see [Eye-openers: what most people never notice](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-13.md))

> **How to learn this chapter.** Read each part once, then close the page and answer the stop-box questions from memory. In a classic study, students who tested themselves three times remembered 61% a week later, against 40% for students who reread four times (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006). Guess before you open each curiosity question, then check the answer. Come back in three days and try the stop-box questions again. 'Learning styles' have no good evidence behind them, and highlighting and rereading help little (Pashler and others, 2008. Dunlosky and others, 2013).

Three short parts, each ending in a stop box. Stop at any box and come back another day.

### Part 1 of 3. The ticket, the seesaw and the resale stall

### 1. Should these four people worry?

Imagine tomorrow's headline: "Bond market crash". Meet four people. They are made up, but their situations are common.

- Aisyah, 23, Kuala Lumpur. First job. RM15,000 in EPF (Malaysia's compulsory retirement fund) and RM5,000 in a fixed deposit, her only cash. A fixed-rate car loan. Plans to study abroad in three years.
- The Rahmans, Penang. A RM400,000 floating home loan (its rate moves with Bank Negara's rate) over 35 years, taken in 2023. RM250,000 in EPF, three months of spending in cash, and RM20,000 in a bond and sukuk fund for school fees in five years.
- Encik Hamid, 60, Ipoh. Retired. RM150,000 in EPF and RM150,000 in fixed deposits that he lives on. No loans.
- Linda, 68, United States. Retired. $240,000 in a broad bond fund she draws on, $300,000 in shares and $60,000 in short US government bills.

Guess now: which of them should care? By the end you can answer for each of them, and for yourself.

### 2. A bond is a ticket

Forget finance for a moment. The government sells you a ticket for RM100. It pays you RM4 every year. In ten years the government buys it back for RM100.

*[Picture on the web page: One ticket carries the whole chapter: RM100 in, RM4 a year, RM100 back.]*

That ticket is a bond. You lent the government RM100, so it owes you, and RM4 a year is your reward for waiting. Two limits of the picture: a concert ticket is worthless after the show, but a bond ends with your RM100 back. And a bond fund holds many tickets and never ends.

**Five words to start with.** 
- **Bond:** A ticket that pays a fixed amount each year and your money back on a set date.
- **Face value:** The amount paid back at the end. RM100 in our ticket.
- **Coupon:** The fixed yearly payment. RM4 in our ticket, or 4%.
- **Maturity:** The end date, when the ticket is bought back.
- **Yield:** What a ticket earns per year if you buy at today's price and hold to the end. It is not the coupon: buy the RM4 ticket for RM92.28 and your yield is about 5%, not 4%.

> **Malaysia note.** About half of Malaysia's government debt is Islamic paper, mostly GII (Government Investment Issues, the government's sukuk, or Islamic bonds). Most GII is built on a deferred sale of a commodity to the government, so holders earn profit, not interest. The ticket picture still works.

### 3. The seesaw: why your ticket's price moves

A month later, new tickets pay RM5 a year: the going yield has risen from 4% to 5%. Nobody will pay RM100 for your RM4 ticket now. Its price drops until a buyer also gets a yield of about 5%.

1. Worked example. Your ticket pays RM4 and has 10 years left. New tickets yield 5%. A buyer pays about RM92.28. They get RM4 a year plus a RM7.72 gain at the end, a yield of about 5%.
2. Your turn, half done. New tickets yield 3% instead. Is your RM4 ticket worth more or less than RM100? (More, about RM108.53, because it pays more than new tickets.)
3. Your turn. A ticket with only 2 years left, when new tickets yield 5%. Does it fall more or less than the 10-year ticket? (Much less, about 1.9%, because only two years of too-small payments are left.)

*[Picture on the web page: Yields and prices sit on a seesaw. When yields rise, old tickets are worth less, and the other way round.]*

*[Interactive tool on the web page: Try it. Drag the yield on new bonds and watch three $1,000 bonds reprice.]*

Two rules fall out of the seesaw. Yields up, prices down. And the longer the ticket, the bigger the swing. A point means one percentage point, say from 4% to 5%. For a one-point rise, a 2-year ticket falls about 2% and a 30-year ticket about 15% (a model). A bond's duration tells you its swing: a fund with a duration of 6 falls about 6% per one-point rise. Fund factsheets print it.

- **Myth:** Government bonds are safe, so you cannot lose money on them.
- **Reality:** They are safe from default (the borrower failing to pay), not from price. In 2022 the main US bond index lost 13.01%, its worst year since the index began in 1976. Hold a single bond to the end and you get every ringgit back. Sell a fund's units after a dip and the loss is real.

### 4. The resale stall: the secondary market

There are two markets. The first sale is the government's auction, a ticket booth. In Malaysia, Bank Negara, the central bank, runs it and 20 principal dealers must bid. Every later sale is at a resale stall, the secondary market: one investor sells to another through a dealer. The government gets nothing from resales, but the resale yield tells it what yield it must offer at its next auction.

*[Picture on the web page: The booth sells new tickets. Old tickets change hands at the resale stall, and the dealer earns the gap.]*

1. To sell, you contact a dealer: a bank's trading desk or a broker.
2. The dealer shows two prices: it buys from you at RM99.50 and sells to buyers at RM99.60. The difference is the dealer's gap, its fee for standing ready. Ordinary buyers usually pay a wider gap than big investors, so ask for both prices.
3. The price shown is the clean price. The buyer also pays you the interest earned since the last payment.

The dealer's gap is what you pay to be able to sell quickly. It widens when everyone wants out. In March 2020 even US government bonds were hard to sell, and the Fed, the US central bank, bought $1.27 trillion in five weeks.

### Go deeper: Who trades, in numbers

| Market | Trading on an average day | When |
|---|---|---|
| US Treasuries | about $1.21 trillion (primary dealer trading) | January to July 2026 (SIFMA) |
| Malaysian government bonds | about RM6.2 billion, up from RM3.8 billion in 2024 | 2025 (Bank Negara) |

| Who | US Treasuries (end 2025, Fed) | Malaysian government securities, share of the whole market (end 2025, Bank Negara) |
|---|---|---|
| Dealers | 25 primary dealers who must bid at auctions | 20 principal dealers, 7 of them Islamic |
| Banks | 6.9% | about 34% |
| Pension funds | pensions and insurers about 6% | about 33% (EPF is the largest) |
| Insurers and takaful | inside the 6% above | about 6% |
| Funds | money funds 12.4%, mutual funds and ETFs 8.4% | asset managers about 3% |
| Foreigners | 32.5% | 21.5% |
| The central bank | the Fed 12.7% (market-value basis) | Bank Negara about 1% |

Malaysian shares of the whole market are computed by multiplying Bank Negara's shares of resident holdings by 78.5%. US shares are from the Federal Reserve's Financial Accounts.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: Who owns most of Malaysia's government bonds, foreigners or Malaysians?
  A: Malaysians. Residents held 78.5% at the end of 2025 and foreigners 21.5%. Pension funds such as EPF and the banks each hold about a third of the whole market (Bank Negara Bond Market Report 2025, worked out from its resident shares). (builds on [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md))
- Q: How much bigger is the US bond resale market than Malaysia's?
  A: US Treasuries trade about $1.21 trillion a day. Malaysian government bonds trade about RM6.2 billion, roughly US$1.5 billion. That makes the US market several hundred times busier. (builds on [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md))

> **Stop here.** Part 1 of 3 done. Close the page and try these three before Part 2.

**Check yourself.** Q: Your RM4 ticket has 10 years left and new tickets yield 3%. Is it worth more or less than RM100?
A: More, about RM108.53, because it pays more than the new tickets.

**Check yourself.** Q: Does the government get money when you resell your bond to someone else?
A: No. Only the first sale at the auction raises money. Resales move tickets and cash between investors.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why do dealers quote two prices?
A: They buy a little lower than they sell. The dealer's gap is their fee for standing ready to trade.

### Part 2 of 3. Where bonds touch your life

### 5. How you can own a bond

If you have EPF savings, you already own bonds. In Malaysia, EPF is the biggest route.

| Route in Malaysia | How much to start | Can you resell? |
|---|---|---|
| EPF (KWSP) | Automatic from your salary. 44.7% of EPF's RM1.41 trillion was in bonds and similar at the end of 2025, mostly government paper | No. You own a share of the fund |
| Bond and sukuk unit trusts | Depends on the fund | Yes, sell units back to the fund at the daily price |
| Bonds and sukuk on Bursa Malaysia, or seasoned bonds through banks | From about RM1,000 | Yes, but trading is often thin, so a quick sale may cost you |

Before buying anything sold as a bond or sukuk with a 'guaranteed' return, check the seller is licensed and not on the Securities Commission's Investor Alert List or Bank Negara's Financial Consumer Alert List.

### Go deeper: Other routes: one-off sukuk, big lots, the US, and US bonds from Malaysia

| Route in Malaysia | How much to start | Can you resell? |
|---|---|---|
| Retail government sukuk | Sukuk Prihatin in 2020 started at RM500 | No. It was a one-off and matured in 2022 |
| Government bonds bought directly | Standard lots were RM10 million (2021 report) | Out of reach for most people |
| US Treasuries through a broker that offers foreign bonds | Broker fees, plus the cost of changing ringgit to dollars | Yes. You also carry the risk that the ringgit moves |

| Route in the US | How much to start | Can you resell? |
|---|---|---|
| TreasuryDirect, buying from the government | $100, no fees | Not inside TreasuryDirect. Move it to a broker first |
| A broker | Varies by broker | Yes, any day at the dealer's buy price |
| Bond ETFs and funds | One share. Big index ETFs charge about 0.03% a year | Yes, any trading day. A fund never matures |

Bank Negara's foreign exchange rules, as summarised by banks: a resident with no ringgit borrowing at home may invest any amount abroad, and one with such borrowing may convert up to RM1 million a year for foreign assets. Check the current Bank Negara notice before relying on this.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: How do bond prices reach your EPF dividend?
  A: Slowly. EPF declares its dividend once a year: 6.15% for 2025. Its bonds returned 4.3% and gave about a third of its income, and its reported income includes paper gains and losses (EPF, as reported by Bernama, February 2026). Higher yields lift future income as old bonds mature and new money is invested. (builds on [Nation Inc.: taxes, interest and the hubs](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-nation.md))

### 6. Where bonds touch you

Rising yields in the news usually means the 10-year government bond yield. Here is what a rise does to a normal person.

*[Picture on the web page: Places bonds reach you. The colour says whether a rise in yields tends to help, hurt, do both or change little. The table below says the same in words.]*

| Where | How it works | If yields rise |
|---|---|---|
| Your EPF | Holds a giant drawer of government bonds for you | Prices dip on paper. New money earns more. Savers with decades ahead gain, if yields stay above inflation |
| Fixed deposits | Rates follow the OPR (Overnight Policy Rate), set by Bank Negara, now 2.75% | Help only if the OPR rises too |
| Home loan in Malaysia | Floating loans taken since August 2022 move only with the OPR. Older ones follow each bank's base rate | Mostly through the OPR: about RM60 a month per 0.25 point step on RM400,000 |
| Home loan in the US | 30-year fixed rates follow the 10-year yield | Hurt new buyers. Existing fixed loans are protected |
| The ringgit | Foreigners hold about a fifth of Malaysian government bonds | Can weaken, raising import prices. Not automatic: in 2026 it held near 4.08 ringgit per US dollar |
| Taxes and services | Interest on government debt competes with schools and hospitals | Hurt slowly. Malaysia's debt service is about 16% of revenue |

> **The one idea to keep.** The same rise in yields hurts people holding long bonds or borrowing now, and helps people who will save for years, as long as yields stay above inflation.

### Go deeper: Six more places bonds touch you

| Where | How it works | If yields rise |
|---|---|---|
| Your job | Companies borrow at the government yield plus a margin | Hurt slowly if high yields last: fewer projects, fewer jobs |
| Prices | A fixed RM4 buys less when prices rise | Rising inflation hurts holders of fixed payments |
| Bank deposits | Banks hold bonds as safe, sellable assets | Little change for you. PIDM insures RM250,000 per depositor per bank |
| Car loans and PTPTN | Hire purchase is mostly fixed when you sign. PTPTN charges a fixed fee | Little change for loans already signed |
| Insurance and takaful | Insurers hold bonds to pay future claims | Mixed: new policies price better, old bonds dip |
| Tabung Haji and Islamic funds | They hold sukuk such as GII | The same seesaw as conventional bonds |

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: When US yields jump, does the ringgit always fall?
  A: No. In 2022 the US 10-year rose from 1.52% to 3.88%, and the ringgit fell about 12% at its weakest, in November, and about 5% over the year. In 2026 the 10-year rose 1.12 points and the ringgit stayed between 3.89 and 4.15 (Fed data). (builds on [How the world gets its dollars](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-04.md))

### Go deeper: What makes yields move: seven forces, and 2026 as an example

Why would new tickets suddenly pay RM5 instead of RM4? Think of a tug of war. The central bank's own rate, expected inflation, how many tickets the government must sell, how many buyers turn up, how fast the economy grows, and how much people trust the borrower all pull on the price of a new ticket.

*[Picture on the web page: Seven forces pull on the yield of a new ticket.]*

| Force | What it means | Which way it pushes |
|---|---|---|
| 1. The Fed's rate path | Short yields track where the Fed sets overnight rates now and where markets expect it to go | Expected hikes push yields up, expected cuts pull them down |
| 2. Expected inflation | Lenders want compensation for prices rising while they wait | More expected inflation means higher yields |
| 3. Term premium | Extra pay for locking money up for years when the future is uncertain | More uncertainty about deficits, inflation or policy pushes long yields up |
| 4. Supply | How much the Treasury must borrow and in what lengths | Bigger deficits and more long bonds push yields up |
| 5. Demand | Who must or wants to buy: foreign central banks, banks, money funds, pensions, stablecoins | Captive or eager buyers pull yields down, a big seller pushes them up |
| 6. Growth | A strong economy competes for money, a weak one frees it up | Booms raise yields, recessions lower them |
| 7. Trust | Confidence in repayment and in the value of the currency repaid | Any doubt raises yields, a crisis elsewhere can lower them as money flees to safety |

*[Picture on the web page: Split the 10-year yield in two. The gold part pays you back for expected inflation. The blue part is the real reward for waiting.]*

You can see several forces at once in 2026. The Fed hiked in September (force 1). Oil prices kept inflation worries alive, and the bond market expected about 2.4% a year of inflation over ten years (force 2). A $1.99T deficit meant heavy issuance (force 4). Japan's recorded holdings of Treasuries fell $171B from February to August while it spent a similar sum defending the yen (force 5). Meanwhile French stress pushed some European money into Treasuries for safety (force 7 in reverse). The result: a 10-year yield of 5.13% on 21 October 2026, after a peak of 5.31% on 5 October.

### 7. Hidden risks, and what protects you

| Risk | How it reaches you | A real number | What reduces it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price risk | Your bond fund falls when yields rise | The main US bond index lost 13.01% in 2022 | Holding a single bond to the end. Shorter bonds |
| Inflation risk | Your fixed RM4 buys less | US bonds bought at 0.52% in 2020 paid far less than 2022's 9.1% inflation | Inflation-linked bonds. Short bonds that reset quickly |
| Forced-seller risk | You must sell at the worst moment | UK pension funds, September 2022: the Bank of England bought £19.3 billion of bonds to stop a spiral | Not borrowing to hold bonds. Emergency cash |

**Chart: Bonds against shares in two bad years (total return, %)**
| Item | US bonds (main index) | US shares (S&P 500) |
|---|---|---|
| 2008, a recession shock | 5.24 | -37.0 |
| 2022, an inflation shock | -13.01 | -18.1 |
In a recession, bonds cushioned the fall. In an inflation shock, both fell. Source: Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index and S&P 500 total returns, as reported in fund filings and index reports.

Why the difference? 2008 was a recession: people fled to safety, yields fell and bond prices rose. 2022 was an inflation shock: yields rose fast and bonds fell with shares. Higher yields today also mean more income tomorrow: in October 2026 a US inflation-linked bond paid about 2.6 points above inflation, against about minus 1 point at the end of 2021.

### Go deeper: Five more risks

| Risk | How it reaches you | A real number | What reduces it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Currency risk | A foreign bond pays in another currency | The ringgit moved between 3.89 and 4.15 per dollar in 2026 | Matching the currency you save in to the currency you will spend in |
| Default risk | The borrower cannot pay | Low for a government borrowing in its own currency. 98.8% of Malaysia's federal debt is borrowed in ringgit at home | Government over small companies. Spreading out |
| Liquidity risk | You cannot sell fast at a fair price | Bonds on Bursa often trade thinly | Funds that redeem daily. An emergency cash buffer |
| Reinvestment risk | When yields fall, money from a maturing bond earns less | The US 10-year was 4.98% in October 2023 and 4.01% in October 2025 | Longer bonds lock a yield in. This is the mirror of price risk |
| Concentration | One fund holds much of a nation's savings, and much of the nation's debt | EPF and the banks hold about two thirds of Malaysian government securities (end 2025) | A government that borrows in its own money, a central bank and deposit insurance. A system risk more than a personal one |

### What is left after inflation

Every yield you see is before inflation, Level 1's rubber ruler. Malaysian individuals generally pay no income tax on interest and profit from government bonds and approved sukuk, so the real return is roughly the yield minus inflation: about 3.95% minus 1.8%, or about 2.1 points (October 2026). In the US, take tax off first.

### Go deeper: The US real-return walk, with tax

On 21 October 2026 the US 10-year yielded 5.13% and the 10-year inflation-linked Treasury 2.76%, so about 2.4 points of the 5.13% was pay for expected inflation.

1. Start with the nominal yield: 5.13% on a 10-year Treasury in October 2026, or $51.30 a year on $1,000.
2. Take out tax. In a 24% federal bracket about $39 is left. Treasury interest is free of state income tax, but not of federal tax.
3. Take out inflation. If prices rise 2.4% a year, about what the bond market expects, $24 of that $39 only keeps up with prices. Your real gain is about 1.5% a year.
4. If inflation turns out higher than expected, the real return drops below zero, even though every payment arrives on time.

*[Interactive tool on the web page: Try it. Set the bond yield, your tax rate and inflation. The bottom bar is what you really earn in buying power. Push inflation up and watch it turn red.]*

### Go deeper: When the safe asset broke: 1979 to 2026, and how a bank failed holding safe bonds

A Treasury is safe from default in dollars. It is not safe from price. Every few years the market reminds people of the difference.

| Episode | 10-year yield, low to high | Price change if the whole jump hit a new 10-year bond at once (model) | What a holder gained or lost, coupons included (model) | What broke |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1979 to 1981, Volcker | 8.76% to 15.84% | -35% | about -14% (price -32%) | Inflation above 13%. The Fed let rates rise until it broke |
| 1994, the bond massacre | 5.19% to 8.05% | -19% | about -13% (price -18%) | A surprise Fed hiking cycle. Orange County went bankrupt |
| 2008, the crisis | 4.27% to 2.08% | +20% (a gain) | about +21% (a gain) | Everything else fell and Treasuries rose. The safe asset worked |
| March 2020, dash for cash | 0.54% to 1.18% in seven trading days | -6% | about -6% | Even Treasuries could not be sold easily. The Fed bought $1.27T |
| 2021 to 2023 | 1.35% to 4.98% | -28% | about -21% (price -24%) | Stocks and bonds fell together. UK pension funds needed the Bank of England in September 2022 |
| 2023, SVB |  |  |  | US banks carried $620B of unrealized bond losses (end 2022). One became a run |
| April 2025, tariff shock | rose sharply within days |  |  | Long yields rose while the dollar fell, a rare case of the safe asset and its currency falling together. Hedge funds unwinding the basis trade were widely blamed, though that is contested |
| 2026 | 3.97% to 5.31%, the highest close since 2002 | -10% | about -8% (price -10%) | A Fed hike, oil, heavy issuance. The 30-year hit 5.67% on 7 October |

Two models, both using the Fed's H.15 daily closes. The first column reprices a 10-year bond as if the whole jump in yields hit it at once. The second follows a real holder who bought a new 10-year at par at the low, still owned it at the high with fewer years left, and collected the coupons along the way (coupons not reinvested, computed for this chapter). Notice the one gain: in 2008 Treasuries did their job as everything else fell. Notice too that 2022 was different. Stocks and bonds fell together, which broke the old idea that one always rescues the other.

How can a bank fail holding bonds that never missed a payment? Walk through a bank shaped like Silicon Valley Bank.

| Step | The bank owns | The bank owes |
|---|---|---|
| 2021: deposits flood in | $100 of 10-year bonds bought at 1.5%, plus $8 of cash and loans | $100 of deposits, and $8 of owners' money |
| 2022: yields rise to 4.5% | The bonds are now worth about $78, plus the $8 | Still $100 of deposits. Marked to market, owners' money is -$14 |
| 2023: depositors leave | Bonds must be sold to pay them | Many deposits were above the $250,000 insurance limit, so they left fast. The hidden loss becomes real. Owners' money is gone |

Accounting rules let the loss stay hidden while the bank promised to hold the bonds to the end. A run forced a sale, and the paper loss became real in a day. The bonds were never in default. SVB's held-to-maturity losses were about $15.1B, close to all of its owners' money. Two days after SVB closed, the Fed opened the Bank Term Funding Program, which lent to banks against Treasuries at their face value, not their market value. A bond's price can fall, but in that panic its value as collateral was held at par by policy.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: How much could a risk-free 10-year Treasury lose?
  A: On price alone, about 32% for someone who bought a new 10-year at 8.76% in July 1979 and still held it in September 1981, when yields hit 15.84%. Counting the coupons collected, the loss was about 14%. From 2021 to 2023 a holder lost about 24% on price and about 21% with coupons (models, Fed H.15 data). Risk-free means free of default, not free of price swings. (builds on [Eye-openers: what most people never notice](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-13.md))
- Q: Someone bought a 10-year Treasury at 0.625% in 2020. What is it worth now, and did they lose money?
  A: About $84 per $100 at today's yields with four years left (model). They lose nothing in dollars if they hold to 2030, but they lose buying power: inflation peaked at 9.1% in 2022. (builds on [The yardstick problem](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-10.md))
- Q: A bank failed in 2023 holding bonds that never missed a payment. How?
  A: Its bonds had lost value as yields rose, about $15.1B at SVB, close to its owners' money, and US banks together carried $620B of such losses at the end of 2022 (FDIC). When depositors ran, the paper loss became real. (builds on [The musical chairs question](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-07.md))

### Go deeper: How governments quietly shrink debt with inflation

This is not theory. In the 1940s the Fed held long-term yields near 2.5% while inflation ran in double digits after the war, quietly shrinking the war debt in real terms. In the 1970s inflation often ran above bond yields. And anyone who bought a 10-year Treasury at its record low closing yield of 0.52% in August 2020 earned about half a percent a year, while US consumer inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022.

> This is the quietest way governments shrink debt. Keep the nominal yield below inflation for long enough and the real value of the debt melts, paid for by bondholders and savers who only look at the nominal number. Level 1's "The seasons of money" called it financial repression. The cure is the split in step 3: always separate a yield into the part that only keeps up with inflation and the part that is truly yours.

> **Stop here.** Part 2 of 3 done. Try these three before Part 3.

**Check yourself.** Q: Does a jump in the US 10-year directly change a Malaysian floating home loan taken since August 2022?
A: No. It moves only with the OPR. The 10-year matters only if it pushes Bank Negara to move the OPR.

**Check yourself.** Q: Name one way rising yields help a young saver, and the condition.
A: New money into EPF earns more for decades, if yields stay above inflation.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why did bonds protect people in 2008 but not in 2022?
A: 2008 was a recession shock, so yields fell and bond prices rose. 2022 was an inflation shock, so yields rose and bonds fell with shares.

### Part 3 of 3. Your gauge and your headline filter

### 8. Your monthly bond weather check

Ten minutes, once a month. It asks questions and never says buy or sell. Four public dials, then six questions about you.

| Dial | Where, free | October 2026 | Look closer if (rule of thumb) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. 10-year government bond yield | BIX Malaysia, US Treasury | Malaysia about 3.95%. US 4.96% (22 October), up 0.95 point in a year | It moved over 1 point in 12 months |
| 2. Inflation and the real yield | DOSM, US Treasury | Malaysia: 1.8% inflation, so about 2.1 points above it. US real yield about 2.6% | The real yield is below zero |
| 3. OPR and the Fed's rate | Bank Negara, the Fed | OPR 2.75% since July 2025. The Fed raised its rate in September 2026 | The OPR changed |
| 4. Ringgit per US dollar | Bank Negara | About 4.08. 2026 range 3.89 to 4.15 | It moved over 5% in 3 months |

### Go deeper: Three more dials for keen readers

| Dial | Where to look, free | October 2026 | Look closer if (a teaching rule of thumb) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5. Foreign share of Malaysian government bonds | Bank Negara monthly statistics | 21.5% (end 2025) | It fell more than 1 point in a quarter while the ringgit fell |
| 6. Auction demand | US auction results. Bank Negara auction results via BIX | US 10-year on 7 October 2026: bids 2.77 times the amount sold | Demand is at its weakest in a year |
| 7. Malaysia's interest bill | Ministry of Finance Fiscal Outlook | Debt service 15.8% of revenue (2026 projection). The 2023 fiscal law sets a 15% limit | It rises further above the limit |

**Self-check: Your personal gauge.** Answer for yourself. Nothing is stored or sent anywhere.
1. Do you have a floating-rate loan?
   - (0 points) No, or only fixed-rate loans
   - (1 points) Yes, and two small rate rises would be easy to pay: Two 0.25 point OPR steps add about RM120 a month on RM400,000 over 35 years.
   - (3 points) Yes, and two small rate rises would hurt: Watch dial 3, the OPR.
2. Do you hold bond funds, or bonds you may sell before they end? EPF does not count.
   - (0 points) No
   - (1 points) Yes, not needed for 10 years or more: Dips have time to recover.
   - (2 points) Yes, needed in 3 to 10 years
   - (3 points) Yes, needed within 2 years, or I draw on it now: Money you need soon should not ride on a long bond's price.
3. How big is that bond money, compared with all your savings, EPF included?
   - (0 points) None, or under a tenth
   - (2 points) A tenth to a third
   - (4 points) More than a third
4. What is its duration? The fund factsheet prints it.
   - (0 points) None, or under 3
   - (2 points) 3 or more, or I do not know: Duration 6 means about 6% down per one-point rise.
5. Will you spend money in another currency within 3 years?
   - (0 points) No
   - (1 points) Yes: study, travel or family abroad: Watch dial 4, the ringgit.
6. Could you be forced to sell at a bad moment?
   - (0 points) No: I keep 3 to 6 months of spending in cash or fixed deposits
   - (1 points) I have some cash, but not much
   - (2 points) I have no emergency cash: This is what turns a dip into a real loss.
- Score up to 3: Low exposure right now. A bond-market move is less likely to change your payments or savings this month. Watch inflation against what your savings earn, and the ringgit if you will spend abroad.
- Score up to 7: Some exposure. Watch the dials that match your answers: the OPR for a floating loan, the 10-year for bond funds, the ringgit for spending abroad.
- Score up to 99: High exposure. Bond headlines are about you. Read your loan and fund documents slowly, and get a second opinion before big decisions.
A teaching model, not advice. The points and bands are a rule of thumb, tested on the four people in this chapter.

| Question | Aisyah | The Rahmans | Hamid | Linda |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Floating loan | 0 | 1 (easy) | 0 | 0 |
| 2. Bond funds, and when | 0 | 2 (in 5 years) | 0 | 3 (draws now) |
| 3. Share of savings | 0 | 0 (about 7%) | 0 | 4 (40%) |
| 4. Duration | 0 | 2 | 0 | 2 (about 6) |
| 5. Another currency | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 6. Cash buffer | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Points and band | 2, Low | 5, Some | 0, Low | 9, High |
| Is a crash headline about them? | Mostly no | Partly | No, but his FD income follows the OPR | Yes |

Back to your guess. The headline is about Linda. The Rahmans feel it partly. Aisyah and Hamid are barely touched by bond prices. But if Hamid had put his RM150,000 into a bond fund he draws on, keeping a little cash, he would score 10, High. Run the gauge again next month.

### 9. Weigh the headline on the SCALES

Many bond headlines are written to grab attention. Before you feel one, weigh it. One short list is enough, and it spells SCALES.

| Letter | Ask | Example |
|---|---|---|
| S | Size: compared with what? | RM5.6 billion of foreign selling is 0.43% of RM1.309 trillion |
| C | Change or level: how much, over how long? | 'Yields soar' can mean 0.05 point in a day or 1 point in a year |
| A | Adjusted: before or after inflation? | Debt hits a record almost every year just from inflation |
| L | Long view: since when? | 'Highest since 2007' can still be lower than most years from 1977 to 2007 |
| E | Exposure: what does it do to me? | A US yield jump moves a US mortgage directly, a Malaysian floating loan mostly through the OPR |
| S | Source and stake: who says it, and what do they gain? | Clicks, a product, a political side, or an honest warning |

> **Real alarms leave tracks.** The filter is not there to make you cynical. Take a headline seriously when you also see forced sellers, a central bank emergency operation, the dealer's gap widening, weak auctions, or the currency and the bonds falling together. The UK in 2022 and Silicon Valley Bank in 2023 showed several at once.

| Real headline | On the SCALES | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Foreign investors disposed RM5.6 billion of Malaysian government bonds in July (Business Today, August 2026) | Size: 0.43% of the market. Long view: about RM11 billion came back into government bonds in August. Exposure: the ringgit was 4.09 at the start of July and 4.08 at the end | Accurate, missing scale. No alarm tracks |
| Bank of England intervenes to end bond market panic (September 2022) | Tracks: forced sellers, an emergency operation, and the 30-year yield up 0.67 point within a few hours on 27 September | A real alarm. The filter flags it rather than dismissing it |

### Go deeper: Two more headlines, from the US

| Real headline | On the SCALES | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 30-year Treasury yield rises to highest since 2007 (August 2026) | Long view: the 30-year was above that level in most years from 1977 to 2007. Exposure: real for US borrowers, as mortgage rates rose | Accurate, and it got worse: 5.67% on 7 October. But 'since 2007' made a return to old levels sound unheard of |
| China is dumping Treasuries (April 2025) | Change: the US 10-year rose 0.47 point in a week and a tariff pause followed within days. Source: Treasury's monthly data did not show large Chinese selling at the time | Half right. The alarm was real, the named cause was not proven |

**Check yourself.** Q: A headline says: "Bond yields soar to a 19-year high." Name three SCALES questions you would ask first.
A: For example: how much did they rise and over how long (Change), what were they in the decades before (Long view), and what does it do to my loans and savings (Exposure).

### 10. Go deeper: the government's side and the machinery

The boxes below are optional. They cover why governments borrow, how auctions and repo work, duration in detail, the yield curve and Malaysia's bond market.

### Go deeper: The government's side, in one page

Why do governments sell tickets? Much of each year's new borrowing repays old tickets that are ending. The rest covers the gap when spending is more than taxes. For a government that issues its own money, borrowing is also a rule it sets for itself: in the US the Fed may not buy new Treasuries straight from the government (Level 1, "How money is born today"), and safe bonds help a central bank steer interest rates. Banks, pension funds and central banks also need a safe ticket to hold. Each new ticket is sold at an auction where dealers must bid. The resale price then works like a vote that never stops: if buyers doubt a government's plans, yields rise and its interest bill grows.

That bill is already large. Malaysia's debt service is projected at RM57.3 billion in 2026, 15.8% of revenue, above the 15% limit Malaysia set itself in its 2023 fiscal law (Act 850). In the US, net interest passed $1 trillion in fiscal 2026, more than defense.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: How much of Malaysia's tax money goes on interest?
  A: Debt service is projected at about RM57.3 billion in 2026, about 15.8% of revenue, and near 16% in 2027 (Ministry of Finance). In the US, net interest of about $1.05 trillion in fiscal 2026 was more than defense. (builds on [The musical chairs question](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-07.md))

### Go deeper: Why the whole system rests on bonds (the backbone test)

*[Picture on the web page: Picture a champagne tower at a wedding. Government bonds are the bottom row of glasses. Every glass above rests on them.]*

- The Fed's money rests on them. The Fed creates bank reserves and cash, and the main asset it holds against them is Treasuries: $4.57T of its $6.47T of securities, about 71% (21 October 2026).
- They are the financial system's pawnshop ticket. In repo markets, banks and funds hand over Treasuries to borrow cash, often overnight. About $12.6T of US repo was outstanding on an average day in the third quarter of 2025 (Office of Financial Research).
- Banks and money funds park cash in them, because rules treat them as the safest liquid asset.
- Stablecoins must hold them. Under the GENIUS Act, compliant dollar tokens must be backed by cash-like reserves: deposits, central bank money, government money funds, repo, or Treasuries with 93 days or less left. Short bills are the dominant choice.
- Foreign central banks keep their savings in them. That is how the world holds dollars without holding cash.
- They set the base price of money. Mortgages, car loans and company loans are priced as the Treasury yield plus a margin for risk.

Level 2 does not take a title on trust. Here is a number on each job a Treasury does.

| Job | Measure | Size |
|---|---|---|
| Base under the Fed's money | Treasuries as a share of the Fed's securities | 71% ($4.57T of $6.47T, 21 Oct 2026) |
| The world's savings | Treasuries held by foreign governments, as a share of all world currency reserves | about 28% ($3.76T of $13.22T, mid 2026) |
| The pawnshop ticket | US repo outstanding on an average day, 69% backed by Treasuries | about $12.6T (Q3 2025) |
| Bank survival kit | Treasuries, agency bonds and cash at US banks | $7.88T, 30% of bank assets (Sep 2026) |
| Money funds | Total money fund assets, mostly government paper | $7.98T (Sep 2026) |
| New rails | Treasury bills held by the largest stablecoin issuer, Tether | about $115B (mid 2026, press) |
| Price of all other credit | Mortgages and company loans are priced as a Treasury yield plus a margin | every day |

The title passes, with one correction. Bonds are the backbone of the system's plumbing: collateral, reserves, liquidity and stablecoin backing. They are not what most bank deposits lean on. At US banks, loans are $14.1T of $25.9T of assets, Treasuries and agency bonds $4.8T. In normal years most new deposits are born from loans. In 2020 to 2021 most came from the Fed buying bonds and the government spending (Level 2, "Who really creates money"). Either way, the system settles, pledges and saves in Treasuries.

### Go deeper: How big the bond world is, and who owns America's IOUs

**Chart: The world's bonds and shares, end of 2025 (US Treasuries: 30 September 2026)**
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| All the world's bonds | 160.7 |
| All the world's listed shares | 157.8 |
| US bonds (38.1% of the world) | 61.2 |
| US Treasuries (marketable) | 31.8 |
Bonds and shares are market values at the end of 2025 (SIFMA). The Treasury bar is the face value of marketable Treasuries on 30 September 2026. The top two bars are close, so a big sell-off in either market can flip their order. Source: SIFMA Capital Markets Fact Book 2026, US Treasury Monthly Statement of the Public Debt (30 Sep 2026)

At the end of 2025 the world's bonds were worth slightly more than all its listed shares, $160.7T against $157.8T. Many people picture the stock market as the giant. The gap is small and flips with prices, but the point holds: the market for promises is as large as the market for ownership. About 38% of the world's bonds are American, and the Treasury market alone trades about $1.2T a day.

**Chart: Who owns America's IOUs: share of all Treasuries held, 1970 to 2025**
| Series | 1970 | 1980 | 1990 | 2000 | 2007 | 2014 | 2019 | 2021 | 2023 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Foreigners | 8.3 | 20.9 | 20.8 | 36.0 | 54.5 | 48.8 | 40.9 | 33.7 | 32.8 | 32.5 |
| The Fed | 15.2 | 12.4 | 5.8 | 11.7 | 11.8 | 21.7 | 14.0 | 25.0 | 17.3 | 12.7 |
| Banks | 30.6 | 20.6 | 9.7 | 7.1 | 2.8 | 4.0 | 5.2 | 7.2 | 6.3 | 6.9 |
| Money funds | 0.0 | 0.6 | 2.2 | 3.3 | 4.2 | 3.8 | 6.6 | 7.9 | 9.4 | 12.4 |
Foreigners rose from 8% to a peak of 54.5% in 2007 and fell back to 32.5%, while their dollar holdings kept rising. Banks fell from 31% to 7%. Money funds grew from almost nothing to about the Fed's share. Pensions and insurers held 21% in 1990 and 6% in 2025. The rest in 2025: mutual funds and ETFs 8.4%, states and cities 5.6%, and households and hedge funds about 9.5% (a residual, so treat it as rough). Source: Federal Reserve Financial Accounts (Z.1) table L.210, year-end, via DBnomics. Shares use market values, so the Fed's level differs from its weekly balance sheet.

> **Insider eye-opener.** Your cash in a money market fund is mostly lent to the government. Money funds held 0.6% of all Treasuries in 1980 and 12.4% in 2025, close to the Fed's 12.7% on this measure. The quiet giant of the bond market is ordinary savers' cash, pooled.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: Which is bigger, the world's stock market or its bond market?
  A: Bonds, just: $160.7T against $157.8T of listed shares at the end of 2025 (SIFMA). Many people guess stocks by a mile. A market value is a price tag, so the order can flip in a big sell-off. (builds on [When markets fall: buckets, collateral and rotation](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-buckets.md))
- Q: In 1970 US banks owned almost a third of all Treasuries. What do they own now?
  A: About 7% (2025). Banks moved from lending to the government to lending to households and firms, while foreigners and funds took over. (builds on [How money is born today](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-06.md))
- Q: Japan cut its US Treasuries by $171B in six months. Did foreigners flee US debt?
  A: No. Total foreign holdings were $9.33T in August 2026, near the record, and the UK ($1,010B) is now almost level with Japan ($1,068B) (Treasury TIC data). The foreign share fell because everyone else bought even more. (builds on [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md))
- Q: A private token company holds about $115B of Treasury bills. Where would that rank among countries?
  A: Around 20th, close to the UAE and Bermuda in the August 2026 TIC table. The figures are two months apart and Tether's is from press reports of its attestation, so treat the rank as rough. A stablecoin issuer now owns more Treasuries than most nations. (builds on [Crypto: Set 2 money, dissected](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-crypto.md))

### Go deeper: How a bond is born: one real US auction

1. Announcement. The Treasury offered $39.0B of a 10-year note with a 4.625% coupon, maturing 15 August 2036, for auction on 7 October 2026.
2. Bidding. Bids came in for $109.0B, 2.77 times the amount offered. The 25 primary dealers are required to bid for their share every time, so every auction is fully covered by design.
3. One price for all. Every winner pays the same yield, the highest one accepted: 5.300%, a price of $94.86 per $100. It was the highest yield at a 10-year auction since November 2000.
4. Who won. Indirect bidders (foreign and domestic investors bidding through dealers) took 79.6%. Direct bidders took 17.0%. The dealers kept only 2.5%, the smallest share in the data.
5. Settlement on 15 October. Buyers' banks pay, and the money goes up into the Treasury's account at the Fed. If the buyer was a fund or a person, their deposit is gone until the Treasury spends it (Level 2, "Who really creates money", Step 3).

What the Treasury sells changes what happens to your money. Bills, about 22% of tradable debt, are bought heavily by money market funds. From June 2022 to October 2026 those funds pulled $1.97T out of the cash they had parked at the Fed, much of it to buy bills, and that cash came back into bank deposits when the Treasury spent it. Notes and bonds bought by investors from their own bank deposits drain those deposits until the Treasury spends. Level 2, "Who really creates money", Steps 3 and 4, walks through both cases.

**Chart: Who wins the 10-year auction: share of the bonds sold, 2008 to 2026**
| Series | 2008 | 2009 | 2010 | 2011 | 2012 | 2013 | 2014 | 2015 | 2016 | 2017 | 2018 | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 | 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Primary dealers | 71.8 | 57.3 | 44.2 | 41.6 | 41.8 | 40.0 | 38.6 | 29.2 | 27.3 | 29.1 | 27.2 | 26.1 | 25.4 | 17.2 | 16.6 | 14.3 | 14.6 | 11.0 | 8.8 |
| Indirect bidders | 27.1 | 37.8 | 42.3 | 48.5 | 38.2 | 40.3 | 46.1 | 58.8 | 63.3 | 63.8 | 64.2 | 60.0 | 60.7 | 65.9 | 65.3 | 66.9 | 68.5 | 70.5 | 73.3 |
| Direct bidders | 1.1 | 4.9 | 13.5 | 9.9 | 20.0 | 19.8 | 15.3 | 12.0 | 9.4 | 7.2 | 8.6 | 13.9 | 14.0 | 16.9 | 18.0 | 18.7 | 16.9 | 18.5 | 17.9 |
The dealers' job has shifted from buyer to backstop. Indirect bidders, foreign and domestic investors bidding through dealers, now take most of each sale. 2026 is to date. Source: US Treasury auction results (fiscaldata), 10-year notes including reopenings.

**Check yourself.** Q: At the October 2026 auction the dealers, who must bid, kept only 2.5%. Is that a good or a bad sign for the Treasury?
A: Good in the short run. It means investors wanted the bonds at that price, so the backstop was barely needed. The cost was the price itself: the Treasury had to pay 5.30% to get that demand.

### Go deeper: Repo: how a bond is pawned overnight

Repo is a loan secured by a bond. You sell a bond for cash today and agree to buy it back tomorrow at a slightly higher price. The difference is the interest. The lender keeps a cushion called a haircut, for example lending $98 against $100 of bonds. Here a hedge fund buys a $100 Treasury and funds it in repo through a dealer, and a money market fund supplies the cash.

| Who | What they now own | What they now owe | What changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hedge fund | $100 Treasury (pledged) | $98 repo loan, plus $2 of its own money | It holds a $100 bond with only $2 of its own money. In practice this is usually one leg of a hedged trade (the cash-futures basis trade), not a bare bet |
| Dealer (a bank's arm) | $98 loan to the fund | $98 borrowed from the money fund | It is the middleman and nets the two |
| Money market fund | $98 repo loan, safe and overnight | nothing new | It swapped a bank deposit for a loan backed by a Treasury |
| The two floors | Reserves move between banks | Deposits move from the fund to the bond's seller | Public money only moved. Nothing was created |

The US repo market had about $12.6T of loans outstanding on an average day in the third quarter of 2025 (Office of Financial Research). That is why a Treasury is worth more than its coupons: it can be turned into cash overnight at a small haircut. It is also where the system breaks. When haircuts jump or dealers run out of room, funds must sell bonds, prices fall, haircuts rise again. That loop drove March 2020.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: Why is a Treasury worth more than the interest it pays?
  A: Because it is a pawnshop ticket. About $12.6T was outstanding in US repo on an average day in late 2025, mostly against Treasuries. Being able to turn a bond into cash overnight is worth something, so investors accept a slightly lower yield for it. (builds on [What money really is](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-01.md))
- Q: Why would the Fed buy more Treasuries in five weeks than it owned in total in 2007?
  A: In March and April 2020 even Treasuries froze as everyone sold to raise cash. The Fed bought $1.27T in five weeks, against total Treasury holdings of $0.75T at the end of 2007 (Fed H.4.1). (builds on [When markets fall: buckets, collateral and rotation](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-buckets.md))

### Go deeper: Duration and convexity: the bond's lever

Duration is the number that tells you how hard a bond swings. Roughly, a bond's price moves by its duration, in percent, for each one point move in yields, the other way. It is also about the average time until you get your money back, with near payments counting more than far ones. A 2-year Treasury has a duration near 2, a 10-year near 8, a 30-year near 15.

| Bond (yields of 21 October 2026) | Price per $100 | Duration (the lever) | If yields rise 1 point | If yields fall 1 point |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2-year, 4.75% coupon, yield 4.81% | $99.89 | 1.9 | -1.9% | +1.9% |
| 10-year, 4.625% coupon, yield 5.13% | $96.09 | 7.9 | -7.5% | +8.3% |
| 30-year, 5.00% coupon, yield 5.42% | $93.81 | 15.0 | -13.4% | +16.8% |

Look at the last two columns. For the same one point move, the gain when yields fall is bigger than the loss when they rise: +16.8% against -13.4% on the 30-year. That bend is called convexity. It is why long bonds are loved in a crash and feared in an inflation. Duration figures are a model computed for this chapter with half-yearly coupons. Coupons for the 2-year and 30-year are illustrative, the 10-year is the real note auctioned on 7 October 2026.
