### Go deeper: The yield curve, and the bond market as a voter

*[Picture on the web page: One move in the 10-year yield, four ripples.]*

Take a $400,000 mortgage over 30 years. At 6.40% the monthly payment is about $2,502. At 7.40%, one point higher, it is about $2,770. One point on the bond market costs that family about $267 a month, about $3,210 a year, for thirty years.

*[Picture on the web page: The yield curve: yields lined up from short to long. Normal curves slope up. An inverted curve, drawn here as an example, often warns of a slowdown.]*

Line up yields from short to long and you get the yield curve. Normally it slopes up, because waiting longer deserves more pay. In October 2026 it does: about 4.81% at 2 years, 5.13% at 10 years and 5.42% at 30 years. When short yields rise above long ones (an inverted curve), markets are betting the Fed will have to cut, usually because a slowdown is coming. Inversions have come before many US recessions, though the timing is loose. The longest inversion of the 2s and 10s on record, 541 trading days from April 2022 to September 2024, has not been followed by a recession so far, and by 22 October 2026 the curve sloped up again by 0.31 points.

> "I used to think if there was reincarnation, I wanted to come back as the president or the pope or as a .400 baseball hitter. But now I would want to come back as the bond market. You can intimidate everybody." (James Carville, adviser to President Clinton, 1993)

> The bond market is a voter that votes every second. When it dislikes a government's plans, yields rise and the government's own interest bill rises with them. US net interest reached $1,051.8B in FY2026, more than defense. That bill is the bond market's running verdict, and it is why Treasury secretaries watch auctions more closely than polls.

### Go deeper: Malaysia's government bonds in detail

| Malaysia's government bonds | Value | Date |
|---|---|---|
| All government bonds (conventional MGS plus Islamic GII) | RM1.31T | March 2026 |
| Share of government securities held by foreigners | 21.5% | end 2025 (Bank Negara) |
| 10-year MGS yield | 3.985%, against about 4.8% for the US 10-year | end August 2026 |
| Bank Negara's reserves | US$132.6B | end June 2026 |
| Main domestic holder | EPF, with 44.7% of its investment assets in fixed income, mostly government paper | end 2025 |

Here is a Level 2 surprise. At the end of August 2026 Malaysia could borrow for ten years at 3.985%, about 0.8 points cheaper than the United States. Lower inflation, a lower policy rate and a large captive saver in the EPF all help. It does not mean Malaysia is safer for a foreign investor, who also carries the risk that the ringgit falls. Nearly half of Malaysia's government debt (47.9%) is Islamic paper, mostly GII, a structure the US does not have.

The weak spot is the foreign fifth. When US yields jump, foreign money can leave ringgit bonds, the ringgit can weaken and Bank Negara may sell dollars to steady it. It is not automatic: in 2026 the ringgit held near 4.08 while US yields rose.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: Why can Malaysia borrow for ten years more cheaply than the United States?
  A: At the end of August 2026 the 10-year MGS yielded 3.985% against about 4.8% for the US 10-year. Lower inflation and a captive domestic saver (the EPF) help. The risk is the foreign fifth of holders, who leave when US yields jump. (builds on [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md))

### Go deeper: Two stories about bonds, both half true

| Story | When it is right | When it is wrong |
|---|---|---|
| Treasuries are safe | Safe from default in dollars. In 2008 they rose 20% while other assets fell | Not safe from price: a holder lost about 14% from 1979 to 1981 and about 21% from 2021 to 2023, coupons included (model). Not safe from inflation |
| China and Japan are dumping, the bond market is breaking | Japan's holdings fell $171B in six months and China's $109B in a year. The foreign share fell from 54.5% to 32.5% since 2007 | Total foreign holdings were $9.33T in August 2026, near the record. The UK added $108B in a year. The October 10-year auction was covered 2.77 times |
| Bonds are a bubble | Right for bonds bought near the August 2020 low of 0.52%, which paid far less than the inflation that followed | Wrong as a rule: on 21 October 2026 the 10-year inflation-linked Treasury yielded 2.76% above inflation, a real reward for waiting, not a bubble price |

### Go deeper: Where the ticket picture breaks

- A concert ticket is worthless after the show. A bond ticket ends with a RM100 buy-back.
- Resale ticket prices swing on hype. Bond prices swing mostly on yields and on trust in the borrower.
- A ticket buyer is a customer. A bond buyer is a lender: the borrower owes them.
- Most Malaysian government sukuk (GII) rest on a deferred sale of a commodity, so holders earn profit, not interest.
- Bond prices are less visible than app prices. Most trading is between dealers.
- A central bank can buy tickets with newly created money. No concert has a buyer like that.
- For a single bond held to the end, the resale price matters only if you sell. A fund never ends, so its price always matters when you sell units.

### Go deeper: Who pays whom when a bond is bought: four cases

| Case | What changes | Public money (deposits and cash) |
|---|---|---|
| A person buys a new bond at auction | Their deposit falls. Their bank's reserves move up into the government's account at the central bank | Falls until the government spends it, then comes back |
| A person buys from another person on the resale market | One deposit falls, another rises. The dealer earns the gap. The government is not involved | Only moves. Nothing created or destroyed |
| A fund such as EPF buys a bond from a bank | The fund's deposit falls and the bank's bond holding falls | Falls. A bank selling a security to a nonbank destroys a deposit, the mirror of a bank buying one |
| A foreign fund sells Malaysian bonds and takes its money home | A local buyer pays ringgit. The fund swaps the ringgit for dollars at a bank, or Bank Negara sells dollars from reserves | Resident deposits fall if a nonbank bought. The ringgit weakens, reserves fall, or yields rise until a local buyer steps in |

### Go deeper: Dates that would change this chapter

| When | What to watch | What it would change |
|---|---|---|
| November 2026 | Bank Negara moves the OPR from 2.75% | The Rahman numbers and FD rates |
| 31 December 2026 | Foreign share of Malaysian government bonds below 20% or above 23% | The 'about a fifth' line and the ringgit touch point |
| February to March 2027 | EPF's 2026 dividend and asset mix | The EPF lines. Fixed income below 40% of assets would change them |
| 31 March 2027 | US 10-year closes above 5.5% or below 4.5% | Dial 1 and the headline examples |
| 30 June 2027 | Ringgit above 4.40 or below 3.80 per dollar while the US 10-year stays above 5% | Whether 2026's calm ringgit was a one-off |
| 31 December 2027 | A new retail government sukuk or savings bond in Malaysia | The routes table |

### Go deeper: More practice, a Day 3 card and Malay words

**Check yourself.** Q: A fund's factsheet says duration 4. Yields rise 1 point. Roughly what happens to its price?
A: It falls about 4%.

**Check yourself.** Q: Hamid keeps his savings in fixed deposits. Which dial matters most to him?
A: The OPR, because FD rates follow it, and inflation against what his FDs pay.

**Check yourself.** Q: A headline says foreigners sold RM5 billion of Malaysian bonds. Which two SCALES questions come first?
A: Size (compared with about RM1.3 trillion of government bonds) and Exposure (did the ringgit or my loan actually move?).

**Check yourself.** Q: Why is 'a price dip only costs you if you sell' not true for a bond fund?
A: A fund never ends, so there is no date when you are sure to get your money back. Its price on the day you sell is what you get.

> **Day 3 card.** Come back in three days and answer without looking: what is a yield, which way does a bond's price move when yields rise, and which of the four people is a crash headline about?

| English | Bahasa Malaysia (common usage) |
|---|---|
| Bond | Bon |
| Islamic bond | Sukuk |
| EPF | KWSP (Kumpulan Wang Simpanan Pekerja) |
| Interest rate | Kadar faedah |
| Overnight Policy Rate | OPR (Kadar Dasar Semalaman) |
| Fixed deposit | Simpanan tetap |

### 11. Say it back

**Check yourself.** Q: New tickets yield 5%. Your RM4 ticket has 10 years left. Roughly what is it worth, and why?
A: About RM92.28, because a buyer can get RM5 a year on a new ticket, so yours must be cheaper to compete.

**Check yourself.** Q: What does the dealer's gap tell you in a crisis?
A: It widens when everyone wants out. A widening gap is one of the tracks a real alarm leaves.

**Check yourself.** Q: Which of the four people is a bond crash headline really about, and why?
A: Linda. A big share of her savings is in a long bond fund she draws on now, so she scores High. The Rahmans feel it partly. Aisyah and Hamid are barely touched.

**Check yourself.** Q: A Malaysian government bond yields 4% and inflation is 2.5%. You are a Malaysian individual. Roughly what is your real return?
A: About 1.5 points a year. Malaysian individuals generally pay no income tax on government bond interest, so take off only inflation. In the US you would take tax off first.

# Who really creates money: banks, the Fed and the Treasury

Rulebook Level 2 (The machinery), chapter 02. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-moneymake.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-moneymake . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Bank loans are one door, the busiest one in normal years. Level 2 adds the others: the Fed, the Treasury, the sponges that soak money up, the shredders that destroy it, the brakes on each printer, and how other countries do it.*

**In short**
- Money lives on two floors. Upstairs, banks and the Treasury hold accounts at the Federal Reserve. Downstairs, you and every business hold bank deposits. You can only spend the downstairs kind.
- In normal years banks create most new downstairs money when they lend (1971 to 2007, 87% to 96% of the two printers combined). They also create it when they buy a bond or anything else from someone who is not a bank. In 2008 to 2014 and 2020 to 2021 the Fed did most of it.
- The Fed creates upstairs money, called reserves, every time it buys a bond. Whether new downstairs money appears too depends on who sold the bond: a bank (no) or a pension fund or other nonbank (yes).
- The Treasury moves money between the floors. Selling bonds and collecting taxes pulls deposits up into its Fed account. Spending pushes them back down.
- So money is not created only by bank loans. In 2020 and 2021 the Treasury and the Fed together created most of the $4.7 trillion rise in bank deposits.
- The Fed is not allowed to buy new bonds straight from the Treasury. It must buy in the open market, through 25 primary dealers.
- In short: banks are the everyday printer. The government and the Fed together are the emergency printer, and when both switch it on, as in 2020, it is bigger than anything the banks do.
- From 1971 to 2026, bank loans grew about $13.79T and the Fed's bonds about $6.43T: two thirds downstairs, one third upstairs, with the upstairs third arriving in two bursts, 2008 to 2014 and 2020 to 2021.

**Five key words.** 
- **Reserves:** Banks' own accounts at the Fed. Upstairs money. About $2.97 trillion on 21 October 2026. Only banks and a few institutions can hold them.
- **Deposits:** The money in your bank account. Downstairs money, a promise from your bank. About $19.6 trillion at US commercial banks.
- **Treasury General Account:** The government's checking account at the Fed. About $945 billion on 21 October 2026. Money in it is out of public hands.
- **Primary dealer:** One of 25 big dealers that must bid at every Treasury auction and that trade directly with the Fed.
- **Open market:** The market where bonds already issued change hands. The only place the Fed may buy Treasuries.
- **Risk-weighted assets:** A bank's assets, each scaled by how risky the rules say it is. Capital rules ask for owners' money of at least a set share of this total.

Level 1's "How money is born today" showed that a bank loan creates a deposit. In normal years that is the most common way money is born, but not the only one. This chapter finishes the picture. It adds the Fed, the Treasury and the dealers in between, and shows exactly which moves create money you can spend and which only shuffle money that banks use among themselves.

**Built on Level 1: recall these before you start.** 
- [How money is born today](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-06.md): A bank loan creates a deposit and repaying it destroys one. There is no fixed money multiplier.
- [What money really is](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-01.md): Money is a ledger of who owes what, so always ask whose ledger a dollar sits on: the Fed's or a bank's.
- [Nation Inc.: taxes, interest and the hubs](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-nation.md): Taxes are the state's subscription fee. Here you see them leave the public's books.
- [The seasons of money](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-08.md): In wartime and after it, the Fed held interest rates down while inflation shrank the war debt (the 1941 to 1951 season of capped rates).
- [Bonds: a ticket you can resell, and where it touches your life](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-bonds.md): Treasuries are what the Fed buys, the Treasury sells and stablecoins hold. Read chapter 1 of this level first.

**Map of this chapter: Two floors, two printers, many drains**
- The everyday printer: Banks create deposits when they lend (see [How money is born today](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-06.md))
- The upstairs printer: Fed reserves reach you through nonbanks (see [Bonds: a ticket you can resell, and where it touches your life](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-bonds.md))
- The Treasury's staircase: Taxes up, spending down, deficits netted (see [Nation Inc.: taxes, interest and the hubs](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-nation.md))
- The sponges: Treasury account and reverse repo absorb (see [When markets fall: buckets, collateral and rotation](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-buckets.md))
- The shredders: Repayments, taxes, auctions, QT destroy (see [The musical chairs question](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-07.md))
- The brakes: Capital, mandate, law, inflation (see [How money is born today](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-06.md))
- Money outside banks: Money funds, repo, stablecoins, eurodollars (see [Crypto: Set 2 money, dissected](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-crypto.md))
- Other printers abroad: ECB, Bank of Japan, Bank Negara (see [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md))

This chapter comes in three parts of about ten minutes each. Each part ends with a stop box and three quick questions. Stop at any box and come back another day.

### Part 1 of 3. Two floors and three printers

### The whole idea in three rows

Here is the whole idea before any numbers. Steps 1 to 3 explain each row, and after Step 3 the full table puts sizes on every channel in four kinds of year.

| Who | Creates money you can spend when | Destroys it when |
|---|---|---|
| Banks | they lend, or buy anything from someone who is not a bank | loans are repaid, or they sell to someone who is not a bank |
| The Fed | it buys bonds. Reserves rise every time, your deposits only if the seller is not a bank | it shrinks its bonds (QT) |
| The Treasury | it spends | it collects taxes or sells bonds to savers, until it spends the money again |

### Two floors of money

Picture the dollar system as a building with two floors. Upstairs are the Fed's books. Banks hold reserves there, the Treasury holds its account there, and money funds can park cash there overnight. Downstairs are the public's books: deposits at banks, plus paper cash. When you pay rent or buy groceries, you move downstairs money. Banks settle with each other upstairs.

> **Picture this.** Think of a big market hall. Upstairs is the wholesale floor, where only licensed traders deal, and they settle in special tokens issued by the hall's owner, the Fed. Downstairs is the shop floor, where everyone shops with receipts issued by the traders, which are bank deposits. Some deals happen only upstairs, between traders and the owner. Some happen only downstairs. And some go through the staircase and change the amount of receipts on the shop floor. This chapter is a guide to the staircase.

*[Picture on the web page: Upstairs: reserves, the Treasury's account and cash parked at the Fed. Downstairs: deposits and cash held by the public. Arrows show which moves cross the staircase.]*

| Floor | What is there | Size, October 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Upstairs (the Fed's books) | Bank reserves | $2.97T (21 Oct 2026) |
| Upstairs | Treasury General Account | $945B |
| Upstairs | Cash parked by money funds at the Fed (overnight reverse repo) | $0.2B (it peaked at about $2.4T in late 2022) |
| Upstairs | What the Fed holds against all this: Treasuries and mortgage bonds | $4.57T and $1.90T |
| Both | Paper cash (a Fed liability that the public holds) | $2.49T |
| Downstairs | Bank deposits | $19.6T (September 2026) |
| Downstairs | M2, the broad measure of the public's money | $23.3T (August 2026) |

**Check yourself.** Q: Can a family spend bank reserves at a shop?
A: No. Reserves are accounts at the Fed that only banks and a few institutions hold. A family spends deposits or cash. Reserves only matter to the family when a move also changes deposits.

### Step 1. Banks create deposits, and not only by lending

When a bank lends you $100, it adds a $100 loan to its assets and a $100 deposit to its debts at the same moment. New downstairs money appears. When you repay, both disappear. That is Level 1 chapter 6. The second way is less known. When a bank buys a $100 bond from a pension fund, it pays by crediting the fund's account with a new $100 deposit. No loan was made, but money was created all the same. When a bank sells a bond to a nonbank, money is destroyed.

> "Whenever a bank makes a loan, it simultaneously creates a matching deposit in the borrower's bank account, thereby creating new money." (Bank of England, Money creation in the modern economy, 2014)

1. A bank lends $100 to a household: the household's deposit rises $100. New money.
2. The household repays: the deposit and the loan both shrink $100. Money destroyed.
3. A bank buys a $100 bond from a pension fund: the fund's deposit rises $100. New money without a loan.
4. Upstairs, nothing changed in total. Reserves only move between banks when the money is spent at another bank.

**Check yourself.** Q: Your bank buys a building from a developer for $1 million and pays into the developer's account at the same bank. Did the money supply change?
A: Yes, it rose by $1 million. The bank gained an asset (the building) and a new deposit liability (the developer's balance). Any purchase by a bank from a nonbank creates a deposit.

### Step 2. The Fed creates reserves when it buys, and the seller decides the rest

The Fed holds $4.57 trillion of Treasuries. It got them by buying in the open market from the 25 primary dealers, paying with reserves it creates on the spot, and by rolling over bonds as they mature. That is real money creation, but upstairs. Whether it reaches downstairs depends on who sold the bond in the end.

| Who sells the bond to the Fed | Upstairs (reserves) | Downstairs (deposits) |
|---|---|---|
| A bank | Up $100 | No change. The bank swapped a bond for reserves. |
| A pension fund, insurer, money fund or foreign investor | Up $100 | Up $100. The seller's bank gets reserves and credits the seller's deposit. |
| A dealer selling from its own stock | Up $100 | Up $100 at first. If the dealer uses the cash to repay a loan from a bank, the deposit disappears again. |

*[Picture on the web page: Two paths for the same $100 purchase. From a bank, only reserves rise. From a pension fund, reserves and deposits both rise.]*

> "When the Federal Reserve purchases securities from a nonbank seller, it creates new bank deposits." (Castro, Cavallo and Zarutskie, Federal Reserve FEDS Notes, 2022)

> The primary dealer in the middle is only the pipe. Many of the 25 primary dealers belong to big banking groups, and many act for customers. To know whether a Fed purchase added money you can spend, follow the cash to whoever holds it at the end. In 2020 to 2022 much of the selling came from nonbanks, which is why quantitative easing then added deposits as well as reserves.

**Check yourself.** Q: The Fed buys $1 billion of Treasuries, and the sellers turn out to be three banks. How much new money can the public spend?
A: None directly. Bank reserves rose $1 billion, which is upstairs money. Public deposits change only if the sellers are nonbanks, or later when banks spend or lend.

### Step 3. The Treasury moves money between the floors

The Treasury keeps its account at the Fed, upstairs. When a fund buys a new Treasury bond at auction, the fund's deposit falls, its bank's reserves fall, and the Treasury's account rises. Money has gone upstairs. When the Treasury pays a Social Security check, the reverse happens: the account falls, and the retiree's deposit and the bank's reserves rise. Taxes work like an auction: deposits go up the stairs. You can watch it happen. In the week to 21 October 2026, on weekly averages, the Treasury's account rose $69 billion and bank reserves fell $60 billion.

*[Picture on the web page: Auctions and taxes lift money into the Treasury's account at the Fed. Spending sends it back down. A deficit means more goes down than comes up.]*

So does a budget deficit create money? It depends on who buys the new bonds. In fiscal 2026 the deficit was $1.99 trillion.

| Who buys the new debt | Effect on the public's deposits |
|---|---|
| Households and funds, paying from their deposits | None overall. The deposits taken at auction come back when the Treasury spends. The buyers now hold a bond instead. |
| Banks | Deposits rise. Banks pay with reserves, the spending lands in someone's account. |
| The Fed, indirectly, buying later from nonbanks | Deposits and reserves both rise. This is the legal route to printing money for a deficit. |
| Money funds using cash parked at the Fed | Deposits rise. Cash that was upstairs comes down when the Treasury spends. |

**Check yourself.** Q: The Treasury runs a $100 deficit and a pension fund buys the whole $100 bond with its bank deposit. What happens to deposits?
A: Nothing overall. The fund's deposit fell $100 at the auction, and the Treasury's spending added $100 to someone else's deposit. The private sector holds $100 more in bonds, not more money.

### The whole map with sizes

| Channel | Adds (+) or drains (-) the public's deposits | Normal year 2019 | Emergency 2020 to 2021 | Shrinking 2022 to 2023 | Latest year |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bank loans, net of repayments | + when lending beats repayment | +$0.45T | +$0.68T | +$1.56T | +$1.00T |
| Banks buying (selling) securities from nonbanks | + buy, - sell | +$0.33T | +$1.86T | -$0.61T | +$0.14T |
| Fed buying (QE) or shrinking (QT) | Reserves always. Deposits only when the seller is a nonbank. Treasuries plus mortgage bonds | -$0.13T | +$4.52T | -$1.04T | +$0.16T (Sep 2025 to Sep 2026) |
| Treasury account at the Fed | - when it rises, + when it falls | fell $0.02T | fell $0.07T | rose $0.43T | rose $0.23T |
| Money funds' cash parked at the Fed (reverse repo) | drains reserves when it rises | flat | rose $1.64T | fell $0.82T | flat |
| Result: bank deposits |  | +$0.79T (+6.4%) | +$4.71T (+35.7%) | -$0.50T (-2.8%) | +$1.23T (+6.7%) |
| Result: M2 |  | +$0.96T | +$6.15T | -$0.72T | +$1.25T (Aug 2025 to Aug 2026) |

Windows run December to December, except the latest year (September 2025 to September 2026 for banks, the Fed and deposits, August to August for M2). Sources: Fed H.8 (banks), H.4.1 (the Fed), H.6 (M2), Treasury Monthly Statement (deficits). Memo, not a deposit flow: the federal deficit was $0.98T (2019), $5.90T (2020 to 2021), $3.07T (2022 to 2023) and $1.99T (fiscal 2026). Whether it added money depends on who bought the bonds (Step 3). The rows do not add exactly to the result, because some channels have no clean series: banks buying back their own shares, fees and interest, and foreign official purchases. In 2019 bank lending and bank bond buying explain the whole rise. In 2020 to 2021 the Fed's channel was 6.6 times bank lending. In 2022 to 2023 deposits fell even though banks lent $1.56T, because QT, bank bond sales and a rising Treasury account drained more.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: In 2020 and 2021 bank deposits rose $4.71T while bank loans rose only $0.68T. Who printed the rest?
  A: The emergency printer. The Fed bought $4.52T of bonds and banks bought $1.86T of securities while the Treasury ran $5.90T of deficits (Fed H.8 and H.4.1, Treasury statements). (builds on [How money is born today](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-06.md))

> **Stop here.** Part 1 of 3 done. You can now say which floor a dollar sits on and which of the three printers made it. Before Part 2, try these three.

**Check yourself.** Q: The Fed buys $100 of bonds from a pension fund. What rises upstairs, and what rises downstairs?
A: Upstairs, bank reserves rise $100. Downstairs, the fund's deposit rises $100. From a bank seller, only the reserves would rise.

**Check yourself.** Q: A household repays a $100 bank loan. What happens to the money supply?
A: It falls $100. The loan and the deposit both disappear.

**Check yourself.** Q: In 2020 to 2021 bank deposits rose $4.71T. How much came from new bank loans, and what did most of the rest?
A: Only $0.68T. Most of the rest came from the emergency printer: Treasury spending, with the Fed buying $4.52T of bonds and banks buying $1.86T of securities.

### Part 2 of 3. Sponges, shredders, brakes and other printers

### Step 4. Drains, sponges and new pipes

- The overnight reverse repo facility: money funds can lend cash to the Fed overnight. While it sits there, it is out of the banks. It peaked at about $2.4 trillion in late September 2022. On 21 October 2026 it held $0.2 billion, so this drain is empty.
- The Treasury General Account: every rise drains reserves and often deposits, every fall adds them back.
- The standing repo facility (since July 2021): a door that works the other way. Banks and dealers can swap Treasuries for new reserves at a set rate whenever they need them, which limits how far short-term rates can spike in a squeeze.
- Stablecoins: buying a dollar token moves your deposit to the issuer, who buys Treasury bills. Bank deposits do not grow, and if the bill comes from a bank or the Treasury, they shrink. The token is a new private dollar outside M2.
- Interest on reserves: the Fed pays banks interest by creating new reserves, about $115 billion a year at current rates (desk estimate). Deposits grow only if banks pass it on.
- Fed profits and losses: when the Fed earns more than it pays, it sends the profit to the Treasury. From late 2022 it paid more than it earned and built up a $245.9 billion IOU to itself by January 2026. That IOU is now shrinking ($232.7 billion), so it again earns slightly more than it pays, and payments to the Treasury restart once the IOU is cleared. The 'taxes go to the Fed's owners' story has it backwards.

**Check yourself.** Q: A money fund pulls $50 billion out of the Fed's reverse repo facility to buy new Treasury bills, and the Treasury spends the cash. What happens downstairs?
A: Deposits rise about $50 billion. The cash was upstairs at the Fed, it passed through the Treasury's account, and the spending landed in public accounts.

### The puzzle of the missing shrinkage

| Date | Fed's bonds | Reverse repo (money funds' cash at the Fed) | Treasury account | Bank reserves |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 26 Feb 2020 | $3.85T | $0.00T | $0.39T | $1.68T |
| 29 Dec 2021 | $8.27T | $1.64T | $0.28T | $4.04T |
| 1 Jun 2022, QT starts | $8.48T | $1.97T | $0.78T | $3.36T |
| 28 Sep 2022 |  | $2.37T, the peak |  |  |
| 31 Dec 2025 | $6.27T | $0.11T | $0.87T | $2.85T |
| 21 Oct 2026 | $6.47T | $0.0002T | $0.95T | $2.97T |

From June 2022 to October 2026 the Fed's bonds fell $2.01T, yet bank reserves fell only $0.39T. Where did the shrinkage go? Into the sponge. Money funds pulled $1.97T out of the Fed's reverse repo pool to buy Treasury bills, and the cash came back into the banks as the Treasury spent it. QT mostly emptied the sponge, not the banks. Now the sponge is dry, so any further drain hits bank reserves one for one. That is a large part of why the Fed stopped shrinking its Treasuries in December 2025 and has added $0.34T since.

### The shredders: six ways money is destroyed

1. Repaying a bank loan. The loan and the deposit both vanish.
2. Paying taxes. The deposit goes upstairs into the Treasury's account and comes back only when the Treasury spends.
3. Buying a new Treasury at auction with a deposit. The same as taxes, until the Treasury spends.
4. Fed QT. When a bond the Fed holds matures and the Treasury repays it with money raised from a nonbank, a deposit and reserves both disappear.
5. A bank selling a bond to a nonbank, or buying back its own shares or bonds. The buyer pays with a deposit, which the bank cancels.
6. Money moving into the Fed's reverse repo pool. It leaves the banks while it sits there. In 2020 to 2021 the pool rose $1.64T, more than twice the $0.68T of new bank loans in those two years.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: The Fed shrank its bonds by $2.01T from mid 2022, yet bank reserves fell only $0.39T. Where did the shrinkage go?
  A: Into an empty sponge: money funds drained $1.97T from the Fed's reverse repo pool to buy bills (Fed H.4.1). The sponge is now dry. (builds on [When markets fall: buckets, collateral and rotation](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-buckets.md))
- Q: When you pay your taxes, does the money still exist?
  A: It leaves the public's books and sits upstairs in the Treasury's account at the Fed, $945B on 21 October 2026, until it is spent again. (builds on [Nation Inc.: taxes, interest and the hubs](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-nation.md))
- Q: The Fed lost money for three years. Did anyone have to rescue it?
  A: No. It booked an IOU to itself, a deferred asset, which peaked at $245.9B in January 2026 and is now shrinking ($232.7B). It is earning slightly more than it pays again. (builds on [What money really is](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-01.md))

### Why the Fed cannot just buy from the Treasury

Section 14 of the Federal Reserve Act says US government bonds may be bought "only in the open market". Congress added that rule in 1935 so that the Treasury would have to face market buyers and could not finance itself at its own central bank. A wartime exception from 1942 allowed up to $5 billion of direct purchases. It was renewed several times, last in 1979, and lapsed in 1981. The Fed can still roll over bonds it already owns by taking new ones at auction, which gives the Treasury no new cash.

> A ban on direct buying is not a ban on financing. From 1942 to 1951 the Fed promised to keep bill rates at 0.375% and long bond yields under 2.5%, buying whatever the market sold at those prices. That financed the war debt cheaply without a single direct purchase. The Treasury-Fed Accord of 4 March 1951 ended the deal.

### The brakes on each printer

| Printer | Hard limit (law or rule) | Soft limit (price or demand) |
|---|---|---|
| Banks | Capital rules: owners' money of at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets plus buffers. Liquidity rules: enough safe assets for 30 days of stress. Reserve requirement: 0% since 26 March 2020 | Borrowers must want loans and pass checks. A loan must beat the bank's funding cost, which the Fed anchors by paying 3.90% on reserves |
| The Fed | May buy Treasuries only in the open market (Federal Reserve Act section 14, since 1935). Its mandate: maximum employment, stable prices, moderate long-term rates | Inflation. Buying bonds while inflation runs high fights its own mandate. The current chair calls QE a tool to use sparingly, if at all |
| The Treasury | Congress must approve spending. The debt limit caps total debt | Auctions must clear. The bond market sets the price, and net interest passed $1T in fiscal 2026 |
| Government plus Fed together | Both keys must turn: Congress spends, the Fed buys from nonbanks | Inflation and the bond market. 2020 to 2021 shows how fast it runs when both keys turn |

Notice the reserve requirement: zero since March 2020. The old textbook picture of banks lending out each deposit ten times over has no legal base in the US today. What stops banks is owners' capital, liquidity rules, the price of money and borrowers who must repay. What stops the emergency printer is a law that makes the Fed shop in the open market, a mandate that puts inflation first, and the bond market's price.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: US banks have had to hold zero reserves since March 2020. So what stops them lending forever?
  A: Capital rules (owners' money absorbs losses), liquidity rules, the 3.90% the Fed pays on reserves, which sets the cost of money, and borrowers who must want and repay loans. (builds on [How money is born today](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-06.md))
- Q: The Fed has been banned from buying bonds straight from the Treasury since 1935. How did it end up with more than half of the new debt of 2020 and 2021?
  A: It bought in the open market from dealers and investors, days or months after the auctions. In wartime, 1942 to 1951, it got the same result by capping yields. (builds on [The seasons of money](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-08.md))

### Money outside the banks

| Money-like claim | Size | Counted in M2? |
|---|---|---|
| Money market fund shares | $7.98T (Sep 2026) | Retail funds yes, institutional funds no |
| Repo, cash lent against bonds | about $12.6T outstanding on an average day (Q3 2025) | No |
| Stablecoins | about $308B (Aug 2026) | No |
| Dollars borrowed outside the US by non-US firms and governments (eurodollars) | $14T, 55% as bonds (Sep 2025) | No |

Who prints the $14 trillion of dollars borrowed outside America? Bond investors hold over half of it (55% at the end of September 2025, BIS). The rest is loans written by banks abroad, in London, Singapore or Kuala Lumpur, which create dollar loans and deposits on their own books exactly as a US bank does. They settle through accounts at US banks, and in a crisis they need dollars from the Fed's swap lines. So the Fed is the last-resort supplier, while private foreign banks and bond markets are the everyday sources of offshore dollars.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: Money market funds hold $7.98T, about 40% as much as all US bank deposits. Is that money?
  A: Partly. Retail funds are counted in M2, institutional funds are not, and both are mostly lent to the government. They work like money for their owners, but they rest on Treasuries and on bank deposits. (builds on [What money really is](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-01.md))
- Q: Who prints the dollars borrowed outside America?
  A: Mostly banks and bond markets abroad, about $14T at the end of September 2025 (BIS). The Fed steps in only in a crisis, through swap lines with other central banks. (builds on [How the world gets its dollars](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-04.md))

### Other printers abroad

|  | Fed (US) | ECB (euro area) | Bank of Japan | Bank Negara Malaysia |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reserve requirement | 0% since 2020 | 1% since 2012, paid 0% since September 2023 | Small ratios still apply | 1% since May 2025 |
| Ban on financing the state | Open market only | EU Treaty Article 123 bans direct purchase of government debt | Barred from underwriting new bonds without the Diet's approval | Central bank credit to the government is limited by law |
| Extra door |  | Large loans to banks (mostly repaid now) | Yield curve control 2016 to 2024, and about 47% of government bonds, excluding bills (June 2026) | The currency door: buying dollars creates ringgit, selling dollars destroys it |

The two-floor picture works everywhere, but the doors differ. In Malaysia a large share of changes in central bank money comes through the currency door: when Bank Negara buys dollars to steady the ringgit, it pays with new ringgit reserves, then usually soaks them back up. In Japan the central bank owns so much of the bond market that who sold a bond matters less than how much the Bank of Japan chose to buy.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: When Bank Negara buys dollars to steady the ringgit, does it create ringgit?
  A: Yes, at first: it pays with new ringgit reserves. It then usually soaks them back up in its money market operations, so the ringgit money stock need not change. (builds on [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md))
- Q: The Bank of Japan owns about half of its government's bonds. Who is the printer in Japan?
  A: The central bank, on a scale no other big economy matches. It held about 47% of government bonds, excluding bills, in June 2026, after its share first fell below 50% at the end of 2025, for the first time since 2022 (Ministry of Finance). (builds on [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md))

> **Stop here.** Part 2 of 3 done. You now know the sponges that soak money up, the shredders that destroy it, the brakes on each printer and how other countries do it. Before Part 3, try these three.

**Check yourself.** Q: From June 2022 the Fed's bonds fell $2.01T, yet bank reserves fell only $0.39T. Where did the difference come from?
A: The reverse repo sponge. Money funds took $1.97T out of it to buy bills, and the cash came back to banks as the Treasury spent it.

**Check yourself.** Q: US banks have had no reserve requirement since March 2020. Name two things that still stop them lending without limit.
A: Any two of: capital rules, liquidity rules, the 3.90% the Fed pays on reserves, and borrowers who must want and repay loans.

**Check yourself.** Q: When Bank Negara buys dollars to steady the ringgit, what does it pay with?
A: New ringgit reserves, which it usually soaks back up afterwards.

### Part 3 of 3. Who printed, year by year, and what the critics say

### What the critics add

| School | Its strongest point | What it adds to this chapter |
|---|---|---|
| MMT and post-Keynesian | Treat the Fed and the Treasury as one. The state spends first, taxes and bond sales drain afterwards. The limit is inflation, not money | Deficit spending is the only source of net financial assets for the non-government sector as a whole, which means the domestic private sector plus foreigners (Stephanie Kelton, The Deficit Myth, 2020). A country's private sector can also gain them from a trade surplus. |
| Austrian and hard money | New money enters unevenly. The first receivers, banks and asset owners, gain before prices rise. Credit without savings breeds booms that end in busts | Ask who receives new money first, not only which floor it lands on (Murray Rothbard, The Case Against the Fed, 1994) |
| Monetarist | The quantity of money matters for inflation, with a lag of one to two years | M2 rose about 40% in 2020 to 2021 and inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022. Then M2 fell in 2022 and 2023 (Tim Congdon, 2025) |
| Official view (Fed, Bank of England) | Central banks set the price of money. Banks and borrowers choose the quantity | QE works mainly through bond yields and portfolios, not only through the deposit count |

We found no school whose strongest objection points to a channel missing from this chapter. Each points to a missing consequence. The Austrian asks who got the money first. The monetarist asks what it did to prices. The MMT economist asks why we pretend the Treasury needs to borrow its own currency. A complete Level 2 reader can hold all three questions at once.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: M2 fell in 2022 and 2023, the first full-year falls since the record starts in 1959. Why was there no deflation?
  A: Prices respond with a lag, and the stock of money was still about 35% to 40% above early 2020. Inflation slowed but stayed positive. (builds on [The deflation debate: would anyone spend a money that grows?](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-defl.md))
- Q: Is today's two-printer system the old empire habit of debasing money, or a safeguard against it?
  A: Both readings have evidence. M2 grew about 37 times since 1970 (Fed H.6). But the open market rule, the 1951 Accord and the 2022 to 2023 contraction show a brake that empires lacked. (builds on [Why empires and their currencies fall](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-09.md))

### Putting sizes on it

*[Picture on the web page: Every channel that creates or destroys the public's deposits, with rough sizes for the latest year and for 2020 to 2021.]*

In an ordinary year, bank lending is the biggest engine. In the pandemic it was the government and the central bank: the Treasury spent borrowed money straight into household accounts, and the Fed and banks ended up holding about 68% to 72% of the new bonds, so nothing drained the deposits back. M2 rose about 40% in two years, from $15.5 trillion in February 2020 to $21.7 trillion in February 2022.

- **Myth:** All money is created by banks making loans.
- **Reality:** Loans are the main channel in normal years (87% to 96% of the two printers from 1971 to 2007), but banks also create money when they buy securities, the Fed creates reserves whenever it buys and deposits when the seller is a nonbank, and Treasury spending adds deposits unless the public funded it from its own accounts. In 2020 to 2021 the Treasury and Fed channel created most new deposits.

- **Myth:** The Fed prints money and hands it to the government.
- **Reality:** The Fed may not lend to the Treasury or buy at auction. It buys bonds from dealers in the open market and pays the sellers. That holds down yields and can turn bonds held by the public into deposits, which finances deficits indirectly. Its profits go back to the Treasury, and since 2022 it has been running losses.

### So who is printing? The everyday printer and the emergency printer

Put all of this together. In a normal year, banks are the main printer: new spendable money appears mostly because people and firms borrow. In the year to September 2026, bank loans grew by about $1.0 trillion and deposits by about $1.2 trillion. But the government and the Fed together can do the same job, and in some years they do it far more than the banks. That combination is printing money in everything but name.

*[Picture on the web page: Two ways new spendable money is made. The banks run every day. The government and the Fed switch on in emergencies, and then they are bigger.]*

1. The government spends more than it collects in taxes. When it pays a salary, a pension or a stimulus check, a new deposit lands in someone's bank account. Spending is what actually puts the money in public hands.
2. To cover the gap, the Treasury sells bonds.
3. Whether new money is left over depends on who ends up holding those bonds. If households and funds buy them with savings they already had, money only moves around and nothing new is left. If banks buy them, or the Fed buys them in the market from dealers and pension funds, the public keeps the new deposits and the bonds sit with the banks or the Fed. New money remains.

| Who ends up holding the new bonds | Is new spendable money left over? |
|---|---|
| Households and funds, paying with savings they already had | No. Money moves to the government and comes back |
| Banks | Yes. The public has the deposit, the bank has the bond |
| The Fed, buying from dealers and pension funds in the market | Yes. The Fed has paid for it with new reserves it created |

> **Picture this.** Think of two printers in an office. The banks' printer runs all day, printing a little each time someone signs a loan, and it shreds the pages again as loans are paid back. The government and the Fed share a second printer kept in a locked room. It needs two keys: Congress must approve the spending, and the Fed must choose to buy the bonds. When both keys turn, as in 2020, it prints faster than anything the banks can do.

The clearest case is 2020 to 2021. Bank deposits jumped $4.7 trillion, about 36% (December 2019 to December 2021). Most of it came from government spending on stimulus checks, business support loans and unemployment benefits, while the Fed ended up with about 56% to 59% of the new marketable Treasury debt, depending on the source. Bank loans rose only $0.68 trillion, a seventh of the deposit rise.

### Then why do people say the government cannot just print?

- The Fed decides, not the Treasury. The law lets the Fed buy only in the open market, for its own reasons such as interest rates or market stability, and it can stop or reverse. Since 2022 it has been shrinking its bond holdings, which pulls money back out.
- The bond market votes. If investors think a government is leaning on the printer, they demand higher interest rates. That is part of why the US 10-year yield is near 5% and the interest bill passed $1 trillion a year.
- There is friction. Congress must approve the spending, the debt ceiling has to be dealt with, and every auction has to find buyers.

> The two kinds of money behave differently over time. Bank-loan money is temporary: when the loan is repaid, the money disappears. Deficit money can stay, because the government rarely pays its debt down overall and rolls the bonds over. So the old worry that governments finance themselves by creating money is right when banks or the Fed end up holding the bonds, as in 2020 to 2021 (about 68% to 72% of the new debt). It is wrong when savers buy the bonds with money they already had.

**Check yourself.** Q: In 2020 bank deposits rose by trillions while bank lending barely grew. Which printer was running, and what two things had to happen?
A: The emergency printer. The government had to spend far more than it taxed, and the Fed and banks had to end up holding much of the new debt. Together that left trillions of new deposits in public hands.

### Fifty-five years of money creation: downstairs banks versus the upstairs printer, 1971 to 2026

Since the dollar left gold in 1971, how much new money came from banks lending, and how much from the Fed buying bonds upstairs? The chart below puts the two printers side by side for every year, using the Federal Reserve's own data. The gold bars are the yearly change in commercial bank loans. The blue bars are the yearly change in the bonds the Fed holds (Treasuries plus mortgage bonds). The dots are the actual change in the money supply (M2).

*[Picture on the web page: Yearly change in commercial bank loans (gold) and in the Fed's bond holdings (blue), with the change in M2 (dots), 1971 to 2026. Bars below the line mean that printer was shrinking. 2026 runs to September for loans, 21 October for the Fed and August for M2.]*

| Era | New bank loans (downstairs) | Fed bond buying (upstairs) | Upstairs share of the two | Change in M2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1971 to 1979 | $548B | $43B | 7% | $847B |
| 1980 to 1989 | $1.11T | $50B | 4% | $1.68T |
| 1990 to 1999 | $1.39T | $173B | 11% | $1.49T |
| 2000 to 2007 | $3.11T | $453B | 13% | $2.84T |
| 2008 to 2014 | $1.14T | $3.44T | 75% | $4.24T |
| 2015 to 2019 | $2.43T | minus $449B | none (the Fed was shrinking) | $3.63T |
| 2020 to 2021 | $681B | $4.52T | 87% | $6.15T |
| 2022 to 2025 | $2.60T | minus $2.00T | none (the Fed was shrinking) | $853B |
| 2026 to date | $784B | $201B | 20% | $988B |
| 1971 to 2026 | $13.79T | $6.43T | 32% | $22.72T |

- 1971 to 2007: the banks did almost all of it. In every decade the Fed's share of the two printers was only 4% to 13%. Its bond buying in those years was about the size of the paper cash people came to hold: the Fed's bonds rose about $0.72T from 1971 to 2007, and currency in circulation was about $0.83T at the end of 2007.
- 2008 to 2014: the first emergency. Bank loans actually fell by $481 billion in 2009, while the Fed bought bonds worth $3.44T over the period. Upstairs took about 75% of the work.
- 2015 to 2019: the banks took over again, adding $2.43T of loans while the Fed shrank its holdings by about $449B.
- 2020 to 2021: the biggest switch-on ever. The Fed bought $4.52T of bonds against $681B of new bank loans, about 87% upstairs. M2 jumped $6.15T in two years, the fastest rise in the record.
- 2022 to 2025: the printer ran backwards. The Fed shrank its bonds by about $2.00T while banks lent $2.60T. M2 rose only $853B over four years, and fell in 2022 and 2023, the first full-year falls in the official M2 record, which starts in 1959.
- 2026 so far: both printers are adding again, banks about $784B and the Fed about $201B.
- The whole period: banks added about $13.79T of loans and the Fed about $6.43T of bonds. Roughly two thirds downstairs and one third upstairs, but the upstairs third came in two short bursts. M2 grew from about $0.63 trillion at the end of 1970 to about $23.3 trillion in August 2026, roughly 37 times.

> How to read the bars fairly. They are the two main engines, not a complete accounting, so they do not add up exactly to the change in M2. Banks also create deposits by buying Treasuries themselves (about $1.9 trillion over the period), the Treasury's cash balance at the Fed swings up and down, and people move money in and out of cash. The blue bar is also the upper limit of upstairs money reaching the public, because Fed buying adds spendable deposits only when the seller is not a bank. Bank loans here are commercial banks only.

**Check yourself.** Q: Looking at the chart, in which two periods did the upstairs printer do most of the work, and what happened to the money supply right after the second one?
A: 2008 to 2014 and 2020 to 2021. After 2021 the Fed shrank its bonds by about $2 trillion, and M2 fell in 2022 and 2023 for the first time in the official record.


---

# The world's balance sheet: what it owns, what it owes, and how countries are built

Rulebook Level 2 (The machinery), chapter 03. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-worldbs.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-worldbs . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*You may have heard that the world owes $300 trillion, or $500 trillion, or more. Each can be true, depending on what you count, and the world owes all of it to itself. This chapter shows what the world really owns, why its debts cancel but still matter, how the numbers grew, and how each big country is built.*

**In short**
- Which debt? On the usual meaning, loans and bonds, the world owes about $348T (end 2025) to over $365T (mid 2026, IIF, via press). Its net wealth is about $518T (UBS, households) to $600T (McKinsey, all sectors, via press). Count everything owed on paper, deposits and other claims included, and the debt side is about $1,200T (computed from McKinsey).
- You cannot subtract one from the other. Every debt is somebody's asset, so at world level the debts cancel. What is left is real things, about two thirds of them real estate (McKinsey's 2021 study, Level 1).
- The debts cancel for the world, not for each family. Who owes whom, in which currency, and how soon decides the danger.
- In 2025 about four fifths of the rise in household wealth was higher prices and inflation, and about a fifth was new investment (McKinsey, via press).
- Debt grew from about 1 year of world output in 1971 (a model estimate) to about 2.5 years (3 counting the financial sector's own debts). It jumps in crises, 2008 and 2020. After 2020 the debt ratio fell while dollar debt kept rising, except in 2022, when a strong dollar shrank it.
- The dollar is the ruler. Japan's debt fell by a third in dollars from 2020 to 2025 while it rose in yen. Nobody repaid anything.
- Countries are built differently. The US is the richest country and the largest net debtor to the world. Japan's state owes mostly its own central bank and savers (foreigners about 13%). Italian families owe little (36% of output) while their state owes 137%. China borrowed to grow and saved at home.

**Built on Levels 1 and 2: recall these before you start.** 
- [The titled world: why abundance runs on credit, and who keeps the balance](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-titled.md): Most wealth is a price, not a pile, and every financial asset is someone's debt.
- [The musical chairs question](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-07.md): Debt is a claim on future income, and the musical chairs stop when everyone wants cash at once.
- [The yardstick problem](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-10.md): The ruler stretches. Always ask what a number is measured in.
- [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md): Money flows to the deepest market, which is why the world holds dollar assets.
- [Who really creates money: banks, the Fed and the Treasury](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-moneymake.md): Every new loan creates a deposit, so new debt always arrives with a new asset attached.

**Map of this chapter: Every debt is someone's asset. So what is the world worth?**
- Many counters, one ladder: Net wealth, loans and bonds, every claim (see [The yardstick problem](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-10.md))
- The great cancellation: Every IOU has two equal sides (see [The musical chairs question](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-07.md))
- Price, not pile: In 2025 about four fifths of the gain was price (see [The titled world: why abundance runs on credit, and who keeps the balance](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-titled.md))
- The ruler moves: Dollar swings resize the whole world (see [The yardstick problem](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-10.md))
- Two crisis jumps: 2008 and 2020 lifted every ratio (see [The seasons of money](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-08.md))
- Countries built differently: Debtor, creditor, saver, borrower, hub (see [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md))
- Who holds the paper: Central banks, foreigners, or the family (see [Bonds: a ticket you can resell, and where it touches your life](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-bonds.md))
- Brain-sized numbers: Village, household, per person, per dollar (see [Eye-openers: what most people never notice](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-13.md))

This chapter comes in three parts of about ten minutes each. Each part ends with a stop box and three quick questions. Stop at any box and come back another day.

### Part 1 of 3. What the world owns and owes

### The question that started this chapter

> "If the world wealth is 300T+ and 500T+ world debt, now show others a brief timeline of how others, maybe the G7 or G10, are different in structure, so users can understand and quantify the numbers around the world." (The owner of this guide, October 2026 (lightly edited))

It is a sharp question, and the honest answer starts with a question back: which debt? Both numbers can be true, depending on what you count. Count loans and bonds, the usual meaning of debt, and the world owes about $348 trillion to $365 trillion, while its net wealth is about $518 trillion to $600 trillion. On that count the order in the question flips. Count everything owed on paper by every part of the world, bank deposits and other claims included, and the total is about $1,200 trillion, far above $500 trillion. So "300T+" is right as a floor for wealth, and "500T+" is too high for loans and bonds and too low for everything owed. One thing holds on every count: none of these debts can be subtracted from wealth, because the world owes all of them to itself. The words below come first, then the numbers.

**Seven words to pin down first.** 
- **Net wealth:** What you own minus what you owe. A $500k house, $100k of savings and a $300k mortgage make $300k.
- **National net worth:** The net wealth of a whole country or the world, all sectors together.
- **Financial asset:** A claim on someone else: a deposit, a bond, a loan, a share. One side's asset is the other side's debt.
- **Gross debt:** Every IOU counted once, from the borrower's side, with nothing subtracted.
- **Nonfinancial debt:** Debt of governments, firms and households only. The financial sector's own borrowing is left out, so the same lending is not counted twice: a bank borrows in order to lend to the other three.
- **Yardstick:** World totals are in dollars. When the dollar moves 10%, non-US numbers move about 10% with nothing real changing.
- **Net foreign position:** What a country owns abroad minus what it owes abroad, shares and firms included. It is not the same as foreign debt.

**Chart: One world, many counters: what the world owns and owes ($ trillions)**
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Everything on every balance sheet, gross (McKinsey, 2025) | 1800 |
| All IOUs on paper, every sector (computed, 2025) | 1200 |
| National net worth (McKinsey, 2025) | 600 |
| Household net wealth (UBS, end 2025) | 517.7 |
| Financial assets of financial firms (FSB, end 2024) | 503.7 |
| Debt, loans and bonds, four sectors (IIF, mid 2026) | 365 |
| Debt, loans and bonds, four sectors (IIF, end 2025) | 348.3 |
| Debt without the financial sector (BIS, end 2025) | 262.7 |
| Debt without the financial sector (IMF, 2024) | 251 |
Blue bars count what is owned, orange bars what is owed. On the usual debt measures, loans and bonds ($251T to $365T), net wealth is bigger than debt. On the widest count of everything owed on paper (about $1,200T), the order flips. Neither comparison tells you how rich the world is, because every one of these claims is owed by the world to itself. Source: UBS Global Wealth Report 2026, McKinsey Global Institute global balance sheet 2026 (via press), Fortune on McKinsey (27 Jul 2026), FSB Global Monitoring Report 2025, IIF Global Debt Monitor (Feb and Sep 2026), BIS total credit statistics, IMF Global Debt Database (blog, Sep 2025).

Where could "500T+" come from? We do not know which source the question had in mind, so here are five candidates. As for "300T+", it is right as a floor for world wealth on every count. It is also roughly how world debt was reported from 2021 to 2024, about $300 trillion to $320 trillion (IIF), the figure many popular videos quoted.

- An estimate this guide's owner once made: the world's gold times ten, about $500 trillion. Level 1's "How money is born today" explains why a fixed times-ten multiplier does not hold.
- The financial firms of the world, central banks, banks and other funds, held $503.7 trillion of financial assets at the end of 2024 (Financial Stability Board). That is a count of claims. It includes much of the world's debt seen from the lender's side, plus shares and claims on each other.
- People's net wealth: $517.7 trillion at the end of 2025 (UBS). The number may simply belong on the other side of the ledger.
- Everything owed on paper by every sector: about $1,200 trillion (computed from McKinsey). On that count "500T+" is true, more than twice over.
- Derivatives: over-the-counter contracts with a notional value of $846 trillion at the end of June 2025 (BIS). Notional is the size of the thing bet on, not money owed. Their gross market value, closer to what is actually at stake, was $21.8 trillion. Never add notional derivatives to debt.

> **Popular claim.** "The world owes $500 trillion and is only worth $300 trillion." What it gets right: the world's paper claims are enormous, and on the widest count of everything owed (about $1,200 trillion) they are far bigger than $500 trillion. What it gets wrong: on the usual meaning of debt, loans and bonds, the world owes about $348 trillion to $365 trillion, while its net wealth is $518 trillion to $600 trillion. And on any count the two cannot be subtracted, because the world owes all of it to itself.

| Measure | Value | What it counts | What it leaves out |
|---|---|---|---|
| Household net wealth (UBS) | $517.7T, end 2025 (McKinsey's household count: $570T) | People's houses, savings, shares and private pensions, minus their debts. 56 markets with over 92% of world wealth | Wealth of governments and firms not owned by people, state pension promises |
| National net worth (McKinsey, via press) | $600T, 2025 (5.1 times world GDP) | Real assets of every sector plus net claims | Human and natural capital |
| Financial assets of financial firms (FSB) | $503.7T, end 2024 | Assets of central banks, banks and nonbanks in 29 jurisdictions with over 90% of world GDP | Real assets. It counts claims, which cancel against debts |
| Debt, loans and bonds, four sectors (IIF) | $348.3T at end 2025, over $365T by mid 2026 (via press) | Households $64.6T, firms $100.6T, governments $106.7T, financial sector $76.4T | Shares, derivatives (notional $846T at mid 2025, BIS, which is not debt), unfunded pension promises |
| Nonfinancial debt (IMF, BIS) | $251T (2024) to $262.7T (end 2025) | Governments, firms and households | The financial sector's own debts, left out so lending is not counted twice |
| Everything owed on paper, every sector (computed from McKinsey, via press) | about $1,200T, 2025 | Nearly $1,800T of assets minus $600T of net worth: deposits, bonds, loans and other claims owed by one part of the world to another | Real assets. It is a gross count, so almost all of it cancels at world level |

> Every one of these numbers comes from a different counter with a different purpose. UBS counts people's wealth for a wealth manager's report. The IIF is a bank industry body and counts the financial sector's own debts, so its figure is the biggest of the usual debt counts. The FSB counts financial firms' assets to watch for risk. McKinsey counts every balance sheet, which is how it reaches nearly $1,800 trillion. When two headlines disagree, first ask which counter they used.

Two kinds of pension sit in different places. Private pension funds are inside household wealth: the savings belong to people. Unfunded state promises, such as public pensions and health care paid from future taxes, are in none of these debt counts. They are real claims on future taxpayers, and hard-money writers often add them to debt. This chapter does not, and has no checked figure for them yet.

### The great cancellation: why the world cannot owe anyone outside itself

Every debt has two sides. When a family owes a bank $300,000, the bank owns a $300,000 claim. When the US Treasury owes $1,000 on a bond, a pension fund, a bank, the Fed or a foreign central bank owns that claim. Add up every balance sheet on Earth and each IOU appears once as a debt and once as an asset. They cancel. There is no bank on Mars that the world owes.

> Imagine a family of four who lend each other money all year: the teenager owes the parents for a phone, a parent owes the grandmother for a car, the grandmother owes the teenager for help with the shop. At the end of the year the IOUs on the fridge add up to $50,000. Is the family $50,000 poorer? No. The IOUs are owed from one member to another. The family is worth its house, its car and its shop. The IOUs only matter if one member cannot pay another.

The debts cancel for the world, not for each family. Creditors and debtors are different families, so interest flows from one group to another. In the United States, the top 10% of households took 67.5% of the rise in household net worth since the end of 2019, and the bottom half took 3.1% (Federal Reserve distributional accounts, mid 2026).

Walk through two real kinds of deal. First, a young family buys an existing flat from a retired couple with a $300,000 mortgage.

| Who | Owns | Owes | Net wealth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Young family | + the flat, $300,000 | + mortgage, $300,000 | No change |
| Bank | + the mortgage loan, $300,000 | + the sellers' new deposit, $300,000 | No change |
| Retired couple | - the flat, + a $300,000 deposit | nothing | No change. The asset changed form |
| The world | + $300,000 of claims | + $300,000 of debt | Unchanged. Debt rose, wealth only moved |

Debt went up and nobody got richer or poorer. Now the second deal: the US government runs a $1 trillion deficit, and half the new bonds are bought by a US pension fund, half by Japanese investors.

| Who | What happens | Net wealth |
|---|---|---|
| US government | Owes $1T of new bonds, spends the money on wages and transfers | Falls $1T |
| US households | Receive $1T of new deposits, then move $0.5T into a pension fund that buys bonds | Rise $1T: $0.5T in deposits and $0.5T in pension claims backed by bonds |
| Japanese investors | Buy $0.5T of bonds with dollar deposits they already held from selling goods to the US | No change, they swapped a dollar deposit for a bond |
| The US as a nation | Owes Japan the same amount as before, in a new form: a bond instead of a deposit | No change in this deal. Its foreign position fell earlier, when the US paid for the goods |
| The world | Every IOU has an owner | Unchanged |

Inside the US, the government's new debt is the private sector's new asset, so "we owe it to ourselves" is right for that half. The foreign half is a claim of Japan on future US income, and it was created when the US bought more from the world than it sold. That is why only countries, not the world, can owe outside. The US's net foreign position was about minus $26.5 trillion at the end of 2024 (IMF) and minus $27.5 trillion at the end of 2025 (BEA), while Japan's was about plus $3.5 trillion (end 2024). A net foreign position is not the same as foreign debt: part of the US figure is foreigners owning US shares and companies, and stock prices move it a lot (BEA).

So what survives the cancellation? Three things. Real assets: land, houses, offices, factories, machines, roads and software, worth roughly the world's $600 trillion of net worth (McKinsey, via press), about two thirds of it real estate (Level 1, "The titled world"). Assets that are nobody's IOU, like gold bullion and bitcoin, which are small next to property. And, in household wealth only, the market's view of companies' future earnings above what their books show, because shares are counted at market price. In national net worth that extra cancels, because a share is also a claim on the company. World wealth, measured in dollars, is mostly the price of real things.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: If every debt is somebody's asset, who is the world in debt to?
  A: Itself. The $348T of debt the IIF counts is matched by $348T of claims held by people, pension funds, banks and central banks. Only countries can owe outside: the US's net foreign position was about minus $26.5T at the end of 2024, Japan's about plus $3.5T. (builds on [The musical chairs question](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-07.md))
- Q: Why is the richest country also the biggest debtor?
  A: Because lenders lend against assets and income, and because the world wants dollar assets. The US holds about 35% of world household wealth and owes about 29% of world nonfinancial debt. Its net foreign position, about minus $26.5T at the end of 2024, is part debt and part foreign ownership of US shares and firms, and the US can owe it in its own currency. (builds on [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md))

> **Stop here.** Part 1 of 3 done. You can now say what the world owns, what it owes on each counter, and why the two cannot be subtracted. Before Part 2, try these three.

**Check yourself.** Q: Someone says world debt is $500 trillion. What is your first question, and what are the two main answers?
A: Which debt? Loans and bonds come to about $348T to $365T. Everything owed on paper, deposits and other claims included, comes to about $1,200T.

**Check yourself.** Q: A young family buys an existing flat with a $300,000 mortgage. Is the world richer or poorer?
A: Neither. Debt rose $300,000 and so did someone's claim. Wealth only moved.

**Check yourself.** Q: If the world's debts cancel, why can they still be dangerous?
A: They cancel for the world, not for each family. Creditors and debtors are different people, and if one borrower cannot pay another, the chain of IOUs breaks.

### Part 2 of 3. How it grew, and how to hold it in your head

### Price, not pile

Debt and wealth can both grow at once, for four reasons. A loan that builds a new house adds a debt and a new real asset. A loan that buys an existing house adds a debt and a deposit, and more credit chasing the same houses lifts their price, which shows up as more wealth. Inflation lifts both in dollars. And the two are counted differently: debt is a gross count of IOUs, net worth is what is left after they cancel.

How much of new wealth is new things? McKinsey's 2026 report, as summarized in the press, found that only about 20% of the rise in household wealth in 2025 came from net new investment, and about 58% came from higher valuations above inflation. The rest was inflation itself. The report was not opened for this chapter, so treat the split as approximate. The direction matches Level 1's "The titled world": the same buildings became worth more.

Here is every way world debt and world wealth can grow or shrink, with a size for 2025 and for a stress year.

| What moves | Debt | Wealth | 2025 | Stress year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| New borrowing | Up | No change on the day, up if it builds something | +$28.8T in dollars, flattered by a weaker dollar (IIF, $319.5T to $348.3T) | 2020: a record +$35T (IIF) |
| New real investment | None or up | Up | about $8T, a fifth of the $40T household gain (McKinsey, via press) | not sized |
| Higher prices of existing assets | None | Up, or down when prices fall | about $23T, 58% of the household gain (McKinsey, via press) | 2022: household wealth fell 2.4%, to $454.4T (UBS and Credit Suisse, via press) |
| Inflation | Up in dollars, down as a share of output | Up in dollars | The IIF ratio fell for a fifth year, to about 308% | 2020 to 2024: the BIS ratio fell from 285% to 235% |
| The dollar ruler | Up when the dollar falls | Up when the dollar falls | The euro rose almost 9% against the dollar (UBS) | 2022: IIF debt fell about $4T as the dollar rose |
| Repayment and default | Down | Moves from lender to borrower, no change for the world | not sized | not sized |

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: World wealth rose about 10.8% in 2025 (UBS). Did the world build 10% more things?
  A: No. Only about a fifth of the household gain came from new investment, and most of the rest from higher prices. A weaker dollar also lifted the dollar value of non-US wealth. (builds on [The yardstick problem](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-10.md))
- Q: Real estate is about two thirds of world net worth. What happens to world wealth if house prices fall 20%?
  A: Measured wealth falls by roughly 13% of net worth (two thirds times 20%, a model using McKinsey's 2021 finding that real estate is about two thirds of net worth). No house is lost and no debt is repaid. Debt stays at face value, so everyone's debt looks bigger next to what they own. (builds on [The titled world: why abundance runs on credit, and who keeps the balance](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-titled.md))

### The ruler moves: the dollar resizes the world

Every world total is counted in dollars. When the dollar rises, everything outside the US looks smaller, and when it falls, everything looks bigger, with nothing real changing. Japan shows how large this effect can be.

| Japan's nonfinancial debt | End 2020 | End 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| In yen | 2,273 trillion | 2,340 trillion | +3% |
| In US dollars | $22.05T | $14.94T | -32% |
| As a share of Japan's GDP | 410% | 351% | -59 points |

Japan's debt rose 3% in yen and fell 32% in dollars, because the yen fell from about 103 to about 157 per dollar. Its debt also fell as a share of its economy, because inflation returned and lifted nominal output. Nobody repaid anything. The same ruler worked the other way in 2025: the euro rose almost 9% against the dollar, which is part of why wealth in Europe, the Middle East and Africa grew about 17.5% in dollars that year (UBS).

In 2022 the ruler worked the other way for the whole world. The dollar rose, and world debt measured in dollars fell about $4 trillion, to just under $300 trillion, the IIF's first annual fall since 2015. World household wealth fell too, about 2.4% to $454.4 trillion on the UBS and Credit Suisse count (via press), as higher interest rates cut asset prices. Nobody repaid anything.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: Japan's debt fell by a third in dollars from 2020 to 2025. Did Japan repay?
  A: No. In yen it rose 3% (2,273 to 2,340 trillion yen, BIS). The yen fell against the dollar, so the ruler shrank the number. (builds on [The yardstick problem](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-10.md))
- Q: World wealth rose 10.8% in dollars in 2025. Measured in ounces of gold, did it rise or fall?
  A: It fell, by about a third. Gold rose about 66% in 2025 (press), so 1.108 divided by 1.66 is about 0.67 (a model). Neither ruler is the right one alone. Check big claims with more than one ruler. (builds on [The yardstick problem](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-10.md))

### A brief timeline, 1971 to 2026

**Chart: The world's output, debt and net worth, 1971 to 2025 ($ trillions)**
| Series | 1971 | 1980 | 2000 | 2001 | 2005 | 2007 | 2008 | 2020 | 2021 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Net worth | None | None | 156 | None | None | None | None | 514 | None | None | 600 |
| Debt | 3.3 | 11.5 | None | 60.1 | 88.2 | 113.5 | 118.6 | 222.0 | 228.3 | 237.0 | 262.7 |
| World GDP | 3.33 | 11.48 | 33.97 | 33.75 | 47.94 | 58.57 | 64.38 | 86.39 | 98.78 | 111.67 | 118.35 |
Debt is nonfinancial debt (governments, firms, households) in dollars. The 1971 and 1980 points are a model: world output times the IMF's finding that this debt sat near 100% of world output until about 1980, from an early sample made up mostly of rich countries. BIS data from 2001, on the BIS's own country coverage. Net worth is McKinsey's national net worth (2000, 2020, and 2025 via press). Output grew about 36 times since 1971, debt about 80 times (the 1971 debt point is a model). Source: World Bank (GDP, current dollars), BIS total credit statistics (aggregate of reporting countries), IMF Global Debt Database (model years), McKinsey Global Institute.

| Year | What was happening | World debt | Debt as % of output (BIS on its own coverage, or IIF) | World wealth |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1971 | The dollar leaves gold | about $3T (model) | about 100% (model) | no reliable series |
| 1980 | Interest rates near 20% | about $11.5T (model) | about 100% (model) | no reliable series |
| 2000 | Rates falling, credit booming | $60T (2001, BIS) | 191% (BIS) | $156T (McKinsey) |
| 2008 | The global financial crisis | $119T (BIS) | 202%, rising to 229% by 2010 (BIS) | a fall of about $21T in 2007 to 2008 (press) |
| 2020 | Covid | $222T (BIS). A record $35T added in one year (IIF, four sectors) | 285% (BIS) | $514T (McKinsey) |
| 2022 | Inflation and a strong dollar | just under $300T (IIF, four sectors), after a fall of about $4T, the first since 2015 | fell (IIF) | household wealth fell 2.4%, to $454.4T (UBS and Credit Suisse, via press) |
| 2025 | Weak dollar, fiscal push, AI borrowing | $263T (BIS) or $348T with the financial sector (IIF) | 246% (BIS) or about 308% (IIF) | $518T (UBS, people) to $600T (McKinsey, all, via press) |
| Mid 2026 | Health, energy, AI and defense spending | over $365T (IIF, via press) | about 305% in Q1 2026 (IIF) | no estimate yet |

Three things stand out. Debt grew faster than output in almost every period since 1971, from about one year of world output (a model) to about two and a half. It grew in jumps, in 2008 to 2010 and above all in 2020, when a record $35 trillion was added in one year (IIF). And after 2020 the world ratio fell for years while the dollar amount kept climbing, apart from 2022, when it fell about $4 trillion as a strong dollar shrank everything counted outside the US. Inflation and the ruler did that, not repayment. The fall did not last in dollars: debt rose about $46 trillion from the end of 2024 to mid 2026 ($319.5 trillion to over $365 trillion, IIF), and the BIS ratio rose again in 2025.

This was not the first time. After the Second World War the US and the UK shrank their government debt as a share of output without repaying it, by growing and by keeping interest rates below inflation (Level 1's "The seasons of money", citing Reinhart and Sbrancia, 2011). The years after 2020 were a short replay.

> The sources do not always agree on direction. In 2025 the BIS measure of world debt to output rose (235% to 246%) while the IIF's fell (to about 308%). The likely reason is how each converts currencies when the dollar falls during a year. It is a reminder that a single year's move in a world ratio can depend on who is counting.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: The world debt ratio fell for years after 2020 while dollar debt kept climbing. How can both be true, and what happened in 2022?
  A: Inflation raised nominal output faster than debt. On the BIS measure world nonfinancial debt went from $222T (285% of output) in 2020 to $237T (235%) in 2024. Nobody paid it down. In 2022 dollar debt even fell, by about $4T on the IIF count, because a strong dollar shrank everything measured in dollars outside the US. (builds on [The seasons of money](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-08.md))
- Q: When did world debt jump most: 1971, 2008 or 2020, and who borrowed?
  A: 2020: a record $35T in one year, with governments borrowing about $14T of it (IIF). In 2008 to 2010 the BIS ratio rose from 202% to 229%. In 1971 there was no jump: debt sat near 100% of world output (IMF). (builds on [1971, oil and the petrodollar](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-05.md))

### Make the numbers brain-sized

A trillion is too big to picture, so shrink it. One trillion seconds is about 31,700 years. Counting the IIF's $348 trillion at a dollar a second would take about 11 million years. Here are three better ways to hold the world in your head.

**Chart: If the world were 100 adults: share of all wealth held by each group**
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| 42 adults with under $10k | 0.6 |
| 41 adults with $10k to $100k | 12.2 |
| 15 adults with $100k to $1m | 38.8 |
