| 1.5 adults with over $1m | 48.4 |
UBS sample of about 3.85 billion adults in 56 markets, grouped by wealth per adult, end 2025. Source: UBS Global Wealth Report 2026 wealth pyramid, end 2025.

Of every 100 adults in UBS's sample, 42 own under $10,000 and together hold 0.6% of all wealth. The one or two millionaires hold almost half. Averages hide this: counting every adult on Earth (World Bank), wealth per adult is about $93,000, yet 42 of every 100 adults own less than $10,000.

| If the world were one household earning $100,000 a year | Amount |
|---|---|
| Income each year (world output) | $100,000 |
| What the family members own, net (household wealth) | $437,400 |
| What the whole household is worth, with the family business and the town hall (national net worth) | $507,000 |
| IOUs written inside the household (all four sectors) | $294,300 |
| of which the town hall (government) owes | $90,200 |
| of which the family business (companies) owes | $85,000 |
| of which the family bank (financial sector) owes | $64,600 |
| of which family members (households) owe | $54,600 |

In household terms, the $294,300 of IOUs are owed from one member of the household to another. The household as a whole owes nobody outside. Its true worth is the house, the land, the tools and the business, about five years of income. The danger is not the size of the IOU pile. The danger is that one member cannot pay another and the chain of IOUs breaks.

| Split across 8.2 billion people | Each |
|---|---|
| Household wealth per person | $63,000 |
| Household wealth per adult (all 5.6 billion adults) | $93,000 |
| Debt per person, all four sectors | $42,000 |
| Output per person per year | $14,400 |

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: Split world wealth and debt across 8.2 billion people. What does each own and owe, and why is that misleading?
  A: About $63,000 of household wealth and $42,000 of debt each. But 42 of every 100 adults own under $10,000, and the debt is owed between governments, firms, banks and households, not by each person. (builds on [Eye-openers: what most people never notice](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-13.md))

> **Stop here.** Part 2 of 3 done. You can now explain how world debt and wealth grew, why the dollar resizes them, and how to picture them. Before Part 3, try these three.

**Check yourself.** Q: Japan's debt fell 32% in dollars from 2020 to 2025. Did Japan repay?
A: No. In yen it rose 3%. The yen fell against the dollar, so the ruler shrank the number.

**Check yourself.** Q: World household wealth rose in 2025. Was most of the rise new houses and machines?
A: No. About a fifth was new investment. Most of the rest was higher prices and inflation (McKinsey, via press).

**Check yourself.** Q: If the world were 100 adults, how many would own under $10,000, and what share of all wealth would they hold together?
A: 42 adults, holding 0.6% of all wealth.

### Part 3 of 3. How countries are built, and what would change the picture

### Who contributes the numbers: G7, G10 and the giant left out

The owner asked about the G7 or the G10. The G7 is the US, Japan, Germany, the UK, France, Italy and Canada. The G10 is, confusingly, eleven countries: the G7 plus Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden and Switzerland. Neither includes China, which now holds about 16% of the world's household wealth (18.5% counting Hong Kong and Taiwan) and about 22% of its nonfinancial debt. So China and India are added here.

**Chart: Who contributes: each country's share of the world (%)**
| Item | Share of world wealth | Share of world debt | Share of world output | Share of world people |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States | 35.09 | 29.03 | 26.0 | 4.16 |
| China | 16.18 | 22.09 | 16.47 | 17.12 |
| Japan | 4.25 | 5.74 | 3.75 | 1.5 |
| Germany | 4.56 | 3.87 | 4.27 | 1.02 |
| United Kingdom | 3.02 | 3.51 | 3.38 | 0.85 |
| France | 3.51 | 4.27 | 2.84 | 0.84 |
| Italy | 2.65 | 2.26 | 2.16 | 0.72 |
| Canada | 2.56 | 2.78 | 1.96 | 0.51 |
| India | 3.13 | 2.57 | 3.34 | 17.82 |
Debt here is nonfinancial debt. Each country's debt is BIS (Q4 2025) and the world total it is divided by is the IIF's $271.9T, so the shares are approximate. Country wealth is derived from UBS wealth per adult times adults, and China's and India's use end-2022 wealth figures, so treat them as rough. Source: UBS Global Wealth Report 2026 and Databook 2023, BIS total credit statistics (Q4 2025), World Bank (2025).

| Group | Share of world wealth | Share of world debt | Share of world output | Share of world people |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G7 (US, Japan, Germany, UK, France, Italy, Canada) | 56% | 51% | 44% | 9.6% |
| G10 (really 11: the G7 plus Belgium, Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland) | 60% | 56% | 48% | 10% |
| G10 plus China, India and Malaysia | 79% | 81% | 68% | 46% |

Read the chart in pairs. The rich are also the big borrowers: the G7 holds about 56% of world household wealth and owes about 51% of world nonfinancial debt, with under 10% of the world's people. Lenders lend against assets and income, so debt follows wealth. The US has a bigger share of world wealth (35%) than of world debt (29%) or output (26%). China's share of debt (22%) is above its shares of wealth and output on these mixed-year figures. McKinsey says China's balance sheet grew through debt more than through rising asset values (via press), though its property boom was also a price story. India has 18% of the world's people and about 3% of everything else, and its low debt partly reflects a small formal financial system.

### Six ways to build a country's balance sheet

| Country | Government debt, % of GDP | Household debt, % of GDP | Company debt, % of GDP | Who holds the state's debt | Owns abroad minus owes abroad |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States | 116% | 68% | 72% | Fed 14%, foreigners 29% (of debt held by the public) | -$26.5T (-91% of GDP), end 2024 |
| Japan | 193% | 61% | 113% | Bank of Japan 43%, foreigners 13% (end 2025) | +$3.5T (+83%) |
| Germany | 63% | 48% | 87% | Bundesbank 20%, outside Germany 51% | +$3.6T (+77%) |
| Italy | 137% | 36% | 58% | Bank of Italy 19%, outside Italy 34% | +$0.35T (+15%) |
| France | 116% | 59% | 155% | Bank of France 17%, outside France 54% | -$0.7T (-22%) |
| United Kingdom | 102% | 74% | 58% | foreigners about a third | -$0.35T (-10%) |
| Canada | 100% | 100% | 119% | non-residents about 45% of the bond market | +$1.3T (+59%) |
| Belgium | 108% | 57% | 118% | National Bank of Belgium 15%, outside Belgium 63% | +$0.38T (+57%) |
| Netherlands | 45% | 94% | 169% | De Nederlandsche Bank 21%, outside the Netherlands 49% | +$0.72T (+60%) |
| Sweden | 35% | 82% | 147% | Riksbank 4%, foreigners 23% | +$0.39T (+65%) |
| Switzerland | 25% | 123% | 129% | not confirmed | +$1.15T (+119%) |
| China | 99% | 58% | 143% | not confirmed | +$3.3T (+18%) |
| Malaysia | 65% | 70% | 89% | foreigners about 20% of MGS (July 2026) | about zero |

Notes: debt ratios are BIS, Q4 2025. Shares of government debt are 2025 (Eurostat for the euro members and Sweden, where "outside" includes other euro area investors and the ECB). Net foreign positions are end 2024 (IMF). What households own differs too: financial assets are 79% of gross household wealth in the US but 44% in Germany, where homes weigh more (UBS).

> **The US and Japan.** The US is the richest country and the largest net debtor to the rest of the world, about minus $26.5T at the end of 2024. It can borrow abroad in its own currency because the world wants dollars. The bigger currency risk in world debt sits outside the US: about $14T of dollar credit owed by borrowers abroad at the end of September 2025 (BIS), which gets heavier for them when the dollar rises. Japan's government owes about twice its output, yet Japan as a nation is owed $3.5T by the world. The Bank of Japan held about 43% of the government's bills and bonds at the end of 2025 (41% by June 2026) and foreigners about 13%, so Japan's debt is mostly owed from one Japanese pocket to another, in yen. Its government debt is 193% of output on the BIS basis, about 207% gross on the IMF's, and about 136% net of the government's own financial assets (IMF). Each figure is right on its own basis. The risk shows up as a weak yen, not as foreign creditors walking away.

> **Germany and Italy.** One currency, opposite structures. Germany's state owes 63% of output, Italy's 137%. Yet the typical Italian adult is richer than the typical German one: median wealth $131,001 against $53,485 (UBS, modelled). Italian families owe little, 36% of output against 48% in Germany. The usual explanation is home ownership, which is more common in Italy, though this chapter has not checked the figures. Italy's state is the debtor, its families much less so. Neither country prints its own currency, so investors can charge either one a risk premium when they worry. Countries with their own central bank pay such premia too, as Britain found in 2022.

> **France.** Same euro, a different worry. The French state owes about 116% of output, less than Italy's 137% (BIS), and French companies carry the heaviest debt in this table, 155% of output. Investors outside France, including other euro area investors and the ECB, hold about 54% of French government debt (Eurostat), and France owes the world a net $0.7T (end 2024). Yet in early October 2026 investors charged France more than Italy to borrow for ten years: about 1.4 points over Germany for France, against about 1.2 for Italy (press). They were reacting to France's deficit and politics more than to the size of its debt. A debt ratio is where the analysis starts, not where it ends.

> **The UK and Canada.** House-rich households with heavy mortgages. Canadian household debt is about 100% of output and British about 74%, among the highest in the G7. When interest rates rise, these families feel it first, because their mortgages reset within a few years. Canada is a large net creditor abroad, partly thanks to big pension funds investing overseas, while the UK is a small net debtor.

> **Switzerland.** A tiny state and heavy private balance sheets. The Swiss government owes only 25% of output, Swiss households 123%, the highest in the table, much of it mortgages that owners often keep rather than repay. Yet Swiss adults are the richest on Earth on average ($910,382) and the country owns far more abroad than it owes. High gross debt, very high net wealth: proof that gross debt alone says little.

> **China.** Debt-built growth, saved at home. China's total nonfinancial debt is about 300% of output, above the US, and its companies, including local government financing vehicles, carry most of it (143%). Yet China is a net creditor abroad, because its savings are lent at home, through Chinese banks, in yuan. Falling property prices have dragged on its household wealth.

> **Malaysia.** A smaller currency with a foreign window. Malaysia's nonfinancial debt is about 224% of output: government 65%, households 70% (high for an emerging market, including mortgages and car loans), companies 89%. It owes the world about as much as it owns abroad. Foreigners hold about a fifth of Malaysian Government Securities (20.1% in July 2026), enough that a jump in US yields can pull money out and push the ringgit down, as Level 1's "The view from a smaller currency" described.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: Japan's government owes about twice its GDP. Why is it not treated like Greece was?
  A: Its debt is in yen, the Bank of Japan held about 43% of it at the end of 2025, foreigners only about 13%, and Japan as a whole is owed $3.5T by the world. Greece borrowed in a currency it could not print, much of it from foreigners. (builds on [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md))
- Q: Germany, Italy and France share the euro. Why did France, with less government debt than Italy, pay more to borrow in October 2026?
  A: Investors price the risk that worries them now, not only the size of the debt. France's deficit and politics worried them more than Italy's higher debt: about 1.4 points over Germany for France against about 1.2 for Italy (press, early October 2026). None of the three can print euros. (builds on [Why empires and their currencies fall](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-09.md))
- Q: Is a country with high government debt but rich households poor or rich?
  A: Look at the whole national balance sheet. Japan: state debt 193% of output, yet a net creditor of 83% of output abroad. Switzerland: tiny state debt, households owe 123% of output, still the richest adults on Earth. (builds on [Nation Inc.: taxes, interest and the hubs](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-nation.md))
- Q: China is not in the G7 or the G10. Why does that change the picture?
  A: China holds about 16% of world household wealth (18.5% counting Hong Kong and Taiwan) and 22% of world nonfinancial debt, and it added more than $4.8T of the roughly $10T rise in world debt in the first half of 2026 (IIF, via press). Leave it out and you miss nearly half of the rise in world debt in 2026 so far. (builds on [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md))

### What would change the picture

These are the signs to watch. Each one would change a number or a story in this chapter, and each has a date or a source.

| Watch | What it would change | When | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| House prices fall 20% | Measured world net worth falls by roughly 13% (a model: real estate is about two thirds of it). Debt stays at face value, so it looks bigger | Any year | McKinsey, Level 1 "The titled world" |
| The dollar moves 10% either way | Every world total moves about 6% to 7% in dollars with nothing real changing (a model) | Check on 30 June 2027 | Fed broad dollar index |
| World debt above $375T, or the debt ratio rising for the first time since 2020 | Ends the "ratio falling" story | IIF release with Q3 2026 data, mid November 2026 to February 2027 | IIF |
| BIS world debt ratio above 250% | Confirms the 2025 rise was not a one-year quirk | BIS release with Q2 2026 data, early December 2026 | BIS |
| France's 10-year spread over Germany well above its early October 2026 level of about 1.4 points | A sovereign scare inside a currency union, where no member can print its way out | Weekly | Market data, press |
| Private credit growing much faster than output for several years | The warning sign post-Keynesian economists watch, measured by the BIS credit-to-GDP gap (country values not yet checked) | Quarterly | BIS |
| Inflation staying high, or falling back | High inflation keeps shrinking debt ratios at savers' expense. A fall back would stop the ratio falling | Monthly | National statistics |
| World household wealth below $500T for end 2026 | Prices, not piles, went into reverse | UBS report, about 30 June 2027 | UBS |

### What people say, and what the schools add

| What people say | Verdict |
|---|---|
| The world is in debt, but to whom? (a 14-second meme, 27 million views) | The right question. The world owes it to itself |
| Global debt is $300 trillion | Right for 2021 to 2024 (about $300T to $320T, IIF). Now $348T (end 2025) and over $365T (mid 2026, via press) |
| Debt is three times the world economy | True on the widest count, about 3.1 times. About 2.4 times without the financial sector |
| The global debt bomb is about to go off | Overstated as one bomb, wrong to dismiss. The IIF ratio fell five years running to 2025, but dollar debt rose about $46T from end 2024 to mid 2026 and the BIS ratio rose in 2025. The risks are specific: refinancing in emerging markets, dollar debt owed abroad, a few governments |
| Debt is bigger than wealth | Depends on the counter. On loans and bonds, wealth is 1.4 to 1.7 times debt (517.7 / 365 to 600 / 348.3). On everything owed on paper, about $1,200T, the reverse. Neither comparison should be a subtraction |
| We owe it to ourselves | True for the world in total and for debt held at home. Not true between families, and false for debt in a foreign currency and for net debtor nations |

| School | Strongest point | What it would add |
|---|---|---|
| Official (IMF, BIS, IIF) | Debt is high and shifting to governments. Interest bills are eating fiscal room | Watch debt to GDP and refinancing needs |
| Post-Keynesian and MMT | Government debt in its own currency is the private sector's asset. Private debt is the real danger | Look harder at Chinese firms and Canadian and Swiss households |
| Austrian and hard money | Unanchored money let debt outgrow output since 1971. Cheap credit inflates asset prices, so part of measured wealth is a bubble | Treat the fall in the debt ratio after 2020 as quiet default through inflation |
| Historians (Reinhart and Rogoff, This Time Is Different, 2009) | Crises cluster after rapid debt build-ups, above all debt owed abroad in a foreign currency | Watch fast debt growth and foreign-currency debt, not the world total |

### Say it back

**Check yourself.** Q: A friend says the world is $500 trillion in debt and only worth $300 trillion. What would you ask first, and what two things would you tell them?
A: Ask: which debt? Then, first: on the usual meaning, loans and bonds, the world owes about $348T to $365T and is worth $518T to $600T net, so the order flips. Only the widest count, everything owed on paper including deposits, passes $500T, at about $1,200T. Second: whichever count they mean, it cannot be subtracted from wealth, because the world owes it to itself. What matters is who owes whom, in which currency, and how soon.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why can Japan owe twice its output and still be a creditor nation?
A: Its government owes mostly its own central bank, banks, insurers and savers, in yen, while Japan as a whole owns $3.5T more abroad than it owes.

**Check yourself.** Q: World debt to output fell in 2023 and 2024 while the dollar amount rose. What did the work?
A: Inflation. Nominal output grew faster than debt, so the ratio fell without anyone paying debt down.


---

# The money clubs: who writes the rules, who can really print, and the game the world plays

Rulebook Level 2 (The machinery), chapter 04. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-clubs.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-clubs . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*The G7, G10 and G20 are clubs, not governments. This chapter shows what they can and cannot do, which countries can really print money and which cannot, why Malaysia sits outside every club but inside the game, and five questions that turn the world into a game board.*

**In short**
- The G7, G10 and G20 are clubs, not governments: no treaty, no money of their own, no power to force anyone.
- The G20 moved fast in the 2008 to 2009 crisis and slowly in calm years. That is the usual pattern, with exceptions.
- Printing power is a ladder with three locks: its own currency, debt owed in that currency, and markets that let it print without a crash.
- Euro members, Ecuador and Panama cannot print on their own. Turkey, Argentina and Sri Lanka owed much of their debt in dollars and paid with inflation or default.
- Malaysia is in no club but lives by club rules. It sits on rung 3 of the printing ladder, where rung 1 is the top: 98.8% of its federal debt is borrowed in ringgit at home, yet foreigners hold about a fifth of its government bonds. Its brakes are the ringgit and its own fiscal laws.
- Five questions open the game board, and a four-step routine turns any headline into a game.

**Built on Levels 1 and 2: recall these before you start.** 
- [The world's balance sheet: what it owns, what it owes, and how countries are built](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-worldbs.md): The G10 is really eleven countries. Greece borrowed in a currency it could not print, much of it from foreigners.
- [Who really creates money: banks, the Fed and the Treasury](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-moneymake.md): Banks are the everyday printer, the government plus the central bank the emergency printer. Buying dollars creates ringgit.
- [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md): In September 1998 Malaysia imposed capital controls and pegged the ringgit at 3.80 to the dollar, until July 2005.
- [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md): Everyone uses the dollar because everyone else does. After 1997, countries short of dollars built reserves.
- [Why empires and their currencies fall](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-09.md): The US owes dollars it can create. Spain owed silver it could not.

**Map of this chapter: Who can make money, and who writes the rules**
- The clubs: G7 inside G10 and G20 (see [The world's balance sheet: what it owns, what it owes, and how countries are built](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-worldbs.md))
- What clubs cannot do: No treaty, no money, no force (see [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md))
- The scorecard: Fast in crises, slow in calm (see [The seasons of money](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-08.md))
- Three locks: Law, debt, market permission (see [Who really creates money: banks, the Fed and the Treasury](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-moneymake.md))
- The ladder: From reserve issuer to no printer (see [Why empires and their currencies fall](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-09.md))
- Malaysia: Rung 3, two kinds of brake (see [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md))
- The games: Six boxes, five real questions (see [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md))
- Your routine: Read any headline as a game (see [Eye-openers: what most people never notice](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-13.md))

Four parts, each ending in a stop box. Stop at any box and come back another day.

### Part 1 of 4. The clubs, and whether they deliver

### 1. Three clubs, no government

*[Picture on the web page: The G7 sits inside both bigger clubs. Belgium, the Netherlands and Sweden are in the G10 and sit inside the G20 only through the EU. Switzerland is in the G10 but not the G20. China and the big emerging economies are only in the G20. Malaysia is in none of them.]*

| Club | Started | Who is in | Why it started |
|---|---|---|---|
| G7 (Group of Seven) | 1975 (Canada joined 1976) | US, Japan, Germany, UK, France, Italy, Canada. The EU attends | The oil shock and the end of fixed exchange rates |
| G10 (Group of Ten) | 1962 | The G7 plus Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden and Switzerland: eleven countries | A standing credit line to the IMF (the International Monetary Fund, which lends to countries in trouble) |
| G20 (Group of Twenty) | 1999, leaders' summits from 2008 | 19 countries plus the EU and, since 2023, the African Union | The 1997 to 1998 Asian crisis, then the 2008 crash |

| Group | World output | World people | World exports |
|---|---|---|---|
| G7 | 44.5% | 9.6% | 30.2% |
| G10 (11 countries) | 47.6% | 10.3% | 38.1% |
| G20 with the EU | 86.3% | 61.0% | 75.8% |
| G20 with the EU and the African Union | 88.5% | 78.8% | 77.5% |
| Malaysia | 0.38% | 0.44% | 0.93% |

Malaysia's share of world exports is about two and a half times its share of world output. It lives by trade, so it lives by rules made in rooms it is not in. For each club's share of world wealth and debt, see the Level 2 chapter "The world's balance sheet".

None of these clubs has a treaty (a binding agreement between states), a binding vote, its own money or a large staff. They cannot pass a law, print a dollar or force a private lender. They work through bodies their members control: the IMF, the Financial Stability Board, the Basel committee that writes bank rules, and the OECD tax talks. Each member must still pass its own laws.

### Go deeper: Membership is not the same as power

| Source of power | Who has it |
|---|---|
| Reserve currency (share of world reserves, mid 2026) | US dollar 56.70%, euro 20.60%, yen 4.96%, Chinese yuan 2.11% |
| A veto at the IMF | The US alone can block decisions that need 85% of votes |
| Standing swap lines from the Fed | Five central banks: the ECB, Japan, the UK, Switzerland and Canada |
| Open money markets (0 closed to 1 open, 2023) | 1.00 for the US, Japan, the UK, euro members, Singapore. 0.42 for Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand. 0.16 for China and India |

Singapore and Switzerland are not G20 members, yet both run open, trusted money centres. China is a G20 member with capital controls, so its yuan is only 2.11% of world reserves despite about 17% of world output. Openness matters more than membership, along with size, trust in the law and deep markets.

### 2. Is the G20 just playing around?

Many people suspect the G20 is just playing around. Here is its record on ten big promises, chosen by one rule: every headline pledge with a target you can check, every crisis programme, and the latest summits. The grades are our judgment of the evidence.

| Promise | What happened | Grade |
|---|---|---|
| 2009 crisis package ($1.1 trillion, plus $5 trillion of national spending plans) | Made, including a new SDR allocation in August 2009 (SDRs are reserve money the IMF creates and hands to its members). Most of the $5 trillion was plans already announced | Delivered |
| A Financial Stability Board | Created in April 2009, still running | Delivered |
| 2021 SDR allocation for all IMF members | Made in 2021, with G20 backing | Delivered |
| Basel III bank rules | Phased in from 2013. The US re-proposed the final part in March 2026, no final rule yet | Partly |
| 2020 debt pause for poor countries | $12.9 billion paused for 48 of 73 eligible countries. One private lender joined | Partly |
| The Common Framework for debt deals | Each case took about 2 to more than 5 years (Chad, Zambia, Ghana, Ethiopia) | Partly, slow |
| A 15% global minimum tax | In force in the EU, UK, Japan, Korea and Malaysia. The US never passed it and won a carve-out in January 2026 | Partly, then diluted |
| No new protectionism (2009) | Members kept adding barriers. The 2025 US tariffs broke the spirit outright | Not delivered |
| Phase out fossil fuel subsidies (2009) | Global subsidies were still very large in 2022 | Not delivered |
| The 2025 and 2026 summits | The US boycotted Johannesburg in 2025, then as host shut South Africa out of Miami | Stalled |

Score: 3 delivered, 4 partly, 2 not delivered, 1 stalled. So the suspicion is half right, and the answer depends on which promises you count, which is why the rule for choosing them is stated above. The quick actions all came in crises: the 2009 package, the 2020 debt pause and the 2021 SDRs. The pause itself was fast, but the debt deals that should have followed took years. In calm years the G20 has moved slowly, and in 2025 and 2026 it split in the open. So the suspicion fits October 2026. It would not have fitted April 2009.

> **The game behind the scorecard.** In a crisis the G20 plays a stag hunt (part 4 explains this game and the next): acting together pays most, but each member acts only if it expects the others to, and a shared shock makes everyone expect it. Even in 2009 some did less than others. In calm years it plays free-rider games. A club with no treaty can coordinate the willing, not force the unwilling.

> **Stop here.** Part 1 of 4 done. Try these three before Part 2.

**Check yourself.** Q: Which club is Malaysia in: the G7, the G10 or the G20?
A: None. It sits in ASEAN, APEC and the Chiang Mai pool, and is a BRICS partner, but in none of the three money clubs.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why can a G20 promise be broken without penalty?
A: The G20 has no treaty, no court and no money of its own. A promise binds only if each member passes its own law.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why did the G20 move fast in 2009 but slowly on poor countries' debts?
A: In 2009 shared fear made each member expect the others to act. Debt relief by one lender frees cash to pay the others, so each prefers to let others give it.

### Part 2 of 4. Who can really print money

### 3. Three locks on the printing press

Here printing means a state and its central bank creating the money that the state's debts are owed in. Banks are the other printer, which the Level 2 chapter "Who really creates money" covers. To print freely, a country must open three locks.

1. Lock 1, the law. Does it issue its own currency? Italy, Ecuador and Panama do not. They use the euro or the US dollar, made by someone else.
2. Lock 2, the debt. Does the state owe its debt in money it can create? Sri Lanka could print rupees, but owed dollars, and stopped paying on 12 April 2022.
3. Lock 3, the market. Can it print a lot in a crisis without a currency crash or runaway prices? That depends on whether the world wants its money, how open its markets are, and its inflation record. Turkey and Argentina had their own money but owed a large part of their debt in dollars, and saw inflation reach 72% (2022) and 220% (2024). They failed lock 3 and partly lock 2.

Each lock is needed and none is enough alone. Passing locks 1 and 2 lets a country pay in its own money, if its law allows and its parliament does not block payment, as the US debt-limit fights of 2011 and 2023 threatened. It cannot choose what that money will buy.

### 4. The ladder

*[Picture on the web page: Six rungs of printing power, with rung 1 at the top (rung 5 has two halves, 5a and 5b). Malaysia sits on rung 3, highlighted: the middle of the ladder, at the strong end of its rung.]*

| Rung | What it means | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Reserve issuer | All three locks open with room. In a crisis the world buys its money | US by far, then the euro area as a whole, Japan, the UK |
| 2. Sovereign printer | All three open, but the world holds little of its money | Canada, Australia, Switzerland, Korea |
| 3. Constrained printer | Locks 1 and 2 open, lock 3 partly. Printing shows fast in the currency, in foreign selling or behind capital controls | China (controls), India, Brazil, Mexico, Indonesia, South Africa, Russia, Malaysia |
| 4. Fragile printer | Own money, but recently paid for printing with a crash, high inflation or default | Turkey, Argentina, Sri Lanka, Zimbabwe |
| 5a. Tied by choice | Could print, but tied its money to the dollar. A peg fixes the exchange rate. A currency board backs every note with dollars | Saudi Arabia (peg), Hong Kong (currency board) |
| 5b. No printer of its own | Must earn, tax or borrow the money it owes | Euro members one by one, Ecuador, Panama |

The rungs are our grading, not an official list. Two edges: Indonesia's central bank holds about 29% of its government's debt (June 2026), after buying from 2020 to 2022 and again in 2026, yet inflation was 1.9% in 2025. A rung 3 printer can print for a while if markets trust its brakes. Germany sits on rung 5b with the cheapest borrowing in the euro area, because markets trust its budget. And the euro area as a whole can print through the ECB, on conditions.

### Go deeper: Lock 2 evidence and the full printing matrix: 28 countries

| Lock 2 evidence | Foreign-currency government bonds sold abroad, % of output (BIS, mid 2026) | Share of government bonds held by foreigners |
|---|---|---|
| United States | 0.0% | 32.5% of Treasuries (end 2025, Fed) |
| Japan | 0.1% | about 13% (end 2025) |
| Malaysia | 0.8% | 21.5% of government securities (end 2025, Bank Negara) |
| Indonesia | 6.3% | 12.8% (June 2026, ADB) |
| Thailand | none reported | 9.3% (March 2026, ADB) |
| Turkey | 7.4% | not checked |
| Argentina | 9.8% | not checked |
| Sri Lanka | 7.0% | not checked |
| Saudi Arabia | 11.7% | not checked |
| Ecuador | 16.1% | not checked |
| Panama | 41.7% | not checked |

Read the BIS column with care. It counts only bonds sold abroad in foreign money, so it misses IMF and bank loans and dollar bonds sold at home, which is why it understates Argentina and Sri Lanka. By a World Bank series, about 42% of Turkey's central government debt was in foreign currency in 2024 (as reported by an aggregator, to confirm). Canada's 9.6% is borrowing abroad by choice, mostly hedged.

| Country | Own currency | Exchange rate (IMF, 2023) | Foreign-currency bonds abroad, % of output (BIS, mid 2026) | Openness (0 to 1) | Rung |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States | Yes | Free floating | 0.0% | 1.0 | 1 |
| Euro area as a whole | Yes | Free floating | n.a. | n.a. | 1 |
| Japan | Yes | Free floating | 0.1% | 1.0 | 1 |
| United Kingdom | Yes | Free floating | 0.0% | 1.0 | 1 |
| Canada | Yes | Free floating | 9.6% | 1.0 | 2 |
| Australia | Yes | Free floating | 0.1% | 1.0 | 2 |
| Switzerland | Yes | not checked | n.a. | 1.0 | 2 |
| Korea | Yes | Floating | 0.7% | 1.0 | 2 |
| China | Yes | Other managed | 0.2% | 0.16 | 3 |
| India | Yes | Floating | n.a. | 0.16 | 3 |
| Brazil | Yes | Floating | 3.0% | 0.16 | 3 |
| Mexico | Yes | Free floating | 8.4% | 0.7 | 3 |
| Indonesia | Yes | Floating | 6.3% | 0.42 | 3 |
| South Africa | Yes | Floating | 6.2% | 0.16 | 3 |
| Russia | Yes | Free floating | 2.2% | 0.16 | 3 |
| Malaysia | Yes | Floating | 0.8% | 0.42 | 3 |
| Turkey | Yes | Crawl-like | 7.4% | 0.16 | 4 |
| Argentina | Yes | Crawling peg (changed since) | 9.8% | 0.16 | 4 |
| Sri Lanka | Yes | Crawl-like | 7.0% | 0.0 | 4 |
| Zimbabwe | Yes, since 2024 | Other managed | n.a. | 0.42 | 4 |
| Saudi Arabia | Yes, pegged | Conventional peg | 11.7% | 0.7 | 5a |
| Hong Kong | Yes, currency board | Currency board | 6.0% | 1.0 | 5a |
| Germany | No (euro) | Euro | 0.3% | 1.0 | 5b |
| France | No (euro) | Euro | 1.2% | 1.0 | 5b |
| Italy | No (euro) | Euro | 0.5% | 1.0 | 5b |
| Greece | No (euro) | Euro | 0.0% | 1.0 | 5b |
| Ecuador | No (US dollar since 2000) | No own legal tender | 16.1% | 0.7 | 5b |
| Panama | No (US dollar since 1904) | No own legal tender | 41.7% | 1.0 | 5b |

Sources: IMF de facto exchange rate classification for 2023 (some regimes have changed since), BIS debt securities statistics (general government, international market, foreign currency, mid 2026, over 2024 output), Chinn-Ito capital openness index (2023), Fed and Bank Negara holder data, the ADB for Indonesia and Thailand. Central bank holdings of government debt: Fed 14% (October 2026), Bank of Japan about 43% (end 2025), Bank Indonesia 29.4% (June 2026), Bank Negara 3.8% (June 2026). In 2023 about two thirds of IMF members did not let their currency float in the IMF's sense.

### Go deeper: What people say, and what the schools say

| What people say | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Printing more money just raises prices (a short with about 75 million views) | Half true. Printing beyond what people want to hold raises prices. How much depends on the rung |
| Any country can print its way out | False for rungs 4 and 5. Even the economists who stress printing power limit it to countries that pass locks 1 and 2 |
| The US can print forever | Partly true. It can pay in dollars unless Congress blocks payment through the debt limit. It cannot choose what those dollars buy or what yield markets demand. Its interest bill passed $1 trillion in 2026 |
| The G20 is a useless talking shop | Half true: true in calm years, false for 2008 to 2009 |

| School | Who can print, in its strongest form | Its blind spot |
|---|---|---|
| MMT | A state with a floating currency that borrows only in it cannot be forced to default. The limit is inflation. Best example: Japan | Lock 3 for small open economies, whose currency falls when they print |
| Hard money | Every paper printer debases in the end. The only real limit is lost trust. Best example: the long fall of paper money against gold | Timing. The dollar has held rung 1 for 55 years since 1971 |
| Mainstream | Room to print depends on the currency of the debt, who holds it, and interest rates against growth. Foreign holders of local bonds can still trigger a currency run | It underweights politics and security |

> **Stop here.** Part 2 of 4 done. Try these three before Part 3.

**Check yourself.** Q: Italy and Japan both owe more than their yearly output. Which lock does Italy fail that Japan passes?
A: Lock 1. Italy cannot issue euros. Japan issues yen and owes them mostly to itself. The euro area as a whole can act through the ECB, on conditions.

**Check yourself.** Q: Sri Lanka had its own currency. Why could it not print its way out in 2022?
A: Lock 2. Its foreign debts were owed in dollars, and a rupee printer cannot make dollars.

**Check yourself.** Q: Name one country on rung 5b and say why it is there.
A: Any euro member, Ecuador or Panama. None issues the money its debts are owed in.

### Part 3 of 4. Malaysia, outside every club

### 5. Malaysia: outside every club, inside the game

Malaysia sits in no money club. Indonesia is the only Southeast Asian G20 member. Malaysia's seats are ASEAN (a founder in 1967), APEC, the IMF, the Chiang Mai reserve pool with China, Japan and Korea, and a BRICS partner seat, announced in October 2024 and in effect from 1 January 2025. Yet it applies rules written elsewhere, such as the 15% global minimum tax from 1 January 2025, a deal the US helped write and later won a carve-out from.

| Who holds Malaysia's federal government debt, Ministry of Finance measure (end June 2026) | Share |
|---|---|
| EPF | 30.5% |
| Banks | 28.5% |
| Insurers | 5.2% |
| Bank Negara | 3.8% |
| KWAP (civil service pensions) | 2.2% |
| Development finance institutions | 2.1% |
| Other domestic investors | 6.2% |
| Mostly foreigners (the rest, implied) | about 21.5% |

Bank Negara counts only government securities traded in the market, and on that count it holds near 1%. The Ministry counts all federal debt, which gives 3.8%. Both are right for what they count. The same difference explains why government bonds alone (MGS and GII) were RM1.309 trillion in March 2026 while federal debt, which also counts Treasury bills and loans, was RM1.38 trillion in June.

Federal debt was RM1.38 trillion at the end of June 2026, 63.1% of output. 98.8% of it is domestic debt: borrowed in ringgit in Malaysia's own market (Ministry of Finance). That does not mean held by Malaysians: foreigners hold about a fifth of the government bonds. Nearly half the debt (47.9%) is Islamic paper. Bank Negara, the central bank, holds only 3.8%, against about 29% at Indonesia's. Malaysia has not used its printer to fund the budget.

| Malaysia's own brakes | The rule | Where Malaysia is |
|---|---|---|
| Debt target (2023 fiscal law, Act 850) | Bring federal debt down to 60% of output over the medium term | 63.1% (end June 2026) |
| Debt-service limit (Act 850) | Debt service no more than 15% of revenue | 15.8% (2026 projection) |
| Statutory ceiling | MGS, GII and Islamic Treasury bills no more than 65% of output | Expected to stay under 65% in 2026 (Ministry of Finance, as reported) |
| Central bank law | The Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009 governs any lending by Bank Negara to the government | Bank Negara holds 3.8% of federal debt |

So Malaysia has two kinds of brake. The laws are the legal brakes, and today it is above two of its own lines. The ringgit is the market brake.

Malaysia did not take an IMF programme in 1998, while Thailand, Indonesia and Korea did. Today Bank Negara calls its regime a managed float, and the IMF calls it floating. Both are true: the IMF's floating allows smoothing, which is what Bank Negara means by managing. Offshore ringgit trading is still not allowed.

Against Indonesia, Thailand and Singapore, Malaysia is typical in most ways: its own currency, a float with smoothing, debt at home, low inflation, a partly managed capital account (some limits on moving money in and out). It is an outlier in five: the 1998 controls and peg, the highest foreign share of the three ASEAN peers checked (about 21.5% against 12.8% for Indonesia and 9.3% for Thailand), a compulsory pension fund as its biggest lender, nearly half its debt in Islamic form, and a central bank that holds very little government debt.

### Go deeper: Malaysia in dates, and against its neighbours

| When | What happened |
|---|---|
| Early 1997 | About 2.50 ringgit per US dollar |
| January 1998 | The worst point, about 4.885 |
| 1 September 1998 | Selective capital controls |
| 2 September 1998 | The ringgit fixed at 3.80 per dollar |
| 21 July 2005 | The peg ends. A managed float against a basket of currencies begins |

Since December 2016 Bank Negara's foreign exchange measures have pushed ringgit hedging onshore. The IMF classes them as capital flow management measures, and the authorities disagreed with its advice to phase them out (2022 Article IV, as reported by The Edge).

|  | Malaysia | Indonesia | Thailand | Singapore |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Club seat | none | G20 | none | none |
| Openness (0 to 1) | 0.42 | 0.42 | 0.42 | 1.00 |
| Foreigners hold of government bonds (ADB, same source) | 21.4% (Mar 2026) | 12.8% (Jun 2026) | 9.3% (Mar 2026) | not checked |
| Central bank holds of government bonds | 3.8% | 29.4% | 8.0% | not checked |
| Reserves, 2024 | $116 billion | $156 billion | $237 billion | $384 billion |

> **Where Malaysia sits.** Rung 3, the middle of the ladder, at the strong end of its rung. It opens lock 1 (its own currency) and lock 2 strongly (98.8% of federal debt borrowed in ringgit at home). It only partly opens lock 3: about a fifth of its government bonds sit with foreigners, the ringgit is not a reserve currency, and reserves are about 0.9 times its short-term foreign debt (foreign debt due within a year), below a common rule of thumb of 1. If Bank Negara printed for the budget, it would break Malaysia's own fiscal lines, foreigners and savers could leave, and a falling ringgit would raise import prices.

> **Stop here.** Part 3 of 4 done. Try this one before Part 4.

**Check yourself.** Q: Name Malaysia's two kinds of brake on printing for the budget.
A: The legal brakes in its fiscal laws (a 60% debt target and a 15% debt-service limit, both above the line today) and the market brake, the ringgit.

### Part 4 of 4. The game the world plays

### 6. Game theory in five minutes

Game theory asks: what is each player's best move, given what the others might do? The table lists six common games. Each one is then drawn as a box, seven boxes in all because the run game gets two, with two players, two moves each, and what each gets in every cell, from best to worst. Stag hunt and focal point are both coordination games: in the first, everyone must act at once, in the second, everyone just follows the habit.

| Box | Game | The shape | Where it settles |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Stag hunt | Everyone gains most if all act. Acting alone is costly | All act or none. Each acts only if it expects the others to |
| 2 | Free rider | A shared good is paid for by some and enjoyed by all | Each player's best move is to let others pay |
| 3 | Prisoner's dilemma | Each gains by cheating whatever the other does | Both cheat and both end up worse off |
| 4 | Focal point | Many choices would work, so players pick the one everyone expects | The habit wins, even if others are as good |
| 5 and 6 | Run | Lenders who expect others to stay, stay. Those who expect others to flee, flee first | The same borrower can be safe or bust depending on belief. Big reserves or a backstop make staying the best move |
| 7 | Chicken | Two players drive at each other | Each tries to look more committed so the other swerves |

> **What game theory leaves out.** Domestic politics (a leader facing an election may choose the worse national outcome), ideology, accidents and plain error. Use the games as a lens on incentives, not as proof that every move was planned.

### 7. Five questions that open the game board

Guess each answer before you open it. Each one opens a game, and each game is a real case.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: Why did the G20 move within months in 2008 to 2009, but take years on poor countries' debts?
  A: Two games. 2009 was a stag hunt (box 1): the shared fear of collapse made each member expect the others to act, and out came a $1.1 trillion package. Debt relief is a free-rider game (box 2): relief from one lender frees cash to pay the others. The 2020 pause covered $12.9 billion, but only one private lender joined, and Ethiopia's deal took more than five years to reach agreement in principle. (builds on [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md))
- Q: If every country wants a tariff edge or a cheaper currency, what happens when they all try at once?
  A: Tariffs are the clean prisoner's dilemma (box 3): all lose when all raise them, as in the tariff war of the early 1930s. Currencies are murkier: in the 1930s devaluing helped the countries that did it, and historians find that devaluing together would have sped recovery (Eichengreen and Sachs, 1985). Exits have been deals like the 1985 Plaza Accord, or truces like the October 2025 US and China pause, which can lapse. Two giants trading threats are playing chicken (box 7). (builds on [The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-leader.md))
- Q: Why does the world keep saving in US dollars even while complaining about the US?
  A: A focal point (box 4). Money is useful because others use it. The dollar was 56.7% of world reserves in mid 2026, nearly three times the euro. The yuan was 2.1%, largely because China keeps capital controls. (builds on [How the world gets its dollars](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-04.md))
- Q: Why did Malaysia and its neighbours pile up dollars after 1998 instead of spending them?
  A: To change the payoffs of a run on their currency (box 5). In 1997 to 1998 the ringgit fell from about 2.50 to about 4.88, and Thailand, Indonesia and Korea had to accept IMF conditions. Malaysia's reserves rose from $21.5 billion in 1997 to $132.6 billion in June 2026. Big reserves make attacking a losing bet, and mean the country need not accept the IMF's terms. (builds on [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md))
- Q: Why can Japan owe about twice its economy and borrow cheaply, while Sri Lanka defaulted?
  A: A run on the debt (box 6): who holds it, and in which money, largely decides it. Japan owes yen mostly to itself: its central bank holds about 43% and foreigners about 13% (end 2025). Sri Lanka owed dollars to foreigners and stopped paying on 12 April 2022. Malaysia borrows in ringgit, but foreigners hold about a fifth of its bonds, so its risk is a weaker ringgit, not default. (builds on [The world's balance sheet: what it owns, what it owes, and how countries are built](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-worldbs.md))

| Box 1. Stag hunt: London 2009 | Others stimulate | Others hold back |
|---|---|---|
| You stimulate | Best: your spending leaks abroad, but theirs comes back as exports | Worst: your spending leaks abroad and you carry the debt |
| You hold back | Middle: safe, but you add little to the recovery | Middle: safe, but the slump deepens |

Settles: all act or none. In April 2009 shared fear made each expect the others to act. Misses: leaders were also rescuing their own banks, and some did less than others.

| Box 2. Free rider: debt relief | Other lenders give relief | Other lenders hold out |
|---|---|---|
| You give relief | Good: the borrower recovers and pays more later | Worst: your relief pays the others in full |
| You hold out | Best: you are paid in full from cash others freed | Bad: the borrower stalls or defaults |

Settles: holding out pays each lender whatever the others do, so relief needs a rule binding all. The 2020 pause had none for private lenders. Misses: China's lenders had their own rules on losses.

| Box 3. Prisoner's dilemma: tariffs | Other keeps tariffs low | Other raises tariffs |
|---|---|---|
| You keep tariffs low | Good: trade grows for both | Worst: you lose sales and gain nothing |
| You raise tariffs | Best: you gain at the other's cost | Bad: trade shrinks for both |

Settles: both raise and both lose, unless a deal or fear of next year's reply holds them back. Misses: tariffs also serve home aims such as revenue, jobs and security.

| Box 4. Focal point: the dollar | Others keep the dollar | Others switch |
|---|---|---|
| You keep the dollar | Good: deep markets, cheap to trade | Bad: you are left in the old money |
| You switch | Bad: thin markets, costly hedging | Good, after a costly move |

Settles: all keep or all switch, and the habit is the dollar. Misses: sanctions risk. Freezing Russia's reserves in 2022 raised the cost of holding dollars for some.

| Box 5. Run on a currency: 1997 to 1998 | Other funds attack | Other funds stay |
|---|---|---|
| You attack | Small reserves: best, the currency breaks. Big reserves: bad, the defence holds and the bet costs you | Worst: you bet alone and lose |
| You stay | Middle: you miss the gain, or the loss | Middle: nothing happens |

Settles: with small reserves, all attack or none. Big reserves make staying each fund's best move, and the IMF becomes an outside option, not a must. Misses: in 1998 Malaysia used controls, not only reserves.

| Box 6. Run on a government's debt | Other holders stay | Other holders sell |
|---|---|---|
| You stay | Good: paid in full | Worst: left holding as the price or the currency falls |
| You sell | Bad: you give up the yield | Bad, but better than staying: you got out first |

Settles: all stay or all sell. A pension fund at home mostly cannot leave the currency, a foreign fund can, so a state that owes its own money at home risks a weaker currency, not default. Misses: who pays the loss.

| Box 7. Chicken: the US and China, 2025 to 2026 | Other backs down | Other escalates |
|---|---|---|
| You back down | Middle: calm trade, nobody wins face | Bad: you lose face and the other gains |
| You escalate | Best: you win the standoff | Worst: a full trade war hurts both most |

Settles: each tries to look committed so the other swerves first. Real case: in 2025 the US and China raised tariffs on each other step by step, then agreed a pause after their October 2025 leaders' meeting. That truce is due around 10 November 2026. Misses: both sides also act for audiences at home.

### 8. Read any headline as a game

1. Players: who can act? Include the quiet ones.
2. Moves: what can each do? Two moves each if you can.
3. Payoffs: what does each get from each pair of moves? Best, good, bad or worst.
4. Order and information: who moves first, and who sees what?

Then name the game, and ask what it leaves out: elections, ideology, accidents and plain error.

| Step | Worked example: "Why Foreign Investors Disposed RM5.6 Billion In Malaysian Govt Bonds In July" (Business Today, 10 August 2026) |
|---|---|
| Players | Foreign funds, local holders such as EPF and the banks, Bank Negara |
| Moves | Funds sell or stay. Locals buy or wait. Bank Negara can sell dollars |
| Payoffs | Selling early dodges a ringgit fall but gives up the yield. Locals mostly cannot leave the ringgit |
| Order | Funds watch US yields. Flow data come out a month later |
| Game | A run on the debt (box 6) that did not start: 0.43% of the market, about RM11 billion back into government bonds in August, the ringgit 4.09 to 4.08 in July |
| Left out | The research house blamed outside events: US and Iran tension, oil and US yields |

**Check yourself.** Q: Your turn. The US and China truce is due around 10 November 2026. Fill in the four steps and name the game.
A: Players: the US and China. Moves: extend or escalate. Payoffs: both gain from calm trade, each gains more if the other backs down, both lose most from a clash. Order: each watches the other before the date. Game: chicken.

### Go deeper: Tripwires: dates that would change the picture

| Game | Players | Real case | Tripwire to watch |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stag hunt | G20 governments and central banks | London, 2 April 2009: $1.1 trillion package | Does the Miami summit (14 to 15 December 2026) end with a declaration all present sign? |
| Free rider | Official lenders, private bondholders, the borrower | 2020 debt pause: one private lender joined | Does Ethiopia's bond exchange settle by 31 March 2027? |
| Prisoner's dilemma and chicken | Big trading economies | Early 1930s tariff war, the 2010 currency war, 2025 tariffs | Do the US and China extend their truce, due around 10 November 2026? |
| Focal point | Central banks, exporters, borrowers | Dollar 56.7% of reserves, yuan 2.1% | IMF reserve data for Q3 2026, due about end December 2026 |
| Run on a currency | Speculators, Asian central banks, the IMF | Malaysia's reserves: $21.5 billion (1997) to $132.6 billion (2026) | Malaysia's reserves below 0.8 times short-term foreign debt in any 2027 release |
| Run on debt | Holders of a state's debt | Japan borrows cheaply, Sri Lanka defaulted, Greece needed bailouts | Malaysia's foreign share above 25% or below 18% in a 2027 release |

### Go deeper: A sixth game: the race to the bottom on tax

Countries gain by undercutting each other's tax rates to attract company profits, and all lose revenue if all undercut. That is a prisoner's dilemma, and the 2021 deal set a 15% floor. Malaysia applied it from 1 January 2025. The US did not enact it, and in January 2026 the OECD package shielded US-based groups from the main top-up rules. The largest player took the defector's payoff, and the others accepted it to keep the rest of the deal. The US argues its own minimum taxes do a similar job, which is a real debate, not only defection.

### Go deeper: Three balance-sheet walks: the dollar privilege, defending the ringgit, a euro member borrowing

The dollar privilege. A US household buys Malaysian-made chips. The exporter sells the dollars to its bank, which sells them to Bank Negara, which buys US Treasury bills. No dollars were created abroad. Dollars moved from a US household to a foreign central bank, which lent them back to the US government. The US got goods for IOUs in its own money. Bank Negara created ringgit to buy the dollars, and usually soaks them back up later.

Defending the ringgit. A foreign fund sells Malaysian bonds and wants dollars. Bank Negara sells dollars from its reserves and receives ringgit, so banks' ringgit reserves fall. It then usually tops them back up to keep its interest rate at 2.75%. The cost is dollar reserves, which is why the 0.9 times ratio matters. A defence that lasts too long runs reserves down, as in 1997 to 1998.

A euro member borrowing. Italy spends more than it taxes. It must sell bonds to banks, funds, households and foreigners. The ECB can create euros and buy Italian bonds on the resale market, but only by a decision taken for the whole euro area. In a panic, deposits can move to banks in another euro country, as in Greece, where about EUR 41 billion left before the June 2015 controls.

### Say it back

**Check yourself.** Q: A friend says any country can print its way out of debt. What three locks would you ask about?
A: Does it issue its own currency, does it owe its debt in that currency, and will markets let it print a lot without the currency crashing or inflation taking off?

**Check yourself.** Q: Malaysia borrows 98.8% of its federal debt in ringgit at home, yet a sell-off by foreigners can still weaken the ringgit. Why, and which rung is it on?
A: Domestic debt means borrowed in ringgit in the local market, not held by Malaysians. Foreigners hold about a fifth of its government bonds and can leave the currency, so it only partly opens lock 3. Rung 3, the middle of the ladder, at the strong end of its rung.

**Check yourself.** Q: Which game explains why the world still saves in dollars?
A: A focal point. Money is useful because others use it, so switching pays only if many switch together.

**Check yourself.** Q: From the Bonds chapter: a foreign fund sells Malaysian government bonds. Which part of your life can it reach, and is it automatic?
A: The ringgit, and through it import prices. Not automatic: in 2026 the ringgit held near 4.08 while US yields rose.

> **Day 3 card.** Come back in three days and answer without looking: name the three locks, the game behind the 2020 debt pause, and Malaysia's two kinds of brake.

# Digital credit, dissected: Saylor's 12% and money moving between baskets

Rulebook Level 4 (Futures and debates), chapter 01. Stack: Fundamentals. Id: rb-strc.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#rb-strc . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Michael Saylor pitches Bitcoin as digital capital, STRC as digital credit paying 12%, and a future dollar token paying 8%. This chapter takes the pitch apart claim by claim, follows the money step by step, and asks what really moves when money moves between baskets.*

**In short**
- In October 2026 Michael Saylor of Strategy (once MicroStrategy) pitched a ladder of new money in five layers: Bitcoin as digital capital, STRC as digital credit paying 12%, the company's shares as digital equity, one day a dollar token paying 8%, and digital yield, income paid as often as daily.
- STRC is a preferred share, not a loan or a deposit. It has no end date, no right to your $100 back and no vote, and the company sets its 12% each month. Bitcoin covers it about 4 to 6 times today, and new borrowing would lower that.
- Of 28 claims checked, 11 hold, 11 are spin (true facts in a misleading frame), 3 are wrong and 3 cannot be checked. The numbers about today hold. The labels are where it slips: "strongest credit in the world" for a junk-rated issuer, and a dollar token paying 8% that US law does not allow.
- The flywheel runs both ways. In 2025 Strategy bought more Bitcoin than was mined. In the third quarter of 2026 it raised $5.41 billion, spent only $0.59 billion on Bitcoin and sold Bitcoin to help pay dividends.
- Money moving between baskets? Read three meters. Dollars: trades only move them, bank loans against Bitcoin create new ones. Ownership and risk: these cross, Bitcoin into listed companies, its risk onto savers. Market value: it changes with no dollar crossing.
- Before you believe any account paying 12%, ask who promises the $100, where the 12% comes from, and what happens if the asset halves. Nothing here is advice.

**Built on Levels 1 and 2: recall these before you start.** 
- [Crypto: Set 2 money, dissected](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-crypto.md): Money sits in two baskets: Set 1, the old anchors (gold, government bonds, bank credit), and Set 2, the new rails (stablecoins, tokens, crypto). Stablecoins are Set 1 wearing Set 2 clothes.
- [Today's board: old anchors, new rails](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-12.md): Under the US GENIUS Act a compliant stablecoin holds cash, deposits or short government bills (loans to the government that are paid back within a year), and may not pay holders interest.
- [Bonds: a ticket you can resell, and where it touches your life](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-bonds.md): A bond is a ticket you can resell. Free of default is not free of price.
- [How money is born today](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-06.md): A bank loan creates a new deposit. Repaying it destroys one.
- [Who really creates money: banks, the Fed and the Treasury](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-moneymake.md): Trades between people only move money. Banks also create it when they buy from someone who is not a bank.
- [The money clubs: who writes the rules, who can really print, and the game the world plays](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-clubs.md): Game theory asks each player's best move, given what the others might do.

**Map of this chapter: Digital credit: a pipe between baskets**
- The pitch: Capital, credit, equity, money, yield (see [Crypto: Set 2 money, dissected](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-crypto.md))
- What STRC really is: A preferred share: no end date, no vote (see [Bonds: a ticket you can resell, and where it touches your life](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-bonds.md))
- Claim by claim: 11 hold, 11 spin, 3 wrong (see [Eye-openers: what most people never notice](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-13.md))
- The flywheel and its brakes: Bitcoin down 30%, 50%, 70% (see [When markets fall: buckets, collateral and rotation](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-buckets.md))
- Three meters: Dollars, ownership and risk, value (see [Who really creates money: banks, the Fed and the Treasury](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-moneymake.md))
- The wrapper map: Old and new wrappers, old and new assets (see [Today's board: old anchors, new rails](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-12.md))
- The players: Who gains in a boom, who pays in a bust (see [The money clubs: who writes the rules, who can really print, and the game the world plays](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-clubs.md))
- Before you believe 12%: Ten questions and a ringgit example (see [The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-em.md))

This chapter comes in four parts. Parts 1 to 3 take about ten minutes each. Part 4 is about twice as long. Each part ends with a stop box. The six words you need are in the box below. Nothing here is advice. The aim is to make you a sharper judge of a big pitch.

**Six words you need.** 
- **Preferred stock:** A share paid before the ordinary shares (also called common stock, traded as MSTR) but after every lender. Not a loan, so nothing has to be repaid.
- **Par:** The $100 STRC aims to trade at. A target the company works to hold, not a promise.
- **Perpetual:** No end date. You get money back only by selling to someone else.
- **Convertible note and put:** A loan the lender can swap for shares at a set price, the conversion price. The put lets the lender ask for cash back on set dates instead. Lenders do that when the share price is below the conversion price, because swapping would give them less.
- **mNAV:** What the market says the company is worth (the price of all its shares, with or without its debt and preferred added) divided by the value of the Bitcoin it holds. Above 1, the market values the company at more than its Bitcoin. Today it is about 1.1 counting its debt and preferred, about 0.9 counting the ordinary shares alone (4 November 2026).
- **Gross and net coverage:** How many times over the Bitcoin could pay the claims, meaning what the company owes to lenders and preferred holders. Net first subtracts the company's cash from the claims, so it reads higher.

### Part 1 of 4. The pitch, and what STRC really is

### 1. The pitch in five layers

In a talk recorded in October 2026, Michael Saylor, executive chairman of Strategy, laid out a ladder. It is worth knowing because it is one of the boldest ideas about future money in circulation.

| Layer | What he means | His example |
|---|---|---|
| Digital capital | Bitcoin as digital gold: scarce, capped at 21 million, something a robot cannot make | Bitcoin itself |
| Digital credit | A security paying a steady income, backed by Bitcoin, the way gold once backed credit | STRC, paying 12% a year |
| Digital equity | Whatever is left after the credit is paid: the company's ordinary shares | MSTR, Strategy's common stock |
| Digital money | A future dollar token with no price swings, paying 6% to 8% | Not yet built |
| Digital yield | Income from all of the above, paid as often as daily | STRC has paid daily since 3 November 2026 |

His argument in one line: if gold rising 10% a year let you sell credit paying 5%, then Bitcoin rising 20% a year lets you sell credit paying 10%. Strategy sells that credit to the public, buys Bitcoin with the money, and hopes Bitcoin rises faster than the 12% it pays. Any gap goes to its ordinary shareholders, and the gap can be negative. The 12% itself is owed in dollars. Part 2 tests this argument against history.

### 2. What STRC really is

Read the contract, not the label. STRC is preferred stock: a share in a company that gets paid before the ordinary shares but after every lender. It is not a loan, a bond or a bank account.

| Question | The answer in STRC's own documents |
|---|---|
| Does it end? | No. It is perpetual. There is no date when you get your money back |
| Can I demand $100 back? | No. Only if someone takes over the company. Otherwise you sell at the market price |
| Who sets the 12%? | The company, each month, at its "sole and absolute discretion". It can cut by up to 0.25 point a month. If one-month SOFR (a short-term dollar rate, about 4%) also falls, it can cut by that fall too. It can never go below SOFR |
| Must it pay? | Only "when, as and if declared" by the board. Missed dividends pile up and must be paid before any dividend on shares ranked below STRC, such as the ordinary shares |
| Where does it rank? | Behind about $6.75 billion of debt, almost all convertible notes, and behind another preferred, STRF. Strategy's other preferreds (STRE, STRK and STRD) rank behind STRC |
| Can I vote? | No, not even to elect directors if dividends stop. Only on changes that hurt STRC and some mergers |
| Can claims be put ahead of mine? | Yes. Any new debt ranks ahead of STRC without asking you |
| What backs it? | 849,327 Bitcoin (about $68 billion at $80,500) and a $4.79 billion dollar reserve. Nothing is pledged to STRC alone |
| How big is it? | About $8.2 billion on 1 November 2026, down from about $10.5 billion in July, after buybacks |
| How is the issuer rated? | B- from S&P, a credit rating agency (October 2025). That grade is called junk: riskier than the safer investment grades |

So why does it trade so close to $100? The company sells new STRC only above $100, buys it back below, and raises the rate when buyers lose interest. That $100 is a target, not a promise. And the board that sets your rate owes its main legal duty to the ordinary shareholders. Your rights are only what the contract says.

- **Myth:** STRC is like a bank account that pays 12%.
- **Reality:** A bank account is a debt the bank must repay, and in Malaysia PIDM insures it up to RM250,000 (in the US, the FDIC insures up to $250,000). STRC is a share with no repayment date and no insurance, and its price at the end of trading on 26 June 2026 was $74.57. It is well backed today, but it is not a deposit.

### Go deeper: Two questions, eight instruments compared, and the accounting

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: STRC's daily dividends started on 3 November 2026. Did the change raise what it pays?
  A: No. Shareholders approved it on 28 October with about 99.3% of votes cast. The company's filing says the total paid, the rate and its obligations are unchanged. Only the timing changed. (builds on [Bonds: a ticket you can resell, and where it touches your life](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-bonds.md))
- Q: Can you get exactly $100 back from Strategy?
  A: Not on demand. You can sell to another investor at whatever the market pays, which was $99.98 on 4 November 2026 and $74.57 at the close on 26 June. The company may buy all of it back at $101 if it chooses. (builds on [Eye-openers: what most people never notice](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-13.md))

| Instrument | What backs it | Who promises par | Worst loss on record |
|---|---|---|---|
| STRC | Strategy's Bitcoin and dollar reserve, after all debt and STRF | Nobody. The company aims at $100 | Closed at $74.57 on 26 June 2026, 25% below par |
| British consol (perpetual government debt) | The UK state's power to tax | Nobody had to repay. Redeemed in 2015 | About 85% below its peak by 1974, before inflation (model from yields) |
| Gold-standard credit | Gold reserves plus the issuer | The issuer, by law | The US cancelled gold clauses in 1933 and raised gold from $20.67 to $35, a 41% loss in gold terms |
| Bank preferred stock | The bank's assets after depositors and lenders | Nobody | Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferreds lost about 95% in 2008. Lehman's went to zero |
| Closed-end fund preferred | A diversified portfolio, at least twice the preferred by law | Nobody, but the law forces the fund to cut leverage | Auction-rate versions froze in February 2008. Holders were repaid at par in most cases, after months to years |
| Money market fund | Short government bills and loans | The fund aims at $1, no guarantee | The Reserve Primary Fund fell to $0.97 in 2008 |
| Payment stablecoin | Cash, insured deposits, short bills, by law | The issuer, one for one | USDC fell to about $0.87 for a few days in March 2023 |
| High-yield bond | The company's cash flow, ahead of all shares | The company must repay at the end date | The US junk bond index fell about 26% in 2008 |

What STRC does better than most of this table: its backing is published every Monday in SEC filings, it is large today against the claims ahead of it, it is not pledged to anyone else, and it trades more each day than any other US preferred stock checked (about $156 million a day).

Accounting and law, briefly. Since 2025 Strategy carries Bitcoin at market value, so reported profit swings with the price: $19.53 billion of net income in the third quarter of 2026 came from unrealized Bitcoin gains, not cash. The preferred shares sit in its accounts as temporary equity. Delaware law lets a company pay dividends only out of surplus, which on today's numbers binds only if Bitcoin falls to about $17,700 to $23,500. The founder's class B shares carry ten votes each, about a third of all votes on the company's share counts (to be confirmed in the proxy).

> **Stop here.** Part 1 of 4 done. You know the five layers of the pitch and what STRC really is. Try these three before Part 2.

**Check yourself.** Q: Is STRC a loan, a bond, a bank account or a share?
A: A share: preferred stock. It is paid after every lender and has no repayment date.

**Check yourself.** Q: Who decides STRC's rate each month?
A: Strategy, at its own discretion, within limits: no more than about 0.25 point down a month plus any fall in one-month SOFR, and never below that rate.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why does STRC usually trade near $100?
A: Because the company sells new STRC above $100, buys it back below, and raises the rate when demand falls. It is a target, not a promise.

### Part 2 of 4. Claim by claim

We checked 28 of the talk's claims against Strategy's own SEC filings (reports to the US market regulator), market data, history and the law. "Spin" means the facts are true but the frame misleads. The claims about today's numbers hold. The words wrapped around them are where it slips.

| What he said | Verdict | The honest version |
|---|---|---|
| STRC is "six times over-collateralized" | Holds, on his method | 6.1 times if you subtract the company's cash first, 4.2 without. Nothing is pledged to STRC, and new debt would lower both |
| About 48 years of dividends are covered | Holds, with both yardsticks | About 46 years in Bitcoin, 3.2 to 3.4 years in dollars, and he gave the dollar figure himself. Paying from Bitcoin means selling it |
| It is "the strongest credit in the world" | Wrong | The issuer is rated junk (B-) and STRC is a share behind about $8 billion of claims. Fair version: well covered for now |
| For a New Yorker it is like a bank account paying 24% | Spin | Only for a top-bracket New York City taxpayer, and only as a delay: each payment is treated as part of your own money handed back, so the price you are counted as having paid goes down, and the tax comes back when you sell |
| Gold rising 10% a year let you sell credit at 5%, so Bitcoin rising 20% lets you sell it at 10% | Spin | Gold-backed credit never paid out of gold's rise: the gold price was fixed by law ($20.67 an ounce in the US until 1933) and British consols (government bonds with no end date) paid 3% from taxes. STRC's 12% is owed in dollars whatever Bitcoin does |
| Money needed in four months to four years belongs in digital credit | Spin | STRC fell 25% below par within weeks in June 2026, and swung about five times as much as a US bond fund over the year. It pays more than a money fund because it can fall like a share |
| A Bitcoin-backed dollar token could pay 6% to 8% | Wrong for a US payment stablecoin | The GENIUS Act bans issuer yield and Bitcoin reserves. Offshore a token can hold some Bitcoin (USDT does), but it still pays holders nothing |
| Since August 2020, Bitcoin returned 37% a year and MSTR 51% | Spin | Bitcoin's 37% checks out when we redo the sum. MSTR's comes out near 46%. Of seven start dates tested, MSTR led from five, gold led from the November 2021 peak, and MSTR was last from January 2025 |

> **The pattern behind the verdicts.** The claims that hold are about today's numbers on the company's own method. The claims that fail come in three kinds: labels that borrow trust from safer products (credit, bank account, stablecoin, strongest), stories with the dates bent (the return table above), and sums that skip a step (the claim that selling $10 billion of credit "made" $10 billion). The full audit box has more of each. So ask first what a thing is in law, then what it pays.

And in fairness, the critics' sharpest claim, that it is a Ponzi scheme, also fails the test. A Ponzi scheme pays old investors only with new investors' money and hides that it has no real asset. Strategy owns a real, public asset worth several times STRC, and discloses every week where the dividend money comes from. The true point inside the criticism is narrower: the dividends depend on the company continuing to raise new money, because its software business earned only $14.3 million of cash from its normal business in nine months. So the 12% is paid in dollars from three places: the dollar reserve, money from selling new shares (ordinary or preferred) and, when those run short, selling Bitcoin. Bitcoin's rise pays nothing unless Bitcoin is sold.

### Go deeper: The full audit: 28 claims and what each flips on
