> **Stop here.** Part 2 of 4 done. You can separate the numbers from the labels. Try these three before Part 3.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why do "48 years" and "3.4 years" of dividends both hold?
A: 48 years (about 46 today) counts the Bitcoin, which pays only if it is sold. 3.2 to 3.4 years counts the dollars on hand, which pay without selling anything. Saylor gave both.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why can a US payment stablecoin not pay 8% backed by Bitcoin?
A: The 2025 GENIUS Act bans issuers from paying holders yield and allows only cash-like reserves, not Bitcoin or preferred stock.

**Check yourself.** Q: What does the return table depend on most?
A: The start date. From August 2020 Bitcoin and MSTR lead. From the November 2021 peak, gold and the S&P 500 beat both, and from January 2025 MSTR is last.

### Part 3 of 4. The flywheel, and what turns it backwards

Saylor calls it a triple flywheel. Sell credit, buy Bitcoin, the price rises a little, the company's shares are worth more than the Bitcoin it holds, so selling shares buys even more Bitcoin per share, the cushion under the credit grows, and the credit gets cheaper to sell. Each link pushes the next.

*[Picture on the web page: Eight links. In a bull market each pushes the next. In a bear market each link can run backwards, and the question is which brake holds first.]*

The key link is the premium, mNAV: the company's value compared with its Bitcoin. Above 1, selling new shares buys more Bitcoin per share. For example, if each share stands for $100 of Bitcoin but sells for $110, each new share brings in $110 of Bitcoin, so every share ends up with a little more. Below 1, it does the opposite: a new share sold for $90 brings in less Bitcoin than each old share already holds, so every share ends up with a little less. The company has said it may then sell Bitcoin instead (reported December 2025). The premium was about 2.5 to 3.5 at the late-2024 peak (press estimates). On 4 November 2026 it was about 1.1 on the company's measure, which adds its debt and preferred to the share value and takes away its cash, and about 0.9 on the shares alone.

| Brake | Where it bites | Reading in early November 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Bitcoin against what Strategy paid | Below $75,451 the whole pile is worth less than it cost | $80,500, only 6.7% above cost. The 2026 low was about $57,700 on 1 July |
| The premium (mNAV) | Below 1, selling shares to pay dividends shrinks Bitcoin per share, and the company says it may sell Bitcoin instead | About 1.1 on the company's measure, 0.9 on the shares alone (4 November) |
| Dollars on hand | Company policy, as reported: keep at least 12 months of dividends | $4.92 billion of dollar assets (the $4.79 billion reserve plus $0.13 billion of other cash), about 39 months |
| STRC's price | Below $100 the company stops selling and starts buying back | $99.98 (4 November). It paid about $99.50 a share in buybacks in the week to 1 November |
| Convertible notes | Holders can demand cash when the share price is below the conversion price | $5.91 billion can be put back for cash from September 2027 to September 2028. Every conversion price is above today's share price |

> **The real stress point.** Not the 12% dividends. The convertible notes. Two years of dividends (about $3 billion) plus the $5.91 billion of notes holders can cash in come to about $8.9 billion, against $4.92 billion of dollars on hand, a gap of about $4 billion. Strategy can refinance, sell shares or sell Bitcoin. Closing the gap by selling Bitcoin would take about 99,000 coins if Bitcoin halved, 60% of a year's new supply. When note holders ask for their cash, it tests whether Strategy can borrow again or sell new shares to pay them. It is not a default, as long as lenders and share buyers are still willing.

| If Bitcoin falls | Price | Bitcoin over all debt and preferred (gross, cash not counted) | Months of dividends the dollars on hand can pay (does not change with the Bitcoin price) | Bitcoin to sell a year for dividends once the reserve runs low, if no shares are sold | Bitcoin to sell for the 2027 to 2028 note puts, if not refinanced |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Today | $80,500 | 3.4 times | 39 | about 19,000 (11% of a year's new coins) | about 50,000 (30%) |
| Down 30% | $56,400 | 2.4 times | 39 | about 27,000 (16%) | about 71,000 (43%) |
| Down 50% | $40,300 | 1.7 times | 39 | about 37,000 (23%) | about 99,000 (60%) |
| Down 70% | $24,200 | 1.0 times | 39 | about 62,000 (38%) | about 165,000 (a full year) |

This is a model, not a forecast, with debts and reserve held fixed. First, the reserve could pay about 27 months of dividends before it reaches the 12-month floor (39 months on hand minus the 12 months the company keeps). That is the best case, not a promise: in the third quarter of 2026 Strategy sold Bitcoin for dividends with about $5 billion in the reserve. Second, see the ladder below for where each kind of cover runs out. Third, the note puts, not the dividends, are the big bill: at minus 70% they would take a full year of new Bitcoin. Fourth, cover is not price: STRC fell 25% in June 2026 while its Bitcoin was still worth more than twice every claim up to STRC.

| One backing ladder (1 November 2026, model) | Times covered today | Bitcoin price where it falls to 1 time |
|---|---|---|
| STRC, company method: claims up to STRC, less dollars | 6.1 | about $13,250 |
| STRC, gross | 4.2 | about $19,000 |
| All debt and preferred, less dollars | 4.5 | about $17,700 |
| All debt and preferred, gross | 3.4 | about $23,500 |

If you remember one number, take the last row: everything the company owes is covered 3.4 times today, and that falls to 1 time if Bitcoin drops to about $23,500. If you remember one danger, take the note puts: from September 2027 holders can ask for $5.91 billion in cash, more than the dollars on hand, and a falling share price makes them more likely to ask.

### It already ran backwards once

In the third quarter of 2026 Strategy raised $5.41 billion by selling shares, but spent only $0.59 billion on Bitcoin. The rest went into its dollar reserve, buying back STRC below $100, and dividends. It sold $348.6 million of Bitcoin in the quarter (at the value on its books), $239.9 million of it to pay dividends. The share sales were defending the credit instead of buying Bitcoin. The talk did not mention it.

### Go deeper: Two questions, and precedents: when reflexive structures turned

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: Does Strategy really buy all the Bitcoin that is mined?
  A: Sometimes. In 2025 it bought 225,030 against 164,250 mined, 137%. In the third quarter of 2026 it bought about 18% of the new coins but sold most of that back, adding only about 4%. Its buying swings with the premium. (builds on [Crypto: Set 2 money, dissected](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-crypto.md))
- Q: What is the biggest bill Strategy faces before 2029: the 12% dividends or something else?
  A: Something else: $5.91 billion of convertible notes that holders can cash in from September 2027, because every conversion price is above today's share price. (builds on [Bonds: a ticket you can resell, and where it touches your life](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-bonds.md))

| Case | What powered it | What broke it, and how fast | Who was paid first | Same and different now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| South Sea Company, 1720 | A premium: shares above the value of its real asset, interest-paying government debt, let it take in more debt cheaply | Shares fell from about £1,000 in June to about £135 by the end of 1720, within about three months | Insiders who sold early, and the government, which refinanced its debt | Same: a premium over a real asset can vanish while the asset stays. The company survived, but late buyers lost about 85%. Different: Strategy's asset is public and trades every day |
| Mississippi Company, 1719 to 1720 | The issuer pegged its own share price by printing notes | The peg was dropped and shares fell about 90% within a year | Holders who switched to land or coin early | Same: an issuer defending its own paper. Different: Strategy defends STRC with a finite reserve, so the defence ends when the reserve does |
| Goldman Sachs Trading Corporation, 1928 to 1932 | Trusts stacked on trusts, financed with preferred stock and debt | Issued at $104, above $220 in early 1929, under $2 by 1932 | Debt and preferred before common | Same: common shares levered by preferred and debt, priced above their assets at the peak. Different: Strategy holds one asset directly, with no cross-holdings |
| MicroStrategy itself, March 2000 | A dot-com valuation | A restatement of results cut the stock 62% in one day | No debt crisis | Same founder and company. Different: the asset can now be checked on the blockchain by anyone |
| UK split-capital zero shares, 2001 to 2002 | Low-risk shares sold to savers, paid at a set date if the trust's assets were enough | A bear market plus hidden cross-holdings and bank debt, over about two years. Compensation averaged about 40% of losses | Bank lenders, then the zeros | Same: a safe-sounding class resting on a volatile pool. Different: zeros had an end date and hidden holdings. STRC has none and Strategy's holdings are public |
| Closed-end fund discounts, a standing puzzle | A fixed pool on an exchange with no right to redeem | Discounts can last for years and widen in stress (Lee, Shleifer and Thaler, 1991) | Not applicable | Same: MSTR's shares alone trade near 0.9 of its Bitcoin. Different: Strategy can buy back shares or sell Bitcoin faster than a fund board usually acts |
| GBTC premium to discount, 2021 to 2022 | The only easy wrapper for Bitcoin in a brokerage account | Rival wrappers arrived. A premium of about 35% became a discount of about 47% to 50% within about 22 months | Holders who sold at the premium, and the sponsor's fees | Same: a premium from wrapper scarcity. Different: ETFs now offer the wrapper at no premium, and GBTC had no fixed claims |
| Celsius, BlockFi and Terra, 2022 | Double-digit yields on crypto, payable on demand | Runs within days to weeks. Withdrawals frozen, then bankruptcies | Secured lenders and early redeemers | Same: a yield far above bills sold to savers. Different: STRC has no right to redeem, so a run shows up as a lower price, not a frozen account |

What is the same across the table: the premium is the engine, the premium rests on one volatile asset, the issuer defends its own paper with a finite pool, and the product is sold to savers as near-cash (the talk's four-months-to-four-years ladder).

> **Stop here.** Part 3 of 4 done. You know the loop, its brakes and where it bit in 2026. Try these three before Part 4.

**Check yourself.** Q: What is mNAV, and why does it matter if it falls below 1?
A: The company's value compared with the Bitcoin it holds. Below 1, selling new shares to pay dividends or buy Bitcoin shrinks the Bitcoin each share owns. The company's measure adds its debt and preferred, so it reads higher (about 1.1) than the shares alone (about 0.9).

**Check yourself.** Q: What happened to Strategy's new money in the third quarter of 2026?
A: It raised $5.41 billion from shares but spent only $0.59 billion on Bitcoin. The other 89% went to the dollar reserve, STRC buybacks and dividends, and it sold Bitcoin to help pay them.

**Check yourself.** Q: What is the binding stress point before 2029?
A: About $5.91 billion of convertible notes that holders can cash in from September 2027, more than the dollars on hand.

### Part 4 of 4. Money moving between baskets: three meters

Here is the big idea to test. It comes from the person who runs this site, not from Saylor: future money moving between baskets. The pitch says digital credit pulls money out of the old basket (money funds, government bills, bank deposits) and into the new one (Bitcoin). To see what really moves, read three meters, not one.

| Meter | What moves it | Digital credit | Stablecoins |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Dollars | Trades move dollars between people. A bank loan, or a bank buying from a non-bank, creates new ones. Repaying destroys them | Buying STRC and Bitcoin moves dollars to the Bitcoin seller. A bank loan against Bitcoin creates new ones | Buying a bill moves dollars to the bill's seller |
| 2. Ownership and risk | Who holds which asset and carries its swings | Bitcoin into a listed company, its risk onto savers | Bills behind crypto tokens, the issuer's risk onto holders |
| 3. Market value | The last trade sets the price of every unit. If one buyer pays $1,000 more for one coin, all the coins are counted as worth $1,000 more each, though only one buyer paid | Buying can lift all 20 million mined coins by more than was spent, or fail to | Near $1 while the backing holds |

*[Picture on the web page: Follow one $10,000. The saver's dollars pass through the wrapper (the legal package around an asset, here STRC and Strategy) to whoever sold the Bitcoin and stay in the dollar basket. What crosses the line is Bitcoin, into a listed company, and Bitcoin's risk, onto the saver. A bank loan against Bitcoin, not drawn here, would add new dollars.]*

1. A saver moves $10,000 from a money market fund into STRC. The fund sells $10,000 of bills. If a household or another fund buys them, dollars only move. If a bank buys them, it creates a new deposit to pay. The saver's dollars go to Strategy.
2. Strategy buys $10,000 of Bitcoin from a miner or an early holder. The dollars go to the seller, who parks them in a bank, a bill or a money fund. No dollar enters Bitcoin. Bitcoin enters a listed company.
3. Strategy pays the saver a daily dividend from its dollar reserve, which was raised by selling new shares. In effect new shareholders pay the preferred holders.
4. In a bear market Strategy sells Bitcoin to pay the dividend. A Bitcoin buyer's dollars go to the saver, and Bitcoin leaves the wrapper. This happened in the third quarter of 2026.
5. A different door: a bank lends $10,000 to someone who pledges Bitcoin. The bank creates a new $10,000 deposit, so the new basket helps create old-basket dollars. Repaying destroys it. Saylor calls this a tailwind. Its size today is unknown: no public total was found.

> **What really crosses the line.** In steps 1 to 4 dollars change hands inside the dollar basket, adding a little only if a bank buys the bills in step 1. What moves is ownership and risk: a listed company holds the Bitcoin in boom years, outside buyers in bust years, and the saver's claim on bills becomes a share resting on Bitcoin. In step 5 this site's picture is literally true: pledged Bitcoin brings new dollars into being. And market value moves with no dollar crossing. So money does move between baskets, as ownership, risk and value, and at the edges as new money.

| Channel | Direction | 2025 (Bitcoin boom) | 2026 to date (the turn) | 2022 (crypto bear) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategy preferred sales, including STRC | Toward Bitcoin | $7.04 billion | $7.53 billion in nine months, none in the third quarter | none |
| Strategy ordinary share sales | Toward Bitcoin, or into the dollar reserve | $16.27 billion | $13.66 billion in nine months | $0.05 billion |
| Strategy Bitcoin purchases (the pipe's exit) | Dollars to Bitcoin sellers | $22.47 billion | $14.26 billion in nine months, $0.59 billion in the third quarter | $0.29 billion |
| Bank loans against Bitcoin | Creates new dollars | no public figure | no public figure | no public figure |
| Strategy's dollar reserve | Back into bills and money funds | set up with $1.44 billion in December (reported) | up $3.35 billion to 1 November | did not exist |
| STRC buybacks below $100 | Back: dollars to sellers of STRC | none | about $2.04 billion | did not exist |
| Strategy Bitcoin sales | Back: Bitcoin out of the wrapper | none | $431.8 million in nine months | $11.8 million (for tax) |
| US spot Bitcoin ETFs | Both ways, no leverage | not checked | about minus $5.8 billion by mid July, about plus $0.3 billion to $1.2 billion by early October (press reports) | did not exist |
| Stablecoin supply | Bills and cash put behind crypto tokens | up $100.5 billion | down $9.1 billion to 5 November | down $24.5 billion |

Read it by period: boom, turn and bust. In the 2025 boom the channels toward Bitcoin ran hard. In the third quarter of 2026 the channels back to dollars took over. In the 2022 bear the pipe barely existed. The biggest flow, stablecoins, is not digital credit at all.

### Go deeper: The ledger in detail: both floors, and the smaller channels

Two floors. Upstairs are bank reserves and the Fed's reverse repo. Downstairs are the deposits the public holds. A money fund that pays out by drawing on the Fed's reverse repo pushes new reserves and deposits into being, but money funds and other non-banks used only about $0.2 billion of it on 28 October 2026, so today the pipe barely touches the upstairs floor. Downstairs, the final buyer decides: a bill sold to a household or another fund only moves deposits, a bill sold to a bank creates them, and when Strategy's reserve buys bills from a bank, deposits shrink again. Nobody publishes who the final buyers were, so the net effect is not known.

| Smaller channel | Direction | 2025 | 2026 to date | 2022 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Strategy convertible notes | Toward Bitcoin | $2.0 billion | none | none |
| Convertible notes bought back | Back | not checked | $1.38 billion | none |
| Strive's SATA preferred | Toward Bitcoin | not checked | $1.29 billion outstanding on 30 September | did not exist |
| Other listed Bitcoin companies | Toward Bitcoin | No yearly flow found. Listed companies hold about 1.30 million Bitcoin in all, 849,327 of it Strategy's |  |  |
| Preferred dividends paid in cash | Inside the dollar basket | $0.38 billion | $1.05 billion in nine months | none |
| US money fund assets | Into the old basket | up $0.95 trillion | not checked | up $0.02 trillion |

| Pool (late 2026) | Size | Digital credit (about $14.7 billion: Strategy's preferreds plus SATA, a similar preferred from another company, Strive) as a share |
|---|---|---|
| US money market funds | $7.9 trillion | 0.19% |
| US government bills | $7.1 trillion | 0.21% |
| US bank deposits | $19.6 trillion | 0.08% |
| Dollar stablecoins (dollar claims on new rails) | $295 billion | 5.0% |
| All Bitcoin | $1.62 trillion | 0.9% |
| New Bitcoin mined in a year | about $13 billion | about 110% |

Against the dollar pools digital credit is under a quarter of one percent. Against new coins it is large. But Bitcoin's price is set by everyone holding the 20 million coins already mined. Strategy bought more than every new coin in 2025 and in the first nine months of 2026, yet Bitcoin fell from about $126,000 in October 2025 to about $57,700 on 1 July 2026. Big buying can lift the price. It cannot promise to.

Now run the same test on stablecoins. When an issuer buys a bill, its dollars go to the bill's seller. What changes is who owns the bills: in 2025 stablecoin growth put about $100.5 billion more of bills and cash behind crypto tokens, about 14 times Strategy's preferred sales ($7.04 billion). In 2026 it shrank by $9.1 billion. From 18 January 2027 at the latest, a licensed US issuer must hold only cash-like reserves. Offshore issuers are not bound the same way: Tether's USDT reported about $8.4 billion of Bitcoin and $19.1 billion of gold among about $191 billion of assets on 30 September 2026 (as summarized from its accountant's report).

| Wrapper, then what sits inside | Old-basket asset inside (bills, deposits, gold) | New-basket asset inside (Bitcoin) |
|---|---|---|
| Old-basket wrapper (US law, listed, regulated) | Money market fund, bank deposit | STRC and other digital credit, spot Bitcoin ETFs, Strategy's shares, a bank loan secured on Bitcoin |
| New-basket wrapper (a token on a blockchain) | Compliant stablecoins such as USDC, tokenized bill funds | Bitcoin itself. USDT, with some Bitcoin and gold behind it, is a partial case |

Saylor's 8% digital money would stack three layers: a token (new wrapper) holding digital credit (old wrapper) holding Bitcoin (new asset). Ask of any product which wrapper it wears, what sits inside, and which meter it moves.

| Reading of "Set 1 absorbs Set 2" | Evidence to November 2026 | Test that would settle it, and when |
|---|---|---|
| A. Absorption: old-basket wrappers swallow Bitcoin | Listed companies hold about 1.3 million Bitcoin, 6.5% of coins mined so far. US spot ETFs hold about $106 billion to $111 billion (press) | Wrappers' share of Bitcoin keeps rising through a bust. Each quarter end, next 31 December 2026 |
| B. Leakage: old-basket cash drains into Bitcoin | $7.53 billion of preferreds sold in nine months of 2026, but the dollars stay, and digital credit is 0.19% of money funds | Money fund assets or bills fall in a quarter of heavy digital credit sales. First quarter 2027 |
| C. Two-way valve: toward Bitcoin in booms, back in busts | 2026 shows both: $431.8 million of Bitcoin sold and $3.35 billion parked in dollars | Bitcoin sold for dividends two quarters in a row. Reports for late 2026 and early 2027 |
| D. Risk transfer: savers carry Bitcoin's risk under a credit label | STRC closed 25% below par in June 2026 | STRC below $90 for 20 trading days while Bitcoin is above Strategy's cost. Any month |
| E. Collateral bridge: Bitcoin starts backing new dollars | Bank loans against Bitcoin have no public total. USDT holds about $8.4 billion of Bitcoin | Bitcoin's share of the biggest stablecoin's reserves rises. Tether's next report, early 2027 |

> **Verdict on the project's earlier view.** An earlier finding of this project was that Set 1 is absorbing Set 2. On the evidence to November 2026, A and D fit best, C is live, B fails the money meter, and E is real but too small to measure. Extended: old wrappers absorb Bitcoin, some savers take on its risk under a credit label, in a bust the wrapper sells Bitcoin back into dollars, and at the edges Bitcoin starts to back new dollars. That is money moving between baskets, read on three meters.

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: You pay $100 for STRC. Where are your dollars a week later?
  A: With whoever sold Strategy its Bitcoin, or in Strategy's dollar reserve. In the third quarter of 2026 only about $0.59 billion of the $5.41 billion raised reached Bitcoin sellers. (builds on [Who really creates money: banks, the Fed and the Treasury](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-moneymake.md))
- Q: A bank lends you $10,000 against your Bitcoin. Did money move between baskets, or was new money made?
  A: New money was made. The loan creates a new $10,000 deposit, backed by new-basket collateral. It is the clearest case where the new basket helps create old-basket dollars. When you repay, that money disappears again. (builds on [How money is born today](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-06.md))
- Q: The biggest stablecoin holds about 100,000 Bitcoin. Is that already Saylor's digital money?
  A: Partly. USDT is a dollar token with some Bitcoin and gold behind it, issued offshore. But it pays holders nothing, and its Bitcoin is about 4% of its assets. Saylor's version would pay 6% to 8%, which a US payment stablecoin may not do. (builds on [Today's board: old anchors, new rails](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-12.md))

> **Before you believe any account paying 12%.** Ask ten questions. Is it a deposit, or a share? Who promises the $100, if anyone? Who sets the rate, and can they cut it? Where does the money come from: profits, new investors, or selling the asset? What happens if the asset behind it halves? What do I rank behind? Can I vote? Who is selling it to me, and what do they earn? What tax applies to me? What currency risk do I take? This is general education, not advice.

> **For a Malaysian saver.** PIDM covers bank deposits up to RM250,000, not shares. Malaysia does not tax foreign income that resident individuals bring home until the end of 2036, with conditions and exceptions (check the latest guideline from LHDN, Malaysia's tax office). There is no US tax treaty with Malaysia: Strategy expects its payments to be return of capital, but a broker may still hold back 30%, and getting it back means filing a US tax return. US estate tax (a tax on what a person leaves when they die) can apply above $60,000 of US shares. And the currency cuts both ways: when the ringgit rose about 22% against the dollar from February 2024 to February 2026 (from 4.77 to 3.91 ringgit per dollar), a dollar asset lost about 18% in ringgit. Fewer ringgit per dollar means a stronger ringgit.

Worked example (a model, not a forecast): RM10,000 at 4.05 ringgit to the dollar on 5 November 2026 buys $2,469 of STRC at $100. A year at 12% pays $296. The end rates are past levels, used only to show the range.

| After one year | Dividend kept | Ringgit per dollar | Worth | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| No US tax held back, ringgit unchanged | $296 | 4.05 | RM11,200 | gain of 12.0% |
| 30% held back, ringgit unchanged | $207 | 4.05 | RM10,840 | gain of 8.4% |
| 30% held back, ringgit as strong as February 2026 | $207 | 3.91 | RM10,465 | gain of 4.7% |
| 30% held back, ringgit as weak as February 2024 | $207 | 4.77 | RM12,767 | gain of 27.7% |
| 30% held back, sold at the June 2026 low close of $74.57 | $207 | 4.05 | RM8,297 | loss of 17.0% |

### Go deeper: The players, their payoff boxes, and the classic yield traps

| Box 1. The treasury-company race (outcome for your company) | Others buy Bitcoin with new paper | Others hold back |
|---|---|---|
| You buy Bitcoin with new paper | Middle: everyone's premium shrinks toward 1 as Bitcoin exposure becomes common | Best: you keep the premium and become the default wrapper |
| You hold back | Worst: your premium vanishes as rivals grow | Middle: nothing changes |

Where it ends up: everyone issues while any premium exists, so the premium is competed away. By June 2026 two rivals, Metaplanet and Nakamoto, traded near 0.9 times their Bitcoin (press reports). What it leaves out: Strategy's size gave it an edge, and Bitcoin ETFs cap plain exposure at 1 time.

| Box 2. A run on the preferred | Other holders sell | Other holders hold |
|---|---|---|
| You sell | Outcome for you: a lower price, as low as $71.25 during 26 June 2026 and $74.57 at the close | Best outcome for you: you got out near $100 before the fall |
| You hold | Bad outcome: the price gaps, but dividends continue while the reserve lasts | Good outcome: 12% at a steady price |

Where it ends up: with no right to redeem, a run only moves the price. The issuer can change the outcomes by raising the rate and buying back below $100. That worked in 2026, at the cost of the reserve and new shares. What it leaves out: funds that must value their holdings at market prices every day sell regardless, which is why June gapped.

| Box 3. The regulator's choice on stablecoin yield | Industry pays yield through exchanges and sister companies | Industry pays no yield |
|---|---|---|
| Regulator allows yield | Stablecoins compete with money funds and deposits, and an 8% Bitcoin-backed token becomes possible in form | Same, with less friction |
| Regulator bans yield, sister companies included | Fights over enforcement. Yield moves into tokenized funds or tokenized STRC | Today's rule: issuers keep the bill income, banks keep deposits |

Where it ends up: banks want a full ban, exchanges a narrow one. The winner decides whether "digital money paying 8%" can ever be a payment stablecoin or only an investment product. What it leaves out: tokenized money funds already pay holders the bill yield legally.

| If this happens | What the pipe does | Who gains | Who loses | Tell to watch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bitcoin boom, premium above 1.2 | Toward Bitcoin: shares and credit sold, Bitcoin bought, perhaps more than is mined | Common holders, Bitcoin sellers | Short sellers | The premium above 1.2 for a month, in Strategy's weekly filings |
| Bitcoin bust, premium at or below 1 | Backwards: buybacks, a bigger dollar reserve, Bitcoin sold to pay dividends | Bitcoin buyers at low prices | Common holders first, then STRC's price | Bitcoin sales in a weekly filing, or the reserve below 12 months |
| Interest rates fall | Easier: 12% looks better against 4% bills | Strategy | Money funds | Federal Reserve decisions |
| Interest rates rise | Harder: savers compare 12% with 4% to 5% risk-free | Money funds, stablecoin issuers | Bitcoin treasury companies | The 10-year yield above 5% (4.90% on 4 November) |
| Stablecoin yield allowed | A competing yield, but also a door to Bitcoin-backed digital money | Stablecoin issuers, exchanges | Banks, through lost deposits | The final stablecoin rules and the market-structure bill in Congress |
| Tax treatment changes | STRC's tax edge shrinks if its payments become taxable dividends | No one in particular | STRC holders | Strategy's 2026 annual report and tax notice, early 2027 |
| MSTR dropped from an index | Passive selling, the premium falls | Arbitrageurs | Common holders | MSCI's November 2026 review (press reports) |

| Player | Wants | Best move in a boom | Best move in a bust |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strategy's management | More Bitcoin per share, an unbroken dividend record | Sell shares and credit, buy Bitcoin | Build the dollar reserve, buy back STRC, sell Bitcoin if needed |
| Common shareholders | Bitcoin per share up faster than Bitcoin | Hold | They pay for the reserve through dilution |
| STRC buyers | 12% near $100, liquidity, a tax delay | Buy near par | Hold through price gaps, or sell at a discount |
| Convertible note holders | Their money back | Convert into shares | Demand cash from 2027 |
| Bitcoin sellers (miners, early holders) | Dollars at a good price | Sell into Strategy's demand | Buy back cheaply from forced sellers |
| Copycat companies | A premium of their own | Issue and buy Bitcoin | Trade below their Bitcoin |
| Bitcoin ETFs | Fees | Offer plain Bitcoin at no premium | Absorb redemptions |
| Banks | Keep deposits, lend against Bitcoin once they can hold it | Offer Bitcoin-backed loans, which create new dollars | Take losses on those loans |
| Stablecoin issuers | Keep the bill income | Grow supply | Shrink, as in 2026 |
| US Treasury | Cheap funding for its bills | Welcome stablecoin demand for bills | Note that digital credit competes with bills for savers |
| The Fed | Stable prices | Higher rates make 12% look smaller | Cuts help the spread story |
| Index providers (MSCI, S&P) | Credible indexes | Include MSTR, bringing passive buying | Exclude it, forcing passive selling |
| Short sellers and arbitrageurs | Spread income | Sell the premium | Cover |
| US regulators (SEC, OCC) | Disclosure and stability | Few moves | Scrutiny of words like credit and bank account |
| Malaysian regulators (Securities Commission, Bank Negara) | Protect local savers | Keep a list of licensed brokers | Warn about unlicensed platforms on an alert list |

| Yield trap | Promised | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| Goldman Sachs Trading Corporation, 1928 to 1932 | Leveraged returns on stacked trusts | Issued at $104, above $220 in early 1929, under $2 by 1932 |
| UK split-capital zeros, 2000 to 2002 | Low-risk fixed growth | Many lost most of their value. Buyers were not told about cross-holdings |
| Terra's Anchor, 2021 to 2022 | About 19.5% on a dollar stablecoin | Fell to near zero in May 2022 |
| Celsius, 2020 to 2022 | Double-digit yields on crypto deposits | Froze withdrawals in June 2022 |

What STRC is not, in fairness: a hidden-leverage scheme. Its terms, holdings, reserve and dividend funding are disclosed in SEC filings every week. Its yield is high because its risk is real, and the prospectus says so.

### Go deeper: Tripwires: dates that would change the picture

| Tripwire | When | What it would mean |
|---|---|---|
| Strategy sells Bitcoin to pay dividends in two quarters in a row | Quarterly reports, next early 2027 | The reverse valve is the normal state, not a one-off |
| The dollar reserve falls below 12 months (about $1.5 billion) | Any weekly filing | The company's own floor is breached |
| STRC below $90 for 20 trading days while Bitcoin is above Strategy's cost | Any month | Buyers price STRC as equity, not credit |
| Convertible note holders demand cash | From 15 September 2027 | The first real refinancing test |
| Strategy's payments become taxable dividends | 2026 annual report and tax notice, early 2027 | STRC's tax edge shrinks for US holders |
| A US rule allows stablecoin yield, or bans it through sister companies too | Stablecoin rules and the market-structure bill, 2026 to 2027 | Decides whether digital money paying 8% can exist |
| STRC's rate cut below 12% with the price at or above $100 for three months | Monthly rate notices | The bull case working: buyers accept less for the same paper |
| Three years of unbroken STRC dividends | August 2028 (Saylor's own test) | Digital credit passes the test its promoter set |
| Bitcoin's share of the biggest stablecoin's reserves rises | Tether's quarterly reports, next early 2027 | The collateral bridge (reading E) is growing |
| MSCI's new screen drops MSTR from its indexes | November 2026 review (press reports) | Index funds must sell, and the premium brake bites |

**Curiosity questions**
- Q: Strategy holds about 4% of all the Bitcoin that will ever exist. The US government holds 8,133 tonnes of gold. What share of all gold is that?
  A: About 3.6% of the roughly 224,200 tonnes above ground at the end of September 2026. One company now holds a bigger share of Bitcoin than the largest official holder does of gold. (builds on [Commodity money and the gold standard](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-02.md))
- Q: Is digital credit a new asset class or one company's funding tool?
  A: Today it is about $14.7 billion, about 91% of it from one issuer ($13.4 billion), plus a few copies. Saylor says credit investors want three years of unbroken dividends. STRC has about 15 months. Ask again in 2028, after the convertible notes come due. (builds on [Crypto: Set 2 money, dissected](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/rulebook/rb-crypto.md))

### Say it back

**Check yourself.** Q: When a saver buys STRC and Strategy buys Bitcoin, where do the saver's dollars end up?
A: With whoever sold the Bitcoin, who usually puts them back into deposits, bills or money funds. The trade moves dollars. It does not create or destroy them.

**Check yourself.** Q: Name the three meters, and one thing each shows.
A: Dollars: trades move them, bank loans against Bitcoin create them. Ownership and risk: Bitcoin moves into a listed company and its risk onto the saver. Market value: every trade reprices all the coins, with no dollar crossing.

**Check yourself.** Q: Name three questions to ask before believing an account that pays 12%.
A: For example: is it a deposit or a share, who promises the $100, where does the 12% come from, can they cut it, and what happens if the asset halves.

# Glossary (Fundamentals)

- **Algorithmic stablecoin:** A token that tries to hold $1 using its own sister token instead of real reserves. TerraUSD collapsed this way in 2022.
- **Asian Dollar Market:** The offshore market for US dollar deposits and loans that Singapore opened in 1968.
- **Asset:** Something you own that has value, such as cash, a house, a bond or a share in a company.
- **Bank deposit:** Money in a bank account. Legally it is the bank's debt to you.
- **Bank note reporter:** A booklet from the free banking era listing what each bank's notes were worth and which were forgeries.
- **Bank reserves:** Money that commercial banks keep in accounts at the central bank, used to settle payments between banks.
- **Barter:** Trading goods directly for other goods, with no money in between.
- **Base money:** Paper cash plus the reserves that banks hold at the central bank.
- **Blockchain:** A ledger copied across thousands of computers and updated in blocks, very hard to change after the fact.
- **Bond:** An IOU sold by a government or company: it pays a fixed rent (the coupon) and returns the money on a set date.
- **Breakeven inflation:** The inflation rate the bond market is pricing in, read from the gap between ordinary and inflation-protected bond yields.
- **Bretton Woods:** The 1944 system that pegged other currencies to the dollar and the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce.
- **Cantillon effect:** The idea that those who receive new money first gain, while those who receive it last face higher prices first.
- **Capital account:** The record of money moving in and out of a country for investment. An open one lets money leave freely.
- **Capital controls:** Rules that limit how much money can move in or out of a country.
- **CBDC:** Central bank digital currency: digital money issued directly by a central bank to the public. A retail US version is banned by law.
- **Central bank:** A public bank that issues a country's base money and manages its interest rates.
- **Chartalism:** The idea that money gets its value from the state, mainly because taxes must be paid in it.
- **Citizenship-based taxation:** Taxing citizens wherever they live. The US is the main example. Eritrea charges its citizens abroad a flat 2% diaspora tax.
- **Collateral:** Something valuable you pledge to a lender, which the lender can take if you do not repay.
- **Coupon:** The fixed interest a bond pays each year, set when it is issued.
- **CPI:** The Consumer Price Index, which tracks the prices of a basket of goods and services households buy.
- **Credit:** Trust that lets someone receive something now and pay later. Also the debt that results.
- **Current account deficit:** When a country pays more to the world for imports and income than it receives, it must borrow or sell assets to cover the gap.
- **Debasement:** Lowering the precious metal in coins while keeping their face value. The ancient form of printing money.
- **Debt deflation:** A spiral where paying down debt pushes prices down, which makes remaining debts heavier.
- **Deep market:** A market where huge sums can move quickly at fair prices under rules that will not change on you.
- **Deflation:** A general fall in prices, so each unit of money buys more. Debts get heavier in real terms.
- **Dutch disease:** When a resource export boom lifts the currency and makes other industries uncompetitive. Named after the Netherlands' gas boom of the 1960s.
- **Economic rent:** Income earned from owning something scarce, such as land or a license, rather than from producing more.
- **Exorbitant privilege:** The advantage the US gets because the world wants dollars and Treasuries, letting it borrow cheaply in its own currency.
- **Face value:** The amount a bond repays at maturity, usually $1,000 per bond. Also called par.
- **Federal Reserve (the Fed):** The US central bank. It sets short-term interest rates, supervises banks and acts as lender of last resort.
- **Financial hub:** A city where money, banks, investors and talent concentrate, such as New York, London or Singapore.
- **Financial repression:** Keeping interest rates below inflation so that debts, especially government debts, shrink in real terms.
- **Floating exchange rate:** A currency whose price against others is set by markets every day.
- **Four Horsemen of leveling:** Walter Scheidel's name for the four forces that historically shrank inequality: mass-mobilization war, revolution, state collapse and pandemics.
- **Free banking:** The period from 1837 to 1863 when US banks issued their own paper notes, each trading at its own discount.
- **GENIUS Act:** The US law setting rules for payment stablecoins, including reserves of cash, deposits and short Treasury bills, and no interest to holders.
- **Gold standard:** A system where a currency is defined as a fixed weight of gold and paper notes can be swapped for gold.
- **Gresham's law:** When two moneys have the same face value, people spend the worse one and hoard the better one.
- **Halving:** The cut in Bitcoin's new-coin reward about every four years. The April 2024 halving set it at 3.125 coins per block.
- **IMF:** The International Monetary Fund, created in 1944 to lend to countries with payment problems and oversee exchange rates.
- **Imported inflation:** Rising prices caused by a weaker home currency or dearer foreign goods, not by anything happening at home.
- **Impossible trinity:** The rule that a country cannot fix its exchange rate, allow free movement of money and set its own interest rates all at once.
- **Inflation:** A general rise in prices, so each unit of money buys less. Debts get lighter in real terms.
- **Jubilee:** The fiftieth-year release in Leviticus 25, when land returned to its original families and bonded servants went free. The release of debts every seventh year comes from Deuteronomy 15.
- **Leverage:** Using borrowed money to buy assets. It magnifies gains and losses.
- **Liability:** Something you owe, such as a loan. One person's liability is always another's asset.
- **Maturity:** The date a bond repays its face value.
- **Medium of exchange:** Whatever people hand over to settle a trade. Money's spending job.
- **Meme coin:** A token with no purpose beyond attention and speculation.
- **Middle-income trap:** When a country grows fast to a middle level and then stalls, often because the next step needs reforms its elites resist.
- **Minsky moment:** The point when a long calm period of rising debt suddenly turns into forced selling and crisis.
- **Money multiplier:** An old textbook idea that banks lend a fixed multiple of their reserves. Central banks now say it does not describe how lending works.
- **Net worth:** Everything owned minus everything owed.
- **Nominal:** Measured in current money, without adjusting for inflation.
- **Nominal yield:** The interest rate as quoted, in dollars, before tax and inflation.
- **Open market operations:** The Fed buying or selling securities in the market, with dealers, rather than directly from the Treasury.
- **Peg:** A fixed exchange rate between one currency and another, defended by a central bank.
- **Petrodollar:** The 1970s arrangement in which oil was priced in dollars and Gulf oil money was recycled into US Treasuries and banks.
- **Primary dealer:** One of 25 banks and dealers that must bid at US Treasury auctions and trade with the New York Fed in its open market operations.
- **Primary deficit:** The government's deficit before counting interest payments.
- **Prisoner's dilemma:** A game where each player gains by cheating, but if all cheat, all end up worse off.
- **Private key:** The secret code that controls tokens in a wallet. Whoever holds it controls the tokens.
- **Provident fund:** A compulsory national savings scheme for retirement, such as Malaysia's EPF or Singapore's CPF.
- **Quantitative easing (QE):** When a central bank creates reserves to buy bonds in the open market, to push down long-term interest rates.
- **Real:** Adjusted for inflation, so values can be compared across time.
- **Real yield:** The return left after inflation. In bond markets it is read from inflation-protected bonds (TIPS).
- **Repo:** A short loan backed by bonds as collateral. The financial system's overnight pawnshop.
- **Reserve currency:** A currency that foreign governments hold in large amounts as savings and for crisis use. Today mainly the dollar.
- **Resource curse:** The pattern where countries rich in oil or minerals grow slower and govern worse than countries without them.
- **Revaluation:** A change in the price of assets already owned, with no new things produced. Falling interest rates revalue assets upward.
- **Reverse repo facility:** A Fed facility where money funds and others park cash overnight, taking it out of the banking system while it sits there.
- **Riba:** The Arabic term for interest or unjust gain on loans, forbidden in Islam.
- **Seigniorage:** The profit from issuing money, the gap between what money costs to make and what it buys.
- **Sovereign wealth fund:** A state-owned fund that invests a country's surplus, often from oil, gas or trade, in assets at home and abroad.
- **Stablecoin:** A crypto token designed to stay worth one unit of a currency, usually one dollar, backed by reserves.
- **Store of value:** A way to carry buying power from today into the future. Money's saving job.
- **Sukuk:** Islamic bonds that pay returns linked to real assets instead of interest.
- **Tax competition:** Countries cutting taxes to attract people, companies and capital from other countries.
- **Term premium:** The extra yield investors demand for locking money up for many years when the future is uncertain.
- **Time preference:** The fact that people value having things sooner rather than later. It is why waiting must be paid for with interest.
- **Time price:** The number of hours of work needed to buy something.
- **Title:** The legal record of who owns something, such as land, a building or mineral rights.
- **Token:** A unit recorded on a blockchain. It can represent a coin, a dollar, a share, a vote or nothing at all.
- **Tokenization:** Recording ownership of a real asset, such as a Treasury bill or a building, on a blockchain.
- **Toll booth:** In this guide, any player who earns by owning a crossing point others must pass, such as a platform, a payment rail or land.
- **Treasury bill (T-bill):** Short-term US government debt, sold at a discount and repaid at full value within a year.
- **Treasury General Account:** The US government's main checking account, held at the Federal Reserve.
- **Treasury securities:** Debts of the US government. Bills last up to a year, notes 2 to 10 years, bonds 20 or 30 years.
- **Triffin dilemma:** The conflict between supplying the world with enough of a reserve currency and keeping that currency's backing believable.
- **Unit of account:** The measuring unit for prices, wages and debts, such as the dollar. Money's measuring job.
- **Velocity:** How many times a unit of money is spent in a given period.
- **Watt-dollar:** This project's name for dollar loans backed by energy assets such as power plants, data centers and chips.
- **Yield:** The return on a bond or investment, expressed as a yearly percentage of its price.
- **Yield curve:** Bond yields lined up from short to long maturities. Upward sloping is normal, inverted often warns of a slowdown.

## The report

Facts as of 2026-10-22. Live page: https://claude.ai/artifact/2QJg4KuARQPAhm6FRbKmLq (private until shared from its Share menu).

### The answer in one paragraph
Energy will not replace the dollar you spend. It is replacing gold's old job: the scarce physical thing that caps how much real output any money can claim. In an AI and robot economy output scales with delivered power, and power cannot be printed. Energy is also entering the system as collateral inside the dollar (power plants, data centers, PPAs and GPUs backing dollar loans, compute futures settling in dollars), a "watt-dollar" descended from the 1974 petrodollar. It fails as spendable money because it is perishable, location-bound and getting cheaper. Musk's "currency measured in wattage and tonnage" is a post-scarcity accounting idea close to the 1930s Technocracy plan, and its real problem is who allocates. Confidence 65 (Plausible).

### How the Fed and Treasury are tackling the debt
They are managing who must buy it, not shrinking it. Captive demand is the chosen strategy: stablecoin reserves forced into short bills from 2027-01-18, bank leverage relief, bills sized to money funds, long-bond buybacks, a Fed repo line Japan promised to use but has not (FIMA unused from 18 February to 14 October 2026). The Fed under Warsh is hiking. Inflation above the 3.5% average debt cost erodes the ratio quietly. No gold revaluation, no Bitcoin buying, no formal accord. Set 1 (gold, bonds, credit) and Set 2 (stablecoins, crypto rails) are joining on Set 1's terms. Round 8 restated the old one-line view ("Set 1 is absorbing Set 2, an acquisition, not a merger") as five readings with dated tests: A absorption (old wrappers swallow Bitcoin, fits), B leakage (dollars drain into Bitcoin, fails the money meter), C two-way valve (toward Bitcoin in booms, back in busts, live), D risk transfer (savers carry Bitcoin's risk under a credit label, fits), E collateral bridge (Bitcoin starts to back new dollars, real but too small to measure). First check: 31 December 2026.

### Scenario probabilities (regime at end of horizon)
| Horizon | S1 Dollar extension | S2 Neutral layer | S3 Energy/compute | S4 Disorderly reset |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| H0 now to 2028 | 62 | 15 | 1 | 22 |
| H1 2028 to 2035 | 44 | 23 | 3 | 30 |
| H2 2035 to 2050 | 31 | 28 | 10 | 31 |

Round 3 values from round3/scen.json (Round 2 had H1 45/22/3/30 and H2 32/28/10/30). H0 is unchanged at 62/15/1/22. The likeliest H0 S4 path is now an oil-shock inflation and term-premium episode with the euro periphery as the weak link, met by a Fed that hikes. The repression episode (S4-lite) sits mostly in H1. Conditional: if China's Announcement 70 lapses with no replacement on 10 Nov 2026, move 2 points from S1 to S4 in H0.

### Calibration result
Given only the raw X post, the engine rebuilt the expert's anomaly (euros sold, not dollars) and went further: Treasury's own fund statement shows the US leg was $500M against Japan's ~$97B, and the France-Germany spread only blew out six weeks later. Verdict: the literal "Bessent sold France" is Refuted, the narrow version (cost routed onto the euro) is Plausible.

### Round 2 in one paragraph
New rails, old anchors. Money changes its plumbing (stablecoins, tokenized funds, AI agents paying in dollar tokens) while the anchors stay: Treasuries back the tokens by law, gold is the neutral asset between states, and borrowing against future income stays with regulated lenders. UHI can help you qualify for credit but should not be pledgeable as cash, and every country can only pay what its taxes, funds and currency carry. For an 18-year-old the old ladder still exists but its housing rung is broken and its launch rung is cheaper but crowded. Ownership, not credit, decides who keeps up. Full answers on the Round 2 page and in round2/DEBATE_R2.md.

### Round 3 in one paragraph
The pipes held and the pressure moved: rent, tax and hardware now decide what a dollar buys. Stablecoins were flat for a year ($304.9B to $303.8B) while the Fed added $370B of bills and money funds about $505B, and through the Hormuz shock the FIMA repo line sat at zero while foreign governments sold $254B of Treasuries instead. A UHI is limited by rent and the tax base, not robots. Housing takes 40% to 48% of each UHI dollar and its supply grows about 1% a year, so a printed Musk-scale UHI runs about 5.8% to 9.8% inflation now, and income and payroll taxes carry 86.2% of federal receipts while a tax on watts or compute would raise under 1%. Cheap production does not reach people on its own: land is 40% of US home value (68% in San Jose), platforms take a rising slice of every sale, and the bottom half own 0.58% of directly held stocks, which Trump Accounts as designed lift only to about 0.60% to 0.70% by 2045. China extended the truce politically to 10 January 2027 but left the legal cliff on 10 November (court odds of a full lapse 12%), and markets price the next Fed hike for 9 December, not 28 October. So the scenario odds barely move. Full rulings in round3/DEBATE_R3.md, earlier-round corrections appended to round2/DEBATE_R2.md and round1/RELOOP.md.

**Decoded intent.** What the Trump, Musk, reset and CBDC, and seigniorage and gold narratives are really aiming at: four decode lanes in round3/decode/ (DCA to DCD) and the panel ruling in round3/DECODE_PANEL.md (that panel may still be in progress).

### Round 4 in one paragraph
If a giant falls, nobody inherits it whole and Europe's money keeps going West. The dollar's share of world reserves fell from about 71% to 56.70% since 2000, but the yuan has only 2.11%. The lost share went to gold (now about 26% of all reserves, worth about 1.8 times all euro reserves) and to many smaller currencies. China cannot inherit with capital controls, and if it opened, money would first run into dollars. The premise that everyone prays for a US downfall fails, because the biggest creditors lose first. Europe is sliding slowly, not falling: its income per head in purchasing power has held at about 70% to 75% of the US since 2000, and the sharp edge is France (OAT-Bund 171.8bp, Le Pen 46% in a $155.7M market). Breaking away does not help on the evidence (Brexit cost about 6% to 8% of GDP per head). If Europe declines, about 55% of its outbound money goes to North America and about 6% to Latin America, so the owner is right on "West" and wrong on Latin America. Southeast Asia wins factories, not money. Full rulings in round4/DEBATE_R4.md.

### Round 5 in one paragraph
Round 5 answered the fifteen open questions, audited the project's memory and wrote down 72 dated predictions before the events. The 2026 rise in real rates is mostly a higher expected Fed path, with Japan the clearest outside push. A yield cap is unlikely (15 by 2035). Japan pays for yen defense by selling Treasuries, the Gulf has no dollar line yet, and the central banks buying gold are the ones without a Fed backstop. One earlier finding was wrong and is now corrected: producer prices were not flat (the series was consumer foods). Moody's held France at Aa3 negative. Borrowing to invest at 6.19% for 13.6% adds little to the typical result and a lot to the bad one. Full rulings in round5/DEBATE_R5.md, predictions in round5/prereg.json.

NY Fed Q3 FX report (mid-Nov), Treasury refunding (11-04), FOMC (10-28), Q3 GDP and PCE (10-29), CBO higher-rates report 62809, CME compute futures launch, French budget vote, WGC Q3 gold, stablecoin holdings by issuer, AI-agent payment volumes. ## Landscape chapters (the findings reorganized as one story)

- [01. The question and how we answered it](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-01.md): A hunch about Washington, Tokyo and Paris became a test of how to find intent that nobody announces.
- [02. The pressure: the debt treadmill](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-02.md): The US debt grows on its own, mainly because the government spends more than it taxes even before paying interest.
- [03. The response: how Washington is managing it](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-03.md): They are not shrinking the debt. They are managing who must buy it.
- [04. The players and what they want](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-04.md): Intent and outcome are different things. Most players want more than they can get, and the gap shows where the real limits are.
- [05. The rails: Set 1 absorbs Set 2](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-05.md): New digital money is being built on top of the old system, by law. It is an acquisition, not a merger.
- [06. The anchors: gold and Bitcoin](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-06.md): Gold is gaining a job between nations. It is not coming back as the thing behind your dollars, and the math of revaluing it is smaller than the stories.
- [07. Energy: gold's old job](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-07.md): Energy will not replace the dollar you spend. It is replacing the job gold used to do: the scarce physical thing that limits what any money can buy.
- [08. Labor, robots and a Universal High Income](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-08.md): Three tiers behave like two classes. A UHI is limited by rent and the tax base, not by robots, and ownership is what moves people across the line.
- [09. The next generation](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-09.md): The ladder was not pulled up. One rung broke, one got cheap but lottery-like, and ownership decides the climb.
- [10. The rivals and the shocks](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-10.md): The rivals' strongest card is hardware, not currency. The shocks that matter in 2026 came from oil, the yen and Paris.
- [11. Connecting the dots: the interconnection map](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-11.md): Information arbitrage: the most useful insights sit between topics, where a cause in one area quietly drives an effect in another.
- [12. Epilogue: the most probable path from here](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-12.md): Not a prophecy. The single most likely story the evidence supports, the dates where it could fork, and what it means for you.
- [13. If a giant falls: where the money goes](https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/ai/landscape/ls-13.md): The owner asked who takes over if the US declines, whether Europe has to fall, and where its money would go. The short answers: nobody whole, no, and mostly West.
