# The question and how we answered it

Landscape chapter 01. Stack: Intelligence (graded, dated findings). Id: ls-01. Facts as of 2026-10-23.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#ls-01 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*A hunch about Washington, Tokyo and Paris became a test of how to find intent that nobody announces.*

This project started with a post on X and a gut feeling. The post claimed that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had quietly arranged for France to take an economic hit so that Japan could be rescued, as part of a plan to manage a US debt of about $40 trillion. The owner of this project believed it: "Bessent sold France to help Japan... This is about to come (just hasn't priced in yet)." He asked an AI what it thought.

The AI answered the way most careful answers do. It checked the facts it could find, noted there was no public statement from Bessent admitting any such plan, and concluded the idea was "speculative rather than established fact." Then the owner pasted in a long transcript from an expert, Jack Mallers, who laid out a detailed theory. The AI read it and mostly agreed with him. Both answers had the same flaw. The first stopped at "unproven". The second borrowed someone else's frame without checking it.

### Why "unproven" is never the end

People in power rarely announce their intent. A finance minister will not say "we are pushing the cost onto Europe." If you only accept official words as proof, the answer to every question about intent will always be "unproven", which tells you nothing. The project's diagnosis listed seven failure modes, and the first one was exactly this: a fact-check frame that ranks official statements on top, when where money actually moved should outrank what anyone says.

> **Picture this.** A detective does not wait for a confession. She asks what the suspect would normally have done, notices what he did instead, and follows the money. The odd choice is the clue. In this case the odd choice was simple: when the US helped Japan defend the yen on 31 July 2026, it sold euros, not dollars. Every modern US intervention before that had sold dollars. That one detail was the story.

### The method: seven moves and an evidence ladder

From that lesson the project built a Revealed Intent Engine. Every agent runs seven moves: spot the anomaly, state the default move, map incentives, read the actor's history, build the mechanism chain, test it with data, and separate fact from inference with a confidence number.

*[Picture on the web page: The evidence ladder. T0 is money that actually moved, T1 is law, T2 is officials on the record, T3 is market prices, T4 is specialists, T5 is commentary. When sources disagree, the higher tier decides.]*

| Status | What it means | Example from this project |
|---|---|---|
| Confirmed | Backed by money that moved (T0) or by law (T1) | Net interest exceeded defense spending in FY2026: $1,051.8B against $965.2B |
| Plausible | Officials' words or market prices plus a mechanism that works | Energy is replacing gold's old job as the real limit on what money can buy |
| Speculative | Only specialists or commentary support it | Bitcoin becomes a neutral reserve between nations by 2050 |
| Refuted | Hard evidence contradicts it | "UHI recipients lose access to credit" under current law |
| Decoded D1 to D4 | Grades for hidden intent: D1 strong, D2 plausible, D3 folklore, D4 debunked | Stablecoins as a deliberate tool to create buyers for Treasury bills: D1 |

### The calibration test: did the engine beat the expert?

Before trusting the engine, the project gave it only the raw X post, with no expert transcript, and asked it to work the case. It rebuilt the expert's key anomaly on its own (euros sold, not dollars) and then went further. Treasury's own fund statement showed the US share of the operation was about $500 million, against Japan's roughly ¥15.4 trillion (about $97 billion). Bessent's photographed desk note had said "$5-10 bil". The France to Germany bond spread was flat in August (78 to 82 basis points) and only blew out from mid-September (87 on 10 September to 157.5 on 21 October), after the Fed hike, the Bank of Japan hike, a French budget fight and oil above $100.

- The literal claim, "Bessent sold France", is Refuted (85). A $500 million euro sale cannot sink a market of about €3.3 trillion of French debt, and the timing does not fit.
- A narrow version is Plausible (50). The US chose a funding currency and a policy mix that pushed the cost of rescuing the yen toward the euro area rather than onto the dollar or Treasuries.
- "Not priced in yet" is Refuted. By October the short Europe trade was described by UBS and Allianz as crowded.

> The signal was the instrument. A photographed note, "I am the house now", and talk of "asymmetric information" moved markets far more than the half a billion dollars that actually changed hands. When an official's words are loud and the money is small, the words are the tool. That gap between saying and doing, recorded for every major actor, turned out to be the most valuable data in the whole project.

### Three rounds and a decoding panel

1. Round 0 calibrated the method on the France case.
2. Round 1 asked the big question: will energy (watts, tonnage, compute) replace the role gold, then bonds, then credit played? Seven research lanes fed four debate courts and a ledger of 419 claims.
3. Round 2 answered the owner's ten follow-up questions on new money rails, a Universal High Income (UHI), the route for an 18-year-old, founders, and rivals.
4. Round 3 tested Round 2 against a year of hard data, and a decoding panel graded what Trump, Musk and the advocates of a "reset" really want.

### The time frames and the four endings

The project uses four horizons: H0 is now to 2028, H1 is 2028 to 2035, H2 is 2035 to 2050, and H3 is a post-scarcity world after that. It scores four possible regimes for how the money system will look at the end of each horizon: S1 dollar extension (stablecoins and tokenized Treasuries carry the dollar onto new rails), S2 neutral reserve layer (gold and possibly Bitcoin settle between nations), S3 energy or compute standard, and S4 disorderly reset (a crisis or overt repression comes first).

| Horizon | S1 Dollar extension | S2 Neutral layer | S3 Energy or compute | S4 Disorderly reset |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| H0 now to 2028 | 62 | 15 | 1 | 22 |
| H1 2028 to 2035 | 44 | 23 | 3 | 30 |
| H2 2035 to 2050 | 31 | 28 | 10 | 31 |

These are judgment odds (Speculative by the project's own rules). Each row sums to 100 and names the regime that best describes the system at the end of that horizon. The scenarios can overlap: S1 plumbing can be the tool of an S4 squeeze.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why did the project treat the euro sale as more important than Bessent's public statements?
A: Because it was money that actually moved (T0), and it broke the default pattern: every modern US intervention had sold dollars. An action that breaks a habit tells you more than words that can be chosen for effect.


---

# The pressure: the debt treadmill

Landscape chapter 02. Stack: Intelligence (graded, dated findings). Id: ls-02. Facts as of 2026-10-23.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#ls-02 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*The US debt grows on its own, mainly because the government spends more than it taxes even before paying interest.*

Everything in this story starts with one pressure. The US government owes $40.44 trillion in total, and $32.566 trillion of that is held by the public, about 100% of the economy's yearly output (GDP). In the fiscal year that ended on 30 September 2026 it collected $5,403.3 billion, spent $7,395.8 billion, and borrowed the difference: $1,992.5 billion, about 6.2% of GDP.

Two numbers inside that deficit matter most. Interest on the debt cost $1,051.8 billion. And the rest, the gap between what the government spends on everything else and what it collects, was $940.7 billion, or 2.92% of GDP. Economists call that second number the primary deficit. It is the engine of the whole problem.

*[Picture on the web page: The debt treadmill. The belt is the interest cost, the runner's legs are real growth, and the steady push is the primary deficit. Ways off: spend less, grow faster, or let inflation shrink the debt.]*

> **Picture this.** Imagine running on a treadmill while someone keeps adding weight to your backpack. The belt speed is the interest rate on your debt. Your legs are economic growth. The backpack is the primary deficit, new borrowing every year just to cover normal spending. Mallers framed the problem as belt versus legs. The project found the bigger issue is the backpack.

### The surprising finding: it is the backpack, not the belt

The popular story says high interest rates are what make the debt explode. The project tested that with Treasury's own numbers. The real interest rate on 10-year debt (2.76%, the yield on inflation-protected bonds) is only slightly above the economy's trend real growth (2.50% a year over ten years). The gap is just +0.26 percentage points. At market rates, the primary deficit explains 92% to 102% of the yearly rise in the debt ratio. Ruling Dc-02: Confirmed, 80.

| Item | FY2026 value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Debt held by the public | $32.566T, about 100% of GDP | The stock that must be rolled over |
| Net interest | $1,051.8B | Third straight year above defense ($965.2B) |
| Primary deficit | $940.7B, 2.92% of GDP | The main engine of the rising ratio |
| Average rate on the debt | 3.518% | Still below today's market rates |
| Market refinancing rate | about 4.88% | What new debt costs |
| Share repricing in 1, 3, 5 years | 35.7%, 56.8%, 70.4% | The old cheap debt is running out |
| Net interest as share of receipts | 19.46% | The project's fiscal dominance tripwire is 25% |

### Repricing: why the bill keeps rising even if nothing changes

The debt is not one loan. It is a pile of loans with expiry dates. Each time one expires, the Treasury borrows again at today's rate. The average rate on the whole pile is 3.518%, but new borrowing costs about 4.88%. Because 70.4% of the marketable debt reprices within five years, the interest bill climbs on its own. If yields hold, the project's model has interest heading to about $1.6 trillion in three years and $1.9 trillion in five.

> The Treasury has been funding itself more with short-term bills, which now make up 22.36% of marketable debt. That keeps costs down when short rates are low, but it means every Fed hike passes through to the federal budget within months. Shortening the debt is a bet that short rates will fall. It makes the budget more sensitive, not less.

### Was the Fed's hike "gasoline on the fire"?

Mallers argued that when the Fed raises rates, it pays more interest into the economy, so hiking is stimulus. The project checked the size. A quarter-point hike costs about $20 billion to $26 billion a year, about 2% of net interest. The real policy rate is mild: about +0.2% on 12-month inflation of 3.7%. And his inputs were overstated: the debt reprices from 3.52% to about 4.9%, not from 2% to 5%. Ruling Dc-07: the "gasoline" claim is Refuted, 70. The deeper point cuts the other way: a Fed that hikes against the President is evidence against fiscal dominance, not for it.

### The quiet helper: inflation

*[Picture on the web page: A shrinking yardstick. Debt is written in dollars, and when prices rise faster than the interest rate on the debt, the real burden shrinks without anyone voting for it.]*

Here is the part almost nobody says out loud. Nominal growth (real growth plus inflation) is running about 5.7% to 6%, while the average cost of the debt is about 3.2% to 3.5%. That gap quietly holds the debt ratio's drift to about 0.4 to 0.6 points a year. The project calls this passive inflation doing the stabilizing work (Dc-09, Plausible, 60). It fades as the debt reprices. And if inflation fell back to 2% while real rates stayed near 2.7%, the ratio would climb faster, which is a strange truth: success against inflation makes the debt math harder.

### Can AI growth fix it?

Elon Musk has said only AI and robots can solve the US debt. The word "only" is Refuted (70): a primary adjustment of about 2.9% of GDP would stabilize the ratio, and history shows growth, inflation, repression and discipline doing the work, never technology alone. But AI can help under three conditions (Dc-03, Confirmed as arithmetic, 75):

- Spending must not rise with the growth. In the project's model, +2.26 points of AI growth with spending held takes the debt to 87% of GDP. If spending scales up with it, 107%.
- Real interest rates must not rise with growth. If they rise one for one, the debt reaches about 129%, the same as with no AI at all. In 2026 the real 10-year yield rose 82 basis points, so this condition is already under strain. Round 5 update: measured from end 2025 to 23 October the rise is 73bp to 2.66%, mostly a tighter expected Fed path with Japan adding about 18bp, not AI demand directly.
- The gains must land in taxable income. In FY2026 corporate receipts fell 15.6%, from $452.1B to $381.4B, as firms deducted AI investment faster. This condition is failing now. Round 5 update: the drag tracks capex growth and should shrink once capex goes flat, and September 2026 receipts were already up 38% on a year.

- **Myth:** Money printing has a hard ceiling, and the US is nearly maxed out.
- **Reality:** There is no fixed ceiling. The real limits are the primary deficit, the real interest rate and how much inflation the public will tolerate. The debt can grow for a long time. What changes is who pays, and how visibly.

**Check yourself.** Q: If the Fed cut rates to zero tomorrow, would the debt problem be solved?
A: No. Interest costs would fall over time, but the primary deficit of about 2.9% of GDP would keep adding debt every year. The backpack stays even if the belt slows.


---

# The response: how Washington is managing it

Landscape chapter 03. Stack: Intelligence (graded, dated findings). Id: ls-03. Facts as of 2026-10-23.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#ls-03 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*They are not shrinking the debt. They are managing who must buy it.*

Faced with the treadmill, a government has a short menu: tax more, spend less, grow faster, inflate, default, or make sure there are always buyers for the debt. Washington's revealed choice, read from where money actually moved, is the last one. The project calls it captive demand: write rules and build plumbing so that banks, money funds, stablecoin issuers and foreign governments end up holding Treasury bills. Ruling Db-01: Confirmed, 75.

### The captive demand toolkit

1. Fund with bills. Coupon auction sizes are frozen with guidance to stay that way for several quarters, and the bill share rose to 22.36% ($7.118 trillion), from 21.53% a year earlier. The refunding statement itself talks about sizing bills to private and Fed demand.
2. Free up bank balance sheets. The enhanced supplementary leverage ratio (eSLR) relief lets banks hold more Treasuries.
3. Write bills into the law of digital money. From 2027-01-18 every compliant US stablecoin must hold cash, deposits or Treasury bills of 93 days or less (the GENIUS Act).
4. Buy back long bonds. Treasury bought back $230 billion of older debt in 2026, funded with bills.
5. Keep foreign holders from dumping. Press Japan to borrow against its Treasuries through the Fed's FIMA repo line instead of selling, and support the yen with euros rather than with dollars.

> "Just as President Abraham Lincoln's National Currency Act of 1863 established a national framework for bank-issued currency, the GENIUS Act establishes a federal framework for payment stablecoins in the digital age." (Scott Bessent, OCC release, 2026-10-21)

> The analogy is the tell. Under the 1863 law, national banks issued notes that had to be backed by federal bonds, which created a permanent buyer for Civil War debt. Bessent names the framework, not the bond backing, so this is intent evidence of moderate weight. But the decoding panel graded "stablecoins as a deliberate captive demand tool for Treasury bills" D1 (80), partly because the Treasury Secretary chose that comparison himself.

### What the 2026 stress test showed

Round 3 checked the toolkit against a year of hard data, and the results corrected some of the project's own earlier lines. Three surprises stand out.

- Stablecoins did not carry the load. Total supply went from $304.9 billion (2025-10-21) to $303.8 billion (2026-10-22), flat for a year after a May peak of $315.5 billion. Over the same year bank deposits rose $1,225 billion, money funds about $505 billion to $7.92 trillion, and the Fed's own bill holdings $370 billion to $565.5 billion. In 2026 the real captive buyers were the Fed and money funds, not tokens.
- The crisis line went unused. The Fed's FIMA repo facility was at zero every week from 18 February to 14 October 2026, apart from a $3.0 billion blip on 4 February. Japan said on 3 August it "plans to utilize" FIMA, then did not. Swap lines peaked at $481 million. Round 5 update: FIMA was still zero on 21 October, 35 straight weeks. Japan's reserve data show both 2026 interventions were paid for by selling dollar securities.
- Foreign governments sold instead. Foreign official Treasuries in Fed custody fell $254 billion (9.1%) from the February peak to $2,549.1 billion, while those holders kept $331.9 billion of their own cash at the Fed. Japan spent ¥27.1 trillion on interventions in 2026.

*[Picture on the web page: The dollar recycling loop. Dollars sent abroad come back as purchases of Treasuries. In 2026 part of that loop ran in reverse: official holders sold $254 billion to raise crisis cash.]*

So the project reworded its own summary. FIMA moved from "chosen tool" to "announced but unused" (R3X-03, Confirmed). The holder base has shifted from steady foreign governments to leveraged, price-sensitive private buyers such as basis traders, money funds and stablecoins (Db-12, Confirmed, 80). That keeps the system working in good weather and makes it more fragile in a funding shock.

### The Gulf asked, then borrowed

The UAE asked for a dollar swap line in April, and Bessent said "numerous" Gulf and Asian allies had asked. No Gulf line had been announced by 22 October. Gulf states instead issued a record $102.7 billion of bonds and sukuk in the first half of 2026. The court's reading: the backstop for non-core states is moving from the Fed's technical lines to Treasury's political ones, which buys loyalty but makes access conditional and nudges states toward gold and self-insurance.

### The Fed under Warsh: hiking, not helping

The Fed raised its rate 12-0 on 2026-09-16 to 3.75% to 4.00%, its first hike since 2023. The President wanted rates "near 1% or lower." Markets on 22 October gave an October hike only 11% to 12% and a December 9 hike 75% to 79%, with year-end rates most likely at 4.25%. Warsh being out as chair by mid-2027 was priced at 9.5%. The Supreme Court kept Governor Cook in June. In plain terms, the one institution standing between the White House's cheap-money wish and the outcome is still standing.

### What they are not doing

| Option | Status on 2026-10-22 |
|---|---|
| Gold revaluation | Not used. US gold still booked at $42.2222 an ounce (2026-09-30) |
| Buying Bitcoin | Zero purchases. The White House said on 2026-10-14 that purchases need Congress |
| A formal currency accord | None. No century bonds or foreign holder fee in any refunding |
| Default or forced term-out | No evidence. Judged below 5% in H0 and H1 |
| Fed yield control | Not hit. Reserve buying paused, bill reinvestment only |

The court's ruling on the overall path (Db-08, Plausible, 60) is a three-part muddle: captive demand at the short end, passive inflation in the background, and hope for AI growth. None is enough alone. The likeliest exit in 2028 to 2035 is managed financial repression: inflation modestly above coupons, regulatory demand for bills, and a Fed whose leadership becomes more cooperative after 2028. The decoders agree that repression through plumbing has already started (DCC-L1, D1, 70).

- **Myth:** The Fed will simply print money to bail out the Treasury.
- **Reality:** In 2026 the Fed did the opposite and hiked. The quiet help comes from rules that make others buy bills, and from inflation running above the average cost of the debt. That is repression through plumbing, not printing.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why does a rising share of short-term bills make the system more fragile?
A: Because bills reprice within months, so any rate rise hits the budget fast, and because the new buyers of bills are leveraged and price-sensitive. When stress comes, they sell or demand higher yields at the worst moment.


---

# The players and what they want

Landscape chapter 04. Stack: Intelligence (graded, dated findings). Id: ls-04. Facts as of 2026-10-23.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#ls-04 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Intent and outcome are different things. Most players want more than they can get, and the gap shows where the real limits are.*

This chapter separates two questions that news coverage usually blends: what does each player want, and what are they actually getting? Wanting is graded with the decoding scale (D1 strong to D4 debunked). Getting is read from money moved and laws passed.

### Trump: a landlord's monetary system

Trump has run one economic worldview for almost 40 years. His paid newspaper letter of 1987-09-02 already said "It's time for us to end our vast deficits by making Japan, and others who can afford it, pay", complained of "a weak yen against a strong dollar", and ended "Tax these wealthy nations, not America." The decoders found four stable wants. In one line: the dollar is the rent everyone must pay, money is cheap for the landlord, and the tenants cover the costs.

| Want | Grade | What he is getting |
|---|---|---|
| Foreigners fund the state (tariffs, allies pay, $1M gold cards) | D1, 85 | Partly. The Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs 6-3 on 2026-02-20. Replacement tariffs left an effective rate near 7%, with up to about $175B of refunds owed |
| Weak but dominant dollar | D1, 75 | Rails yes, cheap dollar only in episodes. A four-year low in January 2026 was "doing great", then EUR/USD fell from 1.170 to 1.123 |
| A Fed that cuts on demand | D1, 85 (intent) | No so far. Warsh hiked 12-0, the 10-year is 5.13%, Cook stayed |
| An owner society instead of welfare | D2, 65 | Trump Accounts for about 70 million children, a 9.9% state stake in Intel, no AI equity deal yet |

The decoders put 75 on this being his real intent and only 35 on him getting most of it by 2029-01-20. The binding constraints are the bond market and the courts, not Congress. His family's crypto ventures made an estimated $2.3 billion pretax from November 2024 to April 2026 (Reuters), a toll-booth model that fits a policy of building legal rails rather than buying Bitcoin for the state.

| Popular decoding | Grade | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Stablecoins are a deliberate buyer for T-bills | D1, 80 | The 93-day reserve rule plus Bessent's 1863 analogy |
| Wall Street and the Treasury market establishment run the plumbing | D1, 80 | TBAC shapes issuance, eSLR relief, buybacks. Visible, not secret |
| Gold revaluation is coming | D3, 10 | Book value unchanged. Bessent: "we're not revaluing the gold" |
| Bitcoin will pay off the debt | D4, 5 | Zero purchases. Bitcoin's total value is a few percent of the debt |
| A planned crash before a reset | D3, 10 | Every self-inflicted drop so far was followed by a retreat |
| Peter Thiel is the hidden architect | D3, 15 | No document, speech or rule shows it |

### Bessent: the trader in the Treasurer's chair

Bessent is the architect of captive demand. He chose the 1863 analogy, said access to the dollar is "no longer unconditional", welcomed "money flow out of some countries of concern" into Treasuries, and called the current system fiat in July 2026. His signal-heavy style (the photographed note, "I am the house now") moves markets more than his money does. The literal "he sold France" story is Refuted (85). The narrow "he chose to let the euro area absorb the shock" version is Plausible (50).

### Warsh: the independent hawk, for now

Warsh hiked against the President, citing 65 months of elevated inflation and hyperscaler competition for capital. He has floated the idea of a new Fed-Treasury accord. The decoders give a crisis-era accord and Fed yield support after the 2028 leadership turnover only D2 (30 by 2032 after Round 5, down from 40). Round 5 update: the accord Warsh describes would shrink the Fed's bond footprint, not cap yields. An explicit yield cap is now judged 15 by 2035. Markets price the Powell governor seat vacated by early 2028 at 64% to 72%. That date is a fork point for the whole story.

### Musk: belief yes, project no

Musk has said since 2023 that money is "a database for resource allocation" and on 2026-10-20 that "currency will be measured in ... wattage and tonnage." The decoders rate this a sincere belief (D1, 75) that also works as a valuation story for his energy, AI and launch businesses (D1, 70). Their best reading is both at once (65). But he has built nothing that would make energy money real.

- X Money is a dollar wallet on Cross River Bank paying up to 6% in dollars, with a Visa card. X said it "never will" launch a token.
- Tesla still holds the same 11,509 BTC it has held since 2022. No buying during his energy-money talk.
- His 200 GW a year solar claim compares with about 0.3 GW of Tesla solar output today, and his pay plan is measured in market cap (up to $8.5 trillion), not watts.
- "Musk is building a private central bank" is D3 (8). "A Technocracy-style energy credit plan" is D3 as a plan (7), though the family influence is D2 (55).

> Musk wants federal dollar checks for a Universal High Income now ("MUST issue dollars") and says money will not matter later. Read together, dollars are his transition tool and physics units are his end state, with no bridge between them. Meanwhile he accumulates dollar claims on exactly the assets that would be scarce in his future: power, launch and compute.

### China, Japan, the Gulf and Europe

| Player | What they want | What they are doing |
|---|---|---|
| China | Reduce exposure to the dollar and hold leverage over the US | Treasuries cut from $694B (Feb) to $590.7B (Aug 2026). The real lever is energy hardware (Chapter 10). e-CNY plus mBridge as a bypass rail: intent D2 75, material bypass by 2030 only 15 |
| Japan | A stronger yen to fight imported energy inflation | Bank of Japan hike on 18 September, ¥27.1T of intervention in 2026, Treasury holdings down from $1,239B (Feb) to $1,068B (Aug) |
| Gulf | Dollar access in a crisis, and a stake in the AI build | Saudi $141.2B and UAE $116.1B of Treasuries, flat. New money goes to US AI equity (MGX and BlackRock's $40B Aligned deal). The UAE warned it could sell oil in yuan while asking for a swap line |
| Europe | Payment sovereignty, and room to pay for defense | Digital euro intent D1 85, issued by end 2030 about 50. Wholesale bridge Pontes live since 2026-09-21. France under bond stress (OAT-Bund 171.8bp on 23 October, above Italy, with Le Pen leading the 2027 market at 46%), Germany's surplus at €146.0B for January to August |

> **Round 4 update.** Round 4 graded the big stories about who wants to take the dollar's place. China wants reserve status and less dollar exposure (D1, 85), not to replace the dollar (D3, 15). 'BRICS plan to replace the dollar' is D4 as a currency plan and D2 as back-up payment rails. 'Everyone is praying for a US downfall' is D3: only Russia and Iran want it, while Germany, China and Japan, the three largest creditor nations, would lose first. On Europe, 'the US wants a weak Europe' holds only in a narrow form, weaker as a regulator and a bloc but stronger as a buyer of defense (D2, 60), and 'Brussels will seize savings' is D4 for insured deposits. Chapter 13 has the full story.

**Check yourself.** Q: Trump strongly wants cheap money. Why is he not getting it?
A: Because the Fed under Warsh is independent and hiking, the courts kept Governor Cook, and the bond market sets long rates. His other wants (private dollar rails, an owner society) advance through rules and private firms that do not need those institutions.

# The rails: Set 1 absorbs Set 2

Landscape chapter 05. Stack: Intelligence (graded, dated findings). Id: ls-05. Facts as of 2026-10-23.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#ls-05 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*New digital money is being built on top of the old system, by law. It is an acquisition, not a merger.*

The owner framed the money world as two sets. Set 1 is gold, bonds and bank credit. Set 2 is crypto, Bitcoin, stablecoins and blockchains, used more and more by AI for commerce. His hypothesis was that both survive and merge into "a new monopoly board". The project's ruling (Db-10, Plausible, 65): right in shape, wrong in one important way. Set 2's rails are being absorbed onto Set 1's balance sheet. Set 1 is buying Set 2.

*[Picture on the web page: Four layers of money. Token rails on top move and settle the money. Treasuries and bank deposits underneath are what it is backed by. Gold sits at the bottom as the neutral asset between nations.]*

### Set 1 is three jobs, not one layer

- Gold is the neutral reserve with no issuer, mostly for states.
- Treasuries are the prime collateral that everything else is priced against.
- Banks create most credit, by making loans that create deposits.

Crypto replaces the rails (how money moves and settles), not the balance sheet (what money is backed by). Payments move to tokens first, some deposit funding second, and the reserve role last and only partly (Round 2 Q1, Plausible, 70).

### A stablecoin is a tokenized T-bill fund with a payment button

From 2027-01-18 every compliant US stablecoin must hold cash, deposits or Treasury bills of 93 days or less. Holders get zero interest by law. So the float belongs to the issuer and its distributors. Circle's Q2 2026 results show the split: $667.7 million of reserve income on $76.5 billion of average USDC, of which $410.4 million (61.5%) went to distribution partners, mainly Coinbase, leaving $48 million of net income. Across the market the float is worth about $11.7 billion a year at a 4.25% bill rate (model). Tether alone made more than $10 billion in 2025.

| Where $50,000 of idle cash sits for a year | Rate | You earn |
|---|---|---|
| Bank savings at the national average | 0.38% | $190 |
| Government money fund or T-bill | about 4.25% | $2,125 |
| GENIUS stablecoin, from the issuer | 0% by law | $0 |
| Exchange reward on a stablecoin | 3.75% | $1,875 (legality case by case from 2027-01-18) |

> This is seigniorage, the profit from issuing money, moved into private hands. The Fed used to send the Treasury large profits ($117 billion in 2015, $107.4 billion in 2021). It stopped in September 2022, because the interest it now pays on bank reserves exceeds what its old bonds earn. Its accumulated shortfall, a "deferred asset", was $233.2 billion on 2026-10-14. Today the cleanest seigniorage in the dollar system goes to stablecoin issuers, whose holders lend to them at zero.

### Who really buys the tokens

When stablecoins grew (end 2023 to October 2025, +$174.9 billion), the best estimate is that about two thirds went to holders outside the US (model range 55% to 81%), and about 41% was genuinely new dollar demand from people converting local currency. Offshore USDT is 61% of supply. Per $1 of new token, a foreign new-to-dollar buyer adds about $0.80 of Treasury demand, a switch from a US bank deposit about $0.72, and a switch from a government money fund about $0.30 (model). But for the last twelve months there was no growth at all. Treasury's advisory committee once projected about $2 trillion by 2028. That now needs about +$1.7 trillion in about 26 months from a flat base, and markets give stablecoins above $500 billion before 2027 only 3%.

*[Picture on the web page: Old petrodollar loop and new stablecoin loop. From 1974, oil dollars came back as Treasury purchases. From 2027, foreign savers buying dollar tokens do the same by law. The new loop is real but cyclical: it ran flat for the year to October 2026.]*

### Do deposits leave the banks?

Mostly no. The famous "$6.6 trillion of deposits at risk" was all US transactional deposits at end 2024, a ceiling, not a forecast, and when an issuer buys a bill the seller's bank gets the deposit back. What changes is cost (retail deposits at 0.38% become wholesale money near 4%), and a slice of money creation tilts from bank loans toward Treasury bills, as in the 1863 design.

### Borrowing stays with regulated lenders

DeFi lends only against collateral you already own, never against future income. All crypto-backed lending was $56.2 billion in Q2 2026, about 0.4% of the $14.10 trillion of US bank loans. A mortgage, car loan or first business loan needs someone who underwrites your future income and absorbs default, so it comes from a bank or a bank-funded lender through at least 2035, even if the money arrives as a token. Banks are moving upstream: their loans to nonbank lenders rose 19.9% in a year to $2.06 trillion, and nonbanks make about 64% of home purchase loans.

### CBDC choices: whose balance sheet holds digital money

| Bloc | Choice | Key date |
|---|---|---|
| United States | Private: statutory ban on a Fed CBDC, GENIUS stablecoins, tokenized deposits (JPMorgan's JPMD live since November 2025), FedNow, proposed Fed "skinny" payment accounts | Ban to 2030-12-31. GENIUS from 2027-01-18 |
| Euro area | Public retail option with a holding cap (about €3,000 discussed) and offline privacy, plus a live wholesale bridge (Pontes) | First issuance 2029 at the earliest |
| China | Public retail e-CNY, interest-bearing and bank-distributed from 2026-01-01, used cross-border via mBridge ($55.49B cumulative to November 2025) | Live |

The fears map unevenly onto these designs. Greater state visibility is real for every digital option, including "private" stablecoins that must be freezable by law (D1). Programmable limits on general balances in G7 countries are folklore so far (D3, 5 by 2035), though targeted vouchers exist (China's Shenzhen lottery, India's food subsidy). Money that expires is D3 (3). The WEF "Great Reset" as a control plan is D3. Calling GENIUS stablecoins a "backdoor CBDC" is D2 (60) as a description of function.

### Why the state keeps Set 1: seigniorage and the freeze button

Every dollar payment ends as a transfer on a ledger the US controls: Fedwire moved $4.59 trillion a day in 2025, CHIPS $2.0 trillion. Foreign central banks keep $2.55 trillion of Treasuries in custody at the New York Fed. That is why one Treasury directive on 2022-02-28 could immobilize Russia's central bank assets held by US persons, and why about €202 billion stayed frozen at Euroclear in June 2026. The power comes from law over the ledger keepers, not from technology. So the state lets new rails grow only on terms that keep both seigniorage and the freeze button (DCD-D01, D1, 80). Stablecoins as a sanctions tool: D1, 85.

**Check yourself.** Q: If stablecoins grow tenfold, does the US government lose control of money?
A: Not under current law. Compliant stablecoins must hold Treasury bills, pay holders nothing, settle through a Fed-controlled system and freeze on lawful orders. Growth would create more demand for US debt and more reach for US sanctions. The open risk is offshore tokens outside that regime.

# The anchors: gold and Bitcoin

Landscape chapter 06. Stack: Intelligence (graded, dated findings). Id: ls-06. Facts as of 2026-10-23.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#ls-06 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Gold is gaining a job between nations. It is not coming back as the thing behind your dollars, and the math of revaluing it is smaller than the stories.*

If Set 1 is buying Set 2, what is left outside the dollar board? Two candidates: gold, which states hold, and Bitcoin, which mostly individuals hold. The project tested both against money that moved.

### Gold: the neutral corner

Central banks bought 863 tonnes of gold in 2025 and 289 tonnes in Q2 2026, buying into a price about 27% below its January high. Poland and China led. France brought 129 tonnes home. 89% of central banks surveyed expect official gold to rise. Round 5 update: the 2026 buyers are central banks without a standing Fed swap line, and 9% of central banks raised domestic storage in the past year, up from 5%. Ruling Db-04: gold as the neutral reserve layer, Confirmed, 75. The say and do gaps are real too: Russia sold 22 tonnes, Turkey sold, and the first half of 2026 (345 tonnes) was the weakest since 2022.

Why the buying? US secondary sanctions now reach dollar, digital and gold channels. Russia's case shows both sides: about €202 billion of its euro assets are still immobilized at Euroclear, while its gold held at home was never frozen. But Western markets banned its bars, so Russia now sells gold at home to fund its budget. The decoders grade "weaponized dollar rails push states into gold held at home" D1 (80).

> **Picture this.** Fire insurance does not need to be worth as much as your house. It needs to pay out in the one disaster you fear. Gold does not insure the world's debt, most of which is owed and settled in the borrower's own currency. It insures a state's ability to pay abroad when its dollar or euro reserves can be frozen. Against that job it is large: official gold is about $5 trillion against $13.2 trillion of allocated foreign exchange reserves, and at end 2025 prices it was 27% of official reserves, more than Treasuries at 22%.

> **Round 4 update.** Measured at market prices, gold is now about 26% of all official reserves (foreign currency plus gold), worth about 1.8 times all euro reserves. The ECB's own count for end 2025 put gold at 27% of global official reserves, against 22% for US Treasuries and 15% for the euro. Gold has quietly overtaken the euro as the world's second reserve asset. Because the dollar's lost share went to gold and to many smaller currencies rather than to one rival, the project now shows its neutral-layer scenario in two parts: gold and Bitcoin (13 to 2028, 17 to 2035, 18 to 2050) and a multipolar mix of currencies (2, 6 and 10). The totals are unchanged.

### Gold supply: not running out, not exploding

About 222,600 tonnes of gold exist above ground, worth about $29 trillion. Known reserves (about 61,000 tonnes) would add about 27% to that, and known resources (114,400 tonnes) about 51%. Mines produced a record 3,672 tonnes in 2025, so the stock grows about 1.5% to 1.7% a year and would be about 39% larger by 2050. Asteroids are no answer before then: metal asteroids hold about 1 gram of gold per tonne, so returning 1,000 tonnes would mean processing roughly a billion tonnes of asteroid metal (model). Asteroid gold breaking scarcity: D3.

*[Picture on the web page: Seasons of money, 1870 to 2026. Gold anchored money by law for most of the first century, the anchor was cut in 1971, and since then gold has returned as a reserve that states choose, not a rule they must follow.]*

### The revaluation math

The US holds 261,498,926 ounces of gold, booked at the old statutory price of $42.2222, so $11.04 billion. At the market price of $4,078, the one-off gain from marking it up would be about $1.06 trillion: roughly half of one year's deficit and about 2.7% of the debt. Here is what larger targets would need (model):

| Revaluation gain equal to | Gold price needed per ounce |
|---|---|
| 10% of debt held by the public | about $12,500 |
| All foreign official Treasuries | about $14,400 |
| All base money (cash plus reserves, $5.51T) | about $21,100 |
| All debt held by the public | about $124,600 |

So the popular $10,000 to $20,000 targets match "cover a slice", not "cover the debt". Precedents exist (1934: $20.67 to $35, 1972 to 1973: $38 then $42.22), but each came when gold still anchored the dollar by law. The gain would also be new base money, and with the Fed paying interest on reserves near the bill rate, swapping debt for reserves saves almost no interest. Odds from the judges: formal US revaluation by 2029-01-20 about 10, by 2035 about 15, an official price of $10,000 or more by 2035 about 3. Market gold at or above $10,000 by end 2030 about 20, at or above $20,000 by 2035 about 7.

### Why not 10x

The owner brought a belief to this project: gold of about $30 to $50 trillion times a 10x collateral multiplier equals the world's debt, and Bitcoin times 10 could support about $300 trillion. Round 1 audited it. The debt to gold ratio has wandered between 12x and 53x, so "gold times 10 equals debt" is a coincidence of one moment. The multiplier also contradicts the owner's own Bank of England citation: banks create money by lending, not by stacking credit on a gold base. Bitcoin times 10 would imply $1.43 million per coin, and real crypto lending runs at about 0.05x. Gold as "what money is backed by": D4.

*[Picture on the web page: The layers of money. Base money is a Fed liability backed mainly by $4.57 trillion of Treasuries. Bank deposits are created when banks lend. Stablecoins are backed by bills. Gold is a separate asset, not the base under any of them.]*

- **Myth:** Gold is what the dollar is really backed by.
- **Reality:** The legal gold cover behind Federal Reserve notes ended in 1968, and convertibility ended in 1971. In today's system bonds are what most money is backed by: the Fed's main asset is Treasuries, stablecoins hold bills, and Treasuries are claims on future taxes. Gold is the asset states hold in case that system is turned against them.

### Bitcoin: politically blessed, not a reserve

The US holds 198,000 to 328,000 forfeited bitcoin, has bought none, and the White House said on 2026-10-14 that purchases need Congress. The proposed ARMA law bars borrowing against, taxing or pledging federal assets and imposes a 20-year hold. US ETFs hold 1.29 million BTC and Tether 98,933. No G20 central bank holding is established. In 2026 Bitcoin rose while gold fell from May to September, fell in hawkish episodes, and traded in a range of $57.7k to $116k over a year. Ruling Db-05: in H0 Bitcoin is a risk asset with political status and a frozen sovereign stockpile, Confirmed, 80. As a future neutral reserve between nations: Speculative, 20 (by 2050).

> Bitcoin is energy-priced, not energy-backed (Da-07, Confirmed, 85). Its difficulty adjustment makes miners' energy spend follow the price, but you cannot redeem a coin for a kilowatt hour. The revealing move was by miners themselves: listed miners signed more than $70 billion of AI and data center contracts, because connected power near fiber now earns more as compute. Stranded remote power still earns most as Bitcoin, the only way to turn it into a globally movable asset.

One correction from the audit: the line often attributed to Putin, that Trump uses crypto to devalue US debt, came from adviser Anton Kobyakov on 2025-09-06 and was about stablecoins. As a devaluation plan it grades D3.

**Check yourself.** Q: A friend says gold must hit $20,000 to match the debt. What would you say?
A: No mechanism links gold to the debt. The ratio has wandered from 12x to 53x, gold fell 27% in 2026 while debt rose, and even a US revaluation to $21,100 would only match base money, not the debt. Gold can rise on central bank and investor demand, which is a different story.


---

# Energy: gold's old job

Landscape chapter 07. Stack: Intelligence (graded, dated findings). Id: ls-07. Facts as of 2026-10-23.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#ls-07 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Energy will not replace the dollar you spend. It is replacing the job gold used to do: the scarce physical thing that limits what any money can buy.*

This was the project's founding question: will energy (watts, tonnage, compute) replace the value role that gold, then bonds, then credit played? The answer, Plausible at 65, has three parts. Energy fails as money you spend. It succeeds as the real ceiling on output. And it is entering the dollar system as collateral, a "watt-dollar".

### Part one: why a kilowatt hour is bad money

*[Picture on the web page: The three jobs of money: medium of exchange, store of value and unit of account. A delivered kilowatt hour scored 1 of 5 on both spending and saving, because it is perishable, tied to a place and getting cheaper over time.]*

- No kWh-denominated stablecoin or token of material size exists. Every energy-linked instrument found in 2025 and 2026 settles in dollars (Da-01, energy as spendable money, Refuted through 2050, 5).
- A kWh has no single price. In 2026 PJM wholesale power rose 41% while California hit historic lows.
- A fixed-kWh unit is unstable in both directions (Da-06, Plausible, 80). Solar modules fell from $132 a watt in 1975 to $0.265 in 2024, so over decades a kWh coin would lose value. In 2026 delivered power got dearer, so right now it would gain. Any fix (cap the units, peg to a share of total energy) turns it back into gold, equity or Bitcoin.
- History: every energy currency proposal since Ford's 1921 energy dollar failed.

### Part two: energy as the binding constraint

Gold limited money by law until 1971. After that the limit was only political: how much debt markets would absorb. In an AI and robot economy, output scales with delivered power, and power cannot be printed. The evidence is money committed: PJM's capacity auction cleared at its cap twice with a 6,623 MW shortfall ($16.4 billion), and data centers explain about 5,100 MW of the peak rise. Ruling Da-03: Confirmed for H0, 80. The refinement matters: the binding input is deliverable firm power plus a grid connection in specific load regions, not energy in general.

| Signal | Value |
|---|---|
| Hyperscaler capex guidance, 2026 | about $700 to 725 billion, up 77% |
| Data center power use (IEA) | 415 TWh (2024), 485 TWh (2025), about 950 TWh (2030) |
| US wholesale power, 2026 | $52 per MWh, up 11%. PJM up 41% |
| Extra energy needed for +2.26 points of AI growth | about 3% a year, against world primary energy growth of 1.4% in 2025 |
| GPU rental (Blackwell) | up 48% in two months |

> The AI debt dividend is an energy-supply bet (Dc-10, Plausible, 55). Musk himself said electricity additions grow about 4% a year while chip output grows far faster. If power lags, the AI boom shows up as power-price inflation and higher real interest rates, not as tax revenue that shrinks the debt. That is the link between this chapter and the treadmill in Chapter 2.

### Part three: the watt-dollar

*[Picture on the web page: Energy as collateral and ceiling under the dollar. Power plants, data centers, power contracts and GPUs back new dollar loans, while delivered power caps how much real output those dollars can claim.]*

Energy is also taking a growing share of the job Treasuries do as prime collateral, but inside the dollar. The Hyperion data center financing ($27.3 billion), 55.9 GW of power purchase agreements, and GPU-secured debt of $48.4 billion (by a T4 tracker) all back dollar loans, and the first compute futures settle in dollars. This is the heir of the 1974 petrodollar, when a physical input became a dollar commodity. Ruling Da-02: Plausible, 75. Two corrections keep it from Confirmed: the collateral is mostly the credit of the big tech firms with energy assets as backup, and the recycling half of the petrodollar (foreign surpluses into Treasuries) is not shown. The scale is still small, about a third of the stablecoin float.

### Musk's physics currency and the allocation problem

Musk's "currency measured in wattage and tonnage" is substantively the 1930s Technocracy plan for energy certificates, a movement his grandfather Joshua Haldeman belonged to from 1936 to 1941. He names no issuer, redemption rule or supply rule. Ruling Da-05: Speculative, 15, for the far future. The robust part of the analysis is the governance problem: a physics unit is either a market price (just a commodity index priced in some money) or an allocation, in which case someone sets the allotments. In Musk's version the natural allocators would be whoever owns generation, launch and compute. That is a concentration of power far larger than central bank discretion.

Compute as a unit of account between machines is Speculative (Da-04, 25). GPU-hours exist as a contract quantity, but nothing is priced in them, and the machine rail actually scaling is the dollar stablecoin.

### Who wins, who loses

The winners are whoever owns firm power and grid connections. People on fixed dollar incomes lose whenever AI demand outruns grid supply (Da-10, Plausible, 60). In the year to September 2026 US energy prices rose 20.4% and real hourly earnings fell 0.7%. No bill anywhere indexes a public transfer to energy or compute. And a tax on watts would not save the budget: 1 cent per kWh on all US electricity would raise about $40 billion, 0.74% of federal receipts.

- **Myth:** Energy will become the new money.
- **Reality:** Energy becomes the new limit and the new collateral, priced in dollars. The sequence the court found: energy as collateral now, energy as an index for bonds or transfers possibly after 2035, and energy as an accounting unit only in a post-scarcity world, where the real question is who controls the allocation.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why would a currency pegged to one kilowatt hour be a poor savings vehicle over 30 years?
A: Because solar keeps pushing the cost of energy down. If a kWh gets cheaper faster than other goods, prices in kWh rise, so each coin buys less. A 4% yearly fall in real kWh cost gives about 4.2% yearly inflation in kWh terms.


---

# Labor, robots and a Universal High Income

Landscape chapter 08. Stack: Intelligence (graded, dated findings). Id: ls-08. Facts as of 2026-10-23.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#ls-08 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Three tiers behave like two classes. A UHI is limited by rent and the tax base, not by robots, and ownership is what moves people across the line.*

Musk has called for a "Universal HIGH INCOME via checks issued by the Federal government." Online voices warn of a "permanent underclass". The owner's own model has three tiers: asset owners, UHI recipients and people still working. This chapter tests all three ideas.

### Where the robots really are

Labor's share of nonfarm business income is 52.8%, the lowest since 1947, while unit profits rose 43.0% annualized and unemployment held at 4.2%. But robots are not yet the cause at scale. About 14,500 humanoids shipped worldwide in 2025, about 90% Chinese. 603,307 industrial robots were installed in 2025 with 5 million operating. A fleet of one million humanoids by 2028 is below 10%. Ruling Dc-05: robots are not a macro labor substitute before 2030, Plausible, 85. The pre-2030 effect is software AI on entry-level hiring.

*[Picture on the web page: Three tiers become two classes. Workers and UHI recipients both live on income streams. Owners' income grows with assets. The decisive line is ownership.]*

Ruling Dd-01: the three tiers collapse into two classes, owners and income-stream dependents, Plausible, 65. Workers and UHI recipients sit in the same structural place relative to capital. Round 2 confirmed the squeeze is shared: both face housing, health cover and, in 2026, energy up 20.4%.

### Credit is not the trap. Ownership is.

The owner feared UHI recipients would lose access to credit. Under current law that is Refuted, conditional (Dd-02, 80). Lenders may not discriminate against public-assistance income (ECOA), and Fannie Mae counts income that will continue at least three years. On that basis $1,000 a month supports roughly a $69,000 mortgage (model). The exception is a UHI whose amount politicians reset each year, like Alaska's dividend, which fails the three-year test.

Selling the stream is another matter. Social Security has been non-assignable since 1935 (42 USC 407) for good reason: pension advance firms charged up to 183% APR, and one veteran got $1,500 for $18,000 of pension. A $1,000 monthly stream is worth about $181,000 in present value, but buyers historically paid 30 to 60 cents on the dollar. The real gap is ownership and compounding (Dd-03, Plausible, 70): a borrower capped by debt to income rules on $2,500 a month can buy about $178,000 of housing, while asset prices follow the capital share.

### The UHI arithmetic

A $30,000 UHI for about 262 million adults costs about $7.86 trillion a year: 24% of GDP, 106% of all FY2026 outlays and 145% of receipts. Financed by borrowing, it takes debt from 101% of GDP to about 128% in year one, 238% in year five and 374% in year ten at constant rates (Dc-08, Confirmed as arithmetic, 90). Even $10,000 is 8% of GDP and reaches about 211% by year ten. Printing does not escape this in the US: bank reserves earn 3.90%, so money finance is overnight borrowing.

*[Picture on the web page: Nominal versus real value of a UHI. The number on the check stays the same. What it buys depends on how it was financed and on how fast the things it buys can be supplied.]*

| Precedent | Size | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| Hong Kong 2020, HK$10,000 each | 2.7% of GDP, from reserves | Inflation 0.3% |
| Mongolia 2010 to 2012 | about 6% of GDP, deficit financed | Poverty 38.8% to 27.4%, then inflation of 10.0%, 8.4% and 14.3%. Stopped after the 2012 election |
| Iran from December 2010 | about 6% of GDP, fixed amount | Lost about 58% of real value in five years |
| Kenya GiveDirectly | about 17% of local GDP, donor dollars | 2.5 local multiplier, 0.1% average inflation |

The lesson: small and funded is safe, large and printed is eroded within two to five years. Real value is nominal divided by one plus inflation.

### Housing is the limit, not robots

Round 3 found the decisive reason. A UHI dollar is spent about 40% to 48% on housing, and housing supply grows about 1% a year. So even unlimited robot goods can meet at most 57% to 76% of the extra demand. Round 5 update: housing supply is shrinking in 2026 (completions down 12.5%), and new homes meet only 15% to 25% of a demand shock within ten years, so the shelter limit is, if anything, tighter. Recalibrated, a printed Musk-scale UHI runs about 5.8% to 9.8% inflation now, 1.4% to 5.8% in 2028 to 2035 and 0.3% to 2.7% after 2035 (model, and a lower bound because it has no interest channel). Round 2's 0.9% case needs housing supply to open first. A UHI of 10% of GDP is much easier: about 1.5% to 3.9% now.

> A printed UHI would feel generous on gadgets and food and thin on rent within two to three years. In nearly every model case, shelter is 50% to 100% of the demand left unmet. Robots make the goods. Landlords capture the checks.

### The tax base is moving the wrong way

Treasuries are claims on future taxes, and those taxes rest on wages. In FY2026 individual income and payroll taxes carried 86.2% of federal receipts, and corporate tax only 7.1%, down from 10.8% in FY2024, as firms expensed AI investment (Microsoft's current tax bill fell from $14.1 billion to $2.5 billion). Each point of labor share lost costs about 0.8% of receipts. Ruling R3-3: the tax base shifting to capital, energy or compute is Refuted for now (70). A 5% excise on hyperscaler capex would raise about $35 billion. The big money is in taxing capital income and equity, not watts or tokens.

### What is actually on the table

No federal UHI or AI dividend bill has moved past introduction, and none found is money financed. Sanders' bill takes a one-time 50% stake in large AI firms and pays about $1,000 per person, which needs a $3.2 to $6.8 trillion stake (model). Inside the administration, Bessent reportedly prefers AI equity seeded into Trump Accounts. Working odds by 2035: a cash UHI or AI dividend about 10, AI equity routed into accounts or a public fund about 25. Five states ban local guaranteed income. The first "AI dividend" you see is more likely a locked account for your child than a monthly check.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why can robots not make a large printed UHI non-inflationary on their own?
A: Because almost half of UHI spending goes to housing, which robots cannot multiply quickly. Housing supply grows about 1% a year, so the unmet demand piles up there and shows up as rent and price inflation.


---

# The next generation

Landscape chapter 09. Stack: Intelligence (graded, dated findings). Id: ls-09. Facts as of 2026-10-23.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#ls-09 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*The ladder was not pulled up. One rung broke, one got cheap but lottery-like, and ownership decides the climb.*

The owner's deepest worry was about children: when a child turns 18 in this new world, is the classic route still open? Labor to cash, then credit backed by income, then a home or a business. The project's answer (Round 2 Q6, Plausible, 70): yes, but it has changed shape.

*[Picture on the web page: The ladder from first job to owning assets. The first job rung still holds. The housing rung broke for entrants since 2020. A new side ladder, launching a brand, got cheap but steep.]*

### Rung one: the first job still exists

Unemployment for ages 20 to 24 was 8.0% in September 2026, down from 9.2% a year earlier. The bend is in AI-exposed white-collar entry roles: recent graduates aged 22 to 27 had 5.6% unemployment against 4.2% for all workers, which used to be the other way round, and the entry share of postings in exposed jobs fell from nearly 60% in 2020 to 44.7%. The facts are Confirmed (80). AI as the main cause only Plausible (55), because rates and post-2021 overhiring are rival explanations.

### Rung two: the housing rung broke

The median first-time buyer is now a record 40 years old, and first-time buyers are a record 21% of sales. For a 20 to 24-year-old saving 10% of pay, a 10% down payment on a median existing home took about 6.2 years in 1990 and about 10.0 years now (model, using NAR's 1990 median of $92,000 as reported in a secondary table). The monthly payment on a median home went from about 40 to about 68 hours of work since early 2020. 49% of adults under 30 live with a parent. The gate is the down payment, not the monthly payment.

*[Picture on the web page: Hours of work needed, then versus now. Since 1990 food at home got 24% cheaper in hours and quality-adjusted cars 54% cheaper. A median home, a family health premium and public tuition got dearer.]*

> This is the honest version of the movie "In Time", where the poor run out of time. Goods got cheaper in hours of work, entry assets got dearer. Of the $78.1 trillion rise in US household wealth since late 2019, the top 10% took 67.5% and the bottom half 3.1%. A price index tracks groceries, not a first home, so a CPI-indexed wage or UHI keeps up with food and falls behind on shelter.

### Can robots and zoning fix housing?

Only together. Land is 68.4% of single-family home value in San Jose and 39.9% nationally. So a 20% cut in building cost lowers prices about 6% in San Jose and about 16% in St. Louis (model). Factory building has a hard record: Katerra burned through more than $2 billion before its 2021 bankruptcy, and robots are under 0.03% of global construction spend. Broad zoning works: Auckland's 2016 upzoning doubled construction, and Austin's median rent fell from $1,546 to $1,296. Narrow reforms do little: Minneapolis's triplex rule produced 47 homes in five years. Ruling R3-5: Plausible, 65, sooner in the Sun Belt, later on the coasts.

### Rung three: launching got cheap, staying visible got dear

A digital brand can launch for about $525 to $2,850 and a small physical brand for about $1,900 to $7,400 (model). Solo founders are a record 63% of Stripe Atlas companies. But median solo founder revenue fell 23% in 2025 while the top decile earned 61 times the median. Family money is the real seed round: 47% of 18 to 29-year-olds got outside help.

*[Picture on the web page: Where $10 of a mass cosmetic goes. Product cost is about $1.76, the retailer keeps about $4.00, marketing about $1.47, other costs about $2.30 and profit about $0.27. A strong robot and energy shock saves maybe 36 cents.]*

The tolls are rising. Amazon's advertising went from 23.5% to 41.9% of its seller services revenue (2019 to H1 2026), Etsy's take rate from 16.5% to 24.2%, and Meta's price per ad rose 12% to 14% a year in 2026 (R3-7, Confirmed, 70). A human-made premium is real as a label effect in experiments but not yet measured as a cash price (Plausible, 60 after Round 5). Round 5 update: the first marketplace data show an AI discount instead, AI models were 17% of CGTrader uploads but 2.6% of sales. Buying a founder's community is the modern exit: the brand rhode added $293.5 million of sales in its first year inside e.l.f.

### Child accounts: real, but measured in tenths of a point

| Trump Account at 18, 5% real, today's dollars | Value |
|---|---|
| $1,000 seed only | about $2,366 |
| Seed plus $25 a month | about $10,913 |
| Seed plus $100 a month | about $36,556 |
| Seed plus the $5,000 yearly cap | about $144,825 |

The seed covers births from 2025 to 2028, so the first seeded cohort turns 18 in 2043. At 18 the account becomes IRA-like, with education and a $10,000 first-home exception but no business exception. The bottom half of households hold 0.58% of directly held equities, a floor since 2010 after a 1996 peak of 1.65%. Trump Accounts as designed lift that to about 0.60% to 0.70% by 2045. Only a grant of about $500 billion of AI equity reaches about 1.27% (R3-11, Plausible, 70). The SEED OK trial showed what works: automatic deposits, not sign-ups.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why does the "permanent underclass" meme get the mechanism right but the conclusion wrong?
A: It is right that ownership decides outcomes. It is wrong that the door is shut. The route becomes permanent only if three things persist: asset returns beating wages, blocked housing supply, and ownership grants too small to matter.


---

# The rivals and the shocks

Landscape chapter 10. Stack: Intelligence (graded, dated findings). Id: ls-10. Facts as of 2026-10-23.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#ls-10 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*The rivals' strongest card is hardware, not currency. The shocks that matter in 2026 came from oil, the yen and Paris.*

A popular story says rivals will dethrone the dollar with a BRICS currency or a Treasury fire sale. The project scored every lever with one formula (cost to the US, times likelihood, times how cheap the move is for the rival, divided by 25) and found the money levers weak. BRICS agreed on no currency in New Delhi in September 2026 (score 0.12). A Treasury fire sale would hurt China most (0.08). mBridge has handled about $55 billion in total (0.60).

### China: Treasury can issue bills, not magnets

| Lever | Threat score | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Solar polysilicon, wafer and cell technology controls | 3.00 (top) | Proposed 16 October 2026: 40 technologies, 12 of them solar, including wafers of 70 micrometers or less. Finished panels excluded. Comments close 15 November |
| Rare-earth and magnet controls | 2.56 | Political truce extended to 10 January 2027, but the legal end date stays 10 November 2026 |
| Energy hardware system play | 2.40 | Thin yuan leg: 94% of Chinese energy loans in 2010 to 2021 were in dollars |
| Battery cell and cathode controls | 1.44 | China supplied 50% of US lithium-ion imports by value |
| Yuan oil and gold settlement | 0.96 | At least two tankers paid Hormuz tolls in yuan |

The court's odds for 10 November: a numbered extension 72%, partial replacement 16%, full lapse 12%. The solar know-how ban finalized in some form: about 25% by end 2026 and about 70% by mid-2027. China holds above 94% of polysilicon and 97% of wafer capacity. Its strategy is precise: sell panels, keep the factories. If the October package lapses with no replacement, the project moves 2 points from S1 to S4 for 2028.

### The battery swap

Electric freight moves goods prices away from dollar oil, but into a different chokepoint. China makes over 80% of battery cells, about 85% of cathode and more than 90% of anode material. On a concentration index, battery mid-stream stages score about 5,250 to 9,400, against oil's 830 to 906 by country. But oil is a flow and a battery is a stock: cut off oil and trucks stop within weeks, cut off batteries and only new vehicles and the 8% to 12% of packs replaced each year are exposed (R3-12, Plausible, 70). The country electrifying fastest is China itself: new-energy heavy trucks were 38.1% of sales in January to September 2026, a hedge against its own Hormuz exposure.

### The 2026 shocks

- Hormuz. A war closed the strait in practice. Brent reached $115.22 and US diesel $6.276 a gallon, up 73% in a year. War-risk insurance jumped to 3.5% to 7.5% of hull value per transit from 0.10% to 0.25%. Markets give normal traffic before 2028 about 48%. The freight spike adds roughly 1 point to CPI, peaking about a year later.
- The yen. USD/JPY neared 164 in July. Japan spent ¥27.1 trillion defending it in 2026 and the Bank of Japan hiked on 18 September. Round 5 update: Japanese yields rose about 85bp this year and account for about 17bp to 18bp of the rise in US real yields. Today it is 157.10, below the 160 to 164 intervention zone.
- France. The France to Germany spread went from 87 to 157.5 basis points between 10 September and 21 October. Tripwires are 175 (ECB adjustments) and 200 (its TPI backstop). Markets put a Le Pen presidency in 2027 at about 46. Moody's decision on France's Aa3 negative rating was due after the close on 23 October: thin markets said 87.5% for a downgrade by 31 October, the court about 70. Round 5 update: Moody's held Aa3 negative on 23 October, conditional on a 2027 budget, so the desk's 70 is a pending score that likely beats the market.

> When the dollar is strong, the US exports inflation. In 2022 the IMF estimated a 10% dollar rise passes about 1 point of inflation to other countries. In 2026 the absorbers were oil importers with weak currencies: the rupee near 96.9, the Philippine peso past 60, the rupiah at 17,315. But the US was not insulated either: energy CPI rose 20.4%. The court's conclusion: the US can export inflation or weaken the dollar to help industry, not both at once.

### What markets say

| Event | Market odds, 2026-10-22 |
|---|---|
| Fed hike on 9 December | 75% to 79% |
| US recession starting in 2027 | about 21% |
| 10-year Treasury at 5.5% before 2027 | 25% |
| Hormuz traffic normal before 2028 | about 48% |
| Stablecoins above $500 billion before 2027 | 3% |
| US Treasury Bitcoin purchase by end 2027 | 20% (thin, desk under 10) |
| Le Pen wins the 2027 French presidency (Polymarket, $155.7M traded, 23 October) | 46% |
| Any member leaves the EU or the euro (every market under $10k traded) | 1% to 8%, too thin to use |

Markets mostly agree with the desk and corrected one date: the next Fed hike is priced for 9 December, not 28 October. They shifted the shape of the main risk. The likeliest disorderly path before 2028 is an oil-shock inflation and term-premium episode with France as the weak link (Round 4 renamed it: France, with Poland as the non-euro fiscal risk), met by a Fed that hikes, not a Fed forced to cap yields.

*[Picture on the web page: Reserve currency eras. The 2026 evidence in this chapter shows pressure at the edges of the dollar's era (gold buying, hardware controls, conditional crisis access), not a handover.]*

### Round 4 update: could a rival inherit?

Round 4 tested succession directly. The dollar's share of allocated reserves fell from about 71% in 2000 to 56.70%, but the yuan holds only 2.11%. The lost share went to gold and a crowd of smaller currencies. China as it is cannot inherit, because a reserve currency must let money leave freely. If it opened its capital account, the court puts about 60% on money first running into dollars, then 9 to 18 years to reach even 10% of reserves. In the US-made shock of early 2025, the market's emergency heirs were the euro, the yen and gold, not the yuan. The desk's odds of any single currency overtaking the dollar are under 1% to 2028, 1% to 2035 and 5% to 2050. Chapter 13 tells the full story.

**Check yourself.** Q: Why is a solar know-how ban more dangerous to the US than a BRICS currency?
A: Because the watt-dollar needs energy hardware that the US cannot print. A rival currency needs others to trust and hold it, which has not happened. Blocking the factories hits the physical base of AI growth directly.


---

# Connecting the dots: the interconnection map

Landscape chapter 11. Stack: Intelligence (graded, dated findings). Id: ls-11. Facts as of 2026-10-23.

Web page: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/#ls-11 . Text built 2026-11-11. Guide for AI readers: https://neetmonetary.netlify.app/llms.txt

*Information arbitrage: the most useful insights sit between topics, where a cause in one area quietly drives an effect in another.*

Most coverage treats debt, crypto, energy, housing and geopolitics as separate beats. The research kept finding the same few pipes running through all of them. This chapter lists the links that are easiest to miss when each topic is read alone. Each is one cause, one effect and the evidence that ties them. Together they explain why a closure of a strait in the Gulf can raise a young American's mortgage rate, and why AI investment can weaken the collateral under the world's money.

> **Picture this.** Think of a city's water system. Houses, factories and fountains look separate, but they all hang off the same mains. A burst pipe across town drops your shower pressure. In the money system the mains are Treasury bills, delivered power and land. Almost every link below runs through one of them.

### Eighteen links

1. Hormuz oil drives the French bond spread: the France to Germany spread was flat in August and blew out from 87 to 157.5 basis points only after Brent passed $100, alongside the Fed and Bank of Japan hikes, which is why the project now sees the likeliest near-term disorderly path as oil-shock inflation with France as the weak link. By 23 October the spread had reached 171.8 basis points, above Italy's.
2. Japan's yen defense feeds into US mortgage rates: instead of borrowing through the unused FIMA line, foreign official holders sold $254 billion of Treasuries in 2026, and the 10-year yield went from 4.68% on 30 July to 5.13% in October.
3. AI investment weakens the collateral under money: firms expensing AI capex cut corporate tax to 7.1% of receipts while wages carry 86.2%, so Treasuries rest more on a labor share that is already at a record low 52.8%, which moved one point from S1 to S4 for 2035 to 2050.
4. Data centers drive household budgets: PJM capacity cleared at its cap with a 6,623 MW shortfall, wholesale power there rose 41%, and US energy prices rose 20.4% while real hourly earnings fell 0.7%, so the AI boom is already taxing every fixed income, including any future UHI.
5. China's solar know-how ban targets the watt-dollar: if AI output is capped by delivered power, the country that controls 97% of wafer capacity holds a lever over the dollar's new collateral, which is why solar technology controls now top the threat table at 3.00.
6. Stablecoin law ties crypto to the bill market: the 93-day reserve rule means every compliant token is a buyer of Treasury bills, so crypto's boom and bust cycle now feeds straight into the Treasury's funding, as the flat $304 billion year showed.
7. Low interest rates would break private seigniorage: Circle's model stops covering costs at a bill yield of about 1.5%, so a future rate-cutting cycle would push issuers to cut distributor payouts and fold into banks, concentrating the new rails in fewer hands.
8. A bill-heavy debt makes the Fed a budget actor: with 22.36% of marketable debt in bills and 35.7% repricing within a year, each hike reaches the federal interest bill within months, which raises the political pressure on Fed appointments after 2028.
9. Sanctions drive gold: the freezing of about €202 billion of Russian euro assets, while its gold at home stayed untouched, is the clearest reason central banks bought 863 tonnes in 2025 and France brought 129 tonnes home.
10. Conditional crisis access pushes toward neutral reserves: the Gulf asked for swap lines and got none announced, borrowing a record $102.7 billion instead, a small push that moved one point toward S2 for 2028 to 2035.
11. Land prices cap both UHI and the robot dividend: shelter takes 40% to 48% of UHI spending and land is 68.4% of home value in San Jose, so robot-built savings and printed checks both end up as land rent unless zoning lets more homes share the land.
12. Platform tolls absorb automation's savings: a strong robot and energy shock saves about 36 cents on a $10 cosmetic while Amazon's ads rose to 41.9% of seller services revenue, so cheaper production reaches shoppers slowly and founders' margins shrink.
13. Interest on the debt flows upward: net interest of $1.05 trillion goes mostly to the top decile, who hold 79% of household-held government securities, while the bottom half owes 51.6% of consumer credit, so a rising interest bill widens the wealth gap on its own.
14. Fed losses turn printing into borrowing: since the Fed pays 3.90% on reserves and carries a $233.2 billion deferred asset, a money-financed UHI or a gold revaluation gain becomes interest-bearing reserves, so neither escapes the debt arithmetic.
15. Europe's savings deepen America's market: European investors hold $16.2 trillion of US securities, 45.9% of everything foreigners hold, and the European Commission counts about €300 billion of EU savings leaving each year, mostly for the US. The same flow that keeps the dollar's market deep keeps Europe short of risk capital at home, which is why 40 of 147 European unicorns moved their headquarters abroad.
16. French politics can strengthen the dollar: a France-led euro crisis would send money into Bunds, Swiss francs, Treasuries and gold, as in 2011 to 2012. That is why the court's rule after such a crisis raises dollar extension for 2028 to 2035 (to 46/24/3/27) instead of lowering it.
17. German power prices move car market shares: industrial electricity in the EU costs more than twice US and Chinese levels, German chemicals output is 24% below 2017 and cars 28% below, and Chinese brands reached a record 11.7% of EU car registrations in August 2026.
18. Frozen reserves raise gold's share: about €202 billion of Russia's euro assets sit immobilized at Euroclear while gold held at home was never frozen. Gold is now worth about 1.8 times all euro reserves, which is why the neutral layer is now shown as gold plus a multipolar mix.

### The three hubs

| Hub | Links that run through it | What to watch |
|---|---|---|
| Treasury bills | 2, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14, 16 | Bill share against the 25% tripwire, stablecoins against 10% of bills, the refunding on 4 November |
| Delivered power | 1, 4, 5, 3, 17 | PJM prices, China's solar catalogue after 15 November, Hormuz traffic |
| Land and ownership | 11, 12, 13, 9 | Land shares, zoning laws, the bottom half's 0.58% equity share |
| Deep markets (where savings land) | 15, 16, 18 | TIC euro-area holdings (mid November), the OAT-Bund spread against 200bp, COFER Q3 (late December) |

> The owner's instinct that "Set 1 and Set 2 merge" and his worry about a "permanent underclass" turn out to be the same story seen from two ends. The state keeps money anchored to bills it can sell and taxes it can raise. Those taxes fall on wages. The interest on those bills flows to owners. So the plumbing that keeps the dollar strong is also the plumbing that widens the gap, unless ownership itself is spread.

**Check yourself.** Q: How can a war near Iran raise the cost of a first home in Ohio?
A: Oil pushed inflation up, central banks hiked, Japan sold Treasuries to defend the yen instead of borrowing through FIMA, long yields rose to about 5.1%, and mortgage rates above 7% follow long yields. Each step is documented in this project.
